title: Stacey Dooley: Down the K Hole review – the weird tale of how you can order ketamine quicker than pizza | Stacey Dooley | The Guardian
description: From incontinence to reconstructive bladder surgery, ketamine’s popularity with the young is a public health crisis in motion. But is Dooley the right person to get to grips with it?
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: From incontinence to reconstructive bladder surgery, ketamine’s popularity with the young is a public health crisis in motion. But is Dooley the right person to get to grips with it?
Content: Stacey Dooley outside the Acorn Recovery unit in Stockport in Stacey Dooley: Down the K Hole.Photograph: BBC/Nine Lives Media/Ryan McNamaraView image in fullscreenStacey Dooley outside the Acorn Recovery unit in Stockport in Stacey Dooley: Down the K Hole.Photograph: BBC/Nine Lives Media/Ryan McNamaraTV reviewStacey DooleyReviewStacey Dooley: Down the K Hole review – the weird tale of how you can order ketamine quicker than pizzaFrom incontinence to reconstructive bladder surgery, ketamine’s popularity with the young is a public health crisis in motion. But is Dooley the right person to get to grips with it?Lucy ManganTue 20 Oct 2026 18.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStacey Dooley’s latest documentary, Down the K Hole, lands as part of a new batch of three from the presenter. One explores the death in barracks of 19-year-old Jaysley Beck and asks how well the army protects its female soldiers from sexual assault and harassment; another investigates the phenomenon of women who are killed by falling and how often domestic abuse may have been involved.Down the K Hole follows the stories of a handful of ketamine addicts in recovery, representatives of what we are told is a 20% increase in UK admissions involving use of the drug since 2023.Dooley spends four months embedded in Acorn Recovery Projects, a rehab centre in Stockport. It is not really made clear what “embedded” means. She appears to turn up in the mornings, rather than live there full-time. And there isn’t a great sense in the interviews with addicts and their families that she is any closer to them than she would be under normal circumstances. Nor, during her reflections after every interaction – usually leaning against a wall in the nearest corridor and sighing – does she come up with any greater insights than she usually does. Dooley’s speciality is empathy and, afterwards, either repackaging what she has just been told, or giving voice to the feelings – sadness, frustration, resignation – she can count on the audience sharing. Which is fine, as far as it goes. But as the programme – indeed, as her career as a documentary maker – continues, you do start to wish she could parlay her established bona fides into something just a bit more rigorous and move us all on from our shared understandings.View image in fullscreenDooley with Acorn resident Jensen – who shows a photo of how he looked before he started his ketamine rehabilitation treatment.Photograph: BBC/Nine Lives Media/Ryan McNamara“From horse tranquilliser to festival favourite,” ketamine is the current recreational drug of choice among under-24s. Presumably the 25-pluses are screaming at them: “Don’t do it! The clue is in thehorse tranquiliserorigin story. It will destroy you, organ by organ, and quickly too. Put it DOWN.” Because, of course, that’s what it does. The staff at Acorn recount their standard experiences of clients beginning treatment because they have “ket bladder” – which means they are in agonising pain, feel the need to wee all the time, and when they do so they pee blood and bits of said organ, which is breaking down inside them. “It looks like phlegm,” says admissions manager Mel. She shows Stacey a picture. It does. Says Mel: “Buying sanitary briefs for 19-year-old lads – like, how did we get here?”There appears, according to Dooley’s film at least, to be no other answer than ketamine’s cheapness and accessibility – and the fact that it doesn’t leave you with a hangover or huge comedown. “You can order pizza and ket, and the ket’ll come first,” says Acorn resident Jensen, who has been using the drug almost every day for eight years and is now six weeks clean. “£40-50 will get you 7g.” It’s a lot of bang for your buck, especially for Jensen, who even enjoyed the k-holes (an intense dissociative state, “like greening out on weed”). Dooley is horrified at the prospect of being so out of control. “It sounds so bleak,” she says afterwards. But the point is surely that being elsewhere, or at least blunting the edges of here, is the point. And so – why?The agony of ketamine addiction: ‘I felt like I was peeing glass’Read moreMost users have something that could at least partly explain their dependence on the drug. Jensen’s mother died in 2019. Lauren has always struggled with depression and is now back in rehab for a second attempt at sobriety; she relapsed after a miscarriage. Like Jensen, Liam’s mother died and, already addicted, he upped his usage. The men especially talk about it enabling them to avoid feelings. But Dooley never drills down into why some people use but most others don’t. And there isn’t much consideration given to the problem that most of them are seeking help only because of the physical damage caused.“If I wasn’t facing consequences,” says Liam, who is in constant pain, “I would definitely still be doing it.” This is after listening to his sisters’ and young nephew’s accounts of what it’s been like looking after him and fearing his death for years. Similarly, Josh lies in bed awaiting bladder reconstruction surgery wishing he could take some ket, while his dad looks on, an expression of quiet devastation on his face.It’s an hour that will bring some attention to ket use as a gathering storm. But it doesn’t do much more than point at the sky and say: “Look at those clouds!” Dooley, these days, could do more.Stacey Dooley: Down the K Hole aired on BBC One and is available on iPlayerExplore more on these topicsStacey DooleyTV reviewTelevisionDocumentaryDrugsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Nige seems tired and bored of himself as Kemi conjures a telepathic budget | John Crace | The Guardian
description: The Tory leader has glimpsed the future and it involves Labour putting every last UK citizen on benefits
Author: John Crace
Headline: The Tory leader has glimpsed the future and it involves Labour putting every last UK citizen on benefits
Content: The Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, speaks to Conservative party members on Tuesday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, speaks to Conservative party members on Tuesday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAThe politics sketchBudgetNige seems tired and bored of himself as Kemi conjures a telepathic budgetJohn CraceThe Tory leader has glimpsed the future and it involves Labour putting every last UK citizen on benefitsTue 20 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTShareIf you’re worried about next week’s budget, then now is your time to chill out. BecauseKemi Badenochhas all the answers. The chancellor, John Healey, has been living rent free in the leader of the opposition’s head for the past few weeks. Lucky man. More than that, she has been perched on his shoulder while he sits at his desk in the Treasury and tries to make the sums add up.And – SPOILER ALERT – Kemi has now read the whole speech that hasn’t yet been written and is in a position to give her budget reply more than a week ahead of time. Opposition by telepathy. Or wish fulfilment. If things don’t work out for her in her current job she could apply to be the next Mystic Meg.In a plush room in Westminster on a wet Tuesday morning, Kemi was giving her verdict in front of an adoring crowd of invited Tory members. They cheered every word. Which was kind. Because she won’t be getting that kind of reception next week. Nobody could be worse than Rachel Reeves, she began. Rachel had been the She-Devil who had implemented £70bn of tax rises. But wait. There was someone worse than Reeves. And that was Healey. Logic is not Kemi’s strongest point.No matter. Healey would be worse because he would do less. Fiscal dialecticism. Yup, the chancellor was going to stand up for an hour and say absolutely nothing. Make no changes to anything. This didn’t seem very likely, but we had to take it on trust.Kemi was John Healey’s brain. And Healey doing nothing was worse than Rachel doing something. It sounded as if Kemi rather missed the tax rises after all. But she had a further warning. The Marxist International Monetary Fund were completely wrong to praise the government for its efforts to reduce the deficit. At best, they had been duped by Healey, at worst they were trying to bankrupt the country.Here’s what was going to happen.Labourwere going to introduce some fictional cuts to benefits that would never be implemented. Because deep down what Labour MPs really wanted was for everyone to live in a country where they could pick up £80,000 a year in benefits. The sign of a functioning nirvana was a world where everyone could be paid not to work. It didn’t seem to have occurred to Kemi that the reason the benefits bill was so high was primarily because the Conservative government in which she had served had increased them substantially during her time in office. And also because many benefits, such as pensions, she was unwilling to cut herself.Surprise drop in UK unemployment to 4.7% as John Healey’s first budget loomsRead moreLabour was doing the wrong things for the wrong reasons, she said. This opened up several philosophical lines of inquiry. Ontologically speaking, was it better to do the wrong things for the right reasons, even if the results were the same? Or what happened if you did the right things for the wrong reasons? Would you then have to negate everything regardless of the outcomes?It turned out that I wasn’t the only one struggling with Kemi’s reasoning. When it came to the questions from the media, several reporters wondered why, if the welfare cuts that she was proposing were so easy to make, previous Tory governments hadn’t got round to making them earlier. And was it just our imagination, or were the same cuts being used to pay for several different items on the country’s balance sheet?Kemi didn’t miss a beat. The cuts she was proposing were the ones Rishi Sunak would have made if he hadn’t been interrupted by the general election that he himself called. It was all very unfortunate. The Tories had been on the brink of success and if only they had had another couple of weeks, everything would have been hunky dory. Tax breaks for the wealthy and benefits cuts for those that need them, that was the Tory way.Then the reverse ferret. Although she had been in previous Conservative governments, she had never inhaled. She had kept her fingers crossed and her mouth shut. Previous prime ministers had taken wrong steps. But sometimes the bravest thing a cabinet minister can do is to do and say nothing. And no one had been braver than Kemi.“In case you hadn’t noticed,” she said patronisingly to one journalist, “we are under new management.” Only it feels very much like the old management. Kemi was still saying nothing her predecessors wouldn’t have said. It was just one of life’s sadnesses that the scales had only fallen from her eyes when the Tories had been booted out of office.Down in Plymouth, Reform was regrouping after yetanother weekend of bad headlines. And the party members who had assembled for the rally didn’t look entirely enthused when the first person sent on stage to act as cheerleader was the charisma-free Danny Kruger. The man who is meant to act as the brains of the party, despite appearing spectacularly dim.“I don’t want to whine,” he said, before going on to do just that. The ITV exposé was just a bit unfortunate, he went on, because he was sure most Reform supporters weren’t racist. “There is no room for that kind of behaviour in the party.” Some of the audience looked a bit disappointed by that. They thought they had been guaranteed a welcome.After a brief and entirely forgettable number from Honest Bob Jenrick – even Reform members think he seems a wrong ’un – out cameNigel Farage. He seemed like a man with the cares of the world on his shoulders. A man who could sense the tide was going out. There was no energy about him as he rolled through a collection of his greatest hits. Forgetting where he was, he even called Plymouth, Portsmouth. That drew a few boos. People like to think they matter a little bit.View image in fullscreenThe Reform leader, Nigel Farage, very briefly mixed up Plymouth and Portsmouth on Tuesday.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/Getty ImagesNige was just tired and bored of himself. Disappointed with a world that had promised him so much and was now crumbling before him. Hell, why hadn’t the riots even spread to this country? Then he could blame lefties and foreigners. He tried to pass off the stories of racism and financial unorthodoxy as just one offs. Every self-respecting party has a few racists. He didn’t sound as if he believed a word of it. And ITV had exposed a 70% hit rate of undesirables. Those aren’t outliers.Come the end, Nige couldn’t wait to see the back of Portsmouth. Or wherever he was. And it felt as though for much of the audience the feeling was entirely mutual.On Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of theGuardian’s year in review event. Joined by fellow Guardian writers, expect candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as they look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. title: ‘It was so satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen’: the people sick of being spied on by their smart TV | Television | The Guardian
description: Is your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacy
Author: George Francis Lee
Headline: Is your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacy
Content: ‘It’s not intimidating, just increasingly enshittified’ … a user and their smart TV.Photograph: SimpleImages/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It’s not intimidating, just increasingly enshittified’ … a user and their smart TV.Photograph: SimpleImages/Getty ImagesTelevision‘It was so satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen’: the people sick of being spied on by their smart TVIs your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacyGeorge Francis LeeTue 20 Oct 2026 10.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 10.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Dan had had enough of his television, he threw a rock straight through the screen. The offence? His smart TV was downloading its third update in three days. “It drove me crazy with what seemed like daily software updates that never fixed anything and ‘features’ that never seemed to work,” says the 71-year-old from Illinois. “And of course, constantly trying to push me to subscribe to paid-for services when all I wanted to do was watch over-the-air TV, play a DVD or stream something from my computer.”Some may accuse Dan of being a luddite, but his master’s degree in computer science and decades of experience in telecommunications would suggest otherwise. “The tech is not intimidating,” he explains, “just increasinglyenshittified.”The first smart TVs entered the market in the late 2000s, when companies introduced operating systems, media players and apps to screens that were becoming wider and thinner. In recent years, the luxury status of smart TVs has waned and increasingly affordable options are widely available. Tom Parsons, TV and audiovisual editor at the electronics magazine What Hi-Fi?, explains that these cheaper models can struggle under more advanced features. “They’re not necessarily super-fast and responsive out of the box,” he says. “And then two, three, four years down the line, they can end up slowing down quite a lot under the weight of all that processing.”Dan is just one of a growing number of tech-savvy watchers wishing their TVs weren’t so smart. Erin McQuiston and Matthew Schroyer, a couple from Connecticut, share his smart-screen scepticism.View image in fullscreenIncreasingly hard to find … a dumb TV.Photograph: Svetlana Lazarenka/Alamy“I don’t think we’ve ever used [our TV] as anything other than just a giant display,” says McQuiston. “There was a period where we were running it through an Xbox. And that was a constant battle because that was constantly being updated and patched and then you’d have to redownload all the apps for it.”Meanwhile, Schroyer says his job as a software engineer has influenced his decision to “intentionally keep it very dumb” by keeping their TV disconnected from the internet. “A rule of the house is: don’t give things the wifi password,” he says. “It concerns me that folks increasingly have to be IT experts to get the bare minimum enjoyable experience out of this stuff.”Instead, the 41-year-old connects his screen to an Apple TV box as a streaming workaround, and cites privacy as well as “highly invasive” advertisements for doing so. “Our living room is not a billboard for sale,” he says.When asked how the couple might cope in a future where TVs may have mandatory internet, McQuiston says her husband is “handy enough to break every terms of service known to man and get in there and unsolder something to manually disconnect it”.For Helen Northmore, a 51-year-old from Wales who works in AI delivery for the UKHealthSecurity Agency, privacy is also a worry. Her grudge against smart screens began four years ago, when her faithful dumb TV broke without warning and she had to quickly find a replacement.“We had already decided that we didn’t want the smart functionality, but it became really clear that it was very hard to find one that didn’t have any,” she says. Northmore, whose partner works in cybersecurity, says the couple wanted to “keep control” over their devices, which cost them a premium. “We were willing to pay more. One of the boundaries in how we live our lives is we want to minimise the smart element. We don’t have smart speakers. We don’t enable or connect to the internet.”View image in fullscreen‘Our living room is not a billboard for sale’ … a smart TV aerial.Photograph: Zdenek Maly/AlamyToday, she watches entertainment through a Sky box connected to her dumb TV, and dreads that when her current telly breaks there won’t be any option but to get a smart model and offer up her data.More consumers are becoming worried about how their information is being used by manufacturers. “There are increasing privacy concerns around to what degree TVs are essentially scraping your data,” says Parsons. “TVs these days are full of sensors, including microphones, and that can make people nervous.”But according to Parsons, despite interest in “dumber” models from some buyers, most shoppers want their TVs to be catch-all entertainment systems. The result is that the dumb TV market is almost nonexistent. “You can buy cheap monitors for signage,” he says, “but from a features point of view, you wouldn’t get the same performance that you would from a consumer TV.”Paul, a public servant from Australia, knows just how hard finding a traditional TV can be. “When my last telly – a glorious 32-inch dumb TV – died recently, aged approximately 10 years old, I spent about three weeks scouring the city looking for something comparable. What I found is that they do not exist any more.”After much searching, Paul discovered a single 40-inch TV without any smart functionality in the back of a shop. “It had zero ways to connect to the internet – just a couple of plugs on the back for making it work with the aerial on the roof and my VHS player, and that was it.” He remembers that it “was very dusty and cost about 200 dollars. Naturally, we fell instantly in love.”“My friends all laugh at it when they come over,” he admits, “but secretly I know the joke is on them. My little telly doesn’t spy on me, and has a DVD player built in.”The punchline may eventually land on Paul, however. In September, the Australian government launched aconsultation into the future of the country’s free-to-air broadcasting, asking citizens for feedback on how TV should be accessed. One of the proposed scenarios would see traditional broadcast services cut in favour of streaming services and video on-demand apps.View image in fullscreen‘My little telly doesn’t spy on me’ … some users such as Paul are clinging hard to analogue.Photograph: Dmitriy Shironosov/AlamyIn the same month, the UK government released amedia green paperoutlining its plan to fully move away from digital terrestrial television to services provided over a broadband connection by 2034 at the earliest. Such a situation would mean viewers having to rely on broadcaster apps and streaming services.If a similar fate befell North America, James certainly wouldn’t care. He is originally from the US but now lives in British Columbia, Canada, and says traditional broadcast TV is “dead to him” and that he prefers to watch shows on streaming services or on YouTube. For the father and husband, privacy is a top priority.“No one expects an end-user licence agreement to include giving up autonomy,” he says. “Having my TV listen to any conversation and use that for monetary or any form of gain is above and beyond expectations on the loss of privacy.”In September, the YouTube channel Gamers Nexus releaseda two-hour investigationinto LG Electronics’ smart televisions, saying that the devices record audio – even when they are offline or powered down. The South Korean companydenied the allegations. In the fallout, some have taken measures to modify their smart TVs, regardless of brand or model. Some videos online show usersreplacing motherboards, cutting out Bluetooth and wifi modules and removing microphones from their TV remote controls.Amid the controversy, James read online advice that modifying a TV remote microphone was a simple procedure. So he surgically removed the sensor himself. “Removing the mic was literally as easy as using a [craft] knife to scrape it off the top,” he says, “and the remote continued to work fine.”James’s willingness to dissect his tech comes from fears for his children. “My kids are not teenagers and they have no agency to protect their private information,” he says. “Someone listening in on a TV gets to find out about my daughter’s first period without her knowing. And that is a level of invasion no one should have without explicit consent.”Frustration and controversies have sparked a DIY interest in opening up and neutering the black rectangles in our living rooms. Though the desire in the first place may lead consumers to ask themselves an important question: have our TVs become too smart for their own good?Gutting any piece of electronic equipment should be left to professionals. However, some may find that, for a complex problem, the simplest solutions are the most elegant. As Dan recalls: “It was enormously satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen.”Explore more on these topicsTelevisionPrivacyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Excessive wealth, extreme emissions – and ecocide: what I learned at Europe’s big superyacht show | The super-rich | The Guardian
description: These yachts are highly popular with the ‘super-bourgeoisie’ – and getting bigger. Can anything be done to stop them destroying our seas?
Author: Sam Wollaston
Headline: These yachts are highly popular with the ‘super-bourgeoisie’ – and getting bigger. Can anything be done to stop them destroying our seas?
Content: Socks away … Sam Wollaston at the Monaco Yacht Show with the 102-metre long Nixie superyacht behind him.Photograph: Sam Wollaston/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSocks away … Sam Wollaston at the Monaco Yacht Show with the 102-metre long Nixie superyacht behind him.Photograph: Sam Wollaston/The GuardianThe super-richExcessive wealth, extreme emissions – and ecocide: what I learned at Europe’s big superyacht showThese yachts are highly popular with the ‘super-bourgeoisie’ – and getting bigger. Can anything be done to stop them destroying our seas?Sam WollastonTue 20 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 10.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWho knew? Apparently everyone did, apart from me: you don’t wear shoes on a superyacht. Now, about to step on to my first teak deck at theMonacoYacht Show, I’ve got to take my trainers off, and I’m having a sock panic. Have they got holes? Do they even match? Do they smell?To be honest, I’ve come dressed all wrong for Europe’s big annual superyacht trade exhibition. The code for men seems to be crisp and tucked in, blazers and chinos, navy and white, sculpted hair and designer sunnies. (I went colourful, loose, casual). For women, it’s something like Riviera elegance. Everyone – whether they’re Italian, French, English, German, American, exhibitors, buyers, brokers, charterers – seems to know each other. The international superyacht community seems to be a close-knit one, and I’m not part of it. Yet.For now, though, I’m boarding my first vessel: a relatively modest Zeelander 8 – 23.9 metres (79ft) long, built in the Netherlands. It has a rather retro look about it, with pleasing curves and a rear end not unlike a Porsche’s. I could imagine James Bond at the wheel. It’s fast too, reaching 40 knots (46mph); I could be in Saint-Tropez in a little over an hour.View image in fullscreenHow much? … the Monaco Yacht Show 2026.Photograph: Syspeo/SIPA/ShutterstockDownstairs there’s a huge owner’s cabin, plus a couple of double guest cabins, all en suite, with lots of nice details, such as a cream-coloured leather floor. In the less opulent crew quarters, there’s room for two or three. How much does it cost? This one is not actually for sale – some of the boats here are, others are for charter, some just for show. But I could order one just like it, it would take a year and a half to build and cost me about €9.5m (£8m).Tempting, certainly, but I need to see a few more before rushing into anything. I can’t help noticing that, compared with some of the others packed into Port Hercules, the Zeelander 8 is a bit … well, small. Is it even a superyacht? There seems to be some debate about how long a yacht has to be to be super – some say 24 metres, others 30.No question about this one – a Fast50, made by Italian builders Baglietto, with room for 12 guests and a crew of nine. It’s not as fast as the Dutch one, despite the name. Its four engines take it to 30 knots, but that’s actually very quick for a 50 metre boat. Perhaps more importantly, its gross tonnage, referring to internal volume, is 499; a sub-500GT yacht isn’t subject to the more stringent safety and environmental rules under the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) that yachts over 500GT are, so they require less frequent surveys and have fewer restrictions on crew size and certification. My favourite features are the large “beach club” (the open deck at the back) and the Jacuzzi right up at the pointy end. Imagine it: sitting with a glass of fizz, in the bubbles, at 30 knots, Céline Dion blasting out … where do I sign?Oh, again. Not for sale. The first Fast50, fresh from the shipyard, is already sold, but they won’t tell me how much for or who to (superyacht owners can be quite shy). The search continues.View image in fullscreenSam at ‘the pointy end’.Photograph: Sam Wollaston/The GuardianThe trouble with superyachting, I’m finding here in Monaco, is that you think you’ve found the perfect vessel, and then you look over there and there’s a bigger, better one. It’s not just me – this is reflected in the Global Order Book, published by Boat International, which tracks construction projects. The2026 GOBcounts the number of yachts over 24 metres under construction globally at 1,093. In 2016, it counted 755 vessels under construction. This year’s figure is actually down 3.95% from last year, but that’s balanced by an increase in average length and gross tonnage. In other words, a few fewer, but they’re getting bigger. New prefixes are required, “mega” and “giga”, but for simplicity’s sake we’ll stick with superyacht. Here at MYS 2026 there are 118 superyachts, with a combined length of 5,508 metres, and a value of €4.5bn.Despite the sock shame, I’m beginning to feel more comfortable. Most people are friendly. It’s a lovely day on the Côte d’Azur – I’m offered ice-cream, branded fans and straw hats. It’s not just the yachts, there are stands for everything connected. Would I like to come to a wine tasting later “exploring superyacht wine trends”? Of course I would. Am I interested in yachting in Saudi Arabia? Hmmm, maybe next year. There are loads of toys on show – jetskis, eFoils, even submersibles. And if you’re still finding life at sea boring, there’s a portable golf simulator, with cameras and sensors, plus a screen, with hundreds of real courses programmed into it. So after dropping anchor off St Barts you can play a round at St Andrews. It costs €170,000 (£143,000).View image in fullscreen‘I could get used to this.’Photograph: Sam Wollaston/The GuardianAnd so on to Nixie, built by Lürssen in Germany, owned by co-founder and CEO of Revolut, Nik Storonsky: 102 metres long, with a helipad, glass-bottomed infinity pool, dedicated spa and wellness zone, and a crew of 34, one of whom is busy polishing a stainless steel cleat on the lowest of its decks. Access, though, is “reserved exclusively for direct, potential clients,” says the Lürssen PR. Perhaps they think the average Guardian reader is not in the market to rent a boat the length of a football pitch. Nixie costs €2.4m a week to hire. A lot, I know, but if you split it between the 12 of you …Anyway, it’s not even the biggest here, which I will be allowed on. First though I pass another – Boardwalk V, only 76.5 metres long and five years old, but this one is for sale, at a discount price! Down €14m, to just €135m. Not including the helicopter. Boardwalk V … it’s ringing a bell. Got it! And now the twin flags on the helicopter’s tail – the American stars and stripes and thetricoloreof Italy – make sense. This boat belongs to Tilman Fertitta, billionaire owner of restaurants, hotels, casinos, and the Houston Rockets basketball team, and now Donald Trump’s ambassador to Italy. Hemade the news in Junewhen hundreds came out to protest after he parked his brand new 117-metre yacht (also named Boardwalk, but without the V) in Venice. He’s got an upgrade – that’s why he’s selling this one.To be honest there are some proper horrors on show. This one looks like a supersized 80s caravan, that one more like a bridge than a boat, another is bright red – like some kind of firefighting ship. “I don’t understand the clients,” says Rick. “They just want something that’s big and flashy and comfortable, they don’t care about anything else.” Rick is also pretty disparaging about the people who sell these boats, the brokers. “They’re like real estate agents, they say: ‘Look at the master cabin, look at all the light, the big windows,’ it’s all about the interior space.”Guess what Rick does? Yup, yacht broker. It’s why we’ve changed his name. He also points out something about the way they look. “I don’t know if you’ve heard the analogy, but they look like irons.” As in electric irons, to do the ironing with, and oh my God, he’s so right – that shape, pointy at the bow, then rising and widening as you go aft, with a squared off swim platform … As Rick says, “once you see it, you can’t unsee it.”In a2024 study, Oxfam identified 23 superyachts owned by 18 billionaires and estimated the average annual carbon footprint of each of these yachts to be 5,672 tonnes. For an average citizen of the world it would take 860 years to produce the same amount.View image in fullscreenSink clearly … a bathroom on one of the superyachts.Photograph: Sam Wollaston/The GuardianOxfam zoomed in further to one family, the Waltons, heirs of the Walmart chain and owners of three superyachts (at this level you’re not talking about the haves and the have-yachts, you’re talking about the have-yachts and the have-lots-of-yachts). They travelled 56,000 nautical miles in a year with a combined carbon footprint of 18,000 tonnes. That’s equivalent to the carbon emissions of about 1,700 Walmart employees.Superyachts use an awful lot of fuel – some of the bigger ones usemore than 500 litres of diesel per hour, releasing CO2as well as nitrogen oxides and sulphur dioxide into the atmosphere. The recreational boating sector as a whole – including yachts – produces about16m tonnes of CO2annually. It’s not just when they’re going along; at anchor they operate onboard generators to run their “hotel loads” (for air conditioning, stabilisation systems, lighting, galleys, hot tubs, etc) which emit further CO2. In addition, the vessels’ big anchors and chains act like the grim reaper’s scythe on the Posidonia seagrass which grows on the Mediterranean seabed and is a vital habitat for sea life as well as a source of oxygen.And there are more and more of them. The big increases came in 2022 and 2023 when, as Boat International puts it, “orders soared as UHNWIs sought private holiday cocoons.” UHNWIs, you’ll know, are ultra-high net worth individuals, but why the big boom? Because a superyacht is “the best way to practise social distancing in a very safe and very comfortable way,” says Grégory Salle. Covid was brilliant for the superyacht sector, in other words. Salle is talking to me by video from Lille where he works at the French National Centre for Scientific Research. He’s also author of the thoroughly researched and surprisingly entertaining book Superyachts: Luxury, Tranquility and Ecocide, which has a whole chapter devoted to Posidonia seagrass.View image in fullscreenJeff Bezos’s 127-metre Koru.Photograph: Giuseppe Catuogno/AlamyEcocide is not the superyacht’s only crime. “It has really become the symbol of excessive, unjustifiable wealth,” Salle says. Even though the gap between most of us and the people who have them is virtually unfathomable, “it looks like provocation, especially when all you’re hearing and reading about is crisis, austerity, poverty – including child poverty.”Superyachts are also a kind of floating paradox that Salle calls “conspicuous seclusion. On the one hand they’re meant to be noticed, they’re massive, you can’t miss them. But at the same time the interior is hidden and of course it can sail away and escape ordinary people.”Salle uses words and phrases such as “plutocracy”, “oligarchy” and the new “global super-bourgeoisie” about the people who own them, a “transnational capitalist class” who operate outside and above borders and rules. Look at the stern of the superyachts, under the name, and they’re almost all registered in places such as the Cayman Islands, the Marshall Islands, the Isle of Man and Malta – flag states offering, among other benefits, tax neutrality.It’s hard to hide a superyacht, or ownership of one. We know about Mark Zuckerberg’s 118-metre Launchpad, and Jeff Bezos’s 127-metre Koru, estimated to have cost €444m. Koru caused a stir in 2022, when a historic bridge in Rotterdam, a Dutch national monument, was going to be dismantled in order to let it through. After the uproar its masts were stepped downstream in the end. Koru is actually a sailing yacht, which might sound like a greener way of doing it, but then Bezos also has a 75-metre support vessel, with additional crew accommodation, helipad, submarine, speedboats and cars, that follows Koru around like a loyal dog. Zuckerberg’s got a couple of support vessels too.View image in fullscreenThe world’s longest superyacht … Azzam.Photograph: David Jalda/AlamyRoman Abramovich is another big fan of a yacht. Using leaked documents,Forbes counted 16belonging to the Russian oligarch. My ship location app tells me that the superest of his fleet – Solaris (140-metres) and Eclipse (162-metres), both registered in the Cook Islands – are now parked in the Sea of Marmara, near Istanbul. When western governments seized Russian oligarchs’ assets after the invasion of Ukraine,Turkey refused to join the sanctionsand became a bolt-hole.Eclipse doesn’t even eclipse everything. The world’s longest superyacht, at 180-metres, is Azzam, launched in 2013 for Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi, who died in 2022, but according toBoat Internationaland theSuperyacht Fan website, Azzam is still in the family. When you get to this level it’s not always clear who owns a yacht, as they can be held in trusts or shell companies, sometimes across several jurisdictions.Take Dilbar for example – a little shorter than Azzam but the world’s largest by volume. In JuneBloomberg reportedthat a court in Germany had ruled that sanctions no longer applied to the yacht after finding insufficient evidence that the Russian billionaire Alisher Usmanov controls The Sister Trust, which formally owns the vessel.Or Kosatka, formerly Graceful, the 82-metre yachtseen being escortedthrough Danish waters by Russian naval vessels in the summer and widely reported to be linked to Vladimir Putin. A bigger, 140-metre yacht, the €620m Scheherazade, which boasts two helipads, anti-drone technology and a cryotherapy room, remains impounded in Italy. Activists working for poisoned Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalnybelievethat one is also owned by Putin.There is no secret about who owns the aptly named Leviathan, the biggest boat at the Monaco Yacht Show. Co-founder and president of the video game company Valve, Gabe Newell doesn’t just own the 111-metre Leviathan, he also owns the 93-metre support vessel Draak, parked up next door.I am allowed on to Leviathan and get a brief look around. I’m shown the huge mess area, which Newell and his guests share with the 42 crew. As well as the pool, there’s an outdoor cinema, basketball court, and a huge gaming lounge with consoles and race simulators, open to everyone. The crew are also keen to point out Leviathan’s diesel-electric hybrid propulsion and battery energy storage system. But it still has a 494,000-litre fuel tank. Fill ’er up? Certainly sir, that’ll be roughly a million euros.View image in fullscreenLeviathan, the biggest boat at the Monaco Yacht Show.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesIt’s not total eco denial at the Monaco Yacht Show however, there’s at least some acknowledgment of environmental impact. I drop in on the Blue Wake awards, “for solutions delivering measurable impact on yachting sustainability”. So there’s a prize for a company using more sustainable materials for yacht interiors. A yacht wins a Blue Wake for having sails, and a marina gets one for planting Posidonia plants.This is all good news … but actually, when you look at it, it’s notthatgood. In five years 3,000 sq metres of Posidonia have been restored – sounds impressive, but then by my calculations that’s an area of about 55 metres by 55 metres. The boat with sails? Great, but actually there are fewer sailing boats here than in previous years, the trend is towards power, more and more of it.It looks like greenwashing, token gestures. I have an Italian friend who calls these superyachtsstronzi di mare– turds of the sea. And you know what you can’t do to a turd. There’s no escaping the truth: that they drink fossil fuels like there’s no tomorrow, which there won’t be if they’re allowed to carry on; that there’s no more monstrous symbol of inequality; and that they look like irons.But before storming off in disgust, maybe I’ll just pop into that wine tasting. In my socks.Explore more on these topicsThe super-richTravel and transportJeff BezosMark ZuckerbergMonacoEuropePollutionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From granny hoods to recycled macs: 13 more sustainable ways to stay dry when it rains | Sustainable fashion | The Guardian
description: Whether it’s Pfas-free tote bags or wash-in waterproofing, here’s how women can stay dry in style – and with less waste
Author: Hannah Rochell
Headline: Whether it’s Pfas-free tote bags or wash-in waterproofing, here’s how women can stay dry in style – and with less waste
Content: Heads up: from top to toe, we’ve got some easy-to-wear ways to stay dry with less waste.Photograph: Hannah Rochell/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHeads up: from top to toe, we’ve got some easy-to-wear ways to stay dry with less waste.Photograph: Hannah Rochell/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterSustainable fashionFrom granny hoods to recycled macs: 13 more sustainable ways to stay dry when it rainsWhether it’s Pfas-free tote bags or wash-in waterproofing, here’s how women can stay dry in style – and with less wasteThe best umbrellas – testedHannah RochellTue 20 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter the hottest UK summer on record, autumn 2026 could be wetter and stormier than usual, partly because of the El Niño climate phenomenon, which is predicted to be the strongest of its kind in living memory. But a lot of wet-weather gear – from flimsy umbrellas that blow inside out within seconds to single-use ponchos that will sit in landfill long after this winter has blown over – often isn’t very sustainable.While waterproofed polyester can keep us dry, there’s no excuse for it not to be made from recycled materials. Look instead for products that are designed to last and, better still, part of a circular system where the brand offers repairs and takes responsibility for reusing or recycling worn-out items. Besides, choosing well-made, thoughtfully designed products means you can use them for years to come.From a water-based spray that can protect your favourite shoes in showers to umbrellas designed to withstand the worst wind and rain, here are 13 of the best.Sustainable ways to stay dry when it rainsReturn of the macFashion editors use this Mark Morrison pun every season, but this time it really makes sense, because Bam’s lightweight trenchcoat is designed to be sent back to the brand for recycling when it wears out. Available in three colours.View image in fullscreenBam Any Weather mac£180 at BamAn update on the granny hoodView image in fullscreenHats off: this umbrella alternative can be worn around the wrist when the rain stops.Photograph: Hannah Rochell/The GuardianUmbrellas aren’t for everyone: if you’re short, like me, they can be difficult to manage on a busy street. I’ve been using one of L-Hood’s shower-resistant hats for the past couple of years. They roll up into a slap band that can be worn around the wrist or stored neatly in your bag.View image in fullscreen£49.99 at L-HoodThe Manchester-proof umbrellaSoaked was founded in notoriously rainy Manchester with a mission to make resilient, sustainable umbrellas. Think wind-resistant vented canopies made from recycled materials and flexible fibreglass ribs.View image in fullscreenSoakedrecycled polyester umbrella£37 at Lotti & WrenFor more, read our roundup of thebest umbrellas for staying dry in the wind and rainDry stridesWhen waterproof trousers look this good, you might be tempted to wear them regardless of the weather instead of keeping them in your bag for emergencies. The oversized silhouette is made to be worn over your normal trousers, and the adjustable drawstring waist and hems make them suitable for cycling, too.View image in fullscreenVivi Marirecycled polyesterrain trousers£69.90 at Vivi MariFuture-proofed shoesI’ve been spray protecting my shoes and boots for years – getting ahead of the weather is the best way to keep them looking good. Liquiproof is amazing stuff, and can be used on leather, suede, nubuck and canvas to protect from not only rain but also mud, oil and other everyday spills such as ketchup. It’s water-based and aerosol-free.View image in fullscreenLiquiproofprotectorspray, 125ml£10 at Liquiproof£14.99 at OfficeShower powerView image in fullscreenFestival weather: this featherlight jacket will help keep the showers at bay without weighing you down.Photograph: Hannah Rochell/The GuardianWhile this isn’t technically a waterproof jacket, I can tell you from experience at a stormy seaside music festival that it does a good job of keeping you warm and dry in a sharp shower or two. It’s also lightweight, folds up pretty smalland is available formenand women. Finisterre also has a great selection of more substantialwaterproof raincoats.View image in fullscreenFinisterrerecycled polyesterhooded jacket£180 at FinisterreFor more, read our guide to thebest waterproof jackets for womenOilskin capSometimes the oldest solution to waterproofing is all you need. This British-made waxed cotton cap has a leather peak and was designed specifically for spending time in unpredictable weather. It’s available intwo coloursand softens with age to look better and better.View image in fullscreenThe Field Cap cotton and leather hatskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion£69 at the Vitamin D ProjectClogged upUnlike many who love the Plasticana Gardana clogs for theirviral fashion credentials, I bought some earlier this year to actually garden in. But it turns out they’re great dog-walking shoes when it’s still too mild to wear wellies or boots. Plus, they’re incredibly lightweight, so you could easily chuck them in a bag.View image in fullscreenPlasticana Gardanarecycled PVC and hempclogs£38 at Straw LondonTote-ally dryThe water-resistant coating on this recycled bag is Pfas-free. It’s padded and strong, with handy compartments for your laptop and other essentials, as well as a removable zip pouch that can be clipped into the bag for safety.View image in fullscreenRainkissherringbone recycled polyester tote bag£111 at RainkissBoil in the bagMy parents refer to rain jackets that store in their own bags as “boils”, and it doesn’t get much more stylish than this unisex one. It has some lovely, incredibly practical features such as thumb straps to keep the sleeves in place, zipped pockets with rain flaps and a toggle to tighten the hood at the back of the head. Available in two colours.View image in fullscreenVoitedrecycled polyesterrain poncho£79 at VoitedA reversible hoodie (and it’s just the hood)When you need warmth as well as protection from the rain, this padded hood has your head, neck and chest covered. Ideal for city commuters because it doesn’t have the added sweat factor of sleeves and a back when you inevitably find yourself on crowded public transport within minutes of needing to put it on.View image in fullscreenFudoonrecycled polyesterpaddedreversiblehood£78 at Smallable£99 at La RedouteWash-in waterproofingUse this clever waterproofer in your washing machine or wash it in by hand. It restores water repellency while maintaining the breathability of fabrics such as Gore-Tex, Sympatex, eVent and Nikwax Analogy. It’s water-based and Pfas-free, and also available as anaerosol-free spray.View image in fullscreenNikwaxwash-in waterproofer, 300ml£9.50 at Blacks£9.99 at TrespassThe circular giletThis gilet is made using fabric scraps from a French mill known for its military-grade textiles. Its outer layer is a 100% recycled waterproof polyamide, with Italian padding made from recycled polyester for the lining. The Re-Pete Project operates a circular take-back system. All its garments and accessories can be returned to be remade or composted, depending on the material.View image in fullscreenRe-Peterecycledwaterproofpolyamidegilet£380 at the Re-Pete ProjectFor more, read thebest waterproof jackets for menand thebest waterproof jackets for womenHannah Rochell is a journalist who specialises in writing about – and experiencing – a slower, more sustainable lifestyle, which she documents on her SubstackSlowette. This involves everything from switching toeco-friendly cleaning productsand advocating fordehumidifiersinstead of tumble dryers, to shopping exclusively at responsible fashion brands and learning to sewExplore more on these topicsSustainable fashionThe FilterAutumnWomen's shoesWomen's coats and jacketsHatsWomen's trousersEthical and green livingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Gay men keep my ego going – they message me all the time!’ Ed Gamble on Traitors, true love, weight loss and people-pleasing | Ed Gamble | The Guardian
description: As a Traitors obsessive, Gamble is in his element hosting its hugely popular companion show, Uncloaked. He discusses keeping the show’s secrets, edgelord comics and how he became known as a ‘mega wife guy’
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: As a Traitors obsessive, Gamble is in his element hosting its hugely popular companion show, Uncloaked. He discusses keeping the show’s secrets, edgelord comics and how he became known as a ‘mega wife guy’
Content: ‘I don’t like it if I think people aren’t playing the game hard enough’ … Ed Gamble in east London.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I don’t like it if I think people aren’t playing the game hard enough’ … Ed Gamble in east London.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianThe big interviewEd GambleInterview‘Gay men keep my ego going – they message me all the time!’ Ed Gamble on Traitors, true love, weight loss and people-pleasingEmine SanerAs a Traitors obsessive, Gamble is in his element hosting its hugely popular companion show, Uncloaked. He discusses keeping the show’s secrets, edgelord comics and how he became known as a ‘mega wife guy’Tue 20 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 05.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEd Gamble does not like seeing himself on screen. “I know a lot of comics who struggle with watching themselves,” he says. “No one should be having to look at their own face so much. It feels simultaneously arrogant and also the most self-flagellating thing you can do.”Unfortunately for him, he is inescapable. Gamble presents the BBC’s wildly successful companion show to the Traitors, The Traitors: Uncloaked, along with thehugely popular podcast Off Menu, with the comedian and current Celebrity Traitors contestant James Acaster.Over the summer, Gamble hosted a new show, Unacceptable, in which comedians try to stand up their worst opinions – a format produced by Romesh Ranganathan, surely the only comic with a heavier workload than Gamble. Another series starts next month. A special for Amazon Prime, based on Gamble’s last two standup tours, will also be available this month. He is, of course, grateful and delighted about all this. It’s a long time since I’ve met someone so self-aware and willing to acknowledge their many privileges without a hint of chippiness.View image in fullscreenLord and lady of the castle … Gamble with Celebrity Traitors host Claudia Winkleman.Photograph: James Green/BBC/Listen EntertainmentGamble has known every twist of The Celebrity Traitors, including the eventual winner or winners, since it was filmed some months ago. How does he handle the pressure of keeping it all in?“Even with my wife, who loves the show, I want to tell her what I’ve been doing on a work day, but I can’t tell her who I’ve met,” he says. Luckily, people don’t generally want to know. If they do ask, Gamble might pretend to be about to tell them. “Then you see their face go: ‘I don’t want that. I want to be part of the national conversation.’”We meet on a mild October day in a pub garden near his east London home. The actor Myha’la, who had just been banished from the show, had made comments on Instagram, addressing suggestions that unconscious racial and cultural bias exists in interactions between the players. “I certainly wouldn’t like to counteract anyone’s lived experience,” says Gamble. “I also think Myha’la said that she signed her own death warrant with the wink [at Richard E Grant shortly before he was unmasked as a traitor]. But that certainly doesn’t mean it’s not true, and it’s something that needs to be discussed and looked at.”View image in fullscreen‘There’s so many things going on with Ross Kemp that I find adorable and very funny.’Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianGamble describes himself as a Traitors “obsessive” (it becomes clear that his capacity for obsessions is part of his personality). “I don’t like it if I think people aren’t playing the game hard enough,” he says, smiling at his own exactness. He knows a lot of the people in this series – fellow comics Ranganathan, Joanne McNally, Rob Beckett and Acaster – but it’s the actor Ross Kemp who, says Gamble, “I was most excited about going in, and I think is bearing out to be my favourite so far.” He and Acaster have had Kemp on their Off Menu podcast. “He’s just such an enigma. He’s obviously got this hard man thing, but also, he’s a proper actor, a total luvvie and, from what we’ve seen on Celebrity Traitors so far, highly sensitive, highly emotional, really cares about the game. I think there’s so many things going on with Ross Kemp that I find adorable and very funny.”Growing up, Gamble initially wanted to be an actor, “because that’s what I knew about. I loved films and TV, and I probably wasn’t really aware of ‘comedian’ as a job.” When he was 13, his mother took him to see Steve Coogan perform, and he began watching comedy shows on BBC2, such asGoodness Gracious Me. He read philosophy at Durham University, where he did sketch comedy and found like-minded friends, including the comic Nish Kumar, with whom he later shared a flat in London.After university, Gamble tried standup, “and fell in love with it – just wrestling with performing on stage.” He gigged regularly, did an influential comedy podcast (Peacock and Gamble, with the comedian Ian Boldsworth), then started appearing on TV in the early 2010s. His career since then has seemed unstoppable.View image in fullscreenMeasured … Ed Gamble in The Great Celebrity Bake Off for Stand Up to Cancer in 2022.Photograph: Mark Bourdillon /Channel 4His new standup show, Fresh Hell, which he will tour next year, is, he says, “another really heavy emotional show. Very political, of course. A lot of it is about toilet brushes. It’s hugely silly. It’s stuff that feels really fun to say.” Gamble can be hilariously revolting, but he’s not interested in being edgy. “I find the attitude of ‘I can say what I like, it’s comedy’ such a teenage opinion. Like, that’s true, you have total free speech. But there might be consequences, and some people might not like it, and they might say they don’t like it, and you can’t censor them for saying that.”There is still a trend for “edgelord” comedians – those who set out to be offensive – but Gamble thinks it’s just part of a cycle. “Quite often they only talk about three topics, and they’ve all got the same angle on it. I think it’s bad for creativity, certainly, but it’ll subside. It’ll keep coming back round again, and it’s often aligned with how things feel politically in the world.”In an era in which comedy clips can circulate without context, is he concerned about what he says? “I guess so, but I’ve always tried to think about what I say and how things can be interpreted. I think that’s a really important thing to do, as anyone who has a public platform. I’ve never been in the game of trying to upset anyone. That’s not who I am, and that’s not what my comedy is.”Being likable is important to Gamble. In his 2023 memoir, Glutton, he unpicks his “desperate need to fit in with people”, as he puts it. His greatest fear is some sort of social banishment. He’s that person, he says, who reads 100 nice comments about himself, then thinks about the bad one for a week (he has a device to lock apps on his phone).Ed Gamble: ‘As a child I was a human dustbin. I’d eat every morsel’Read more“I think it’s that thing of being a desperate people-pleaser, and it’s probably one of the most pathetic elements of my personality. But also, I kind of don’t mind it, because that’s what drives me, and what makes me try to hone what I’m doing. I do wish I had that slight abandon and self-confidence to be like, ‘I’m right about this, fuck you guys,’ but I don’t.”Has his people-pleasing decreased the older and more successful he gets (he turned 40 this year)? “No, because the more people who see you doing things, the wider the field is of people who might potentially not like you, and then you see that happen.” He laughs. Those objective measures of success are “definitely something to lean on, but the brain’s an odd thing, right? It’s not logical a lot of the time. It will just go: ‘Well, think about what that one person said. That’s the real thing.’” He’s getting better, he says, “at going, ‘That doesn’t make sense, so maybe think about how well things are going.’”In his book, he acknowledges the cliche that he has sometimes used humour as a defence mechanism. He grew up in south London, attending the prestigious private school King’s College. There, his brand became the “funny fat guy”, he writes. For the first half of his life, Gamble was overweight. “I was conscious that I could be funny, and of what that could do in a social setting. Just throwing in those jokes, going, like, ‘I know I’m bigger than you, but I’m in control of it, and I can make those jokes before anyone else does.’” But it also legitimised them. “People would then feel freer to make jokes about it around me, and I’d put myself in a situation where I had to laugh or build on those jokes. Whereas internally, I think they hurt a little bit all the same.”He wouldn’t necessarily recommend self-mocking in that situation. “Broadly, what I wouldn’t recommend is making jokes about people’s weight. But you can’t tell kids at school, can you?” He dismisses the idea that he suffered much, though. “I don’t think it was massively difficult.”View image in fullscreenGamble … ‘The only time I really started worrying about my weight was when I lost a lot.’Photograph: Glasgow International Comedy FestivalIn Glutton, a book with a chapter devoted to his love of cheese, Gamble comes across as someone largely accepting of his weight, which increases in direct proportion to his overwhelming love of food. In his early 20s he reached his highest weight, about 120kg (19st). What made him decide to lose it?“The whole thing is so vain that I hate saying it, but I was booked for a TV gig,” he says. “I thought, ‘Right, that’s in four months or whatever, so I’m going to see if I can lose a bit of weight before that.’ I started doing all the things that people say you should do – do a bit of exercise, maybe don’t eat all of that.” The weight began to come off. “I know there’s various reasons why that doesn’t work for a lot of people, so I’m not saying it’s as simple as that. But, for me, it started to be.”It was also a time when he was trying to take control of his health, having been diagnosed with type 1 diabetes a decade earlier, at 13. “The only plus side I would say of type 1 diabetes is your blood glucose levels really tell you what you shouldn’t be eating. So I was keeping an eye on that, and I was trying to eat more nutritiously, and it just worked.” He lost 44kg. Then he became “obsessed” with exercise; he took up running, and ran two London marathons. “It all worked out that way, really. But the basis of it is vanity.”Was it ambition as well? Did he think he would be less successful if he was larger? “Genuinely, no,” he says. “But that is a thing. I do find it quite sad, but also I am the beneficiary of it, that I probably have got way more work since I’ve lost weight. If I continued to be the size I was back then, I don’t think I would have got half the things I’ve got, because of that.” It’s not news that ours is a sizeist society, and this isn’t just in the entertainment industry, says Gamble. “I’ve read plenty of fascinating articles about this, that people above a certain size don’t get considered for jobs. I don’t know what it is, but it’s quite depressing.”Gamble’s relationship with food is a lot healthier now, although he has replaced quantity with quality and become a self-confessed food bore. “I still eat whatever I want. I’ve just managed to draw a distinction between want and need, and I go: ‘That’s delicious, I’ve enjoyed that. I’m full now.’” Does he obsess about his weight? “I do sometimes, in terms of body image stuff, but it’s been way worse than it is now. The only time I really started worrying about my weight was when I lost a lot – you start to worry about it coming back – but I think I’m in a good place with that now.”He is easily influenced by social media, though, he says, and the expectations on men to look a certain way. “If you’re interested in anything fitness, your phone will realise that, and then it’ll just show you pictures of men working out and going: ‘I eat carbs all day, and I still look like this.’ I’m like, ‘Well, you’re 20 and clearly genetically gifted,’ but it will still be ticking over in my mind. I try not to engage in too much of that.”View image in fullscreenHosting Unacceptable.Photograph: Rob Parfitt/TLCI’m fascinated by people’s transformations, and although Gamble’s wasn’t too drastic – if he’s hot now, he was also nice-looking when he was larger – it also coincided with becoming famous and, presumably, fairly rich. Gamble writes that, even at university, his role with girls was as “trusted friend and sexless confidant”, so how did he not go wild with all that must have suddenly been on offer?“I’ve been hugely privileged throughout my whole life, so it’s not like I’ve come from a hard background and suddenly I’ve got loads of money,” he says, matter-of-factly. “In terms of relationships, I met my wife before I lost weight and before I got any massive success within the world of entertainment.” He married Charlie Jamison, a TV producer and musician, in 2021. “So I’ve always had a very supportive home life, and that’s the thing I want to preserve more than anything.”But he must get women approaching him? “Genuinely, no. I talk about Charlie so much – on stage, in interviews, on podcasts – that I think I’ve now become known as a mega wife guy. What I’ve noticed is no approaches from women, almost, and my social media is open. They’re just very respectful, and I appreciate that.” He smiles. “You’ve got to say thanks so much to the gay men for keeping some sort of ego going, because they don’t care, they’ll message me all the time. I can open my message folder and go: ‘I’ve still got it.’”When life is good – great marriage, stellar career – is that helpful to his comedy?“I’d say in some senses, yes, because I’m happy, comfortable, and that’s why I write a lot of silly material. A lot of the comedians I love are more inward-looking, slightly more tortured, if that’s a phrase I can use. I think that’s what some comedy fans prefer, and certainly critically, it’s preferred. But you know what, the trade-off is I’m on stage for an hour a day, and absolutely love the other 23 hours to be nice.”He has nothing, really, to worry about, he says, “in comparison with a lot of other people”. But still, he adds: “I’ll always find things to worry about. It’s almost funnier to have everything laid out in front of you quite nicely and still fuck up.”Ed Gamble Livestreamson Prime Video from 29October. The Fresh Hell tour starts 30 January; details atedgamble.co.ukDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Andy Burnham faces climate revolt after approval of North Sea gas drilling | Fossil fuels | The Guardian
description: Jackdaw gasfield announcement signals UK’s commitment to North Sea industry but undermines green credentials
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Jackdaw gasfield announcement signals UK’s commitment to North Sea industry but undermines green credentials
Content: The Noble Endeavor oil rig in the Cromarty Firth, Scotland. Campaigners say the Jackdaw decision will exacerbate the climate crisis.Photograph: Andy Buchanan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Noble Endeavor oil rig in the Cromarty Firth, Scotland. Campaigners say the Jackdaw decision will exacerbate the climate crisis.Photograph: Andy Buchanan/AFP/Getty ImagesFossil fuelsAndy Burnham faces climate revolt after approval of North Sea gas drillingJackdaw gasfield announcement signals UK’s commitment to North Sea industry but undermines green credentialsWhat does the approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean?Kiran StaceyPolicy editorTue 20 Oct 2026 14.24 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 18.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Jackdaw gasfield will be given the go-ahead on Wednesday, signalling Andy Burnham’s commitment to the North Sea fossil fuel industry and threatening to trigger a row with climate campaigners and Labour MPs.Miatta Fahnbulleh and John Healey, the energy secretary and chancellor respectively, will make the announcement from Aberdeen on Wednesday morning after more than a year of deliberations over whether doing so would violate the UK’s climate commitments.The approval for drilling at one of the biggest undeveloped fields in the declining North Sea basin is a big boost for Britain’s oil and gas industry – and especially for Shell and the Norwegian company Equinor, which operate it.It will be met with outrage from climate campaigners, who say it undermines Labour’s green credentials and will exacerbate the climate crisis.What does the approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean?Read moreTessa Khan, the executive director of the anti-oil campaign group Uplift, said: “Jackdaw will provide around just 2% of our gas demand for roughly 10 years. It has been oversold and won’t stop the overall decline in North Sea jobs, as it will be largely unmanned and operated remotely.”She added: “Labour’s climate credibility is on the line. No new oil and gasfields are compatible with safe climate limits.”View image in fullscreenActivists from Fossil Free London stage a protest against the Rosebank oilfield and Jackdaw gasfield outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockWhen fully operational, Jackdaw will account for 6% of North Sea gas production, making it one of the biggest gasfields not yet under production.Along with the Rosebank oilfield, its status has become symbolic of the government’s commitment to the oil and gas industry, which is facing heavy job losses as reserves decline and platforms become increasingly automated.The fieldwas approvedby the Conservative government in 2022, with ministers arguing it would help shield the UK from the volatility in the energy market caused by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.Labour came to power in 2024 on a promise not to grant any new licences in the North Sea, not expecting to have to make a decision on Jackdaw or Rosebank.However both fields were cast into doubt last year bya landmark rulingthat said their environmental approval had been incorrectly granted.A judge ruled that when deciding whether the two fields would violate the UK’s climate commitments, regulators should have taken into account the carbon emissions generated by burning the oil and gas they would produce.Shell and Equinor resubmitted their application for environmental consent last September. Since then, Fahnbulleh and her predecessor, Ed Miliband, have spent months deciding whether to use their ministerial power to block it.Both the prime minister and his predecessor, Keir Starmer, have come under heavy pressure to allow the fields to go ahead in recent months, not least from Donald Trump, who urged both men to “open up the North Sea”.Burnham signalled he was sympathetic to the US president’s arguments earlier this summer,promising to takea “pragmatic approach” to the decision.“There is a resource there,” he said in July. “When people are struggling – you can’t ignore that.”He told the Commons last week: “I will take a pragmatic approach on oil and gas. We will set out our decisions shortly.”Several sources have told the Guardian that Fahnbulleh has decided not to block the field, allowing the North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA), which regulates the industry, to give the go-ahead based on financial and logistical concerns.Making the announcement alongside Healey and the NSTA’s chief executive, Stuart Payne, they will say that granting the environmental approval does not violate Labour’s manifesto commitment because it is not a new licence.Fahnbulleh is understood not to have made a final decision on the larger Rosebank field, but energy department officials are looking at ways the tax proceeds from the project could go to green projects if it was given. A decision is expected later this year.The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland, where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted.But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party.A poll by Savanta for the climate group E3G and seen by the Guardian shows that nearly a third of voters say they would be less likely to vote Labour if it gives the go-ahead for more North Sea oil drilling.That includes almost exactly a third of those who voted Labour at the last election, and around half of 18- to 24-year-olds.Ellie Mae O’Hagan, the UK energy programme lead at E3G, said: “After a summer of deadly heatwaves, the public has made up its mind: more drilling is the wrong answer.“If the prime minister wants a decade in power to change the country, he should invest in heat pumps and solar, not tax breaks for the oil and gas companies driving up our bills and polluting the planet.”Officials say, however, that the Rosebank decision is likely to be the more sensitive one, partly because it will produce around seven times the CO2 emissions of Jackdaw and partly because most of the oil produced there will be exported.Khan said: “The defining test is Rosebank. Burnham must deliver on his promise and prioritise affordable bills, genuine industrial growth and a safe climate over oil profits. That means rejecting Rosebank.”Explore more on these topicsFossil fuelsEnvironment policyOil and gas companiesEnergy industryEnergyGasClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Senior Reform official cast doubt over legality of huge donations | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Admission from James Orr to undercover reporter came three months before party was given £72m
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Exclusive: Admission from James Orr to undercover reporter came three months before party was given £72m
Content: James Orr was suspended as Reform’s head of policy last month after other comments he made about political donation laws came to light.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJames Orr was suspended as Reform’s head of policy last month after other comments he made about political donation laws came to light.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesReform UKSenior Reform official cast doubt over legality of huge donationsExclusive: Admission from James Orr to undercover reporter came three months before party was given £72mRowena MasonWhitehall editorTue 20 Oct 2026 14.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 18.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA senior Reform UK official raised questions about whether major donations from billionaire backersChristopher Harborneand Ben Delo would be legal under the proposed new foreign donors cap three months before they gave £72m to the party.James Orr, who was then Reform UK’s head of policy and a Cambridge professor, discussed potential difficulties around future donations from Harborne and Delo in undercover footage captured by the investigative reporting group Verbatim.A reporter was posing as a potential donor when Orr talked to him about “filling the war chest in anticipation” of tougher donations rules, describing it as the establishment trying to “kneecap” the party.Orrwas suspended as Reform’s head of policylast month after Channel 4 broadcast some of Verbatim’s undercover filming in which he appeared to discuss ways to get around funding laws to allow donations from a US-based donor.The matter is under police investigation and he remains suspended, although Reform has released its own report clearing Orr and another official of wrongdoing.The new footage has been shared with the Guardian after a public debate about whether thetwo £36m donations from Harborne and Deloto Reform UK will be allowed under the cap. The party maintains the donations are legal, pointing out that the retrospective overseas donor cap has not yet been passed into law.In the footage, recorded in July this year, Orr expressed doubt about whether Delo and Harborne would still be able to donate given that, when it does become law, the £100,000 overseas donor cap is to cover party donations dating back to March this year.Orr believed Delo would probably meet the residency test as long as he was not required to have been a tax resident, in which case he would be “stuffed”. He said Harborne was “probably more of a challenge” in terms of avoiding the overseas cap and he “can’t do anything for 12 months” after moving back.Harborne had been living in Thailand until he registered to vote in Hampshire this summer, and Delo has long been resident in Hong Kong, though he has been on the UK domestic register for some years.The new law willlimit overseas donors to giving £100,000 a yearto a political party. It will apply to donations made after March 2026, and will require any domestic donor who wants to give more than £100,000 to have been resident in the UK for at least a year.In the discussion, Orr was recorded as saying the party was too reliant on Harborne and Delo as “two big whales”. He said the new law was “a retrospective law, which is unheard of. So, we’re going to challenge it in the courts.”James Orr discusses potential problems with future donations from billionaire backers – videoOrr added: “We’ll push it through judicial review. And then … so, we’ll have a big fight. But, yeah, the last few days we’ve been working hard on just filling the war chest as best we can, in anticipation of something quite brutal.”On whether the two men would be caught by the overseas cap, he said: “I mean, there’s going to be a huge fight over that. But Ben, I think it’s probably OK, because I think he is … it depends on how they legislate it, they might just say, you must have been tax domiciled here for X period of time, in which case Ben is stuffed.”Orr went on to say: “It depends what … test for moving back you apply. So, under the common law, there’s a two-limb test, which is actually quite a – not a stringent one. It’s a factual thing, a factual matrix test.“How much time you spend in England, do you have a house here, can you vote, do you have any bills that you pay, you know, it’s quite kind of, it’s not tax … So, on that test, Ben meets it, I think. And then the second then is intention. Do you intend to stay, so, evidence that you intend to stay …”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHaving debated whether Delo would meet the test, Orr said Harborne was “probably more of a challenge”. The Reform official said he would move back to the UK. “But, if he does move back, there’s 12 – he can’t pay – he can’t do anything for 12 months. And, it looks as if they will bring that in.”In his chat with the undercover reporter, Orr also referred to the “complicated backstory” ofDelo, a British-born billionairewho was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls in his cryptocurrency business. He was later pardoned by Donald Trump.0:37James Orr refers to ‘complicated backstory’ of billionaire donor Ben Delo – videoOrr also spoke about having spent time on a boat with Ben Delo in the Peloponnese this summer, talking of mixing work and a holiday in Greece, saying: “We went from Athens down to Ben’s boat in Porto Cheli.” Lawyers for Delo said he did not own a yacht.A Reform UK spokesperson said: “We are 100% confident both [donations] are legal and won’t ever have to be handed back.”Orr did not respond to a request for comment. He has previously denied wrongdoing in relation to electoral laws on overseas funding and dismissed Verbatim as “politically motivated actors trying to discredit a political opponent through dubious legal means”.Lawyers for Harborne described Orr’s comments as private speculation that would not be appropriate to comment on and did not represent established facts. Delo’s lawyers did not respond substantively, saying he would not be drawn into speculation about a conversation he was not party to, or the legal effect of a law yet to be passed. They later added that he had taken extensive legal advice on his donations and had previously set out his rationale for making them.Reform has previously said it intends to take legal action against Verbatim and its directors over the undercover filming.Explore more on these topicsReform UKParty fundingChannel 4Christopher HarbornenewsShareReuse this content

title: US has resumed sharing intelligence with Ukraine about Russian strikes, says Zelenskyy | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Advance warnings of missile attacks were seemingly suspended last week by the White House, but Ukraine’s president says: ‘Now it works’
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Advance warnings of missile attacks were seemingly suspended last week by the White House, but Ukraine’s president says: ‘Now it works’
Content: Zelenskyy (right) with the Finnish president (centre) and US envoy Steve Witkoff (left) in Oslo, Norway.Photograph: Heiko Junge/Pool NTB/APView image in fullscreenZelenskyy (right) with the Finnish president (centre) and US envoy Steve Witkoff (left) in Oslo, Norway.Photograph: Heiko Junge/Pool NTB/APUkraineUS has resumed sharing intelligence with Ukraine about Russian strikes, says ZelenskyyAdvance warnings of missile attacks were seemingly suspended last week by the White House, but Ukraine’s president says: ‘Now it works’Luke HardingTue 20 Oct 2026 15.32 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 19.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has resumed sharing intelligence with Kyiv about Russian missile strikes,Volodymyr Zelenskyysaid on Tuesday after a meeting with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway.He saidUkrainewas again receiving advance warnings of ballistic missile attacks, which were seemingly suspended last week by the White House. “Now it works. It’s great,” he said, adding that the US move would save lives.The Ukrainian president said: “It’s very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic [missiles] is coming. So we are thankful to the American side.”Witkoff will on Wednesday meet Russian president Vladimir Putin after what a US official called “constructive” talks with Zelenskyy inNorway.
