The US envoy would aim to “create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations”, a US official told Reuters.The talks in Oslo took place amid the worst crisis in US-Ukraine relations since Putin’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. Donald Trump has bitterly accused Zelenskyy of failing to end the war and has said Ukraine needs a new leader.On Tuesday Trump again suggested Zelenskyy was the main obstacle to an agreement. “We want Zelensky to make a deal. He can make a deal. He could have made a deal two years ago when wehad our little chat in the Oval Office,” he said.Trump also said he had asked Putin to release Stephen Hubbard – anAmerican taken prisoner by Russian forcesin occupied Ukraine – in a further sign of his growing public alliance with Moscow.The US president’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined Witkoff and Zelenskyy by video for the talks. Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, also took part, alongside EU and British security officials.Zelenskyy said he had held a “positive” phone call earlier with the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio. Asked if Ukraine was now losing the war, after recent hostile US actions, Zelenskyy replied: “Of course we are not losing. But we are losing people because of Russian attacks and time. It’s a pity.”He said he had raised with Rubio restrictions imposed last week on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s satellite internet service. The slowdown has crippled Ukraine’s ability to launch mid-range drone strikes on Russian battlefield positions.Zelenskyy said he had offered to stop Ukraine’s long-range attacks on Russian oil refineries – a key Trump demand – if the US provided Kyiv with Patriot missile interceptors. The Pentagon has blocked the delivery of Patriots to Kyiv paid for by other countries, leaving Kyiv more vulnerable than ever to air attacks.Speaking on Tuesday, Zelenskyy also said he opposed a trilateral summit floated by Putin, which would see the Russian leader, Trump and China’s president, Xi Jinping, meet next month to strike a Ukraine deal. Zelenskyy would be shut out, theWall Street Journal reported.“There can be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in Oslo. He added: “If it’s about Ukraine and our future it can only be acceptable when we are at the table of negotiations.”The Washington-Kyiv crisis began 10 days ago when Trump announced he was lifting US sanctions on Russian diesel, in an attempt to lower fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. He then announced an energy ceasefire, which Kyiv implemented for several days but Russia ignored.Despite this, Trump has bitterly rounded on Zelenskyy. He has effectively positioned the US as Russia’s ally, favouring Moscow over Kyiv, to the dismay of America’s pro-Ukrainian European and British backers. The US’s peace proposals have largely echoed Russia’s maximalist demands.The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, on Tuesday questioned whether US negotiators had been honest brokers in the peace efforts. Witkoff has held numerous meetings with Putin in Moscow, while so far visiting Kyiv only once.“Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now,” Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin’s terms “because Europe has been supporting Ukraine”, Kallas said.Tuesday’s talks came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of US politicians that he believed “some political decision has been made to slow down … support for us”.US officials have denied this but have failed to explain convincingly why satellite communication services were curtailed or intelligence sharing temporarily cut off.Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio insisted nothing had changed. He said Patriot interceptors were in short supply and were needed in other parts of the world, as well as for the US’s own defence. “There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine,” he insisted.At least nine people were killed in Ukraine on Tuesday. They included passengers who were travelling on the Kyiv to Odesa highway. A Russian drone struck two vehicles, killing three people and injuring four. One of the victims was the driver of a shuttle bus, which was on its way from the capital to a military cemetery.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropeUS foreign policyVolodymyr ZelenskyyNorwaynewsShareReuse this content

title: Schools in England must recognise antisemitism as distinct category of harm, report says | Antisemitism | The Guardian
description: Government expected to accept recommendations of review, which found three in five Jewish students had experienced prejudice
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Government expected to accept recommendations of review, which found three in five Jewish students had experienced prejudice
Content: Sir David Bell, who led the independent review, said many cases of antisemitism were not reported by students and teachers.Photograph: David James Wood/David WoodView image in fullscreenSir David Bell, who led the independent review, said many cases of antisemitism were not reported by students and teachers.Photograph: David James Wood/David WoodAntisemitismSchools in England must recognise antisemitism as distinct category of harm, report saysGovernment expected to accept recommendations of review, which found three in five Jewish students had experienced prejudiceRichard AdamsEducation editorTue 20 Oct 2026 16.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 17.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSchools and colleges inEnglandwill be expected to take a tougher stance against antisemitism after a report found that three out of five Jewish students said they had been affected.Sir David Bell, the former chief inspector of Ofsted who was commissioned by the government to lead the independent review, said he found many cases of antisemitism going unreported or unchallenged by students and teachers.Belltold Sky Newsthat “a general commitment to tackling racism or prejudice or hate has not properly identified antisemitism as a particular kind of hate”, with the review, to be published on Wednesday, recommending increased awareness and teaching.“We do need to name antisemitism as a particular kind of prejudice and hate, because I think if you don’t name it, you don’t actually know what you’re tackling or what you’re going to be able to do to respond to it,” Bell said.The review’s conclusions would require schools and colleges in England to recognise antisemitism as a distinct category of harm and take explicit action against it.The government is expected to accept the review’s 27 recommendations, including provision of resources to tackle antisemitism in schools and dedicated teacher training in antisemitism awareness, including a national hotline where school leaders can quickly get advice on tackling antisemitism.Other recommendations include encouraging schools to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance working definition of antisemitism, as well as strengthening teaching of the Holocaust to ensure that antisemitism is seen as a central theme of the genocide.Policies on staff behaviour should also make clear that antisemitism is not acceptable, and that all schools and colleges should have “robust” reporting and response procedures.“This is not just a report for Jewish children in Jewish schools. This is for all children and young people in all schools and colleges. We know that antisemitism crosses all boundaries,” Bell told the BBC.Bell added there needs to be stronger guidance on political impartiality for schools so that students can “debate topical and difficult issues without feeling that teachers are imposing their own views on students”.A survey conducted for the review found that one in five students said they had witnessed antisemitism, and three in five Jewish students had experienced it. However, fewer than half of those surveyed felt it would be addressed if reported.The review was launched by the government in March, after antisemitic episodes including theattack at Manchester’s Heaton Park synagoguein October last year.The Community Security Trust (CST), which provides security and support to the Jewish community and schools, haspublished figuresshowing rising numbers of antisemitic incidents at schools this year.In the first half of 2026 the CST found that reports of antisemitism in schools had reached the highest levels it had ever recorded, from 112 incidents in the first half of 2025 to 178 recorded over the same period in 2026.A spokesperson from the Board of Deputies of British Jews said: “Treating antisemitism in schools as a safeguarding issue will have the benefit of creating an explicit duty on all schools to address this as they would any other threat to children’s safety, and will strengthen accountability.”Bell’s review will be presented to MPs in parliament on Wednesday.Explore more on these topicsAntisemitismSchoolsCollegesStudentsEnglandShareReuse this content

title: Italy to deploy 500 troops to Milan after days of protests and looting | Italy | The Guardian
description: Government planning tougher security measures as France also says military forces will be deployed
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Government planning tougher security measures as France also says military forces will be deployed
Content: Protesters clash with police in Piazza del Duomo in Milan, Italy. The unrest followed ​clashes on Saturday in other northern cities ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin.Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenProtesters clash with police in Piazza del Duomo in Milan, Italy. The unrest followed ​clashes on Saturday in other northern cities ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin.Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/ShutterstockItalyItaly to deploy 500 troops to Milan after days of protests and lootingGovernment planning tougher security measures as France also says military forces will be deployedWhy are people protesting across Europe?Angela Giuffridain Rome andJon Henleyin ParisTue 20 Oct 2026 17.24 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 20.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleItaly’s government is sending 500 soldiers to Milan and vowed a “firm response from the state” after protests against the cost of living descended into clashes with police, vandalism and looting. Further demonstrations are planned on Saturday.The government of the far-right prime minister,Giorgia Meloni, also announced new security measures, including an offence of violent participation in ⁠a demonstration, tougher penalties for ⁠rioters, and financial liability for ​parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting..InFrance, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on Tuesday some military forces would be deployed during ⁠protests ​planned for this Saturday, “mostly to free police and gendarmes in their mission to maintain order”.The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, told parliament that the police presence during Saturday’s demonstrations ⁠would be “massive” and that ​his ​goal was ​for an “immediate return ​to order” ‌after last weekend’s violent riots.Police in Milan, in northern Italy, detained 271 young people after hooded youths set bins ablaze, ransacked shops and smashed windows, including in the area surrounding the city’s cathedral, during the unrest on Saturday and Sunday.Police used teargas and water cannon to disperse the violent groups, who were on the fringes of an initially peaceful protest. Of those detained, 32 have been arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.View image in fullscreenIn Milan’s Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, brands including Chanel, Tiffany ‌and Dior have removed merchandise from ‌their windows as a precaution.Photograph: Stefano Porta/LaPresse/ShutterstockImages of Saturday’s clashes in France, including mobs looting shops and public buildings set on fire, prompted several countries including the US, China and Germany to issue travel advice for their citizens. Nearly 2,400 people were arrested in one of France’s most violent recent bouts of unrest.French authorities on Monday announced partial curfews in several cities, including Paris, Bordeaux, Lille and Nice, and after a night of relative calm, Lecornu said on Tuesday that new curfews would be imposed where they were needed.Authorities in Paris renewed Monday night’s curfew, which would apply from 11pm on Tuesday until 6am on Wednesday to the Place de la République, where many of the weekend clashes took place, and in the central Les Halles shopping district.Paris police ordered a temporary ban on people carrying cans or bottles of petrol or gas, and banned masks and helmets in some areas. A man was also arrested in connection with theburning down of the historic town hall in Limoges.The Italian press agency Ansa reported that one of the security measures being considered in the country was aimed at second-generation immigrant youths, known asmaranza– a slang term used to describe gangs of young people, usually from marginalised areas.Many luxury stores in Milan’s fashion district have stayed closed amid fears of further unrest. Brands including Chanel, Tiffany ‌and Dior removed merchandise from ‌their windows as a precaution.Other stores ransacked included the sports retailers Decathlon and Arc’teryx and the mobile phone operator Vodafone, footage showed.View image in fullscreenThe sports retailer Decathlon was among the stores ransacked in Milan during the protests.Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/Shutterstock“The government will respond firmly to these attacks on the state, ​including through measures aimed at curbing violence by minors,” the foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, who also serves as deputy prime minister, said after Meloni chaired a meeting with top security officials on Monday.Meloni’s coalition, which is facing a general election next year, is reportedly planning tougher penalties for road blockades after days of protests in southern Italy by lorry drivers over fuel prices.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhy are people protesting across Europe?Read moreMeanwhile, Milan is bracing for further protests on Saturday after a new movement, called 17 October, emerged on social media. It said it would organise demonstrations there and in other Italian cities each Saturday afternoon “until this government of thieves collapses”.“You are the violent ones,” the group said. “You, who denied us a future. Now, we are claiming that future ourselves.”Opposition politicians often accuse the government of using security as a propaganda tool, arguing that Italy’s leaders do little to address core issues such as education, housing and living conditions in marginalised areas.There were also tensions during protests at the weekend over the high cost of living in other northern Italian cities, ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, police said.The protests in Italy and France have been mirrored by demonstrations in other parts ofEurope.Thousands rallied in Lisbon and other Portuguese cities on Tuesday evening, hours after police dismantled housing protest camps at dawn and arrested 55 people.Demonstrators inPortugalare protesting soaring housing costs, seeking to align themselves with similar actions in neighbouring Spain, where tents have been set up in central Madrid for weeks.In Lisbon, thousands of people gathered in the central Rossio square, where protesters voted by a show of hands to re-establish their tent camp from Wednesday.“They forced me on to the streets to shout”, read one placard. Another declared: “Lisbon is not for sale”.Anti-government demonstrations have also rocked the Albanian capital Tirana over the past week, driven by fresh demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and a controversial resort development linked to Donald Trump’s family.Clashes between the protesters and police escalated again on Tuesday amid renewed calls for prime minister Edi Rama’s resignation. Riot police used teargas and water cannon to disperse protesters who fired fireworks and hurled molotov cocktails and stones at officers.Earlier on Tuesday, Rama repeated earlier accusations that “foreign actors” were to blame for the violence, having previously accused both Russia and Iran of driving online misinformation.“It is a hybrid war that gains traction precisely because it is rooted in genuine grievances, not mere fantasy,” the prime minister said, citing the rising cost of living, housing affordability and concerns for the future.Explore more on these topicsItalyProtestEuropeGiorgia MeloniCost of living crisisFrancePortugalnewsShareReuse this content

title: Weight loss in middle age can restore cardiovascular health, research suggests | Health | The Guardian
description: UK study of 6,000 patients shows shedding 5% of body weight may help cut the risk of stroke and heart disease
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: UK study of 6,000 patients shows shedding 5% of body weight may help cut the risk of stroke and heart disease
Content: Researchers at University College London said their study showed it was ‘never too late to start making changes to improve your health’.Photograph: Richard Drury/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenResearchers at University College London said their study showed it was ‘never too late to start making changes to improve your health’.Photograph: Richard Drury/Getty ImagesHealthWeight loss in middle age can restore cardiovascular health, research suggestsUK study of 6,000 patients shows shedding 5% of body weight may help cut the risk of stroke and heart diseaseAndrew GregoryHealth editorTue 20 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLosing just 5% of your body weight in middle age can reduce inflammation, lower the risk of stroke and make your heart as healthy as if you had never gained weight, research suggests.Millions of men and women worldwide gain weight as they age, putting extra stress on their body, reducing quality of life and doing significant damage to their cardiovascular and metabolic health.While most know being overweight or obese can affect health, many believe it is an inevitable part of ageing or assume they would need to shed a large amount of weight to reap any benefits.The new study adds togrowing evidencethat small changes in body weight can have a big impact on health risks. While millions of people hope to lose a large amount of weight, it’s much easier to start with a smaller goal and keep it off, experts said.Researchers at University College London found overweight people who lost just 5% of their weight in their 40s and 50s had similar heart health in older age as adults who had always been a healthy weight.By the time they reached the age of 62, both groups had comparable cholesterol levels, blood pressure and signs of inflammation – all key measures of cardiovascular and metabolic health.16:27From paleo to intermittent fasting: are any diets actually good for us? - videoThe study’s lead author, Charis Bridger-Staatz, of UCL’s centre for longitudinal studies, said: “Ageing is often framed in terms of inevitable health decline, but our new research shows that this need not be the case.“Just a modest reduction in weight in people’s 50s may make a real difference to their health, potentially improving their quality of life and reducing their risk of heart issues.”Having poor metabolic or cardiovascular health can raise the risk of serious conditions, including type 2 diabetes, heart disease and cardiovascular events such as heart attacks or strokes.Bridger-Staatz, a senior research fellow in population health, said thousands of lives could be lost needlessly in the next decade because of poor health related to being overweight or obese.“While obesity prevention strategies rightly place strong emphasis on children and young people, these findings indicate that prevention efforts should also extend to people in their 50s,” she added.“Although this is often perceived as a stage of life when meaningful health change is no longer possible, our research shows that it’s never too late to start making changes to improve your health.”In the study, researchers looked at data from more than 6,000 people born in the UK in 1958. They analysed body mass index and noted the highest BMI each person reached by the age of 42.The team then examined whether people had lost or gained at least 5% of their weight by age 50, and if they had maintained this weight difference at age 55. Measurements such as blood pressure, cholesterol and inflammation markers were also analysed.The study found that at the age of 62, the metabolic and cardiovascular health of overweight people who had lost weight in middle age closely resembled that of the consistently healthy weight group.This was an observational study, so conclusions cannot be drawn about cause and effect. The researchers also highlighted other limitations but said the findings had important implications.The study’s co-author, Laura Gimeno, said: “These results show that the benefits of weight loss may extend beyond short-term weight reduction. Our findings support current interest around expanding access to effective weight-loss support, including weight-loss medications.“They also highlight the importance of reducing further weight gain in midlife, as this was consistently linked to the fastest deterioration in heart and metabolic health.”Explore more on these topicsHealthWeight-loss drugsDiets and dietingUCL (University College London)Heart diseasenewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand told woman to ‘clear up the mess you’ve made’ after alleged rape, court hears | UK news | The Guardian
description: Woman says alleged assault at comedian’s London home was one of most painful experiences of her life
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Woman says alleged assault at comedian’s London home was one of most painful experiences of her life
Content: Russell Brand arriving at Southwark crown court with his wife, Laura Gallacher, on Tuesday.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAView image in fullscreenRussell Brand arriving at Southwark crown court with his wife, Laura Gallacher, on Tuesday.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAUK newsRussell Brand told woman to ‘clear up the mess you’ve made’ after alleged rape, court hearsWoman says alleged assault at comedian’s London home was one of most painful experiences of her lifeEmine SinmazTue 20 Oct 2026 14.22 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman has said she “couldn’t speak or breathe” when Russell Brand raped her at his London townhouse after picking her out from a crowd after one of his gigs, a court has heard.She said the comedian looked “horrified” after the alleged attack so she assumed he would apologise but instead he told her: “Clear up the mess you’ve made.”The woman said she “tortured herself” in the years that followed because it was one of the “most painful experiences” of her life.Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.The TV personality sat upright in the dock as the woman’s video-recorded police interview was played to Southwark crown court on Tuesday.The woman told officers she was a “massive fan” of Brand and “giddy” to meet him after one of his stand-up performances at the Hammersmith Apollo in 2009.She alleged he pointed to her and said “you” before inviting her, her friend and a third young woman they did not know to have drinks with him.Brand’s security guard later invited the trio backstage where the woman performed oral sex on the actor but refused to have penetrative sex. By then, the woman’s friend had left, but Brand had sex on a sofa with the third woman, who was 19.The woman said she felt “awful” and “disgusting” when she left the dressing room, which is when Brand asked her why she had refused to have sex with him. She told him she had a boyfriend, to which he replied: “We don’t belong to anyone, we’re all free, the ownership of people is sort of what we’ve been sold.”View image in fullscreenThe woman said Brand was ‘persuasive’ about her visiting his three-storey townhouse in Hampstead, west London.Photograph: Wenn Rights Ltd/AlamyBrand asked for her phone number and began messaging and calling her. She said he was “persuasive” about her visiting his three-storey townhouse in Hampstead, north-west London.Days later, the woman was picked up by Brand’s driver and taken to the star’s home knowing she would have sex with him. “I’ve really struggled for a really long time to accept what happened to me, because I went there knowingly and willingly,” she said.She alleged that when she arrived, Brand told her: “This is the best decision you’ve made.” But when they went to Brand’s bedroom, he ordered her to have a shower because her hair smelled “funny”, and made her brush her teeth.She said it made her feel “really dirty”, adding: “At the time it did feel like a thrilling thing to go to the house of this person I really fancied, and I loved comedy. But all those things didn’t feel that good.”View image in fullscreenThe woman described Brand’s dark bedroom and ‘enormous’ bed.Photograph: Metropolitan PoliceShe described his dark bedroom and “enormous” bed, and the distinctive black toilet paper in his ensuite bathroom. Pictures later shown to the jury showed a crucifix above his bed and black furnishings.The woman told how they had consensual vaginal sex but that she did not enjoy the experience, saying: “It felt very awkward. It didn’t matter who I was, and I just sort of wanted it to be over.”Then Brand anally raped the woman, she told police. “He didn’t give me a warning, he didn’t ask,” she said. “I don’t know how long it took for me between it going on and me asking him to stop. I don’t think it was very long. I felt like I couldn’t speak or breathe, the amount of pain.”She alleged she begged him to stop, at first really quietly and then more loudly, but Brand continued.She said he looked “absolutely fucking horrified” after the alleged attack, adding: “I thought he was going to say sorry … but actually what he said was: ‘You need to clear up the mess you’ve made.’”She said one of Brand’s aides later asked her to leave because the comedian had a gig.“The way I would describe that event to people after was that it was traumatic and that he hurt me and harmed me. And when I asked him to stop, he didn’t,” she said.She told the court she had gone to a sexual health clinic afterwards because she feared she had HIV, and she became unwell and anxious.“In the years that followed, if I spoke to people about it, it was was very much laced with ‘I shouldn’t have gone’, and I think I tortured myself because I think it was one of the most painful experiences I’d gone through.”Earlier on Tuesday, two women who have separately accused Brand of sexually assaulting them at work in front of his entourage gave evidence from behind a screen.The first woman said Brand laughed after “mauling” her by squeezing her breasts and kissing her sloppily while she was working at a radio station in 2004 or 2005.She told the court he “overpowered her with such strength” during the “violent” and “frenzied” attack that took place in the middle of her work day.She said she had “buried” the assault because there was such a culture of fear in the media in the 2000s and Brand was a “big star”.The second woman, who worked at Channel 4, said she was “repulsed” when Brand placed his head in her lap during a filming project after she was asked to give him a massage.She said Brand was with two men – named in court as Jack Bayles and Gareth Roy – during the alleged assault in 2009, which she reported to her line manager.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bad apple effect: study shows how people are influenced by rule-breaking of others | Psychology | The Guardian
description: Research shows how seeing bigger violations by others can lead people to increase their own rule-breaking
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Research shows how seeing bigger violations by others can lead people to increase their own rule-breaking
Content: ‘In many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing,’ one of the study’s authors said.Photograph: Cultura Creative/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘In many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing,’ one of the study’s authors said.Photograph: Cultura Creative/AlamyPsychologyBad apple effect: study shows how people are influenced by rule-breaking of othersResearch shows how seeing bigger violations by others can lead people to increase their own rule-breakingNicola DavisScience correspondentTue 20 Oct 2026 19.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom politicians taking bribes tobullying and harassment in City firms, leaders have been quick to label those who break the rules as the odd “bad apple”. But new research backs up the idiom that one bad apple can spoil the barrel.Researchers have found that when people go beyond the rule-breaking they see in others, general compliance can swiftly turn into widespread rule-breaking.Dr Lucas Molleman, from the University of Amsterdam and the first author of the research, said the goal was to explore how individuals make decisions about rule-breaking in a social context.“Many people think of themselves as making sort of autonomous decisions, especially in these individualist cultures that we are from, like Netherlands, the UK,” he said. “But in actual fact, in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing.”Writing in the journalProceedings of the Royal Society B, Molleman and colleagues report how they recruited 750 people in the US to take part in an online experiment, with the participants approximately evenly split between Republicans and Democrats.The researchers asked each participant to complete an online task in which they saw an animated “shooting star” moving across a row of 100 squares as its intensity varied. Participants were instructed to pick the square that lit up most intensely to receive a monetary reward.However, participants received greater rewards for selecting squares further to the right of the correct square, and smaller rewards for selecting squares further to the left.Participants were then shown whether another participant had followed the rules or broken them, the extent of any rule-breaking, and their political affiliation, and asked if they wished to update their choice. The process was repeated six times.The results revealed participants showed large degrees of rule-breaking even in their initial choices, with 23% of choices involving squares with the highest reward.However, the choices of others mattered: seeing others following the rules slightly reduced an individual’s rule-breaking, while seeing others making small beneficial violations – choosing a square a third of the way to the right, beyond the correct square – slightly increased rule-breaking.Crucially, seeing others flagrantly flout the rules by selecting a square even further to the right led participants to greatly increase their own level of rule-breaking. In some cases they went beyond the violations they had observed.The team say the findings were stronger when a participant had the same political leanings as others – something Molleman said chimed with other research, suggesting people who are politically aligned are more influenced by each other.The researchers used computer simulations to explore how the behaviour they had observed in the experiments would play out in a large group. The results showed that a situation could quickly get out of hand.“A minority of escalating individuals, exceeding the rule violations they observe, they might cause a whole collective to spin out of control,” Molleman said.However, he noted that about a third of participants consistently followed the rules even though it did not lead to the largest reward.Prof Stephen Reicher, of the University of St Andrews, in Scotland, who was not involved in the work, said the study had limitations, including that the experiment was abstract and there was no penalty for rule-breaking, meaning the relevance of the work to real-world examples remained unproven.Reicher also stressed that the results went against the concept of contagion, instead showing that whether we are influenced by others depends on who those others are.“This is important because it implies that, say, we don’t riot simply because we see others rioting,” he said. “In fact, many people who see rioting respond by helping clear up after riots.”Explore more on these topicsPsychologyResearchHigher educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: The ‘Finger cutter’ and the ‘Brazilian Escobar’: the men accused of bringing cocaine cartels to Europe | Drugs | The Guardian
description: A Belgian criminal organisation’s links with a Brazilian cocaine gang have been the focus of a major trial in Brussels, where smuggling links have been alleged between European players and the drug cartels of Latin America
Author: Andrei Netto
Headline: A Belgian criminal organisation’s links with a Brazilian cocaine gang have been the focus of a major trial in Brussels, where smuggling links have been alleged between European players and the drug cartels of Latin America
Content: In the past decade, cells of Latin American drug cartels have been identified by police forces, Europol and intelligence services across Europe and north Africa.Composite: Guardian Design/Belga/AFP/Getty/AP/EuropolView image in fullscreenIn the past decade, cells of Latin American drug cartels have been identified by police forces, Europol and intelligence services across Europe and north Africa.Composite: Guardian Design/Belga/AFP/Getty/AP/EuropolBloodlinesDrugsThe ‘Finger cutter’ and the ‘Brazilian Escobar’: the men accused of bringing cocaine cartels to EuropeA Belgian criminal organisation’s links with a Brazilian cocaine gang have been the focus of a major trial in Brussels, where smuggling links have been alleged between European players and the drug cartels of Latin AmericaSupported byAbout this contentAndrei Nettoin Brussels and ParisTue 20 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early hours of 7 September, a convoy of heavily armed police swept through the sleeping streets of central Brussels towards the Haren district, on the city’s north-eastern outskirts. They made their way to 22 Avenue du Bourget, a militarised bunker-like complex that was the former headquarters of Nato.The modernist complex, with its austere and functional architecture, was hastily built in 1967 and houses the Justitia courtroom, where Belgium’s federal trials are now held. It was here that the perpetrators and accomplices of the 2015Paris terrorist attacksand the 2016Brussels attackswere tried in 2022.Last month, officers armed with assault rifles patrolled the building’s wide corridors, protecting those involved in this decade’s most high-profile trial: theBressers-Carvalho case.For a month, judges and a legion of lawyers shared the main courtroom with journalists and the public on one side of a large armoured-glass partition. On the other side were the defendants, 31 in number, flanked by officers with their faces masked to protect them from possible reprisals. It was a scene more typical of countries ravaged by mafias.During the lengthy hearings throughout the month, two among the many defendants stood out. The first was Flor Bressers, a 40-year-old Belgian born in Lommel, a town of 35,000 in the province of Limburg. Bressers has an unusual profile for criminal circles. A criminology graduate of the Free University of Brussels (VUB), he was often known to his peers as “the professor” or “the academic”.Yet his most commonly used nickname contradicts the image of a refined and scrupulous man: Bressers is best known as“the Finger cutter”.Arrested in 2022at a wine tasting with his wife in a penthouse of the luxury Renaissance Zurich Tower Hotel, Bressers has been facing charges of kidnapping, unlawful detention, extortion involving firearms, and leading a criminal organisation.View image in fullscreenLeft, Sérgio Roberto de Carvalho, known as the ‘Brazilian Escobar’, and the Belgian Flor Bressers, nicknamed the ‘Finger cutter’.Composite: AFP/EuropolThe other key figure alleged to be in the criminal organisation is a 68-year-old Brazilian: Sérgio Roberto de Carvalho. In a joint operation involving Interpol, Europol, the Brazilian federal police and the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA),Carvalho was arrested on 21 June 2022at a luxury hotel overlooking the Danube in the Hungarian capital, Budapest.Based in Mato Grosso do Sul, a Brazilian state in the tri-border region of Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay, which is one of the continent’s centres of organised crime, Carvalho became known in his own country by thenickname “Major”, from his rank when he was a military police officer, a past life in which he blended corruption and crime. In Europe, his moniker was more revealing: “the Brazilian Escobar”.Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’Read moreTogether, the Finger cutter and the Brazilian Escobar are the main defendants in a Belgian courtroom bristling with security as the international cocaine trafficking network between Latin America andEuropeis put under the spotlight.Bressers and Carvalho are alleged to have been behind an organisation suspected of transportingup to 45 tonnes of cocaine to Europe.Prosecutors said they led a lawless multinational operation that moved hundreds of millions of dollars through front companies, one of which, the Antwerpwater treatment firm Kriva Rochem, has given the case its alternative name.The money – allegedly laundered through cryptocurrencies, financial markets and property – financed the complex logistics involved in transporting cocaine produced in Peru and Bolivia along illegal, dusty routes inBrazil, before crossing the Atlantic and being distributed in an unknown number of countries in Europe and beyond.Bressers had been on Europol’s list of most wanted fugitives since 2021. According to the agency’s notice, he was wanted for kidnapping and unlawful deprivation of liberty, extortion involving a firearm and participation in a criminal organisation.An earlier case from 2010, in which he was eventually acquitted in 2015 for lack of evidence, alleged that he had ordered a settling of scores, in which the victim had a finger cut off with pruning shears – giving rise to Bressers’ nickname.View image in fullscreenFlor Bressers after his arrest in 2022. He was on the run for two years.Photograph: Photo NewsIn 2020, five years later, he was convicted in relation to another revenge case: kidnapping a Dutch drug dealer who was beaten, threatened with death and cut with a razor blade after being blamed for a missing cocaine shipment. Bressers then became a fugitive, spending two years on the run.Bressers also appeared as a suspect in at least one other violent case, this time in Guyana, involving the death of a rice wholesaler in the South American country whose seized consignment contained cocaine. His death is believed to have been a cover-up to prevent the gang’s network being dismantled. That case also never went to trial.Bressers’ partner, Carvalho, is perhaps better known in Europe than in Brazil. According to Brazilian court documents, he led the group that acquired dozens of tonnes of cocaine produced in Peru and Bolivia and transported it through the Brazilian midwest to the ports of Paranaguá and Natal, from where the drugs were shipped to Europe.Born in 1958 in Ibiporã, in southern Brazil’s Paraná state, Carvalho grew up in Mato Grosso do Sul and became engaged in criminal activity while a police officer in the state. First sentenced to 15 years in prison for drug trafficking in 1998, hewas not dismissed from the police until 2010. Rather than continue running his operations from Latin America, the Brazilian Escobar moved to Europe, firsthiding in Portugaland then in Spain.View image in fullscreenA customs officer at the Dutch port of Rotterdam, which was a major route used by smugglers to import drugs from South America.Photograph: Kristof van Accom/Belga Mag/AFP/GettyThere, according to Spanish police, he took up residence in a €2m mansion in Marbella on the Costa del Sol, using the identity of Paul Wouter, a wealthy Surinamese citizen. From this base in Spain, a known hub of international cocaine trafficking, prosecutors say he coordinated, between 2017 and 2020, an organised crime network spanning Portugal and Spain, specialising in drug smuggling through ports such as Setúbal, near Lisbon, and Leixões in northern Portugal, and through Lisbon airport, as well as the ports of Rotterdam and Antwerp.Portuguese police suspected that Carvalho had links to thePrimeiro Comando da Capital(PCC, or First Capital Command), Brazil’s leading criminal organisation.Carvalho was cornered – but not arrested –in November 2020 in coordinated raidsinvolving more than 1,000 police officers police from Portugal, Spain, Belgium, the Netherlands, Romania and the United Arab Emirates, as well as Europol. The operation led to 45 arrests and the seizure of more than €13m (£11m) in cash, 70 luxury cars, 37 aircraft and 136 properties.View image in fullscreenSome of the cash seized in the international raids on traffickers in 2020.Photograph: EuropolThe court heard that Carvalho is said to have staged his own death in the same year by obtaining a death certificate for Wouter, who was allegedly the victim of Covid-related complications.He then moved to Budapest, where he was arrested in 2022 while using the identity of Guillermo Díaz Flores, a Mexican national. Carvalho is alleged to have used at least 10 false identities before being detained in Budapest. Extradited toBelgiumin June 2023, he was sent to a high-security prison.In court, he was reunited with the Finger cutter, his alleged accomplice, as they faced charges of orchestrating a transnational criminal organisation. In his trial evidence, Bressers did not admit any of the charges and claimed to be the victim of a media witch-hunt. “I have a strong feeling that all of this was orchestrated by the authorities,” he says.Bresser’s defence team is contesting the admissibility of the evidence and has requested the case be dismissed. When approached, Bressers’ lead solicitor, Hans Rieder, had not commented by the time of publication. During the trial, the defence accused the press of “painting an absolutely monstrous picture of our client”.View image in fullscreenA customs officer simulates a drug search of a ship for the media in a dive tank at Antwerp port.Photograph: Virginia Mayo/APCarvalho, who did not attend all of the proceedings due to health problems, maintained his innocence and claimed to be the victim of persecution by the Brazilian federal authorities. “I have been in prison for five years and nobody is listening to me,” he said at the hearing. “It was a namesake who committed these crimes, not me.”Carvalho’s lawyers, Frédéric Thiebaut and Renaat Landuyt, were approached for comment but did not respond. The Belgian federal prosecutor handling the case also declined to comment.The trial hearings wrapped up on 9 October, with a verdict anticipated on 15 December. Bressers could receive up to 20 years in prison, while Carvalho could be handed up to 15 years.Over the past decade, cases such as the Bressers-Carvalho one have multiplied. During this period, cells of Latin American drug-trafficking groups have been identified by national police forces, Europol and intelligence services in Portugal, Spain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, Italy, the Nordic countries, eastern Europe and the Balkans, as well as north Africa.These criminal offshoots have become embedded in Europe through “brokers” or members of drug cartels that “provide specialised services related to cocaine production in Europe, including extracting cocaine from various carrier materials or the processing of trafficked coca paste”,according to Europol’s Andy Kraag, head of its serious and organised crime centre.“Latin American criminals are heavily involved in this. We see the presence of Latin American criminals in Europe growing, their activities becoming more and more relevant.“It used to be the other way around – it’s a two-way street now. We already saw, for decades, European high-level criminals embedded in Latin America, settling down there. And now you see more and more Latin American criminals permanently or semi-permanently active in Europe too,” Kraag says.High-level sources across Europe and Latin America indicate that these groups are expanding their operations and influence in the real and digital economies, fuelled by cryptocurrencies, gambling companies, and the financial and property sectors.View image in fullscreenBressers’ lead lawyer, Hans Rieder, arrives at the Brussels court.Photograph: Belga News/AlamyAccording to Juan Gabriel Tokatlian, a professor of international relations at Universidad Di Tella in Buenos Aires, and an expert on Latin American organised crime, the “war on drugs”, as waged in Colombia – where he lived for 20 years – made cartels more resilient and dynamic, which explains their ability to adapt and expand internationally.“Europe has become, in recent years, a place where drug consumption has increased in particular. If you look at the UN reports, it is an important market – in the 1980s, particularly as regards cocaine, it was not relevant,” he says.“In that context of European demand and an erratic anti-drug policy that militarises but then coexists, we find a series of situations that end up empowering organised crime,” says Tokatlian.Like Carvalho, dozens of alleged leaders of criminal organisations such as the PCC, Tren de Aragua, the Sinaloa cartel, Clan del Golfo or Los Lobos are being held in prisons across Europe, wanted by national police forces or Europol, or listed on Interpol’s red list of most wanted individuals.They are sought for links to trafficking cocaine to Europe, trafficking arms and synthetic drugs to Latin America, and ties to European organisations in the Balkans or the Italian’Ndranghetamafia.View image in fullscreenSome of the 1,747 packages of Colombian cocaine seized in the Dominican Republic in 2020, disguised as kitchen items and bound for Rotterdam.Photograph: Erika Santelices/AFP/GettyGabriel Feltran, a sociologist at Sciences Po university in Paris and director of research at the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS), say groups such as the PCC or Sinaloa are partnering with European crime organisations such as those in Albania or the ’Ndrangheta in “joint ventures”.How Europe’s most wanted cocaine trafficker turned Sierra Leone into the world’s first true narco stateRead moreHe says they buy coca directly from Latin American producers and are capable of delivering directly at the end – so drug ownership no longer passes from hand to hand along the chain.It is what Feltran calls the “platformisation” of organised crime, in which,like multinational digital platforms such as Amazon, Google and Meta, the cartels integrate theirinfrastructure and economic models with the aim of controlling the entire drug-trafficking chain, from production deep in Latin America to sale on the streets of Europe.It means that everything from communications, payments, precursors (chemicals needed to manufacture drugs) and laboratories to logistics is concentrated at the top, with carriers and local operators often unwittingly hired as paid service providers, such as Uber drivers.Feltran says that, before this platformisation, trafficking was based on routes and several intermediaries who were drug owners in each step of the chain. Now, he says, such “joint ventures get together at the top, buy directly from the producer and deliver directly at the end. They no longer go through intermediaries.”“Ownership of the drug no longer changes hands. They concentrate everything, optimise a lot and grow very quickly. The more people use their services, the more dependent they become – that’s a network effect.”Explore more on these topicsDrugsBloodlinesBelgiumBrazilAmericasEuropeOrganised crimeDrugs tradefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: After dark, these YouTubers watch over an unlikely charge – a shark stuck in a South Korean canal | South Korea | The Guardian
description: A group of self-appointed guardians wearing hi-vis and carrying selfie sticks watch over the animal that has been trapped for a month, drawing more than 1.6 million visitors
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: A group of self-appointed guardians wearing hi-vis and carrying selfie sticks watch over the animal that has been trapped for a month, drawing more than 1.6 million visitors
Content: L-R YouTubers Kim Jong-hwan, Choi Won-jin, Na Tae Soo and Kim Jong-hwan who have been keeping watch over the 3.5-metre shark trapped in a canal in Busan, South Korea.Composite: Supplied/ Yonhap News AgencyView image in fullscreenL-R YouTubers Kim Jong-hwan, Choi Won-jin, Na Tae Soo and Kim Jong-hwan who have been keeping watch over the 3.5-metre shark trapped in a canal in Busan, South Korea.Composite: Supplied/ Yonhap News AgencySouth KoreaAfter dark, these YouTubers watch over an unlikely charge – a shark stuck in a South Korean canalA group of self-appointed guardians wearing hi-vis and carrying selfie sticks watch over the animal that has been trapped for a month, drawing more than 1.6 million visitorsRaphael Rashidin SeoulTue 20 Oct 2026 19.09 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 19.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInSouth Korea, they call themjagyeongdan, a word that sits somewhere between a vigilante group and aneighbourhood watch.Each night they don hi-vis vests, pick up their selfie sticks, and gather around the harbour in Busan to keep watch over an unlikely charge:a stranded sharkaffectionately known as Bukang-i.A month after the shark became trapped in a city canal, the group of self-appointed guardians are taking turns to protect her, patrolling the waterfront at night for visitors who might disturb the animal.Most are YouTubers who livestream the waterway, from where the shark has become a national celebrity. They stay up through the night, calling out anyone shining torches or lasers into the water. Some of their videos have been watched hundreds of thousands of times.View image in fullscreenVisitors watch the shark trapped in a waterway in the south-eastern port city of Busan.Photograph: Jung Yeon-Je/AFP/Getty Images“They bring fishing lamps, or the kind of lights people use at a campsite,” saysChoi Won-jin, one of the shark’s protectors. He arrives as the lights go out along the canal and waits for the offenders Koreans online call “lantern villains”.The shark has been marooned in the canal since 18 September. Named after Bukhang, the Korean name for the city’s North Port, and about 3 metres long, the female dusky shark is one of a species classed as endangered worldwide. More than 1.6 million visitors have come to see her, the city says, at a park that used to draw about 2,000 people on a busy Saturday.Authorities have twice tried to guide her back out to sea and a third attempt is due to take place on Wednesday afternoon.For now though, the shark remains in the canal, drawing crowds by day and leaving a handful of men to keep watch after dark. They patrol the canal’s park to check everything’s in order, eat snacks as the night goes by, and share their grievances on air about the behaviour they witness.“We’re ordinary members of the public,” says Choi, who has had a YouTubechannel for ten years and covers trending issues in South Korea.“So we have no choice but to put it nicely, and get them to understand as best we can.”“Don’t, please don’t switch the torch on,” says one of them, a YouTuber who lives nearby and goes by the nameNa Tae-soo. Most people comply, he says. “The animal thrashes about at night because of the torches, and it’s dangerous.”View image in fullscreenCrowds flock to the waterfront park in Busan to see the shark.Photograph: YONHAP/EPAHis footagehas captured the shark twisting sharply away from a beam of light at 2am and striking the side of the canal. The national institute of fisheries science later confirmed an abrasion on her snout and said a visitor’s torch likely startled the shark into injury.Korean media report that 105 officials from seven agencies watch over her, with a team on standby to reach the water within three minutes. Choi disputes this, saying that after dark it is almost up to him and the others.The waterfront is closed to the public from midnight until five in the morning, a restriction the YouTubers say is impossible to enforce across a park that size. One night, livestreaming from the walkway, Choi filmed a man tipping food waste into the water.Nobody has seen her feed, though experts say that feeding can happen in an instant and sharks her size need not eat often.Further attempts to free the shark have been paused on the grounds that more force would distress her.Cooler water might see her move on. Dusky sharks prefer water between 18C and 26C, the fisheries institute says. Experts put 15C as the point below which her physiological functions would start to decline, and about 11C as the point at which survival becomes precarious. Busan city officials expect the canal to reach that temperature after the middle of November.View image in fullscreenThis aerial photo taken on 29 September shows the South Korean Coast Guard boats spraying water in an attempt to guide the shark back to the sea.Photograph: YONHAP/AFP/Getty ImagesThe fisheries institute recorded 46 large sharks off the east coast in the first half of this year, nearly four times as many as a year earlier, which it attributes to warmer seas and more of the fish sharks feed on.The affection for Bukang-i has meanwhile become an industry, with a commemorative soju, a baseball mascot in a shark cape and an honorary city ambassadorship, and nearby shops reporting a surge in sales. South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, visited the canal in mid-October.The shark’s guardians thinks she should be forced out. Choi says the city should protect her where she is until she leaves of her own accord.Kim Jong-hwan, who runs a small business, keeps watch by day as well and has livestreamed her almost every day.“I went to pass on information [to my followers], and after that I started observing her”, he says. “Watching her over time, with the water pumps being fired and then the nets, I came to find those things being done to her objectionable. So we ended up cheering her on.”“She’s just an animal, and she came in by her own choice,” Kim says.“If it gets cold, if there’s no food, if the water doesn’t suit her, she’ll leave by herself. I’d like her to just be left alone, to rest there comfortably until then, and go.”Explore more on these topicsSouth KoreaWildlifeSharksAnimalsAsia PacificfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Too big to not fail’: Google outage exposes UK reliance on a handful of cloud providers | Datacentres - UK | The Guardian
description: Our dependence on internet services of a few key tech companies leaves us vulnerable to cloud failures, bugs and more, experts say
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Our dependence on internet services of a few key tech companies leaves us vulnerable to cloud failures, bugs and more, experts say
Content: A Google technician diagnoses an overheated CPU at a datacentre in Dalles, Oregon.Photograph: Google Handout/EPAView image in fullscreenA Google technician diagnoses an overheated CPU at a datacentre in Dalles, Oregon.Photograph: Google Handout/EPADatacentres - UK‘Too big to not fail’: Google outage exposes UK reliance on a handful of cloud providersOur dependence on internet services of a few key tech companies leaves us vulnerable to cloud failures, bugs and more, experts sayAisha DownTue 20 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt happened again. Apower outage hit a datacentre in London, and things cascaded from there: multiple banking services faltered, court hearings were put on hold and patients reported temporary glitches on the NHS app.The datacentre in question was in Google’s europe-west2-b zone, one of more than a dozen “zones” that the US search giant maintains in Europe to service its clients.The outages – which have affected, according to the website Downdetector, Royal Mail, Revolut, HSBC and Lloyds bank, among others, are so far not of the scale of a similar cascade this time last year, when Amazon Web Services went down for nearly half a day.That outage hit a far bigger node – Amazon’s us-east-1 – in a concentrated region of Virginia, which hosts the greatest density of datacentres on Earth. It saw cascading effects worldwide: taking out the Roblox game and Signal messaging app and causing smart mattresses worldwide to suddenly heat overnight and toast their occupants.It lasted about 15 hours.Today’s problems appeared to peak at about 9am, and by mid-afternoon were somewhat resolved, according to reports submitted to Downdetector. Because Google Cloud stores data and runs operations for a number of businesses, there were widespread knock-on effects – mostly confined to UK businesses.Revolut confirmed “a service disruption affecting multiple services”, but added that “all our customers’ money and data are safe”. Lloyd’s said its app was working, but “we understand some [people] are having issues with certain online services this morning”.HM Courts and Tribunal Service, which handles remote video hearings in courts across England and Wales, said it was “aware of an issue affecting Cloud Video Platform,” and was “working with our technology partners to restore service”.Like the far bigger outage last year, it’s a reminder of the physical infrastructure – often creaking and provisional – that underpins most of the virtual world.Michał “rysiek” Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert, said the outages were a reminder of the increasing concentration of the internet and vital services on the infrastructure of a few key companies – the “hyperscalers”.“Hyperscalers have become too big to not fail. But worse, they’ve become so deeply ingrained into the very fabric of our digital lives that switching away from them seems unimaginable.”The Guardianhas reportedthat British police keep vital data on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, despite being apparently aware that this exposes sensitive information to US government insiders, hostile foreign actors and outages like today’s. Up to 60% of the UK government’s infrastructure ishostedon cloud services – mostly Amazon, Microsoft and Google.“I am sure Google’s engineers are doing everything they can to mitigate them, but it is unreasonable to have a handful of gigantic companies whose outages time and again cause public institutions or large swaths of the digital economy to stop working en masse,” said Woźniak.Last year’s AWS outage was later revealed to have been caused not by a power outage, but by a bug inautomation software. A separate outage was caused by an AI tool that Amazon hadadoptedafter laying off tens of thousands of staff last autumn.Woźniak pointed at anannouncementthis year from Google indicating that it was also embracing AI, with 75% of all new code “now AI-generated and approved by engineers”.“One can only wonder how that affects the reliability and quality of Google’s services. Multiple large outages at another hyperscaler, AWS, a year ago have been linked to internal AI tooling.”A Google spokesperson said: “We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event. Services have been restored. We will update ourpublic status dashboardwith an analysis of the incident.”Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - UKGooglefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘They said: there’s this part … he’s an idiot!’ SNL UK’s Freddie Meredith on his unlikely route to comedy’s big leagues | TV comedy | The Guardian
description: A few months ago, he was pulling pints. How did he end up writing for Sharon Horgan, acting with Jeff Goldblum and storming the West End?
Author: Rachel Aroesti
Headline: A few months ago, he was pulling pints. How did he end up writing for Sharon Horgan, acting with Jeff Goldblum and storming the West End?
Content: ‘They were looking for an incel consultant’ … Freddie Meredith.Photograph: Rebecca Need-MenearView image in fullscreen‘They were looking for an incel consultant’ … Freddie Meredith.Photograph: Rebecca Need-MenearTV comedyInterview‘They said: there’s this part … he’s an idiot!’ SNL UK’s Freddie Meredith on his unlikely route to comedy’s big leaguesRachel AroestiA few months ago, he was pulling pints. How did he end up writing for Sharon Horgan, acting with Jeff Goldblum and storming the West End?Tue 20 Oct 2026 07.08 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 09.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUntil a few weeks ago, Freddie Meredith’s IMDb page was full of names like “Seb” and “George” and “Philip Noonan”. Lately, however, it’s started saying things like “Olly Murs” and “Liam Gallagher”. The characters that aren’t listed are even weirder: perhaps you’ve come across his recent turn as an east London mosquito? Or Jeff Goldblum’s troubled nephew? How about the tech billionaire tasked with introducing King Charles to a new AI assistant who looks exactly like Diana, Princess of Wales?It’s not just Meredith’s online CV that has had a radical overhaul. At the start of this summer, the 33-year-old was working in a bar, where he would sometimes get recognised by fans of Bafta-winning BBC sitcom Such Brave Girls, in which he played the protagonist’s ludicrously tenacious boyfriend. He mimics punters’ confusion at seeing a guy off the TV serving them: “What’s happened to you?!”Nothing had. Meredith was a jobbing actor saving up for his Edinburgh fringe debut,Need a Light?, an hour of character comedy about a lonely oddball desperately trying to make friends in a nightclub smoking area. But when August arrived, it looked as if the investment might not pay off: Meredith describes the first few performances as “crap. It was just not working.”View image in fullscreenHot ticket … Freddie Meredith.Photograph: Eva Pentel/Sky UKThings have improved immeasurably since then. With a few tweaks, the show found its groove and went on to become one of the festival’s hottest tickets, leading to a best newcomer nomination and an instantly sold-out and twice-extended London transfer. Then, a few days before his final show, his agent got a call from the producers ofSaturday Night LiveUK, “out of the blue”. They wanted to add him to the cast for its second series. Could he start on Tuesday?It’s early October when Meredith bemusedly recounts that “overwhelming” job offer. Yet sitting beside the empty SNL UK stage (he did offer to spend the interview with one leg faux-casually propped up on it, which is what his Need a Light? character would have done), he seems right at home. Between his impressions of Britpop stars (who may actually be Russian operatives), lascivious insects and Silicon Valley bros, he has undoubtedly hit the ground running.Still, it’s been a lot. Acting alongside guest host Jeff Goldblum on his first show was surreal enough to drown out the nerves, but the second instalment was scarier – partly because he’d also written two of the sketches, including a sublimefull-cast X Factor tribute(hence the Olly Murs impersonation).Meredith spent a chunk of last year auditioning for this British version of the US sketch institution, but ultimately wasn’t invited to join the original cast. He suspects it was because his material was too strange: he did his main audition in the guise of “a guy who was completely obsessed with Peaky Blinders” and was told his act might not translate to US audiences. In the end, he got the sense the producers “wanted to make sure the show had this real mainstream pull”.Yet when Meredith tuned in from home, he was surprised to see how “weird” SNL UK had ended up. Instead of courting viewers with broad comedy, the show has leaned into uncompromising Britishness and undiluted idiosyncrasy (see last season’s sketch reimaginingJools Holland as a demonwho appears if you don’t put your clocks forward). An SNL rep tells me producers “don’t provide comments on individual castings”, meaning there’s no official word on the reason behind Meredith’s last-minute addition (they didn’t tell him either), but to me he seems like the obvious missing ingredient in this comedy-nerd-friendly take on the format. Mainly because his speciality – disconcertingly awkward men who cleave to a quintessentially British cringe-comedy heritage (your David Brents, your Alan Partridges) – had no representative in the cast before.Meredith grew up in west London, 10 minutes down the road from the SNL UK studios. At school, he had no particular acting ambitions until he was cast in a sixth-form production of The Libertine, Stephen Jeffreys’ Restoration-set play about the Earl of Rochester (“crazy play to do at school”). The performance was “probably the most fun” he’d ever had, so he decided to apply to drama school. He got into Rada and signed with an agent upon graduating, but momentum soon stalled. Although Meredith is nowhere near as socially inept as his comedy creations, his vibe is clearly not swaggering alpha – yet in his early career he was being put up for the kind of roles that “let’s say, James Norton is doing now. That I’m never, ever going to get in a million years because it’s leading-man stuff. People didn’t really understand who I was.”View image in fullscreenAs Seb in Such Brave Girls.Photograph: Vishal Sharma/BBC/Various Artists LtdAt a loose end during lockdown, he decided to show them. A longtime comedy enthusiast – in his teens he’d seen Tim Key perform and “laughed so much; I’d never seen anything that really properly spoke to me before” – he began uploading left-field character studies to Instagram. The first was a spoof of a post-play Q&A with an actor who is so ill at ease that he seems to be having an out-of-body experience. Somehow, the clip “seemed to find its way through to my comedy heroes” including Jamie Demetriou, Lolly Adefope and the producer Rupert Majendie, who invited him to perform in east London soon after. Meredith was reluctant, but his girlfriend convinced him to grab the opportunity. He was immediately put on a bill with – what are the chances? – Key himself.That was in 2021; in the intervening years, Meredith has combined small roles in TV shows such as Big Boys and Andor, and eccentric live comedy (at one gig I attended a few years ago, he simply did a jig in a football kit and massively long trainers), with social media skits involving various odd men made even more uncanny via glitchy visual distortion and agonised micro-expressions.View image in fullscreenA deeply British antihero … Freddie Meredith in Need a Light? at the Edinburgh fringe.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThis year, he finally decided to write a full show for one of these characters: the sad-case protagonist of Need a Light? arrives at the club on his own in a shirt, tie, skinny jeans and pointy beige brogues, toting a reusable shopping bag and tirelessly attempting to strike up conversation with his fellow clubbers – AKA audience members – by giving out lighters, offering to provide assistance at their next house party or proving his macho status by telling them how he’d deal with the boy in Adolescence if he was the psychiatrist sent to interview him (swiftly and violently). It’s a zillennial update on the deeply British antihero you’re primed to root for and recoil from in equal measure.Working behind bars honed Meredith’s devastating observational comedy about uncomfortable men trying to fit in (“you get so much more material from these sorts of jobs than you ever would just sitting at home”). So did looking at people in the background of TV programmes. Need a Light? features a riff on the men placed at the rear of the Top Gear studio audience: people “trying their best to have a good time. There’s something really pure about that energy.” He has always been fascinated by the “guy behind the guy” – men on the peripheries – and recently started thinking more about the isolated, impressionable types who try to channel masculinity in misguided ways, such as the Peaky Blinders devotees or those who fall prey to manosphere influencers. Meredith personally finds the content “really funny and it’s kind of feeding this comedy vehicle, but if you don’t have the tools to not recognise that as being quite problematic, then you might just be like, wow, sick!”Luckily, Need a Light? ends on a wholesome high, as our genuinely sweet (if incredibly irritating) hero achieves the camaraderie he craves. Yet Meredith has also been mining the manosphere theme elsewhere. He was part of the writers’ room for Sharon Horgan’s new HBO dramedyYouth, drafted in specifically to flesh out the character of her teenage son – played by Cillian Murphy’s son Aran – who flirts with such ideology (“They were looking for an incel consultant,” he jokes). He also ended up getting a role written for him: a blundering intern at the literary agency where Horgan’s character works. “They were like: there’s this part, we’re just calling him Freddie. He’s a completeidiot.”‘Y’awright, our kid, yeh?’ … Meredith as Liam Gallagher on SNL UK.Which means that the week we speak, Meredith is on HBO, live on Sky and in residence at London’s Soho theatre. In the next couple of days, his intense schedule will involve writing and performing sketches with SNL UK guest host Danny Dyer by day, before travelling into town to perform Need a Light? in the evenings. On top of that, Meredith is still learning the SNL ropes: while the rest of the cast had six weeks to get up to speed before going into production, he’s having to catch up in real time. Not that he minds – in fact, he is relishing the manic pace of long-awaited success. “You spend so long not working as an actor,” he says. “There’s something to be said for doing it all.”Saturday Night Live UK is on Sky One and Now; Youth is on HBO Max. Freddie Meredith: Need a Light? is at Soho Theatre from 9 to 14 November and at Fairfield Social Club in Manchester on 19 November.Explore more on these topicsTV comedyTelevisionComedy (Culture)Saturday Night LiveEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Edinburgh festivalfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’ll keep doing this if people pay us!’ The cast of TV hit Ghosts on making a movie – and maybe a caveman spinoff | Comedy films | The Guardian
description: As the haunters of Button House hit the big screen with a plot about an escaped phantom, we hear how the team just missed each other too much – and why grunting Robin may get his own show
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: As the haunters of Button House hit the big screen with a plot about an escaped phantom, we hear how the team just missed each other too much – and why grunting Robin may get his own show
Content: ‘It was like being at a party’ … Mathew Baynton, Martha Howe-Douglas, Jim Howick and Ben Willbond in Ghosts: The Possession of Button House.Photograph: Mandozzi Photography/PAView image in fullscreen‘It was like being at a party’ … Mathew Baynton, Martha Howe-Douglas, Jim Howick and Ben Willbond in Ghosts: The Possession of Button House.Photograph: Mandozzi Photography/PAComedy films‘We’ll keep doing this if people pay us!’ The cast of TV hit Ghosts on making a movie – and maybe a caveman spinoffAs the haunters of Button House hit the big screen with a plot about an escaped phantom, we hear how the team just missed each other too much – and why grunting Robin may get his own showStuart HeritageTue 20 Oct 2026 10.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 11.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the final episode of Ghosts was aired in December 2023, the sitcom felt as if it had reached a definitive conclusion. The show’s central relationships, between Charlotte Ritchie’s Alison and the ghosts who haunt her tumbledown inherited manor house, were neatly tied up, as they encouraged her to sell the place to a hotel developer. It was a tearjerker of an episode for the millions of people who watched it, as well as for the cast and crew behind the scenes.“We had stopped the series with genuinely no intention of coming back,” explains the show’s co-creator Mathew Baynton, who also stars as the callow romantic poet Thomas. “We were all in tears on the last day of filming,” he says, now perched on the uncomfortable end of a chaise lounge in a London hotel suite.“I was so upset that it finished,” addsLolly Adefope, who plays the excitable Kitty, from the better structured end of the chaise. “It was like being at a party and you guys were leaving.”“It was a clear ending, and the guys felt like they had fully explored all of the characters,” says director Simon Hynd, “but I did notice a look of regret in some of their eyes.”All of which is to say that Ghosts is now back. Although the television series remains over, the story will continue in the new film Ghosts: The Possession of Button House. So the question is, who blinked first?“Alison Carpenter, our executive at Monumental, had started to say, ‘We could get the funding for a film if you guys want to do that,’” explains Baynton. “But we just batted it away.”“The fear was that you’d end up making a 90-minute episode of a TV show, and it would feel like, Please Sir! The Movie,” says co-creator and star Laurence Rickard, who plays both caveman Robin and decapitated nobleman Sir Humphrey Bone. “Which I love, by the way.”Eventually Carpenter convinced the show’s six creators and stars (the others being Simon Farnaby, Martha Howe-Douglas, Jim Howick and Ben Willbond, not present) to at least get into a room and discuss the prospect. “We all talked through what we didn’t want it to be, and what it sort of had to be to be a film,” explains Baynton. “That led us very quickly to the concept of possession, which would allow one of the ghosts to get out of the grounds.”double quotation markWhen Ghosts ended, it was the first time that we hadn’t done something together in 18 years“It was the fastest turnaround ever,” laughs Rickard. “We went in at 9:30am going ‘I mean, it’s nice to see everyone, but I think the answer is probably no’ – and then by 11 o’clock, we were going, ‘We have to do this.’”The resulting film is still very much Ghosts, with its unique mix of sharp absurdity (at one point a Ouija board spells out ‘Leave’ to make a point about Brexit) and near-debilitating emotional notes (you may never again look at a scotch egg without crying). But it is undoubtedly a movie, with stakes and a ticking clock and big set pieces.“The possession idea immediately invites a body swap sort of thing, which reminded us of Big,” says Baynton. “Then we were talking about, what if the possession doesn’t last and his spirit is fading, which reminded us of Back to the Future. The group of kids breaking into the house felt like The Goonies. All our touchstones for this were films we loved in our youth.”The film is an astonishing feat, not just because of its quick turnaround – Hynd only learned of the film late last year – but because every member of its ensemble has a vital part to play in the plot.“With the series, we got so used to writing multi-thread narratives,” explains Baynton. “In any episode, the actual stories are told in two or three brief moments, so that had become our mode of writing anyway.”View image in fullscreen‘I was the Gen Z member of the cast’ … Lolly Adefope in the film.Photograph: Mandozzi Photography/PAThis approach meant that, despite no longer living in Button House, Alison and her husband Mike, played by Kiell Smith-Bynoe, find themselves swept up in the action. Smith-Bynoe seems especially pleased with his arc. “Mike gets to prove himself in this one,” he explains, “which felt good after spending a few years not getting to do that.”Smith-Bynoe has arguably always had the hardest acting job on Ghosts, as Mike is often the only person on screen who isn’t a ghost and can’t interact with them. This challenge was doubled for the film’s climax when, without giving too much away, a roomful of characters old and new flit in and out of tangibility. “It took me a minute,” he says. “I had to keep asking Simon who I was supposed to be able to see.”Much of the cast this time around are new, in the form of the aforementioned kids. It takes a lot to steal a film out from underneath a cast as talented as this, but Scott Ellis Watson, who played the young John Davidson in I Swear, is phenomenal here, largely because he spends a lot of time doing a bang-on impersonation of a dead middle-aged Tory MP.The new additions were something that Adefope in particular appreciated. “It was so fun having Scott around,” she says. “I was sort of the Gen Z member of the cast, so we talked a lot about memes and TikTok.”“You were the child whisperer, weren’t you?” says Rickard.“Yes, exactly. I was translating for you,” she smiles back.With the show, the six creators were able to break off and write individual episodes in various permutations of their troupe. But the film is credited to all six of them. Was that a hard thing to accomplish? “It was just a process of who was around at what time,” says Baynton. “So sometimes it was two of us, sometimes three or four. What is lovely about that is that the person who’s absent for a little period of time then becomes your fresh pair of eyes when they return. You get to a point at times where all you can see is A or B and both of them are problematic, but then someone who’s been away for a couple of weeks comes in and goes, ‘Well, what about C?’ And you go, ‘Oh yeah!’”A lot of this is simply muscle memory. The Ghosts team are now veterans, having met while making theHorrible HistoriesTV show almost two decades ago, and continued with the sitcomYonderlandand the 2015 Shakespeare comedy film Bill. It’s hard to think of any writing and performing group this large who have managed to stay intact for so long. Even Monty Python ran out of films and shows in less time, their work together now largely consisting of tweeting hatred at each other.View image in fullscreenWhat a pickle … Baynton and Howick in the Shakespeare comedy Bill (2015).Photograph: Bbc Films/Allstar“Oh, we’ve got that phase to look forward to,” laughs Rickard. “I’ve been drafting some of that stuff.”Rickard is the one who seems to have most keenly felt the absence of Ghosts: “The first year after the series stopped was the first time that we hadn’t done something together in 18 years.” You get the sense that this film exists in part because its creators missed hanging out with each other.So why stop the party now?
