Will there be anything else to look forward to from the gang? “There isn’t something secretly being developed,” insists Baynton. “But we’ve always had the same feeling, which is that we love working together and we’ll keep doing it if people will pay us to do it.”Does that mean more Ghosts films? That prompts a slightly more uneasy response. “This does sort of feel like, you know, the big swan song,” replies Rickard.“Yes, but we said that before, so no one can take our word for it,” adds Baynton. “But there’s no intention. Also, ghosts can’t age, and I’m rapidly getting way too old to play Thomas.”“But Robin could definitely have a spinoff, and that wouldn’t be a problem,” cracks Rickard, noting that he’s looking more and more like a long-dead caveman with every passing year. “It would be great. My makeup call would get shaved right down.”Ghosts: The Possession of Button House is in cinemas on Friday 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsComedy filmsTV comedyTelevisionLolly AdefopefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tom Cruise’s Digger is a commercial flop – but also the perfect climate film for our time | Digger | The Guardian
description: The movie follows Digger Rockwell, whose drilling triggers a vast iceberg that’s five times the size of Washington DC
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: The movie follows Digger Rockwell, whose drilling triggers a vast iceberg that’s five times the size of Washington DC
Content: Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell in a scene from Digger.Photograph: Courtesy of Warner Bros Pictures/Warner Bros Pictures/APView image in fullscreenTom Cruise as Digger Rockwell in a scene from Digger.Photograph: Courtesy of Warner Bros Pictures/Warner Bros Pictures/APDiggerAnalysisTom Cruise’s Digger is a commercial flop – but also the perfect climate film for our timeOliver MilmanThe movie follows Digger Rockwell, whose drilling triggers a vast iceberg that’s five times the size of Washington DCTue 20 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 10.15 EDTShareDigger, the newAlejandro González Iñárritufilm, is bombastic, misanthropic and an epic, critically savaged flop. It is also the near-perfect climate change film for our era.Digger Rockwell, the eponymous protagonist played byTom Cruise, is a bluntly caricatured Texas oilman blase about the environmental ruin of his drilling, even as it triggers a disastrous splitting of the Arctic ice sheet. This causes a vast iceberg, five times the size of Washington DC, to barrel towards Europe and threaten a devastating tsunami.Much like this impending disaster and the real-world retreat of glaciers and coral reefs, though, the mere act of watchingDiggerhas become a forlorn race against time. The box office failure has been resounding, and Digger’s time on the big screen has been brief.Facing a predicted $245m loss– the lavishly made film took $8m in its first weekend in the US before dropping 60% for its second – Digger wasyankedfrom more than 2,500 theatres across the US ahead of its third week. Scrambling to find a single cinema showing Digger, I had to resort to spending a Thursday lunchtime with just two other ticket-buying patrons at a major Manhattan venue.The critical opprobrium and dismal ticket sales shouldn’t be a shock. Fans of Cruise are used to mass appeal movies of clean-cut heroism, not him aged, balding and dressed in a Stetson and cowboy boots and little else as he howls a confected Texan drawl in a dark climate satire.The Digger disaster: what an epic movie flop means for Tom Cruise and HollywoodRead moreThe film also,as critics have pointed out, strays into a “glib and overblown” depiction of elite cowardice and cynicism when it comes to the climate crisis.View image in fullscreenTom Cruise as Digger Rockwell in Digger, a Warner Bros Pictures release.Photograph: Courtesy of Warner Bros. PicturesThere are heavy-handed scenes of Digger eating endangered tuna in front of his aghast chief scientist Nirav Ganesh (a harried Riz Ahmed) and of sneering indifference from a US president (played dyspeptically by John Goodman) when confronted by the looming catastrophe.“You know what, this isn’t my problem,” the president says when confronted with ecological and societal doom. A farcically bellicose, Pete Hegseth-like general dismisses the iceberg as a snow cone and advises the president to “blow that frozen cunt up” with nuclear weapons.At one point, Digger and Ganesh sit in a room gazing at flickering flames, as if they are in hell. It’s not a cheery message, but it is a franker one than the other, scarce attempts to depict the climate crisis on screen. Perhaps we are actually in hell, the movie suggests, and the evil oil tycoons aren’t the only ones to blame for that.It is cathartic to see Ganesh berate Digger for being guilty of the “most heinous act of all time” by knowing, as oil companiesdid in reality for decades, of the consequences of global heating but then fatally obscuring this knowledge in order to rake in more cash. But Digger goes further than just unmasking a single villain.Don’t Look Up, the 2021 climate allegory, frames the problem as frantic scientists being ignored as an asteroid heads towards Earth. Digger’s message is a more sinister but uncomfortably accurate one – that we all know of the cataclysm we are inflicting upon current and future generations but have largely acquiesced to it.“Let’s cut the bullshit, you love oil,” as Digger tells enraged European lawmakers, all dressed in muted beige and grey, in a lengthy rant. “You want to bask in your unsustainable lives.”The oil companies may haveliedandbought offpoliticians, but, in the wealthy west at least, we have all been complicit by failing to punish leaders for this and we remain willing customers for the poison of fossil fuels, even as theychoke,drownandfryus.Any sort of lifestyle change – eating lessmeat, flyingless, switching to a car that doesn’t have a petrol pump on hand at eachcorner– is too much hassle for most of us even as we face the biggest threat to menace humanity. There are always, as Digger points out to the Eurocrats, phones to be charged, TikToks to watch. In holding up a mirror to this, Digger might not be the climate film we want. But it may be the one we need.It’s striking that the possible end of a habitable planet has spawned comparatively little art with only vague nods, if at all, to our culpability. Among movies, there was Waterworld, another flop where Kevin Costner had to drink his own urine on a world flooded by the melted ice caps, and The Day After Tomorrow, where the melting ice causes a storm that plunges society into a new ice age.View image in fullscreenIn Waterworld, the polar ice caps have melted and the Earth is covered by water. The remaining people travel the seas in search of survival.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/AlamyMusically, the best of a meagre bunch is perhaps Smash Mouth’s 1999 hitsongAll Star which includes a lament of thinning ice and the line “my world’s on fire, how ‘bout yours?” The climate crisis may seem too overwhelming and gloomy to depict, but also, maybe we have so closeted and normalized our guilt that it feels shameful to bring it out into the light to be examined in public.Digger forces us to not look away, even as we squirm at what we’ve done. “This film is a disaster movie,” Iñárritu hassaid. “But the disaster is us.”The film is too nihilistic about our lack of response – Digger condemns clean energy as useless and his half-sister Emma (played by a squandered Sandra Hüller) makes endeavors in renewables that are dismissively mocked. Yet in real life the industry isgrowing explosively. We have everything we need to confront the climate crisis, after all, bar the necessary willpower.Digger won’t be the last climate film. Later this year, A Statement, a dramatization of a real-life 1980 meeting of experts on what to do about global warming starring Paul Rudd and Paul Giamatti, will be released.But Digger was the last Warner Bros’s theatrical release before it waspurchasedby Paramount Skydance and the Ellisons. Its commercial failure, along with theideological leaningsof the movie studio overlords, may deter further attempts to give us unvarnished tales of the climate crisis. That would be a huge, iceberg-sized mistake.Explore more on these topicsDiggerTom CruiseFilm criticismClimate crisisFossil fuelsAlejandro González IñárrituOilanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Could this be a Deep Blue moment for the cryptic crossword? | Puzzles | The Guardian
description: A computer program has finally outdone humans at solving cryptic crosswords. Plus, more from around the puzzleverse
Author: Alan Evans
Headline: A computer program has finally outdone humans at solving cryptic crosswords. Plus, more from around the puzzleverse
Content: Garry Kasparov playing Deep Blue at chess in 1997.Photograph: Stan Honda/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGarry Kasparov playing Deep Blue at chess in 1997.Photograph: Stan Honda/AFP/Getty ImagesCluesletterPuzzlesCould this be a Deep Blue moment for the cryptic crossword?A computer program has finally outdone humans at solving cryptic crosswords. Plus, more from around the puzzleverseDon’t get Cluesletter, our weekly puzzles newsletter, delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereAlan EvansTue 20 Oct 2026 11.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 11.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the IBM supercomputer Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov at chess in 1997, it was an early victory for artificial intelligence over the human mind, and the culmination of decades of attempts. Almost 30 years later, a computer program has finally outdone humans at solving cryptic crosswords.Earlier this month, a model called Darmok solved the final puzzle of the Times’s annual cryptic crossword competition about three minutes faster than Liam Hughes, 29, whobecame the contest’s youngest (human) winner.After Deep Blue’s victory, the New York Times’s puzzle editor, Will Shortz,set engineers a challenge. “Is the computer going to be able to solve the clues involving puns and wordplay? I don’t think so,” he wrote. “In a much more wide-ranging and, frankly, complex game like crosswords, we humans still rate just fine.”Less than a decade later, a computer named WebCrowbeat 75 human crosswordersat an AI conference, and by 2021 a program named Dr Fill“won” the American crossword puzzle tournament, the most prestigious of its type for American-style crosswords, which rely on a combination of general knowledge, allusion and double meanings.But cryptics are much trickier, and as recently as 2024 my colleagueAlan Connor was asking: “Will the cryptic crossword remain the last thing AI can’t conquer?”Dr Sid Chatterjee, a computer scientist at the University of Texas in Austin, thought not, and in 2025 set out to prove it. He began work on Darmok, named aftera Star Trek episodein which the crew attempt to converse with a species that speaks only in allegories – an experience akin to solving a cryptic.View image in fullscreenSid Chatterjee and Darmok after solving the final puzzle in the Times’s cryptic crossword championship.Darmok’s first tilt at the Times championship ended in failure when it gave up on the final puzzle after 18 minutes. Its triumph this year was partly as a result of successfully solving a clue that tripped up three of the five finalists, including 14-time champion Mark Goodliffe:double quotation markWolf trap missing its lowest crosspiece? (5)”The letters filled in as part of other clues gave the pattern S_A_F. Both SCARF and SNARF mean “to eat greedily” (synonyms for “wolf”) but the rest of the wordplay relied on a visual element.“Trap” indicates the synonym “SNARE”, and when the bottom line of the E is removed – “missing its lowest crosspiece” – it becomes an F, making SNARF the answer.While one might expect visual clues like these to be more difficult for an AI, Chatterjee said he couldn’t detect a pattern in the types of clues Darmok struggles most with. It does find puzzles by John Henderson (known to Guardian readers asEnigmatist) harder than most, though.If you’d like to challenge yourself against Darmok, it solvedthis Fed crosswordfrom last week in four minutes and 10 seconds. Good luck.Darmok is based on four AI models: Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Fable 5, GPT-5 and GPT-6 Astra. The solving is primarily done by the first two, with the others joining in if needed. Chatterjee attributed Darmok’s improvement this year to the extra power behind these frontier models, as well as some of his refinements, such as making Darmok wait until it had attempted all the clues before inserting answers.The next frontier for AI and cryptic crosswords – setting a satisfying puzzle – will be an even bigger jump. “It is a very, very difficult problem because you have got to make a sentence that parses both in normal English and in cryptic English smoothly, and those two grammars are very, very different,” said Chatterjee. “If [beating humans at cryptic crosswords] was the Mount Everest challenge, I call this next one the Olympus Mons challenge.”Clue of the weekdouble quotation markProportion of inspiration and perspiration? It’s roughly 45% and 42% (5)FromBluebird in the Independent. The answer, RATIO, is hidden in the clue twice, making up five of the 11 letters in “inspiration” – or roughly 45% – and five of the 12 letters in “perspiration” – roughly 42%.Readers’ cluing contestCongratulations toTony Kelly (Montano)for winning this week’s competition with his clue for the wordDEBUT:double quotation markKick-off leads to decisive early goal for PSG (5)Kick-off is the definition. “Leads to” indicates the first letters of decisive and early, ie DE, and “goal for PSG” refers to the football team Paris Saint-Germain, indicating BUT, the French word for goal.This week, as a nod to the word wrongly identified by solvers in the Times championship, we’d like you to come up with a clue for the wordSCARF. title: Devil Woman: why does gen Z suddenly love Cliff Richard? | Cliff Richard | The Guardian
description: His 1970s banger is climbing up the streaming charts, with some young listeners tracking it down on vinyl. How did he become the voice of youth, again, aged 86?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: His 1970s banger is climbing up the streaming charts, with some young listeners tracking it down on vinyl. How did he become the voice of youth, again, aged 86?
Content: Like he never went away … Cliff Richard.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreenLike he never went away … Cliff Richard.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyPass notesCliff RichardDevil Woman: why does gen Z suddenly love Cliff Richard?His 1970s banger is climbing up the streaming charts, with some young listeners tracking it down on vinyl. How did he become the voice of youth, again, aged 86?Tue 20 Oct 2026 09.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Devil Woman.Age:50.Popularity:Never bigger.DevilWoman, the song by SirCliff Richard?That’s right, his most famous song.Well now, that’s hardly fair. Sir Cliffhas been aniconsince the birth ofpopularmusic.Yes, that’s true. His 68-year-old song Move It was potentially the first British rock’n’roll record.He’s had so manyNo 1s, too.True. Living Doll in the 50s, Summer Holiday and The Young Ones in the 60s, We Don’t Talk Any More in the 70s, Mistletoe and Wine in the 80s, The Millennium Prayer in the 90s.And what number didDevilWoman get to?No 9.So it’s far from his mostfamoussong,then?I rebut this. In terms of pure cultural cut-through, Devil Woman represents the pinnacle of Sir Cliff’s career.Cultural cut-through how?The song formed the centrepiece of the video game trailerGrand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look, which has gained 32m views on YouTube since it launched last month.Oh wow. What footage did it soundtrack?Variously: scuba diving, basketball, kayaking, stripping, VR pornography, kidnapping and armed robbery.And how does thefamouslyChristianSir Cliff feel about his song being used for such depravity?He may be stuffing his ears with money as we speak.Outrageous.Yes, but also extremely cool. The song fits the game perfectly. It’s corny and sleazy in equal measure, and as a result people are falling for it again.So this is why it’swildlypopular?Exactly. Streams on Spotify are up 325%, and gen Z is making a big thing of tracking it down on vinyl. The success is being compared to when Kate Bush’s Running Up That Hill surged back up the charts after being featured on Stranger Things.This tends to happen a lot, doesn’t it?In the streaming age, where all music is permanently accessible, yes. Even Murder on the Dancefloor got a bump after it soundtracked Barry Keoghan’s genitals at the end of Saltburn.Well, this is great.It is. Not only is the Devil Woman resurgence a timely validation for a song about being poisoned by a woman who sometimes transforms into a cat, but for Sir Cliff as a whole.How so?The man is 86 years old. It’s only natural that his career should wane a little as he ages. Lately he’s become more famous for his novelty calendars than his music, so this resets the clock a little.How does he plan to capitalise upon this hip resurgence?He’s about to release a reggae version of The Lord is My Shepherd.Sorry I asked.Yeah, me too.Do say:“Cliff Richard is cool again.”Don’t say:“Quick, hide the video where herollerskates around a Milton Keynes shopping centre.”Explore more on these topicsCliff RichardPass notesGrand Theft AutoGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The last bastion is gone’: the US right idolised Orbán’s Hungary. Can they recover now he has fallen? | Hungary | The Guardian
description: The long read: Over the past decade, Hungary has been a beacon for the ‘postliberal’ right, with pro-Trump thinkers making regular pilgrimages to Budapest. Now Orbán is gone, how will the movement adapt?
Author: Brian Goodman
Headline: The long read: Over the past decade, Hungary has been a beacon for the ‘postliberal’ right, with pro-Trump thinkers making regular pilgrimages to Budapest. Now Orbán is gone, how will the movement adapt?
Content: The Lónyay–Hatvany-villa, headquarters of the Danube Institute, in Budapest.Illustration: John KaziorView image in fullscreenThe Lónyay–Hatvany-villa, headquarters of the Danube Institute, in Budapest.Illustration: John KaziorThe long readHungary‘The last bastion is gone’: the US right idolised Orbán’s Hungary. Can they recover now he has fallen?Over the past decade, Hungary has been a beacon for the ‘postliberal’ right, with pro-Trump thinkers making regular pilgrimages to Budapest. Now Orbán is gone, how will the movement adapt?A longer version of this article first appeared inThe DriftBrian GoodmanTue 20 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 05.47 EDTShareEspresso Embassy, a third-wave coffee shop in Budapest’s diplomatic and governmental quarter, is where visiting reporters and academics come to talk politics. On the way in for my morning coffee on 18 March, I passed a poster for Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz party that had been vandalised with a marker pen: “the safe choice” had become “the certain way to get fucked”. From across the cafe, I spotted the American journalist and historian Anne Applebaum locked in conversation, possibly with a source. I heard someone exclaim: “Just like Mussolini!” It was election season in Hungary.It was also a couple of days beforeCpac Hungary, a satellite event of the US-based conservative conference. As members of the international right arrived in town, the notorious Orbánist thinktank known as the Danube Institute was hosting an event called On Censorship, Tolerance, the Left and God. The official line would be: bad, good, bad, good.After dark, I walked along the walls of Buda castle and past the Jesuit stairs to the institute. The featured speakers were Dave Rubin, an American podcaster from the so-called “intellectual dark web”, and Eva Vlaardingerbroek, a Dutch provocateur who claimed the title “shieldmaiden of the far right” on her X profile. “You don’t realise how good you have it” inHungary, Rubin said. “So many things are wrong across the west.” After the panel, an American man introduced himself to me and asked how long I’d been in Budapest. Had I ever considered dual citizenship? If so, he could help. “My friends,” he said, “call me the Harriet Tubman of white people.”For the previous few months, I’d been hanging around the Danube Institute and other state-subsidised gathering places, trying to pass as yet another member of the rightwing intelligentsia making his pilgrimage to Budapest. Founded in 2013 with state funds redirected by the Orbán government, the institute had become known as the central hub in the emerging “postliberal” movement, a loose coalition of heterodox conservative thinkers frequently associated with the idiosyncratic Americanblogger and self-styled Christian dissident Rod Dreher. During Dreher’s first fellowship term at the Danube Institute in 2021, he helped arrangeTucker Carlson’s weeklong press junketin Hungary, which featured a fawning Fox News interview with Orbán. Since then, liberal publications such as the New York Times, the New Yorker and the Atlantic have dispatched journalists to grill Dreher about the institute and his relationship to Orbán’s autocratic regime. This produced a series of breathless reports that showcased the small thinktank as a clearinghouse for dangerous illiberal ideas. As Applebaum wrote in her bookTwilight of Democracy: “The Danube Institute exists, in practice, to make the Hungarian government presentable to the outside world.”In Applebaum’s view, the Orbán regime had “created a political system in which no opposition party could possibly win”, and the foreign intellectuals at the Danube Institute were either cynical propagandists or naive stooges for Orbán’s anti-democratic project. But soon, Orbán would be out of power, ousted in alandslide election in April, and in June the new Hungarian parliament would pass a constitutional amendment dismantling the patronage system that funds the Danube Institute, as well asMCC Brussels, a training ground for Fidesz elites.It was end times for the postliberals in Budapest, even if they didn’t know it yet. What will survive the demise of the so-called Budapest scene is a fractured group of rightwing thinkers who, whatever their fate in Hungary, will continue to hold a frightening level of influence over US political culture. If they were ever Orbán’s puppets, they aren’t any more. But reducing them to the unthinking servants of one particular strongman has made it more difficult to confront the real threat of postliberal ideas – or the crisis to which they are responding.Officially, I was in Budapest to write a book about the western intellectuals who travelled to Hungary to meet the dissident opposition during the final years of the communist era. My family and I were guests of the Institute for Advanced Study, which had once been called the Collegium Budapest before it was effectively closed by the Orbán government in 2011. Now reopened, it was part of the rump of Central European University that still remained in Hungary. The rest of the institution was forced to move to Vienna during a prolonged campaign against George Soros and Hungary’s independent civil society.At the start of this year, I made it my half-ironic mission to infiltrate the Danube Institute. I really did want to see what was actually going on inside this thinktank that had become known as the headquarters of the international postliberal project. Reaching it was not hard. It is housed in the Lónyay-Hatvany Villa, a refurbished building that had briefly served as an SS casino during the second world war and now housed a high-end restaurant on its main floor. One evening, I climbed a steep staircase dimly lit by iron sconces, the yellow light reflecting off wet stone, until I reached a narrow passage closed in by two high walls. Up ahead, I noticed a doorway marked only by a floor lamp on a small red carpet. I hesitated, then entered.View image in fullscreenPéter Magyar celebrates his Tisza party’s victory in the Hungarian general election in April.Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/ShutterstockStraight in front of me was a dining room with a commanding view of the Danube. I snapped a few photos with my phone until I heard someone behind me on the stairs. I hurried into the basement annexe and reached a check-in table. I gave a young assistant my name, and she pointed towards a coat check. It turned out that infiltrating the Danube Institute just required online registration.In the brightly lit basement, a shelf offered complimentary issues of glossy rightwing journals such as The European Conservative and Hungarian Review. I picked up a copy of the then state-subsidised Hungarian Conservative with a painting by Tivadar Csontváry Kosztka on the cover; its title was Mysterious Island.The other guests were beginning to arrive, and I was immediately worried I’d been misled by a New Yorker piece on Dreher, in whichhe told a journalistthat “the Danube Institute had a casual dress code” and he “could usually leave the suits at the apartment” even when meeting with ministers from Orbán’s Fidesz party. But here was a parade of male intellectual fashion: ribbed turtlenecks; crocheted ties and silk cravats; blazers of tweed, linen and corduroy. I looked down at my rumpled blazer – the only one I own – and felt underdressed.In the months to come, I would jot down scraps of overheard conversation. Much of it was unsurprising, especially for anyone who had spent time on X: “We’re going to interrogate him with truth serum”, “No one is linking except Tucker”, “Hitler would have gone broke on her OnlyFans”, “Do you have a contact for Vance?”All the knowing gossip and memes were part of a game of one-upmanship among intellectuals who styled themselves as insiders. Still, there was something jarring about seeing this very online culture in the flesh. Most of the names they dropped were exactly the ones you’d expect. What did catch me off guard was how often I also heard them mention the names of the liberal journalists who had alerted me to the existence of the Danube Institute in the first place. If Hungary looms large for people like Applebaum, she, in turn, haunts the postliberal imagination; these guys all clearly read the Atlantic.“Anne Applebaum, I think she’s great,” I overheard one of the institute’s fellows wisecrack at the bar. “I really respect her.” At the very first event I attended, a debate on How Non-Liberal Regimes Rule Through the Good Life, the main speaker referred to Applebaum as “persona non grata” at the Danube Institute. The postliberal economist Philip Pilkington responded: “I do find the descent into Applebaumism hilarious.”Pilkington was referring to Applebaum’s stubborn tendency to divide the world between liberal democracies and illiberal autocracies, between virtuous and corrupt elites. This “moral purity test” was not only hypocritical, he pointed out, it was intellectually unserious. According to Pilkington, it prevented liberal elites from accurately seeing themselves. The “crude” Applebaum analysis, he said, doesn’t “have a good explanation of why liberalism is falling apart”.Part of the appeal of postliberalism is that it does provide an account of why it feels as though everything is falling apart: a liberal world order could never have turned out otherwise. At least this is Pilkington’s view, as expressed in his 2025 book, The Collapse of Global Liberalism. Born in Ireland, Pilkington is a millennial former leftist who took a job in finance and then moved to Hungary, where until June he was employed at the Danube Institute and the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, then another Fidesz-aligned thinktank. For him, “liberalism is, in the final analysis, a dark and uncivilised philosophy of life that will destroy any civilisation it touches”.Equally comfortable making sweeping claims about “Marxian historical materialism” and offering hot takes about yoga pants as a symptom of civilisational decline, Pilkington argues that the drive to demolish all hierarchies is “self-undermining” and “self-destructive”: “The reality is that equality does not exist in most spheres.” Liberal capitalism, according to this line of thought, only ever appeared stable because it was built on a foundation of pre-liberal hierarchical structures, such as the church, family and classical legal traditions. Now it has become a victim of its own self-undermining success. As Pilkington puts it, “liberal capitalism” became “far too aggressive in its promotion of work and consumption and is undermining the building blocks on which the stability of society rests”, namely “the family and the ability to reproduce the species”.The postliberal movement’s foundational text is 2018’s Why Liberalism Failed by the philosopher Patrick Deneen, another visitor to the Danube Institute. The title of Deneen’s book captures the shared premise of all postliberal thought: that the historical period in which western societies were governed by a “regime of liberalism”, as he put it elsewhere, has already reached a calamitous end. Whether that period began in 1989 with the fall of communist regimes in central and eastern Europe or 500 years ago with the Protestant reformation remains a matter of some obfuscation.For postliberals, the collapse of liberalism was an inevitable outgrowth of its first principles: its anti-hierarchical commitment to formal equality, its faith in human progress and, above all, its emphasis on individual autonomy. In practice, Deneen argues, these values actually produced extreme economic inequality, spiritual debasement and a profound sense of unfreedom. “Liberalism has failed,” he writes, “not because it fell short, but because it was true to itself.”View image in fullscreenArgentina’s president, Javier Milei, on stage at Cpac Hungary in March.Photograph: Gergely Besenyei/AFP/Getty ImagesAt least initially, the postliberals seemed more solicitous of the populist masses than of the Republican old guard: they supported Donald Trump, who was then styling himself as a champion for a new working-class coalition against the elite establishment. Deneen and other postliberals claimed their goal was to transcend the toxic left-right divide in US politics by positioning themselves as both allies of social democracy and enemies of corporate progressivism. Indeed, they insisted the only way to defeat the disastrous post-cold war alliance between neoliberal economics and neoconservative foreign policy was through a novel fusion of social-conservative values and left economic ideas.After postliberalism relocated to Hungary it became more true to itself. The year after its publication, Why Liberalism Failedwas translated into Hungarian, and Deneen met Orbán in Budapest. In the years after 2018, the Danube Institute and other regime-supported institutions hosted nearly every major American postliberal intellectual in Budapest. Many are now familiar figures on the so-called New Right. To use a basketball analogy, if Deneen was the philosopher-coach and Dreher was the veteran point guard on this postliberal squad, the rest of the starting five might include the Catholic integralist Adrian Vermeule; the national conservative Yoram Hazony; the censorious culture warrior Christopher Rufo; and the shapeshifting opinion columnist, UnHerd editor and Compactmagazine cofounder Sohrab Ahmari, with the political theorist Gladden Pappin coming in off the bench.Back in the US, Pappin had been a junior academic before he began writing blog posts for theJournal of American Greatnessunder the pen name Manlius Capitolinus. By now, all of Pappin’s posts as Manlius Capitolinus have been taken down, but he subsequently published a series of revealing essays under his own name in another journal. In Toward a Party of the State, from 2019, Pappinarguedthat the “liberal conservatism” of the old Republican establishment had failed precisely because it became a handmaid to the “governing ideology of neoliberalism”, a form of statecraft without a moral vision of the good life.Drawing on left thinkers such asNancy Fraser, Pappin suggested that neoliberalism maintained its fragile legitimacy by “redefining itself as progressive”, creating an unholy alliance between pro-corporate and socially liberal constituencies. To overcome the “neoliberal ideological hegemony”, according to this theory, we need a national unity government with a strong, activist party-state led by intellectuals, among them, presumably, Pappin himself.At the time, postliberals could still squint and see Trump as a vessel for this project. After Trump’s defeat in 2020, Pappin visited Budapest for the first time, and before long, he had relocated to Hungary. In 2023, he was appointed president of the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, a highly unusual position for a foreign national. Pappin now had the opportunity to learn from the Fidesz party-state and start putting his ideas into practice.To postliberals, Orbán’s governing programme looked like a dream come true. As Rufo, coming off his stint at the Danube Institute,put itin 2023: “Hungary’s leaders are serious people combating the same forces confronted by conservatives in the west: the fraying of national culture, entrenched leftwing institutions and the rejection of sexual difference.” But, compared with the contemporary Republican party, Orbán seemed exhilaratingly willing to use the power of the state to pursue a conservative vision of the good life.Orbán was the great defender of the postliberal trinity: “strong families, strong borders, strong industry,” asPappin saidin an interview with the Atlantic. “Orbánomics” consisted of a series of interventions to build up Hungary’s car manufacturing capacity, ensure access to less expensive Russian energy and increase work requirements for welfare recipients, raising taxes on banks and even nationalising some.Defying the EU, the Orbán regime also pursued a so-called “zero migration” policy. But the postliberals were perhaps most enamoured of Orbán’s efforts to encourage traditional family formation and raise the birthrate. Since 2022, Hungary has spent about 5% of its GDP every year on a suite of welfare initiatives offering generous maternity leave, childcare support and tax breaks for mothers.View image in fullscreenJD Vance meets Patrick Deneen at a panel discussion at Catholic University, Washington in May 2023.Photograph: Francis Chung/POLITICO/APAs Rufo explained, these seemingly “progressive” policies were meant to serve “conservative ends”: first, “to incentivise traditional marriage and family formation”; second, to help ward off “foreign ideologies, such as critical race theory and gender ideology”; and, third, because “raising the native Hungarian birthrate obviates the need for foreign immigration”. Hungary’s student debt policy also allowed new mothers to suspend, reduce or ultimately erase their debt entirely, depending on how many children they had given birth to. In 2023,Pappin pointedto Hungary’s student debt programme as a model for the kinds of policies the Republican party should pursue.During the Biden years, the postliberals yearned for the kind of power and stability in the US that Orbán enjoyed in Hungary. In Deneen’s 2023 book Regime Change: Toward a Postliberal Future, the philosopher was no longer just diagnosing the problem with liberalism; he was suggesting a radical solution. Deneen now called for a revolutionary turn to “aristopopulism”, in which a cadre of elites would act as “class traitors” to help socially conservative workers depose the liberal-meritocratic ruling class in the US, and take control of a newly integrated state and civil society. “What is needed, in short,” he wrote, “is … the peaceful but vigorous overthrow of a corrupt and corrupting liberal ruling class and the creation of a postliberal order in which existing political forms can remain in place, as long as a fundamentally different ethos informs those institutions and the personnel who populate key offices and positions.” As an example of what he had in mind, Deneen pointed to Hungary.By the time I arrived in Budapest in late 2025, Trump was back in power, with the postliberal darling JD Vance as his vice-president. The new administration was armed with a blueprint for Deneen-style regime change. In 2023, the Heritage Foundation, a conservative US thinktank, had released a report titled Project 2025, “75% of which is being implemented”, as Heritage’s’s Paul McCarthy, who’d been involved in drafting the chapter on US foreign aid, claimed at a Danube Institute event this February. (The Danube Institute and Heritage had established a formal collaboration in March 2023, a month before the Project 2025 report was released.)For Applebaum and other post-cold war liberal intellectuals such as the historianTimothy Snyder, the direction of the US right was yet more evidence that “America’s future is Hungary”. According to Snyder, Trump and Vance are “Orbán’s pupils”, and many of their policy decisions “arise in whole or in part from Hungarian sources”.But in Hungary, a funny thing was happening: Orbán’s own government was no longer popular. Péter Magyar, a former Fidesz insider who had broken with the party, was leading Orbán by double digits in independent polls. One of two things was about to happen: either Fidesz would be out of power for the first time in 16 years, or Orbán would prove himself a genuine dictator. The Applebaum theory of Orbán’s regime was about to be put to the test, and so was postliberalism.On the national holiday of 15 March, I joined masses of supporters of Magyar’s new Tisza party as they filled the streets all the way up to Heroes’ Square, where Orbán had made hisfirst major political speechin June 1989. Later that year, Orbán raced back to Budapest from his Soros-funded scholarship at Oxford to participate in the unfolding regime change as a representative of Fidesz, founded as the Federation of Young Democrats. Now, my Hungarian friends were joking that Orbán resembled one of the corpulent bureaucrats he had once sought to replace.In the Hungary of 2026, postliberalism was not working out as planned. Inflation and house prices had risen faster than anywhere else in the EU. Orbánomics was crashing out. Industrial development hadn’t resulted in the promised economic growth, and Fidesz had been rocked by a massive pollution scandal at an electric vehicle battery plant. Though migration was effectively halted, Chinese guest workers streamed in to work in the newly created car industry jobs. After creeping up marginally, the fertility rate seemed to be flattening.Corruption throughout Orbán’s patronage system was so rampant that Hungary was being widely labeled a mafia state. Fidesz had rewritten the constitution, installed party loyalists in key judicial roles, gerrymandered electoral districts, changed election laws to inflate their parliamentary majority, put much of the higher education sector under the control of boards stacked with party members and overseen the sale of media companies to regime-friendly oligarchs. Already, the regime had granted that women with at least four childrendid not have to pay income taxesfor the rest of their lives. In the run-up to the election, they reduced the number of children required to three, and then two. But that wasn’t going to be enough to win an election, let alone replace the global neoliberal economic order.View image in fullscreenA branch of the Scruton cafe chain in Budapest.Photograph: Zoltán Csipke/AlamyBoth Trump and Vance had been rumoured guests at Cpac Hungary, but neither showed up in the end. The event chair still claimed that the “biggest stars of the sovereigntist right” were all on the way to Budapest. Javier Milei, the president of Argentina, was a last-minute addition. They also advertised an appearance by the Czech prime pinister, populist billionaire Andrej Babiš, but he pulled out at the last minute. Maybe they had all been scared off by Orbán’s tanking poll numbers.Lingering outside the gate on the day of the event itself, I saw Pappin walking toward the VIP entrance. I ducked behind a Cpac banner reading “FEL GYŐZELEMRE!” (“ON TO VICTORY!”).I wondered how he was taking the polls. A little over a week earlier, I had run into Pappin after an event at which he had joked that the liberal Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, sounded a lot like a “dangerous postliberal” when he prominently declared that the crisis in the rules-based international order was “a rupture, not a transition”. I was grabbing a coffee at a Scruton cafe – part of a chain named after the conservative English philosopher and Orbán ally Roger Scruton. Exposed lightbulbs hung from the ceiling in front of a stencilled cartoon of a hip, young Scruton in a double-breasted suit, with a speech bubble: “The greatest treasure of Hungarians is their national identity.” When I spotted Pappin at the next table, I decided to introduce myself, playing up the extent to which Scruton himself figures into my research. We talked about life in Budapest, the city he had referred to elsewhere as “Scrutopia”, and he scoffed at the impression of the Danube milieu put forward by the western press. “You know, all these people show up in Budapest looking for some kind of conservative intellectual utopia,” he said. Though the scene had been influential, he added, “There are only like five of us.”Five intellectuals in close proximity to power can do a lot of damage. Take it from Deneen in Regime Change: “Even if relatively small, an elite cadre skilled at directing and elevating popular resentments, combined with the political power of the many, can bolster populist political prospects as a working governmental and institutional force.” But this wasn’t what was happening in Hungary, at least not any more. The political power of the many was no longer cooperating. Though Vance had finally flown in for support, the polls still weren’t moving in Orbán’s direction.On 11 April, the night before the election, I heard Orbán’s voice echoing from the castle during a final torch-lit rally. The next day, the city was all nerves. The final turnout, nearly 80%, would set a national record. After polls closed, I gathered with friends to stream the independent Partizán media feed on YouTube. The first results, released just after 8pm, put Fidesz slightly ahead. Then, at 9.16pm, a new banner crossed the bottom of the screen: Orbán had called Magyar to concede. The convoluted Hungarian election machine had backfired, and Tisza had defeated Fidesz in a landslide. “Looks like the last bastion is gone,” Eva Vlaardingerbroek posted on X.My friends and I rushed to Batthyány Square, where Magyar was set to give hisvictory speech. The crowd throbbed with expectation; drones circled above us. Techno music drifted across the Danube from a dance party next to the floodlit parliament. We eavesdropped on two childhood friends who hadn’t seen each other in years as they embraced and looked deeply into one another’s eyes in wonder. Their meet-cute was interrupted by someone vomiting on the cobblestone at their feet.It slowly dawned on me that what we were witnessing was not a change of government but a regime change. Throughout the campaign, Magyar had used the Hungarian termrendszerváltás, literally “system change”, once reserved for talking about the democratic transition from communism in 1989, and now, somehow, Tisza had made it happen.If Pilkington is right that post-cold war liberals don’t have a good understanding of why their world is falling apart, neither did the postliberals after Magyar’s win. For them, the fact that Orbán had conceded gracefully was proof that he had always been committed to democracy – and that liberal critics such as Applebaum and Snyder had misunderstood him all along. On election night,Rod Dreher respondedto news that Orbán had conceded with a sarcastic post on X: “But … but … but, I was told by so many experts and journalists in the west that this would never happen, that Orbán is a fascist dictator who would never surrender power!”It’s true that Applebaum’s work often relied on a reductive binary between democracy and autocracy that, in this case, had obscured the fact that democratic change was still very much possible in Hungary. But the postliberals were trapped in their own binaries, too: because Orbán wasn’t a dictator, their logic went, Hungary must have ultimately been a democracy. This allowed them to dismiss all the ways Fidesz had held on to power by changing election laws, packing the judiciary, attacking civil society and higher education, and consolidating control over the media.There was one thing that Applebaum and the postliberals could agree on after the election: the demise of the so-called Hungarian model. Applebaum’s post-election column marked the passing of one of her own stock narratives. Orbán’s Hungary would no longer serve,she wrote, “as a model for Americans or Europeans who want to capture their own states, or take apart their own checks and balances, or impose their own illiberal ideologies on people who don’t accept them”. In his own postmortem,Dreher reacheda similar conclusion: “As a model for Maga and other nationalist conservatives in the west, Hungary is over.” But it would be a mistake to think that Orbán’s defeat, or the potential closure of state-supported institutions such as the Danube Institute, means the end of postliberalism.“We are all postliberals now,”Pilkington arguedon Postliberal Order, the Substack newsletter he shares with Deneen, Pappin and CC Pecknold, a historian of theology. As he pointed out, Magyar shared many of Orbán’s views on core issues. “From the standpoint of domestic politics, Magyar effectively ran on Fidesz’s own platform,” Pilkington argued in a differentpost-election column, “promising to keep migration low, maintain Hungarian cultural nationalism, and keep the generous family support system that Fidesz built in place.” But Pilkington wasn’t just making a narrow political point. Postliberalism as an intellectual project was not tied to the fate of any particular political party. “No doubt, Fidesz has been an incubator of alternative thinking in transatlantic conservatism, but these ideas are in the ether and are unlikely to go away any time soon.”View image in fullscreenViktor Orbán awards Roger Scruton the Middle Cross of the Hungarian Order of Merit at the Hungarian embassy in London in 2019.Photograph: Zsolt Szigetváry/EPAIn the narrow, descriptive sense, it’s true that there is no going back to the liberalism of the brief, post-cold war interregnum, circa 1989-2015. Still, postliberals are terrible at predicting what comes next. On X, Pilkington posts regular prophecies of western civilisational catastrophe with the swagger of a former finance guy. “There is an old phrase in investment,” he writes in The Collapse of Global Liberalism, “it is better to be wrong for the right reasons than right for the wrong reasons.”But if Pilkington is right about our new postliberal era, it is for the wrong reasons. Clearly, the world of post-cold war liberalism is over. But the idea that all the challenges brought on by its collapse can be answered by the postliberal programme is a farce. As Hungary has shown, postliberal policies don’t produce a life good enough to win over voters. In the end, Hungary was a false model for our authoritarian future. Now the model we have to worry about is US-made.In all my time in Hungary, there was one person I had never seen at the Danube Institute or at any of the other events I attended: Rod Dreher, an alleged mainstay of the Budapest scene. After a few failed attempts, we finally met on a spring afternoon in early May, the day before Magyar was sworn in as prime minister. Over rosé spritzes and nicotine pouches, I made my confession to Dreher: I told him I had been attending events at the Danube Institute, about all the wild conversations I had overheard, and about how I was just trying to understand what attracted American intellectuals to the dissident right. We both agreed that Hungary was a strange place to look for lessons about the US. But here we both were.“I was never part of any scene here, although I kind of thought I would be,” he told me. Like Pappin, he noted that only a handful of conservative anglophone intellectuals lived in Budapest; most of their companions were only there temporarily, to check out what it was like when their side was in power. But the Scruton cafes were “phoney”, more Ikea than English country house. The Danube Institute, though it was never the Orbánist propaganda factory it was rumoured to be, was overseen by overcautious Hungarian managers, he said, who had held it back from becoming a truly stimulating intellectual environment. “There was a scene,” he admitted, “but it was very superficial.”How liberalism became ‘the god that failed’ in eastern EuropeRead moreAnd now the Budapest scene, however superficial, was coming to an end. Over the next few months, the new Tisza-led parliament would pass a series of laws and constitutional amendments aimed at dismantling the Fidesz party’s system of funding thinktanks and other intellectual institutions. At the end of July, Pappin would resign from the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, and the MCC foundation would be formally dissolved. Already, Magyar had promised not only to end government funding of the organisation that runs Cpac Hungary, but to investigate the former funding through the newly created National Asset Recovery and Protection Office. As Dreher would later put it: “The unsettling atmosphere of vengeance that has overtaken Hungary since Péter Magyar became prime minister [sic] likely means the end of the Danube Institute.” (The Danube Institute did not respond to requests for comment.)I asked Dreher what he would do next. He told me he had briefly considered moving to Vienna, but then he had had a change of heart. It was time to give up the good life in central Europe and return to the American south. My own temporary resident permit was about to expire. As the sun set behind Károlyi-kert, one of the oldest gardens in Budapest, Dreher and I downed our last rosé spritzes. Postliberalism was finally coming home, and so were we.Listen to our podcastshereand sign up to the long read weekly emailhere.

title: Don’t be fooled. The AI that was supposed to save us time is doing just the opposite  | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: The government says it can transform the state with AI, but it is no match for the resulting stream of machine-generated slop. And we all pay the cost, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: The government says it can transform the state with AI, but it is no match for the resulting stream of machine-generated slop. And we all pay the cost, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Since the adoption of ChatGPT, governments around the world are seeing surges in complaints and requests.Photograph: Krongkaew/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSince the adoption of ChatGPT, governments around the world are seeing surges in complaints and requests.Photograph: Krongkaew/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Don’t be fooled. The AI that was supposed to save us time is doing just the oppositeGaby HinsliffThe government says it can transform the state with AI, but it is no match for the resulting stream of machine-generated slop. And we all pay the costTue 20 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 09.06 EDTShareAnother morning, another avalanche of emails. Even after a guilty cull, my inbox is sitting at well over 7,000, but lately I’ve started subscribing to theQuentin Crisptheory of housework: why bother, when after four years or so you stop noticing the accumulating dust? Empty inboxes just fill up again anyway.In theory, email was supposed to save hours of meetings, phone calls and standing over photocopiers. Instead, we just spend hours deleting stuff people wouldn’t have bothered telling us if it had meant picking up the phone, but which they can now spam to their entire database at the click of a button. The glorious ease and convenience of being able to reach the world in seconds came, we now know, with the inconvenience of them being able to reach you right back.And therein lies the challenge to the government’s hopes of AI helping to transform the machinery of the state on the cheap, saving not only time but billions of pounds in public money. It’s early days, but AI seems not so much to be streamlining public service delivery as gumming it up – partly because, as was once the case with email, the public is using it right back at them.In aSubstack postlast week, the former civil servant Sam Freedman noted that governments around the world seem to be experiencing unusual surges in complaints, requests and responses to regulatory and official bodies since the adoption of ChatGPT. It’s the same storyin the courts, withemployment tribunal casesin England, Scotland and Wales reportedly rising by 39% in a year thanks in part to claimants using AI to draft claims, while magistrates and judges face a wave of people who can’t afford lawyers using ChatGPT to build cases that often don’t make sense. And all of this needs patient disentangling by a human, on the grounds that just because a defendant is citing precedents that don’t exist, it doesn’t mean there isn’t a genuine grievance buried in there somewhere.Whitehall special advisers complain of departments drowning in AI-generated freedom of information requests, an abuse of a system originally intended to empower individuals. MPs’ offices are similarly swamped by AI-generated letters, all of which need to be read by humans for fear of missing something important from a constituent.How long before public consultations on changing the law become so spammed by slop that they are in essence useless as a measure of what the country actually thinks? There’s a fine line between the noble aim of making it easier for individuals to interact with an otherwise remote state, and making it so easy that the result is an uncontrollable firehose of meaningless machine-generated guff.The obvious answer to this kind of AI flooding is getting AI tools to detect or sift it, but that doesn’t always work when dealing with potentially vulnerable human beings. Constituents who use AI to express themselves in more fancy-sounding language when writing to their MP, for example, still have the right to expect a personal response from a human being.Employers who thought they were being smart by getting AI to sift job applications, meanwhile, are reaping what they sowed, as resentful applicants automate their end of things too and spray-gun applications across the board, rather than concentrating on the jobs they really want. Now neither side can separate the wheat from an avalanche of chaff.The risk of paralysis is likely only to increase if the public startsadopting agentic AIin the kind of numbers big tech fondly imagines. Early adopters might well find agents save them time and hassle. But shortcuts stop being shortcuts once everyone else is using them too, and risk turning into bottlenecks instead. Think of cars, which have vastly shortened journey times compared with travelling by horseback, except in cities at rush hour when too many other people are also trying to shorten theirs. By 2018, central London daytime traffic was moving on average atjust over 7mph– about the same speed as a trotting pony.Historically, humans have always learned to develop ways around problems of our own making. We have spam filters for email, congestion charges to keep cars out of cities, and in the long term we could well figure out what kind of frictions we need to put back in the system to make it possible to live with the impact of AI.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut for now a useful rule of thumb, if improbable claims start to be made for savings due to AI, will be that more isn’t always better; faster and easier isn’t always more convenient; and time saved in one section of public services has a horrible habit of popping up in another one. Let the Whac-A-Mole begin.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionChatGPTOpenAIComputingEmployment lawEmployment tribunalscommentShareReuse this content

title: After the violence and chaos in France, there’s only one beneficiary: Marine Le Pen | Paul Taylor | The Guardian
description: The far-right leader’s promise to restore order will appeal to many ahead of next year’s presidential elections – the stakes are suddenly much higher, says the European Policy Centre’s Paul Taylor
Author: Paul Taylor
Headline: The far-right leader’s promise to restore order will appeal to many ahead of next year’s presidential elections – the stakes are suddenly much higher, says the European Policy Centre’s Paul Taylor
Content: Firefighters tackled a blaze in Paris as protesters march in the background, 17 October 2026.Photograph: Firas Abdullah/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFirefighters tackled a blaze in Paris as protesters march in the background, 17 October 2026.Photograph: Firas Abdullah/Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionFranceAfter the violence and chaos in France, there’s only one beneficiary: Marine Le PenPaul TaylorThe far-right leader’s promise to restore order will appeal to many ahead of next year’s presidential elections – the stakes are suddenly much higherTue 20 Oct 2026 05.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 10.36 EDTShareThere is only one clear winner so far from France’s chaos: Marine Le Pen. Theviolence and riotingthat engulfed towns and cities across the country over the weekend, six months before a pivotal presidential election, is a godsend for the hard-right, Eurosceptical, anti-immigration candidate. Asbuildings burned, shops were looted and police attacked, the rioting largely drowned out peaceful mass protests over the dilapidated state of schools , fuel prices and the cost of living.Across France and the rest of Europe, people are in shock atscenes of arson and pillagein city centres, the wrecking of symbols of the republic such as the 19th-century town hall in peaceful provincial Limoges and the bust of Marianne in Marseille’s city hall, and the looting of more than 2,000 shops.Though France has along revolutionary tradition, this was not the work of egalitarian insurgents or working-class warriors, but nihilist, anarchist “black bloc” gangs, with opportunist looters and rioters along for the ride.Emmanuel Macron is a lame-duck president who has no practical answers to a crisis that is ruining his legacy. Macronexpressed his “anger and shame”at the violence and the damage to France’s global image in a Sunday-night broadcast to the nation, but he is so widely loathed, including by many who voted for him in two presidential elections, that his pleas for order and dialogue were largely ignored.Le Pen, in contrast, issued asolemn video message, looking presidential as she sat at a desk with the national tricolor (but no EU flag) and bookshelves as her backdrop. Millions of suffering French people were angry about “anarchic immigration” and the cost of living without smashing or burning anything, she said. They would have an opportunity in six months’ time to vote for a different path of “restored authority and security”.View image in fullscreenA screengrab from Marine Le Pen’s video after the riots across France.Photograph: Rassemblement NationalMacron’s minority government is trapped in a vicious circle. France’s debt and deficit squeeze leaves him no spare cash left to buy off protesters. A decade of his centre-right presidency has failed to reform a bloated public sector or improve public services. The country has a youth crisis, characterised by anxiety over aneconomically uncertain futureand amplified by social media, as well as a geopolitical crisis with Russia’s war on Ukraine spreading into acovert war against Europe.Foreign critics of progressive European social policies are fanning the flames with incendiary commentaries. Donald Trumpgloatedon social media that “France is burning!”. Blaming the situation on immigration, he urged the French to “close your borders and take control before it is too late”. Vladimir Putin’s close aide Kirill Dmitriev described events in France as“the suicidal fall of Europe”and also ascribed it in part to chaotic migration.The convergence of crises leaves little room for manoeuvre for a French government struggling to push even a mildly cost-cutting budget through a hung parliament. For now, it is trying to extinguish the violence withselective curfews. One presidential hopeful, Dominique de Villepin, who was a Gaullist prime minister 20 years ago, has even compared the situation to the eve of the fall of theancien regimein 1788, a year before the outbreak of the Revolution, when France was stricken by drought, failed harvests and empty state coffers.That may be a far-fetched parallel. But the sense of a fraying state, a discredited political class and an ossified bureaucracy unable to staunch a slow-motion financial crisis that might suddenly accelerate makes the stakes in next year’s presidential race ever-higher.Until last weekend’s explosion, the school and student protests, unrest over the cost of living and outrage at instances of police brutality against young demonstrators all seemed to be lifting the campaign of radical-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who in some opinion polls hadovertaken the centrist Edouard Philippefor second place. However, Mélenchon’s apparent refusal to clearly condemn the looting or attacks on the police, and hisbelittling of the violenceas “disorder that is part of the events in the life of a society”, may cost him support among more moderate leftwing voters who have boosted Socialist candidate Raphaël Glucksmann in the latest opinion surveys.Investors aretaking frightat the violence and political instability, selling French stocks and bonds. A deepening market run on France could yet change the dynamics of the presidential campaign, rallying a frightened middle-class behind a seasoned centrist candidate seen as a safe pair of hands in a crisis.A month after the May 1968 student-worker uprising that rocked Charles de Gaulle’s staid regime, voters scared by the spectre of civil unrest delivered a landslide victory to his party, which promised to restore order and authority. A year later, De Gaulle was disavowed in a referendum on regional devolution and resigned.Historical comparisons are risky. Last weekend’s violence has increased the likelihood of a law-and-order backlash among voters that could propel Le Pen into the Élysée Palace. But if the financial situation worsens and the campaign turns on who can save the economy, she may yet lose out to a candidate who is firm on security and more orthodox on fiscal policy. Economics is Le Pen’s weak spot.So far, neither Philippe nor other centrist and centre-right rivals have set the campaign alight. But six months is a long time in French politics.Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy CentreExplore more on these topicsFranceOpinionMarine Le PenEmmanuel MacronProtestEuropeParisJean-Luc MélenchoncommentShareReuse this content

title: Worried about what your phone is doing to your brain? This new fad will make it worse | Imogen West-Knights | The Guardian
description: I have long known that internet detritus is bad for me. But with microdramas – stories told in episodes under two minutes – I can actually feel the damage being done, says writer Imogen West-Knights
Author: Imogen West-Knights
Headline: I have long known that internet detritus is bad for me. But with microdramas – stories told in episodes under two minutes – I can actually feel the damage being done, says writer Imogen West-Knights
Content: Images from the microdrama Pregnant By My Ex’s Professor Dad.Composite: DailymotionView image in fullscreenImages from the microdrama Pregnant By My Ex’s Professor Dad.Composite: DailymotionOpinionTelevision industryWorried about what your phone is doing to your brain? This new fad will make it worseImogen West-KnightsI have long known that internet detritus is bad for me. But with microdramas – stories told in episodes under two minutes – I can actually feel the damage being doneTue 20 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 11.06 EDTShareSeven or eight years ago, a new kind of televisual entertainment was born in China. Microdramas: over-the-top, soap opera-type series with splashy, schlocky premises such as infidelity, arranged marriage and secret billionairehood, in which each episode is a mere 60-90 seconds long, took off there among an audience of the phone-addicted.And now, as with many cultural phenomena that start in China, microdramas have made it over here. The form is forecast to take in$1.5bn in revenue in the USby the end of this year. Channel 4 announced recently that it waslaunching its first microdrama, and the UK is already leading Europe in terms of microdrama-watching, with8.2 million of us tuning in to these thingsevery month.Numbers such as this give me a queasy, vertiginous feeling about the vast difference in possible human experiences existing alongside each other at the same time. What do youmean, millions and millions of people are watching this stuff that seems, to me, catastrophically brainless and objectively bad? Who? What do they eat for breakfast? What do they dream of at night?Before I read those numbers, I had only seen tiny snippets of microdramas embedded into news pieces about the phenomenon. I wanted to know what it was like to actually watch one. I downloaded ReelShort, one of the apps that hosts microdramas exclusively, and flicked through the homepage. Recommended for me wereTrapped in the Boss’s Embrace,I Had a Baby Without YouandCarrying His Triplets, Becoming His Wifey. I went to the “HOT” tab and selected the one with the most convoluted title,Pregnant By My Ex’s Professor Dad, althoughLet Me Taste Your Husbandalso appealed.In Pregnant By My Ex’s Professor Dad, it is legible right from the get-go who the bad guy is (the ex) and who the good guy is (the protagonist) and what is going to happen, not least because it is right there in the title. The question of “what is going to happen?” that is supposed to drive you into the next episode, the question that has driven all narrative since time immemorial, is rendered oddly moot.There is no setup, no world-building, no padding whatsoever, just rapidly cut dramatic denouements over and over again: someone being cheated on, someone slapping someone else, a car window getting smashed, a new love interest being introduced, a sex scene. All of this happens in the first three minutes of the series. Helpless women swoon over geometrically jawed hunks on sets lit like a morgue and say exactly what they are thinking in voiceover, so that there is no room at all for nuance to creep in and engage your brain while you watch.You can watch the first few episodes of any given series for free, and then you hit a paywall, which you can get around by watching ads for another form of phone brain rot: colour-matching mobile games. I have been told by loved ones before now that I couldn’t be a newsreader or a jury member because I can’t keep my emotions off my face. This is true. I caught sight of myself in my phone screen reflection while watching microdramas and saw there a person who looked as if they’d just spotted a pile of dog sick on the carpet.I’m not incapable of enjoying bad television. I do not come here having descended from a lofty perch of only watching heritage BBC adaptations of classic novels or whatever. My appetite for dreck is hearty enough. But, my God – and can there be such an entity in a universe producing microdramas? – this stuff is awful. Flagrantly so, though, to the degree that I start to feel there is something wrong with me for desiring quality in this format.Or I sense that I’ve done something wrong by intentionally going to watch one. In apiece for the New York Times Magazine, writer Daniel Kolitz described these shows as happening to people “like a food-borne illness”, rather than something that people elect to get into. They appear on your phone screen, and there you are, watching them in a half-conscious malaise while you wait for the day to end.I would love for this kind of thing to go the way of non-fungible tokens: something we all had to hear about for a short time and that are now patently doomed to the scrapheap of short-lived modern internet detritus.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMaybe this is partly because my own feelings about internet detritus have changed lately. Whereas in the past I had a known, but not felt, understanding that the allure of apps and games and scrolling on my phone was bad for me, nowadays I am regularly experiencing real, bodily panic that my brain is being atrophied. I am scared of my phone, and my sick want for it. So the emergence of an all-new, even more terrible way of being on your phone does provoke the reactionary in me. “Just let people enjoy things!” a better person might think. Not this time.Imogen West-Knights is a writer and journalistExplore more on these topicsTelevision industryOpinionInternetTelevisionSmartphonesDigital mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: That piping hot new TV show I just watched? I can’t recall a thing about it  | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: I’m never fully concentrating, always simultaneously thinking a huge thought about the future or scrolling through Vinted, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: I’m never fully concentrating, always simultaneously thinking a huge thought about the future or scrolling through Vinted, writes Zoe Williams
Content: A rare example of memorable TV … Colin from Accounts.Photograph: BBC/© 2026 CBS Studios Inc., Easy Tiger Productions Pty Ltd, Foxtel Management Pty Ltd, Create NSW/John PlattView image in fullscreenA rare example of memorable TV … Colin from Accounts.Photograph: BBC/© 2026 CBS Studios Inc., Easy Tiger Productions Pty Ltd, Foxtel Management Pty Ltd, Create NSW/John PlattOpinionTelevisionThat piping hot new TV show I just watched? I can’t recall a thing about itZoe WilliamsI’m never fully concentrating, always simultaneously thinking a huge thought about the future or scrolling through VintedTue 20 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 12.35 EDTShareSome friends and I were talking, at the weekend, about the TV shows War (about a couple getting divorced) and The Diplomat (about an entirely different couple, not getting divorced). I hadn’t seen either because I was busy withColin from Accounts. One friend had seen one show but not the other, and couldn’t remember which; a second friend had seen both and couldn’t remember anything that happened in either.It emphatically wasn’t because they weren’t good. The second friend seemed medium-sure, in fact, that they were both great. His thesis is that he just watches so much TV that none of it can find any purchase in his memory.I can’t remember plots because I’m never fully concentrating, always simultaneously thinking a huge thought about the future or scrolling through Vinted, and I don’t even notice I’m only half in it until I try to watch something with subtitles. Then it dawns on me that, having no trace of conversational Korean, I must literally look at the screen if I want to know what’s going on.Relatedly, I can’t remember which series of anything I’m up to, either. I can cheerfully get halfway through episode 3 of series 2 of, say, Slow Horses, before I realise that not only do I know what’s about to happen, I also know that one of those characters is no longer alive.The most elegant rationale came from friend number two, who put it down to the Netflixification of the televisual arts. In its play for world dominance, the streaming company makes all countries look the same, and everyone dress the same, and eat the same sort of food from the same slightly-too-large plates in their implausibly hotel-like kitchens. So what possible choice does your hippocampus have but to merge all the stories into one?‘The word-of-mouth has been crazy!’ How Colin from Accounts stormed the UKRead moreA third friend blamed herself, for watching Game of Thrones too often – twice, all the way through, then some jaw-dropper episodes many more times. It has occupied all her mental RAM, now and for ever. Ask her how any intractable situation resolved – with, say, an organised crime ring or a hostage situation – and she’ll just assume a dragon arrived.Blessedly, it’s impossible to get lost in Colin from Accounts, because only two things happen: they are off, then they are on again. If you can’t remember why they’re off, no problem – it was probably a misunderstanding and soon they will be back on. Sorry. I should have given a spoiler alert.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistThe Guardian’s year in review 2026: on Tuesday 1 December 2026, join your favourite Guardian writers for an evening of candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as we look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. With Zoe Williams, John Crace, Pippa Crerar, Jonathan Liew and Lucy Mangan. title: Trump’s obsession with Ilhan Omar has reached a dangerous new level | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The administration seems intent on stripping the congresswoman of her US citizenship and deporting her. It’s a terrible abuse of power, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The administration seems intent on stripping the congresswoman of her US citizenship and deporting her. It’s a terrible abuse of power, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Omar has been repeatedly attacked by Trump.Photograph: Demetrius Freeman/The Washington Post/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOmar has been repeatedly attacked by Trump.Photograph: Demetrius Freeman/The Washington Post/Getty ImagesOpinionIlhan OmarTrump’s obsession with Ilhan Omar has reached a dangerous new levelArwa MahdawiThe administration seems intent on stripping the congresswoman of her US citizenship and deporting her. It’s a terrible abuse of powerTue 20 Oct 2026 10.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 12.36 EDTShareWhat do you think it is about Ilhan Omar, exactly, that seems to get under Donald Trump’s tangerine-tinted skin? The president hasclaimedhe has a problem with the progressive Democratic congresswoman because she is “unpatriotic” to the US and “disrespectful … to Israel”. However, the extent of his animus towards Omar, the first Somali American in Congress, suggests there’s more to it. Trump hasinsistedhe is “the least racist person there is anywhere in the world”, so I’m sure it has nothing to do with the fact that she’s brown and Muslim. Truly, it’s a mystery.Whatever the reason, Trump’s not a fan. The president has plenty of enemies, but few have been attacked as ferociously and consistently over the years as Omar. He’s called her “garbage”, among other nasty names, suggested (without evidence) that she married her brother, andsaidshe “should be thrown the hell out of our country”. His supporters haveechoed his callsto deport Omar, who fled war-torn Somalia as a child and became a naturalised US citizen at 17.Now Trump’s obsession with Omar has reached a dangerous new level. Trump isn’t just throwing out insults any more; his administration seems intent on stripping the congresswoman of her US citizenship and deporting her. Last Monday, 22 days before the November midterms in which Omar is seeking re-election, federal agentsraidedher house in Washington DC. Her phone was seized and grand jury subpoenas were reportedly issued to some of her relatives as part of an investigation concerning her immigration paperwork. Trump, by the way, denied anyinvolvement. Just a curious coincidence that one of his biggest nemeses is now being treated like a criminal.As House Democratic leadershave said, the raid on Omar’s house “raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponisation of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries”. But it also raises another question: is this “just” a stunt designed to embarrass and intimidate Omar before the midterms? Or is there a real possibility that the congresswoman could be denaturalised and deported?“Certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen,” Tom Homan, Trump’s “border czar”,told Fox Newsover the weekend when asked about Omar being deported. “We’ll let the evidence lead where it leads, but she’ll be held to the same standard you and I are held: if she violated the law, then she’ll be held accountable,”Homan added.Oh, please. I know the Mar-a-Lago set are big on Botox, but I can’t believe Homan was able to preach about accountability with a straight face. Not many people areconvictedof 34 felonies and face no jail time. Trump, however, is in the White House rather than prison because the supreme court’s conservative majority (which he helped create) found that former presidents areentitledto a degree of immunity from criminal prosecution.The US government has every right to uphold its immigration laws, but its appetite seems to vary considerably depending on the person. If Homan really is so keen on accountability, may I suggest he take a look at the Trump megadonor Elon Musk? The tech mogul’s brother, Kimbal Musk, has publicly joked about the fact that the brothers briefly worked in the US without proper documentation in the 1990s. (Elon said it was a “grey area”.) And then there’s Melania Trump: in 2016, theAssociated Pressreported the first lady was paid for 10 modelling jobs in the US before she had legal permission to work in the country. (Melania has denied ever violating the terms of her immigration status.)Omar was just a teenager when her father filled out the paperwork that led to them both being naturalised. I obviously have no idea if there were any errors in that. But I can tell you that this “investigation” is not about accountability. It is a terrifying abuse of power that reflects the way in which the Trump administration is weaponising the immigration system to stamp out dissent. We’ve already seen Trumpdeportnoncitizen student activists to crack down on pro-Palestinian speech. Now he’s applying that strategy to Omar, a sitting congresswoman. As Barack Obamawarnedat the weekend, “If this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her.” Indeed it won’t; Trump is just getting started.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
