title: What’s the future for the Green party? Should it be ecosocialism? | Joe Todd | The Guardian
description: The party must aspire to be more than a Labour pressure group. It should offer a vision for radical reform – and ways to implement it, says political writer and Green party member Joe Todd
Author: Joe Todd
Headline: The party must aspire to be more than a Labour pressure group. It should offer a vision for radical reform – and ways to implement it, says political writer and Green party member Joe Todd
Content: Zack Polanski at a Green party campaign event in London on 4 October.Photograph: Jacqueline Lawrie/LNPView image in fullscreenZack Polanski at a Green party campaign event in London on 4 October.Photograph: Jacqueline Lawrie/LNPOpinionGreen partyWhat’s the future for the Green party? Should it be ecosocialism?Joe ToddThe party must aspire to be more than a Labour pressure group. It should offer a vision for radical reform – and ways to implement itTue 20 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 05.40 EDTShareIt’s a strange time to be a Green. We have just held our largest conference ever, but it was overshadowed by a controversial motion that was attacked by the media as racist. Then, when welost a byelectionin a Camden seat that is so Labour it has estates named after Blair-era ministers, the headlines called for Zack Polanski to resign.It does, however, mark the end of phase one for Polanski’s Greens. Polanski burst on to the political scene in 2025 and ate up attention, enjoying an easy monopoly on hope while Labour was sucked into the black hole of Starmerism. Labour has since escaped, with Andy Burnham giving social democracy with Mancunian characteristics a half-hearted go. But Burnham’s honeymoon already seems to be ending. John Healey’sbudgetof “difficult decisions” and “fiscal responsibility” is likely to disappoint everyone but the financial markets, and a winter energy bill crisis driven by a possibleEl Niñodeep freeze is just one of many problems he’ll soon have to face.One school of thought says Polanski can carry on as before, focusing on points of difference with Labour. Healey announces a no-change budget; Polanski calls for a tax on wealth to fund public services. Angela Raynersides with landlordsover renters; Polanski proposes an emergency rent brake and explores Berlin’s plan to expropriate the properties of corporate landlords.These interventions matter, especially in our attention-driven politics. But on their own they are only tactical manoeuvres in response to the politics ofLabour. If we act like we’re only a Labour pressure group, that’s what we will become. And in doing so, we will neglect to answer the deeper question: what are society’s fundamental problems and what is our plan to fix them?In practice, Burnham’s “radical vision” promises only modest regulation of public utilities, limited devolution and reform of the voting system and of social care after the next election. Weighed against the crises we face – climate breakdown, bankrupt public services, rampant inflation, runaway rents, an epidemic of loneliness, a billionaire-owned media, a deranged elite of tech oligarchs who literally want the world to end – his vision reads more like the managed decline of a system in crisis.If phase two of Polanski’s Green party is about anything, it should be about breaking this spell. Part of this is naming capitalism as the root cause. Naomi Klein made the best-selling case more than a decade ago that the fight of our times iscapitalism v the climate– that a livable world and continued resource extraction are fundamentally incompatible.But Burnham will not go there. He namesneoliberalism as the problemand then neglects to fix it, unceremoniously dumping any intention to expand public ownership and shrink the role of the market.Polanskishouldgo there,rooting his day-to-day interventions in a credible programme to transition away from capitalism – not only imagining the end of capitalism and what might come next, but planning in painstaking detail just how we are going to get there. He must build a credibleGreen partyvision that shows Burnham’s to be meek and hollow.Don’t get me wrong, the Green party isn’t there yet, nor anywhere close. We have 5 MPs, 10% of the vote and we’re still learning to be a mass of 230,000 members. But if we don’t start taking ourselves seriously, why would anybody else? Trust in political parties is on the floor, and that affects the Greens too. Why should people put their faith in us and dare to hope if we don’t have a programme that is honest, rigorous and credible?We only need to look to the French leftwing party La France Insoumise to see what this looks like. In 2016 Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s movement published L’Avenir en Commun, which went straight into the bestseller list and has been read by hundreds of thousands of people. It is a visionary, comprehensive programme that would be written into the constitution so that companies can never take more from nature than they give. It’s a plan to provide free water and energy to every household, to redraw France’s regions around river basins, mountain ranges and forests, and to organise ecological planning. It is more extensive and detailed than any manifesto for ecological transition in Europe, and polls suggest Mélenchon could lead the French left into next May’spresidential runoffagainst Marine Le Pen.The Green party’s programme must be similarly full of strategy and vision: reckoning honestly with the forces arrayed against us and setting out precisely what we’d do in our first year of government. It should also talk about the good life and what we’re fighting for, in words that resonate with voters, rather than dry policy. Written in a big open process where lots of groups are involved: unions, community groups and thinktanks, farmers watching harvests fail, pensioners battling fuel poverty, renters priced out of homeownership and workers whose jobs are vanishing – it should become a comprehensive point of unity that can provide an answer to those who aren’t voting Green because they doubt our credibility, and fill the void currently occupied by single-issue policy motions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPolanski is correct when he says that Burnham isn’t serious about socialism. But we have to be honest: right now, neither are we. If Burnham’s vision is meek and hollow, ours is still being formed. And as Labour faces the tests of governing, now is the time to write it.Joe Todd is a senior fellow at the Autonomy Institute, the co-host of the Life of the Party podcast and a Green party memberDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Do not be distracted by other global crises. Nature cannot wait for a better year – we must act now | Steven Guilbeault | The Guardian
description: In 2022, I helped push through the international agreement to protect biodiversity. Wars and economic pressures can make nature seem like a ‘nice-to-have’. But it is a critical asset, and Cop17 must deliver real action
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In 2022, I helped push through the international agreement to protect biodiversity. Wars and economic pressures can make nature seem like a ‘nice-to-have’. But it is a critical asset, and Cop17 must deliver real action
Content: The Cop17 summit in Yerevan will have to agree on a timetable to deliver on the $30bn public finance promise by 2030, as the last target was missed.Photograph: COP17View image in fullscreenThe Cop17 summit in Yerevan will have to agree on a timetable to deliver on the $30bn public finance promise by 2030, as the last target was missed.Photograph: COP17The age of extinctionCop17 biodiversity summitDo not be distracted by other global crises. Nature cannot wait for a better year – we must act nowSteven GuilbeaultIn 2022, I helped push through the international agreement to protect biodiversity. Wars and economic pressures can make nature seem like a ‘nice-to-have’. But it is a critical asset, and Cop17 must deliver real actionSupported byAbout this contentTue 20 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTShareWhen I was five, property developers came to cut down the woods behind my home in La Tuque, Quebec. My mother encouraged me to climb one of the trees in protest, then told the developers, straight-faced, that there was nothing she could do when they asked her to get me down. A few days later, the tree was cut down anyway.I thought about that tree in the early hours of a freezing Montreal morning in December 2022, as the gavel came down on aglobal agreement between nearly 200 countriesto halt and reverse the loss of nature by 2030. I thought about how important nature is for our health, our food security and our economies, but also how much passion there is around protecting it, and how it has the power to inspire people all around the world.Despite differences in national circumstances, interests, and levels of responsibility, what we agreed to do really did, and still does, have the power to create longer term stability for billions of people across borders.We agreed to protect 30% of the world’s land and oceansand channel $200bn (£150bn) a year into nature. We admitted that far more money was flowing into destroying nature than protecting it, committing to address $500bn of subsidies currently contributing to the problem.View image in fullscreenSteven Guilbeault speaks to journalists after Cop15 in Montreal in 2022.Photograph: Lars Hagberg/AFP/Getty ImagesNearly four years later, the reality is that we are not delivering on those promises.The context has changed. War, extreme weather and homes swept away or burned to the ground are becoming the norm, and public finances are strained everywhere. Leaders feel pressure to choose between protecting biodiversity, which is perceived as a “nice-to-have”, and policies that look like self-preservation.This is a false dichotomy. Nature is a critical asset for national prosperity and economic security, and the evidence is already there.Farmers in Francewho have leant on biodiversity instead of chemical fertilisers have seen crops thrive through extreme drought. In Brazil,Indigenous fire brigadeshave cut blazes by more than 20% in parts of the Cerrado and Amazon, regions vital to the soya and commodity trade with the global north.To the environment ministers preparing for the biodiversity summit starting this week in the Armenian capital, Yerevan, I know what you are about to be told: budgets are tight; there’s a war, an election, a trade dispute. Nature can wait for a better year.But the reality is, there might not be a better year, there is only the one you are in. I and some of the ministerial colleagues that sat beside me in the early hours of that Montreal morning four years ago agree that theship can be turned around,and it can start with three clear next steps in Yerevan.1. Stop public finance from backsliding and deliver on your promisesIn Yerevan, ministers must set out a timetable and interim milestone to deliver on the $30bn public finance promise by 2030, having just fallen shy of the $20bn target by 2025. Overseas development finance dropped23% last year– the largest drop on record – and it is expected to decline further before the end of 2026. Biodiversity-specific funding within that has fallen 17%.Countries such as the UK arepublicly acknowledgingthat ecosystems such as the Congo basin and the Amazon rainforest are also critical for food security within its own borders. Investing in nature overseas is not charity – it is a sure bet on stable food import costs among other things.2. Direct finance ministers to address runaway harmful subsidiesFinance ministers should meet within the next two years to set out a plan for turning off the tap on subsidies that undermine economic security. We have four years left to start shifting $500bn of harmful subsidies, as this is no longer just an issue only for environment ministries.Four years ago countries made a historic deal to save nature. Is it dead in the water?Read moreHarmful subsidies have rocketed to$2.6tn in recent years.Across countries’ biodiversity plans,only 15%had plans to address the gap. The quantity ofmoney spent on destroying nature is 30 times higherthan what is going into protecting and restoring it.3. Close the gap on marine protected areasMinisters must also draw up a plan of action for closing the gap between terrestrial and marine ecosystem protection, building on all the tools that have been used for land, and pushing for progress at the first ever Ocean Cop in New York in January next year. According to national commitments,27% of terrestrial landis protected, which is something that should be celebrated, while oceans have just12% similarly coveredby protective agreements.Ocean ecosystems are remarkable and humbling places with unfathomable potential. The species we have yet to discover, the amount of carbon and heat they absorb each year, and the buffers against extreme weather that coastal ecosystems such as mangroves and coral reefs can provide are well worth the cost of investing in protection.To the ministers heading to Armenia, I say: this Cop is your tree. In Montreal, nearly 200 countries climbed up together. In Yerevan, the pressure to climb back down will be intense. I ask those ministers not to give in to it. Do not let them cut it down. There is no better year coming, only this one, and the choice to drive forward the goals we all set together back in 2022.Steven Guilbeault is a former environment minister of CanadaExplore more on these topicsCop17 biodiversity summitThe age of extinctionBiodiversityWildlifeConservationTrees and forestsOceansClimate crisiscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Covid-19 and care homes: the inquiry’s scathing verdict must be heeded  | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The government did not throw a ‘protective ring’ around social care, and vulnerable people were left exposed
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The government did not throw a ‘protective ring’ around social care, and vulnerable people were left exposed
Content: ‘While there is no “ideal solution” in a situation where the risk of infection must be balanced against the benefit to residents of being visited, it concludes that restrictions were inappropriate and harmful in some cases.’Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘While there is no “ideal solution” in a situation where the risk of infection must be balanced against the benefit to residents of being visited, it concludes that restrictions were inappropriate and harmful in some cases.’Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianOpinionCovid inquiryThe Guardian view on Covid-19 and care homes: the inquiry’s scathing verdict must be heededEditorialThe government did not throw a ‘protective ring’ around social care, and vulnerable people were left exposedTue 20 Oct 2026 13.44 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.52 EDTShareThe families of the 43,000 care home residents in the UK whose deaths between March 2020 and July 2022 were either caused by, or contributed to, by the Covid pandemic, have waited a long time for theofficial verdicton the way they were treated. The report published on Tuesday confirmed what many have been saying for a long time. In the first, panicked stages of lockdown, residents and their care workers were “something of an afterthought”. The “protective ring” around care homes referred to by Matt Hancock, the former health and care secretary, was a fiction.These are scathing judgments. What actually happened, starting in March 2020, was that about 30,000 people were discharged from hospital to care homes in order to free up beds for Covid-19 patients. Since there were not enough tests for all of them, those without symptoms were moved without being tested. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, there was no instruction to isolate newly arrived residents until the second half of April (in Scotland, this happened earlier).As Heather Hallett, the inquiry chair,pointed out, there is no way of knowing how many cases of Covid-19 were transmitted in this way. But this was one of a series of decisions that enabled the virus to “spread like wildfire”. Mr Hancock’s misleading description of the government’s policy has thus been firmly rejected. Plans for isolating newly arrived care home residents in any future pandemic are among the report’s key recommendations.View image in fullscreenHeather Hallett.Photograph: UK Covid-19 Inquiry/PABetter overall planning is another one. Thereporthighlights the fact that the social care minister at the time, Helen Whately, played no role in the decision to order the discharges, and calls for increased clarity around roles and responsibilities, along with new guidance around visitors. While there is no “ideal solution” in a situation where the risk of infection must be balanced against the benefit to residents of being visited, it concludes that restrictions were inappropriate and harmful in some cases.Two further recommendations address deaths explicitly. The report suggests that there could be exceptional circumstances in which an end-of-life visit is not allowed, but it is hard to imagine what these might be. Ministers must decide whether they agree. Lady Hallett’s call for mandatory end-of-life training for care home staff is more straightforward. Her finding that this was lacking is disturbing, given the rise in“do not resuscitate” orderson care home residents in 2020. While the inquiry found that there was no government policy of denying treatment to people based on age or disability, it confirms that such orders were applied inappropriately. Ministers must ensure that this never happens again.This is a report about a pandemic. But Andy Burnham, who has made social care reform an urgent priority, will surely recognise its wider implications. Arguably the report’s most important finding is the harm caused by the division between the NHS and social care, and the way that care home residents, andworkers, became a kind of collateral damage in the battle against the pandemic. A recommendation for a transformed relationship between the centralised health system and the locally led care system would have sat outside this inquiry’s remit. But when confronting many of the problems it describes, one obvious conclusion to be drawn is that social care needs a stronger voice at the heart of government.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Alberta’s referendum: Canada holds together – against Donald Trump | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Voters’ emphatic rejection of separation strengthens Mark Carney’s energy strategy in the face of a US trade war and threats
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Voters’ emphatic rejection of separation strengthens Mark Carney’s energy strategy in the face of a US trade war and threats
Content: A pro-Canada rally in Edmonton, Alberta, on 18 October.Photograph: Timon Johnson/The Canadian Press/APView image in fullscreenA pro-Canada rally in Edmonton, Alberta, on 18 October.Photograph: Timon Johnson/The Canadian Press/APOpinionCanadaThe Guardian view on Alberta’s referendum: Canada holds together – against Donald TrumpEditorialVoters’ emphatic rejection of separation strengthens Mark Carney’s energy strategy in the face of a US trade war and threatsTue 20 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.52 EDTShareCanadians are proving to be a voice of sanity. In roundlyrejectingthe idea of separating from Canada, voters in the oil- and gas-rich province of Alberta sensibly backed thenation-buildingstrategy of the prime minister, Mark Carney. He has put Alberta at the centre of his plan to make Canada an energy superpower that is “much less dependent on the United States”.Donald Trump’s trade war and threatslast weekto make Canada the 51st US state were a fillip for Mr Carney in Alberta, a landlocked western province where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular. The stakes were high: a successful separatist campaign would have handed Mr Trump leverage over Canada’s resource belt. The result instead lets Mr Carney cast Alberta’s mineral wealth as a national asset, rather than allow separatists to define it as a regional grievance.Albertans were not offered a binding secession vote. They rejected the idea of beginning the process towards such a vote. The early result – roughly75%against 25% – looks emphatic. For all the separatists’ talk of “success”, Albertans did not buy their tactical argument: that voting for a future referendum would strengthen the province’s hand against Ottawa. However, the sense of alienation in the province is profound: polls show thatAlbertansthink most of the country does not respect the region.View image in fullscreenMark Carney.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockAddressing that alienation has come at a worrying cost, both politically and environmentally. Mr Carney, who was raised in Alberta’s capital, Edmonton, made a series of pacts with the province’s premier, Danielle Smith. Heagreedto back a new 1m-barrel-a-day oil pipeline and tear up environmental rules. Mr Carney has to deliver tangible gains, or else the sizable faction that supports separatism within Ms Smith’s United Conservative party will entrench itself and look for future opportunities to act.Whatever replaces the “Let Alberta decide” movement will have an uphill struggle. In his bookThe Republic of Alberta, the journalist Tyler Dawson wrote that it has “no charismatic leader like René Lévesque, the suave, smoke-wreathed Quebec separatist who took his province to its 1980 secession referendum. There is no culturally entrenched canon of nationalist literature to fill Alberta bookshelves. The province has no unique language or race or faith that binds its residents together.” Yet victory this month for the Lévesque-founded Parti Québécois in provincial elections reveals that separatists can win power despite their raison d’etre beingunpopular.To those who witnessed the Brexit referendum, the Albertan poll offered adepressingrerun of nationalist gripes and political fantasy. The easy assurance that sovereignty can be recovered painlessly is wearily familiar. Keith Wilson, an architect of Alberta’s separatist movement, calling the task of founding a country “super easy” will prompt a sense of deja vu. Perhaps most importantly, Blackfoot leaders saying that separatists regarded treaty nations as a “speed bump” is a sign that the sovereigntists have not caught up with the fact that First Nations’ rights are belatedly being recognised as a critical part of Canada’s constitutional makeup.Canada’s unity is a political achievement that is continually negotiated among regional interests, Québécois nationhood, Indigenous people’s rights, new arrivals and the continental pull of the US. Paradoxically, theinsecuritythat characterises Canadians keeps them in check – and holds the nation together. Or as one of the country’s most famousnovelistsput it: Canada is “not a country you love, it is a country you worry about”.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Three ways to boost the UK’s fragile food security | Food security | The Guardian
description: Letters: Damien Conrad makes the case for local food hubs, Simon Tompsett promotes growing your own food, and Alex Robinson points to reducing waste
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Damien Conrad makes the case for local food hubs, Simon Tompsett promotes growing your own food, and Alex Robinson points to reducing waste
Content: Waste vegetables discarded after processing for retail sale, Burscough, LancashirePhotograph: EnVogue_Photo/AlamyView image in fullscreenWaste vegetables discarded after processing for retail sale, Burscough, LancashirePhotograph: EnVogue_Photo/AlamyFood securityLettersThree ways to boost the UK’s fragile food securityDamien Conradmakes the case for local food hubs,Simon Tompsettpromotes growing your own food, andAlex Robinsonpoints to reducing wasteTue 20 Oct 2026 13.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.08 EDTShareYour editorial is right to warn that Britain’s food system leaves us dangerously exposed (The Guardian view on food security: we have just-in-time, we need just-in-case, 15 October). But scarcity is only part of the problem. Across the country, good food exists; what is missing is the infrastructure to store it, aggregate it and get it to the people who need it.That failure runs through the whole food chain. Farmers are being pushed to the brink whilemillions of tonnes of edible produce go to waste. Independent retailers and wholesalers face rising costs, while schools, hospitals and community organisations want to provide healthier food but are constrained by tight budgets.Meanwhile, climate shocks are becoming more likely, farming methods remain unsustainable, and poor diets carry a vast economic cost (a shocking £300bn per year in the UK, or £10,000 per household, according to an analysis by the Food, Farming & Countryside Commission). The current system is neither resilient nor rational.There is a practical alternative: local food hubs that can accept surplus food but also enable buying in bulk, combining supplies and shortening the final mile. Hubs can create new markets for farmers, reduce waste and help communities access affordable, healthy food.Many such hubs appeared during lockdown, but too few survived. Thenew hub in Barking and Dagenhamshows what is possible. It redirects surplus food to organisations tackling the causes of poverty, while laying the foundations for collective purchasing and a fairer local supply chain.Britain does not lack food, ideas or demand. It lacks durable local infrastructure. If government wants a food system that is secure, healthy and sustainable, supporting food hubs should be central to the plan.Damien ConradPurley, LondonYour editorial on food security correctly identifies the problem, but centralised food stockpiles can only ever provide part of the solution. A key measure should be to encourage households to grow their own food. Allotments should be given greater protection from destruction by developers and local authorities, an example of which is the takeover of allotments in Teddington by Richmond upon Thames council to extend a cemetery. Feeding the living should take precedence over accommodating the dead.Simon TompsettTeddington, LondonYour editorial makes a compelling argument for government action, but it misses a powerful way we could build our resilience: cutting food waste. In the UK, we wastemore than 10m tonnes a year– over half of it in our homes, whichcosts a household of four £1,000 a year.We tend to hugely underestimate our own potential to make a difference. Halving edible food waste at home would save over 2m tonnes, and put £500 in householders’ pockets. Boosting surplus food distribution and addressing supply-chain waste could also save food and money, and take pressure off food growers.No one chooses to waste food. If the government heeds your editorial’s advice to act, then addressing the structural causes of food waste, backed by a national citizen-focused campaign, would give people benefits they can feel today while protecting us against the shocks of tomorrow.Alex RobinsonChief programmes officer, Waste and Resources Action ProgrammeHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Pleaseemailus your letter and it will be considered for publication in ourletterssection.Explore more on these topicsFood securityFood wasteFoodFarmingClimate crisislettersShareReuse this content

title: Like it or not, we have all benefited from the slave trade | Slavery | The Guardian
description: Letter: Phil Hamlyn Williams responds to criticism of the Church of England’s plans for reparations
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Phil Hamlyn Williams responds to criticism of the Church of England’s plans for reparations
Content: A sculpture of former slave and later abolitionist writer Olaudah Equiano at the International Slavery Museum in Liverpool.Photograph: Russell Contreras/APView image in fullscreenA sculpture of former slave and later abolitionist writer Olaudah Equiano at the International Slavery Museum in Liverpool.Photograph: Russell Contreras/APSlaveryLettersLike it or not, we have all benefited from the slave tradePhil Hamlyn Williamsresponds to criticism of the Church of England’s plans for reparationsTue 20 Oct 2026 13.06 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.07 EDTShareThank you for the excellent research into the rightwing backlash against the Church of England’s proposals for reparations (Lobbying, lawyers and a media blitz: the fight to kill the Church of England’s £100m slavery compensation fund, 13 October). May I offer observations in two areas?We are all beneficiaries of the slave trade, like it or not. The work that the Guardian is doing on the actions of its founders will enhance the historical record, but it is unlikely to change the broader picture identified by Eric Hobsbawm and others.Cheap cotton picked by enslaved people fired the Industrial Revolution. Everything else flowed from it. The need for machinery demanded coal and iron. These begat steam engines, the railways, the factory system.The benefits were not, and are not, evenly shared. My friend’s grandmother, who worked in a cotton mill at the age of 13, and so many like her suffered along with her brothers and sisters transported against their will from Africa.Yet industrialisation transformed our lives. Take the example of cotton: the historian Roger Osborne offers a very telling statistic in his book Iron, Steam & Money: “In 1790, 4 per cent of clothing in Europe was made of cotton … by 1890, it had grown to 73 per cent while the European population had roughly doubled to 400 million.”Industrialisation was not without its critics, not least John Ruskin. But its legacy is a world of disparity in wealth between and within nations, let alone the shadow of global warming. The evil of the slave trade lies at the heart of it. Individuals and families may have been responsible, but they are dead. It is with each of us in the postindustrial western world that discussion of reparations must start.Let me turn now to the Church of England. While working for a C of E diocese, I struggled with hostile parishes refusing to pay their parish share. I can only imagine the current outcry.May I suggest that it isn’t about reparations? These are people clinging to a disappearing world. Too few people are attending church to pay its way. As a bishop once said to me, these people have deep pockets, but very short arms. I suspect that pockets are no longer that deep.Would it be wrong to repeat the oft-misquoted Bible passage from the letter toTimothy? The love of money is the root of all evil.Phil Hamlyn WilliamsOld Dalby, LeicestershireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: A hankering for fresh herring and the proper British name for ‘sea bass’ | Fish | The Guardian
description: Letters: Elaine Hoare recalls her mother buying five fish for a shilling while Michael Heaton draws readers’ attention to an Americanism
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Elaine Hoare recalls her mother buying five fish for a shilling while Michael Heaton draws readers’ attention to an Americanism
Content: An article about bygone seafood recipes reminded Elaine Hoare of her local herring man in the 1950s.Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreenAn article about bygone seafood recipes reminded Elaine Hoare of her local herring man in the 1950s.Photograph: GettyFishLettersA hankering for fresh herring and the proper British name for ‘sea bass’Elaine Hoarerecalls her mother buying five fish for a shilling, whileMichael Heatondraws readers’ attention to an AmericanismTue 20 Oct 2026 13.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.06 EDTShareYour article (Whale meat curry for dinner? Study of bygone seafood recipes shows how UK tastes have narrowed, 13 October) reminded me of the call of “Fresh herring, fresh herring” from the herring man wheeling his cart in the back lane by our house in Douglas, Isle of Man, in the 1950s. My mother went to him with a bowl and bought herring for tea – five for a shilling, if I remember correctly. They were delicious. We cleaned them, scored each side three or four times, dipped them in oatmeal and fried them. We have a fish man from Grimsby call every Monday, but he never has herring.Elaine HoareChalfont St Giles, BuckinghamshireI am perplexed by the Marine Conservation Society’s suggestion that we should eat “wild-caught sea bass” as an alternative to cod (Scale back on hake and coley, seafood charity tells shoppers, 14 October). First, there is no such fish in Britain: “sea bass” is an Americanism they use to distinguish the marine bass from the several species of inedible freshwater bass in US rivers and lakes. We have only one species: bass. Second, it is insulting to suggest it as an alternative to cod. It is infinitely nicer than cod, but unsuited to battering.Michael HeatonWarminster, WiltshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
