title: Parish churches need support to preserve the tradition of choral evensong | Anglicanism | The Guardian
description: Letter: Dr Andrew James Sillett of St Giles’ church in Oxford says parish churches need help to flourish just as cathedrals do
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Dr Andrew James Sillett of St Giles’ church in Oxford says parish churches need help to flourish just as cathedrals do
Content: ‘If we focus only on preserving cathedrals, we risk overlooking the wider musical ecosystem that sustains English choral evensong.’Photograph: Gary Roebuck/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘If we focus only on preserving cathedrals, we risk overlooking the wider musical ecosystem that sustains English choral evensong.’Photograph: Gary Roebuck/AlamyAnglicanismLettersParish churches need support to preserve the tradition of choral evensongDr Andrew James Sillettof St Giles’ church in Oxford says parish churches need help to flourish just as cathedrals doTue 20 Oct 2026 13.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.06 EDTShareDr Coco Parkinson-Huggins (Letters, 13 October) is right to highlight the severe financial pressures facing England’s cathedrals and the threat that this poses to choral music. Yet the future of choral evensong depends not just on cathedrals. Across the country, there are parish churches that sustain choirs, train young organists and offer regular opportunities for children and adults to participate in this living tradition.I am a churchwarden and singer at St Giles’ church in Oxford, where locally recruited choirs of boys, girls and teenagers sing choral evensong every Sunday. Alongside these choirs, around 40 organ students are currently learning through the church, and we are investing in a major new pipe organ to support future generations of musicians.Parish churches often face many of the same financial pressures as cathedrals, but with fewer resources and less professional support. However, they remain uniquely placed to recruit locally and adapt quickly to changing circumstances.At St Giles’ church, we are developing new ways of widening access to choral and organ education that should prove just as important to the future of the tradition as preserving historic institutions themselves.If we focus only on preserving cathedrals, we risk overlooking the wider musical ecosystem that sustains English choral evensong. This tradition will flourish only if both cathedral and parish churches are enabled to pass it on to future generations.Dr Andrew James SillettChurchwarden, St Giles’ church, OxfordExplore more on these topicsAnglicanismChristianityReligionHeritagelettersShareReuse this content

title: Mac Allister double sparks Liverpool’s thrilling comeback win over Villarreal | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Ronald Araújo and Florian Wirtz were also on target as Liverpool hit back from 2-0 down to stun Villarreal 4-3 in the Champions League
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Ronald Araújo and Florian Wirtz were also on target as Liverpool hit back from 2-0 down to stun Villarreal 4-3 in the Champions League
Content: Alexis Mac Allister (left) hugs Kostas Tsimikas after giving Liverpool the lead with his second goal of the night.Photograph: Ryan Browne/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAlexis Mac Allister (left) hugs Kostas Tsimikas after giving Liverpool the lead with his second goal of the night.Photograph: Ryan Browne/ShutterstockChampions LeagueMac Allister double sparks Liverpool’s thrilling comeback win over VillarrealAndy Hunterat AnfieldTue 20 Oct 2026 17.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 18.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndoni Iraola and Iñigo Pérez parked a long and close friendship in the buildup to their first competitive confrontation as coaches. The old Athletic Bilbao teammates will have a humdinger of aChampions Leaguecontest to dissect once communications are restored. Liverpool, ignited by Rio Ngumoha, recovered from two goals down against Villarreal to maintain their 100% record plus their gathering momentum.Alexis Mac Allister struck twice, Florian Wirtz capped recent improvement with his first goal of the season while Liverpool were dreadful for the opening 30 minutes, transformed after the break and fretting in stoppage time after Tani Oluwaseyi had volleyed in a third forVillarreal. The game flipped on Sergi Cardona’s mistake and Ronald Araújo’s equaliser with the final touch of the first half. “We weren’t able to handle the emotion tonight,” conceded Villarreal coach Pérez.Doué and Vitinha burn bright as brittle Barcelona come unstuck against PSGRead moreBut the lasting impression was of Ngumoha seizing responsibility in the absence of big names and drivingLiverpoolon at the age of 18. The winger was electric, the difference maker, and from the right-wing role that he is still adapting to. He supplied the cross for Araújo’s all-important leveller and unravelled the Villarreal defence for Mac Allister’s second, Liverpool’s third on a rollercoaster of a night and performance.“Rio didn’t have it easy tonight,” said Iraola. “They demanded a lot of him defensively with their left-back attacking but he was very difficult to stop. If you can put him in one-v-ones he can make space and produce things, like the lovely assist for Alexis, and endurance-wise he is able to play more and more minutes. He is eager to improve and if he can add things to his game he’ll become the full package.”The regular phone calls between Iraola and Pérez had ceased in the days leading up to the fixture. Had they continued the Liverpool head coach might have told his opposite number to bring a coat and not wear a short-sleeved polo shirt on a day of incessant rain. Iraola rested Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola. A fourth game in 10 days explained the omissions of Wirtz and Barcola, who had featured heavily in the previous three, while Isak’s workload was being carefully managed after his recent thigh injury.Liverpool’s much-changed team fell behind quickly. An error-strewn start by Virgil van Dijk was responsible, and also in keeping with a ponderous opening half hour from the hosts. Villarreal passed their way around Anfield with style and precious little resistance.The Liverpool captain presented Georges Mikautadze with an immediate opportunity when he misjudged a long clearance by Renato Veiga. Van Dijk’s poor touch almost released the Georgia international striker through on goal but Jérémy Jacquet closed off that route. Van Dijk’s second slip followed moments later, and this time there was no reprieve. The defender attempted to head another Veiga long ball back into the safe arms of Alisson. He found Mikautadze instead and Villarreal’s No 9 pounced expertly, controlling well before rolling the ball under the Liverpool keeper. There were apologies all round from Van Dijk.View image in fullscreenAlexis Mac Allister heads home to score Liverpool’s opening goal.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Ed Sykes/Apl/SportsphotoVillarreal doubled their lead with a goal that encapsulated the start made by both teams – the visitors passing their way through Liverpool’s midfield and picking holes in their high defensive line, with the home side slow to react. Pape Gueye, Alberto Moleiro and Nathan Saliba combined to send their rampaging left-back, Cardona, through on goal. Played onside by Kostas Tsimikas, the full-back beat Alisson with a finish a striker would have been proud of.Cardona’s defending was much less impressive as Liverpool clawed their way back into the contest. The recovery commenced when Mac Allister rose superbly to meet a Tsimikas corner and flicked an unstoppable header into the unguarded side of Peter Gulacsi’s goal.Villarreal’s comfort vanished entirely when Ngumoha clipped a cross towards the far post following another Tsimikas corner. Cardona checked his surroundings, then inexplicably let the ball bounce behind him, and right into the spot where Araújo was lurking. The on-loan defender headed home for the second successive week in the Champions League and celebrated with a mass pile-on with fans in the Anfield Road Stand.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAraújo was withdrawn at the interval because Iraola felt Liverpool would match up better to Villarreal with Ryan Gravenberch at right-back and Wirtz restored to the forward line. And so it proved. Liverpool improved vastly after the restart with Ngumoha and Wirtz a constant, marauding threat.View image in fullscreenRonald Araújo heads home Liverpool’s second goal in first-half stoppage time.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersNgumoha took the acclaim of the Kop after creating Mac Allister’s second of the night with a sparkling run down the right. It was some one-two that brought Liverpool the lead. Mac Allister floated a pass out to the winger, whose first touch brought the ball under control and took him away from Cardona in the same movement. He then left the substitute Juan Foyth in his wake before pulling back a pass from the byline for the incoming midfielder to smash a shot in off the underside of Gulacsi’s crossbar.Wirtz completed the comeback after Tsimikas and Cody Gakpo had combined to create space for the playmaker inside the area. The Germany international drilled a clinical left-footed finish inside the Villarreal keeper’s far corner. Oluwaseyi created a nervous finale when converting a cross from the former Newcastle forward Ayoze Pérez but Liverpool held firm. “We started too relaxed and we were too relaxed at 4-2,” Iraola said. “But against a really good Villarreal team I give value and importance to this win.”Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueLiverpoolVillarrealEuropean club footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Doué and Vitinha burn bright as brittle Barcelona come unstuck against PSG | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Amid an ongoing state of civil unrest, Paris turned its attention to football as Vitinha’s late strike helped PSG to a 4-2 win against Barcelona
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Amid an ongoing state of civil unrest, Paris turned its attention to football as Vitinha’s late strike helped PSG to a 4-2 win against Barcelona
Content: Vitinha celebrates after putting PSG back in front late on.Photograph: Matthieu Mirville/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenVitinha celebrates after putting PSG back in front late on.Photograph: Matthieu Mirville/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockChampions LeagueDoué and Vitinha burn bright as brittle Barcelona come unstuck against PSGBarney Ronayat Parc des PrincesTue 20 Oct 2026 17.08 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 18.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFire, noise, fury, a sense of empty energy. And across town, a football match too. Do any of these randomly pitched autumnal Champions League fixtures mean anything? Probably not when you’reParis Saint-Germainand Barcelona, and the only game in town is risk-free TV income and a semi-guaranteed place in the knockout stuff.But this was still a dazzling occasion at the Parc des Princes, where the champions of France and Spain played out a light, open, frictionless, exhibition-style game of football. PSG finished 4-2 winners, having been pegged back to 2-2 midway through the second half. But this was also a game where the score almost did not seem to matter, and where the only really hard message was the frailty of theBarcelonabackline and PSG’s thrilling attacking energy in these midweek A-games.Foden hat-trick helps Manchester City cut through noise and crush AEK AthensRead more“Debris! Debris! DEBRIS!” the insanely loud PA announcer screamed into his mic before kick-off, in what appeared to be a poor-taste tribute to the current state of the nation’s capital, although it may also have been “du bruit”.In the hours leading up to this game France’s interior minister had specifically ruled out postponing the whole thing due to the ongoing state of civil unrest, the kind of statement that is no doubt intended to sound reassuring, but which also generates its own kind of whiplash.Paris is burning. Paris is always burning. No, but Parisreally is burning this time. The main site of the violence of the last few days is three miles east of the Parc, which lurks by the ring road in one of Paris’s slightlynégligéinner quarters, rising up like a vast concrete alien doughnut in between the townhouses.On matchday it required a degree of cognitive dissonance to take in these two opposing spectacles. On one hand the piles of charred bikes and the mass looting which has, in reassuringly Parisian style, seemed to focus on elite high-fashion brands. Chanel will rue the day.In the middle of which Paris also hosted this glittering treat of a football match, stuffed with so many throwaway little delicacies, like an elite artisan patisserie. Before kick-off there were leaping tongues of flame, a laser show spectacular, and a vast tifo at one end showing a ghoulish PSG serial killer type attacking the Barcelona badge with his blood-soaked chainsaw. The message here seemed to be: we are confident. We believe in our process. And we will hack you to death.View image in fullscreenDésiré Doué strikes to give PSG the lead in the first half.Photograph: Julien de Rosa/AFP/Getty ImagesFrom the start this was a high-grade, disarmingly open game. For Hansi Flick’s Barcelona it represented a genuine test of method. Here we have an elite team that plays with a studied disregard for some of the tenets of positional defensive play. We will press forward and trust what lies behind. We will also give up on the basic idea of marking pretty much from the kick-off, as it turned out.With one minute gone PSG should have scored. A quick diagonal passing move from right to left put Khvicha Kvaratskhelia in space. His shot pinged off a post and back to an offside Ousmane Dembélé, who shinned wide of an open goal.There was a fury to PSG in those opening minutes, the front players finding angles and free channels. Pedri and Marc Bernal in central midfield took a while to settle for Barça. Bernal is pure La Masia, a baby-faced 19-year-old Catalan, misleadingly so, as he also has the physique of a rugby union flanker. And Pedri is of course the kind of footballer who glides through these occasions, so casual you half expect to look down and notice he’s playing in flip-flops and holding a Calippo.Before long Barcelona were making chances of their own, Dani Olmo setting off on a couple of surging deep runs, Anthony Gordon almost getting on the end of a cutback.João Cancelo was booked with 16 minutes gone for a lunge on Désiré Doué, a disastrous state of affairs for any full-back faced with this nightmare of feints and fast-twitch feet. And two minutes later Dembélé was off, injured chasing the ball, replaced by Ferran Torres. Maybe he should play a bit more, get match fit.View image in fullscreenXavi Espart scores his first Champions League goal to equalise for Barcelona at 1-1.Photograph: David Ramos/Uefa/Getty ImagesStill the game just zinged from end to end. Raphinha had a close-range shot blocked by Matvey Safonov after a nice pass from Gordon. PSG had three shots blocked or saved in the space of six seconds on 28 minutes, Joan García saving brilliantly low down.And on 38 minutes PSG deservedly took the lead. The goal was in keeping with the game, expertly hi-tech but also strangely easy and open. Lamine Yamal essayed an ambitious chipped clearance. João Neves took the ball back. It fell to Doué, and he had time to jink inside, feel the space around him, and shoot low inside the post.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPSG were bossing this by now, Kvaratskhelia running up and down the gears on the left, such a beautifully inventive presence, socks crumpled down around his ankles, all mooching straggly menace, as though the base player from Shed Seven has reinvented himself as a state of the art elite European inside forward.By the break Barcelona were hanging on, overrun in midfield. And the second half was more of the same: mobile, relentless, high-grade product, lovely attacking interchanges, occasional large spaces in the Barcelona backline.Doué forced another fine close-range save, played in by Vitinha. On 55 minutes Barcelona equalised, Xavi Espart galloping through the left side of the PSG defence and smashing a shot into the net off the hands of Safonov. The PA announcer gave the goal to Lamine Yamal, because, well, great branding. But it was Espart’s first in Europe, the second of his career. He’s 19, hyper-versatile, another dreamy Catalan youth-teamer.Barça brought on Rodri, absent from the starting XI, Flick admitted afterwards, solely with the weekend’sclásicoin mind. For a while order was restored, Rodri strolling around like the only grownup on the pitch.View image in fullscreenVitinha fires in from the edge of the box as PSG retake the lead late on.Photograph: Dave Winter/ShutterstockBut PSG always have tools to hurt you. Doué sliced open the right side again and crossed for Fabián Ruiz to hit the post from six yards out. From the corner Lucas Hernandez had the space to leap and produce a wonderful finish, thumped off the meaty part of the forehead high into the top corner.Seven minutes later it was 2-2. This was a strange goal, scored by Lamine Yamal after a wonderful run in from the right and a lofted near-post finish that in the moment either looked like a mistake from Safonov or a moment of pure invention.Two minutes after that it was 3-2 to PSG as the game kept on running to its own speed, this time a controlled first-time shot from Vitinha, seizing on a bouncing ball near the edge of the box. Ruiz added a fourth four minutes from the end.The game against Lyon at the weekend will mitigate against the usual round of rotations, and injuries did begin to bite a little here. But PSG still finished like a machine built for these occasions, operating always with strength in reserve, and quite clearly the most potent midweek team in Europe once again.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueParis Saint-GermainBarcelonaEuropean club footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Football regulator has ‘absolute power’ to force Manchester City sale if verdict upheld | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: The Independent Football Regulator’s chair, David Kogan, has said the watchdog has powers to make Manchester City’s owners sell the club
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Independent Football Regulator’s chair, David Kogan, has said the watchdog has powers to make Manchester City’s owners sell the club
Content: David Kogan, chair of the Independent Football Regulator, is awaiting the outcome of Manchester City’s appeal before commenting on a potential further investigation.Photograph: Jon Super/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDavid Kogan, chair of the Independent Football Regulator, is awaiting the outcome of Manchester City’s appeal before commenting on a potential further investigation.Photograph: Jon Super/ShutterstockManchester CityFootball regulator has ‘absolute power’ to force Manchester City sale if verdict upheldIFR chair David Kogan insists regulator has power to actCity have appealed against Premier League’s chargesPress AssociationTue 20 Oct 2026 19.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 20.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Independent Football Regulator (IFR) will have “absolute power” to force Manchester City’s owners to sell if they are ultimately found to have run the club improperly, the watchdog’s chair has said.Manchester City have beenfound guilty of circumventing Premier League rulesby an independent commission, which found they set up “sham” commercial arrangements to inflate revenues or reduce costs by over £900m over a nine-season period.David Squires on … Manchester City sailing into unknown Premier League watersRead moreThey were also found to have made “concerted efforts” to “stop and frustrate” the Premier League’s investigation into those arrangements. City have lodged an appeal, claiming the verdict “contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”.David Kogan, the chair of the IFR, told podcastThe Rest Is Footballit was premature to talk about any action his organisation might take while the appeal was ongoing. Kogan did confirm, though, that the IFR had “absolute power” to force a sale by the club’s ownership, if that was felt to be appropriate.“We have the power to ask an owner to step away from a club if we believe that they run a club in a way that is neither fit, fair or done with propriety,” Kogan said. Asked if an owner could refuse to divest, Kogan replied: “No, no, no. We’ve got absolute power to do so.”On the possibility of the IFR investigating City, Kogan said: “I am not going to get pushed into making any judgement on this until we’ve seen all of those questions being answered. Then we will have to decide whether we’re going to mount our own investigation and come to a conclusion on that and what we’re going to do. And pre-empting that would be a colossal mistake.”Manchester City are majority-owned by Abu Dhabi United Group (Adug), an investment vehicle owned by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the Abu Dhabi royal family.Koganhas already pledged to resignif there is any political interference in any investigation the IFR may undertake into City, amid concerns it could create a diplomatic issue between the United Kingdom and the United Arab Emirates.Kogan’s comments came amid fresh scrutiny of Manchester City’s finances by the UK’s accounting watchdog. In a letter to the House of Commons business, innovation, science and trade committee, the Financial Reporting Council (FRC) confirmed it assumed “regulatory consideration” of the matter on 30 September.The FRC said it was examining the independent commission’s findings and making “preliminary enquiries” to establish whether there were grounds for a formal investigation.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityPremier LeagueFootball politicsBusinessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Carrick insists Manchester United board back him after Ten Hag points to ‘toxic culture’ | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Erik ten Hag has claimed Cristiano Ronaldo ‘let the team down’ during their time together at Manchester United
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Erik ten Hag has claimed Cristiano Ronaldo ‘let the team down’ during their time together at Manchester United
Content: ‘I have a really good relationship with everybody at the club,’ said Michael Carrick. ‘We’ve got to win games of football.’Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreen‘I have a really good relationship with everybody at the club,’ said Michael Carrick. ‘We’ve got to win games of football.’Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAManchester UnitedCarrick insists Manchester United board back him after Ten Hag points to ‘toxic culture’Manager acknowledges he needs to start winning gamesTen Hag accuses Cristiano Ronaldo of letting club downJamie Jacksonin ComoTue 20 Oct 2026 17.13 EDTFirst published on Tue 20 Oct 2026 06.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Carrick believes Manchester United’s board continue to back him, although the manager admits he must start winning matches to keep his job. Carrick also denied there is a toxic culture at the club, after Erik ten Hag’s claim there had been when he was manager.Carrick’s side travel to Como on Wednesday for their third Champions League game, aiming for a third victory of the season in all competitions. Sunday’s 1-1 draw at Leeds left United 13th in the Premier League, having won only once.Cristiano Ronaldo receives 30-day suspension and £215 fine over Portugal walkoutRead moreTheir only other success was last month’s4-0 home win against Sabah, of Azerbaijan, in the Champions League. Carrick was asked on Tuesday if he feels backed by the executive.“Yeah – why wouldn’t I?” said the 45-year-old. “I’m in this position, I have a really good relationship with everybody at the club. We’ve got to win games of football and that’s what we’re striving to do.”Despite the poor results Carrick has not sought reassurance from the hierarchy. “Certainly not. I don’t need any reassurance,” he said. “It’s pretty clear. I know the role, my responsibilities. I know we’ve got to win ­football games for everything to flow and ­everything to fall into place.”Ten Hag was Carrick’s predecessor from April 2022 to October 2024. During his tenure the Dutchman claimed that the executive did not support him regarding some disciplinary ­matters. In early 2024 Jim ­Ratcliffe, who had recently become the largest ­single minority stakeholder, assumed control of the football department.View image in fullscreenErik ten Hag and Cristiano Ronaldo in 2022. ‘He let the team down, and he let me down,’ the former Manchester United manager said.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/Reuters“They are continuing the toxic culture, they fuel it, they give power to the players,” Ten Hag told the Athletic, referring to his time in charge.Ten Hag claimed thatCristiano Ronaldo“let the team down” ­when the Dutchman was managing United. The ­forward’s second spell at the club featured him walking out twice.“He let the team down and he let me down, because we planned with him,” said Ten Hag. He also questioned ­Ronaldo’s commitment, saying that after United were beaten 4-0 at Brentford in the second game of his tenure, the ­Portuguese refused to complete a run in training.“I confronted him with this,” Ten Hag said. “Many times I say: ‘Ronnie, everyone wants to work for you to bring you in the right position, but if you can’t bring yourself in the box, you can’t score.”Carrick, who became interim manager in January and was appointed permanently in May, was asked if he has encountered toxicity at United. “No, I haven’t. The players, the staff, they’ve given us everything that they could give,” he said. “I couldn’t be happier with the togetherness.”Ten Hag led United to the FA Cup in 2024, but claimed the owners then failed to meet promises made during talks that led to him agreeing a contract extension.He said: “They promised me ­loyalty, they promised me backing, they promised communication, that we get aligned. We spoke about the issues. But the promises, they didn’t keep. “I said: ‘No selling Scott ­McTominay.’ And in the end they sold him. I got, of course, very embarrassed and disappointed.”Carrick was asked if Ten Hag’s comments about the leadership raised any red flags. In answering he mentioned Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and the chief executive, Omar Berrada.Raya does not care if Arsenal are deemed ‘boring’ as Arteta defends style of playRead more“Not for me, that’s Erik’s opinion, it’s totally wrong for me to comment or get involved, it’s nothing to do with me at that stage. We’re pretty stable. There’s certain conversations we have that we’re really clear with, with Jason with Omar, the owners, and to the players. It’s really important we’re all pulling in the same direction.”Carrick will be without nine players for Como: Leny Yoro is ­suspended and Ayden Heaven is ill, while Luke Shaw, Lisandro Martínez, Kobbie Mainoo, Marcus Rashford, Benjamin Sesko, Patrick Dorgu and Manuel Ugarte are injured.The absence of five frontline defenders (Yoro, Shaw, Heaven, Martínez and Dorgu) will force Carrick to field an unfamiliar backline that may include Matthijs de Ligt, who has not played since last November due to a back problem. An appearance for the 19-year-old left-back, Harry Amass, is also being considered.There is a severe weather warning for lightning and rain in Como on Wednesday that may affect the 5.45pm kick-off.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedErik ten HagCristiano RonaldonewsShareReuse this content

title: Minhas rips through England as Brook’s men wilt against Pakistan in tri-series opener | Cricket | The Guardian
description: The 21-year-old Arafat Minhas scored 59 and then took six for 40 as England were thrashed in their tri-series opener against Pakistan in Rawalpindi
Author: Taha Hashim
Headline: The 21-year-old Arafat Minhas scored 59 and then took six for 40 as England were thrashed in their tri-series opener against Pakistan in Rawalpindi
Content: Arafat Minhas of Pakistan (centre left) celebrates with his teammates after sealing victory against England.Photograph: Aamir Qureshi/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenArafat Minhas of Pakistan (centre left) celebrates with his teammates after sealing victory against England.Photograph: Aamir Qureshi/AFP/Getty ImagesCricketMinhas rips through England as Brook’s men wilt against Pakistan in tri-series openerEngland collapse after fast start to run chaseArafat Minhas scores 59, then takes six for 40Taha HashimTue 20 Oct 2026 12.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 18.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter the embarrassment of their English summer, this was a welcome sight for Pakistan. A contest in front of their own, no Ollie Robinson to wobble down a lethal Dukes, and a format they are far more comfortable with. The result was an impressive victory in Rawalpindi against England, who fell 87 runs short in their first match of this one-day international tri-series.At the centre was Arafat Minhas, playing in only his fifth ODI but already making a serious splash, finishing with astounding figures of six for 40. And he can bat too. The 21-year-old began with a half-century from No 7, resuscitating Pakistan’s innings alongside another newcomer, Hasan Nawaz, as 81 for four turned into a total of 302.England collapse to 87-run defeat by Pakistan in men’s tri-series cricket ODI – as it happenedRead moreMinhas’s left-arm spin was up next, accounting for Harry Brook with a magical delivery as England crumbled in reply, a decent position of 165 for three becoming 215 all out. Fittingly, Minhas was the closer, showing off another skill: a direct hit to run out Gus Atkinson ended the game with 11.2 overs unused.England have powered their way to 350-plus totals in three series deciders this year, but all of those were in the first innings, with work needed on how to handle the chase. Brook lamented his side’s batting against spin. “We were probably a little bit too careful against the spinners,” he said, arguing that Pakistan’s total was under par. “We can probably put them under more pressure in stages.”Nawaz performed the day’s first rescue act after a lethargic start by Pakistan with the bat. Fakhar Zaman clipped the first ball of the innings to midwicket, and while the ball pinged off Babar Azam’s middle against the quicks, the early introduction of Will Jacks’ off-spin stripped away the flow. He fell innocuously, bowled by Jacks for 34 while playing off the back foot.Salman Agha continued his bizarre story arc over the last two months. A fill-in captain for the Headingley Test in August, Agha was dropped from Pakistan’s lineup for the second Test and then discarded from the squad for the third. He returned home to hit a triple hundred in first-class cricket, lost the captaincy of Pakistan’s T20 team, then struck a match-winning ton against Sri Lanka on Sunday in the tri-series opener. A confident start here was quickly followed by a strange dismissal, sweeping a full toss by Adil Rashid into Atkinson’s hands.View image in fullscreenJoe Root is clean bowled by Pakistan's Naseem Shah.Photograph: Aamir Qureshi/AFP/Getty ImagesPakistan needed a shake. Nawaz immediately welcomed Rashid’s flight, sending the ball down the ground for six, his first of three against the veteran leg-spinner. The 24-year-old has plenty of power on him, and he built valuable stands with Saad Baig and Minhas to make up for the failings at the top. Nawaz, dropped on 28 by Atkinson, closed his bashing on 79, the economical Jamie Overton surprising him with an 87mph yorker.Minhas was less brutal than Nawaz but led Pakistan’s final push with 59 off 58, and Faheem Ashraf powered up with a 26-ball 39, with 91 coming off the last 10 overs, four off the final ball to push past 300.With the injured Jacob Bethell missing this series, Tom Banton has another run of games to complicate the question over England’s opening pair. He put on 91 for the first wicket with Ben Duckett and went to a half-century, but the dream of back-to-back ODI tons closed on 57 when he slapped Minhas to midwicket in the 19th over.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSomething special was required for Brook, five of his 15 international hundreds having come against Pakistan. Minhas provided it with Brook on five, a fizzing delivery with enough turn there to knock back off stump.Pakistan lacked any real pace with the ball against Englandin the recent Test series, but Haris Rauf and Naseem Shah were missing then. Rauf’s short ball prompted fatal mistakes from Duckett and Sam Curran, while Naseem skidded one through the defence of a well-set Joe Root.But this was Minhas’s night. While Jordan Cox was undone by another fine delivery for a leg-before, Overton gifted a simple catch to long-on. Jacks, developing his reputation as a finisher, remained, the game still alive while he stuck it out. But he found midwicket – a familiar dismissal on the day – and Minhas trapped Rashid in front moments later. Pakistan have found one.Explore more on these topicsCricketPakistan cricket teamEngland cricket teammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: British Cycling’s best world championships since 2012 overshadowed by off-track issues | Cycling | The Guardian
description: Redundancies beckon as British Cycling restructures while former cyclists and employees raise concerns over return of ‘toxic culture’
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Redundancies beckon as British Cycling restructures while former cyclists and employees raise concerns over return of ‘toxic culture’
Content: British cycling flourished at the world track championships but the backdrop of alleged misconduct and redundancies have cast a shadow over this success.Photograph: Zac Williams/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBritish cycling flourished at the world track championships but the backdrop of alleged misconduct and redundancies have cast a shadow over this success.Photograph: Zac Williams/SWpix.com/ShutterstockCyclingBritish Cycling’s best world championships since 2012 overshadowed by off-track issuesRedundancies beckon as British Cycling restructures while former cyclists and employees raise concerns over return of ‘toxic culture’Jeremy WhittleTue 20 Oct 2026 13.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 18.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish Cycling’s most successful world track championships campaign in over a decade, in which they topped the medal table in the first qualifying event for the 2028Olympic Games, was achieved against a backdrop of allegations of misconduct and looming redundancies.Despite a traumatic buildup to the championships in Shanghai, with star sprinter Matt Richardsonwithdrawn from competitionon the eve of the event due to allegations of “discriminatory remarks”, the British squad recovered to win six gold medals, three silver and three bronze.British Cycling under scrutiny over allegations of ‘toxic culture’ in leadership teamRead moreAnna Morris stepped into the void left by Richardson’s sudden exit, winning three world titles – joining past triple gold medallists Victoria Pendleton and Bradley Wiggins – while Millie Couzens and Erin Boothman won the individual pursuit and Madison, respectively.It was Team GB’s most successful track world championships since Melbourne in 2012, when they also claimed six gold medals.Richardson’s withdrawal, however, sparked further allegations during the championships of discrimination and bullying in the wider organisation at a time when BritishCyclingis also in the midst of a restructuring process expected to lead to multiple redundancies.Attributing the job losses to the body’s new strategy of creating “a stronger organisation”, a British Cycling spokesperson said that the changes “will result in some roles being removed” but that it would be inappropriate to put a figure on those potentially at risk during the restructure.Sources have told the Guardian, however, that up to 17 roles within the national body are considered at risk.It was also revealed last week by the Times, that in a survey commissioned by former British Cycling CEO, Jon Dutton, 31% of riders and staff,when asked whetherthey had “witnessed or experienced thoughtless, inappropriate, or unacceptable behaviour”, responded in the affirmative.When describing the culture of their world-class programme, “driven” was the most commonly used word among the riders and staff, but second-most prominent, alongside “supportive”, was “toxic”.The shadow of a “toxic culture” then lengthened after a LinkedIn post by the former commercial manager, Jack Lindsay, was supported by others with recent experience of British Cycling.View image in fullscreenAnna Morris won three gold medals for Britain at the world track championships.Photograph: Kacper Pempel/ReutersLindsay said that he had complained formally over bullying, but that there was “no action against the individual I had sought to hold responsible”.He added that he had “repeatedly raised incidents of bullying by a member of the executive with members of the senior leadership team, and that management had chosen to address them informally”.“The high-performance programme receives millions of pounds each year in public funding,” Lindsay said. “Athletes, staff, sponsors and the public have a legitimate interest in whether the organisation upholds the standards it promotes.”Lindsay’s post was supported by Georgia Holt, a Commonwealth Games medallist and paracycling world champion, who said that she had “unfortunately experienced the same toxic culture”.Holt described the allegations of bullying as a “peek under the rug at a large scale operation that hasn’t had significant scrutiny because the medals keep coming in”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNeither British Cycling nor UK Sport were able to confirm the date of Lindsay’s complaint being raised, nor the details of any action that was taken. However the Guardian has confirmed that the staff Culture Survey was implemented by Dutton in a direct response to Lindsay’s complaint.Richardson is now under investigation although British Cycling has declined to state when it is expected to conclude, or whether the findings will be made public. UK Sport reiterated that “the highest standards of integrity and athlete welfare are non-negotiable when it comes to UK Sport’s commitment to winning well”.It is a decade since Jess Varnish madeallegations of sexism and bullyingagainst then technical director Shane Sutton. He denied the accusations but Varnish’scomplaint was upheld. Those allegations led to the commissioning of an independent review of British Cycling’s culture in 2017.In the aftermath of that review, which revealed a “culture of fear” and a “dysfunctional leadership”, the national body set out to develop “common values, leadership principles and employee behaviours that British Cycling lives by”.But sources with recent experience of British Cycling have told the Guardian that past cultural issues have now returned.On the condition of anonymity, one former British Cycling employee, who also worked in an advisory capacity, said that “the problems went round and round, people left, others took their place and no progress was made. The only thing that mattered was more medals, as with that the budget was secure. The culture was based solely on the result and how that was achieved came under no scrutiny.”In response to the criticisms of culture, British Cycling said that it was “committed to delivering our strategy and ambitions in an environment where people feel supported, valued and able to do their best work.“Our most recent staff Culture Survey recorded a 71.2% favourability score across the organisation, which is categorised as ‘very good’. However, we recognise some colleagues have raised concerns, and we are committed to listening and acting wherever this is the case.“The GB Cycling Team has developed an action plan that is being implemented, alongside wider work across British Cycling focused on leadership, development, feedback and wellbeing.”Dutton, who was also a director of Grand Départ GB to oversee the visit of the 2027 men’s and women’s Tour de France, left British Cycling this summer. He was appointed as CEO of the British Olympic Association in January this year, assuming his new role in July.Explore more on these topicsCyclingTeam GBOlympic GamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m in a bad place’: Mark Allen says his snooker career may be over after defeat | Snooker | The Guardian
description: Mark Allen has said he ‘doesn’t see a future with snooker in it’ in an emotional interview after losing his first match since April’s Crucible semi-final defeat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Mark Allen has said he ‘doesn’t see a future with snooker in it’ in an emotional interview after losing his first match since April’s Crucible semi-final defeat
Content: Mark Allen’s first-round loss in Belfast was his first appearance at a tournament since an agonising semi-final defeat at the Crucible in April.Photograph: George Wood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMark Allen’s first-round loss in Belfast was his first appearance at a tournament since an agonising semi-final defeat at the Crucible in April.Photograph: George Wood/Getty ImagesSnooker‘I’m in a bad place’: Mark Allen says his snooker career may be over after defeatFormer world No 1 loses 4-2 to Jordan Brown in Belfast‘I don’t see a future with snooker in it,’ says tearful AllenPress AssociationTue 20 Oct 2026 14.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 17.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark Allen said he was in a “bad place” and his snooker career could be over after losing to Jordan Brown in the first round of theNorthern IrelandOpen in Belfast.The 40-year-old was playing his first match since his world championship semi-final loss to Wu Yize in April. Allen missed a match-ball black off the spot at 16-15 in front and went on to lose the deciding frame to Wu, who went on to win the title.Allen has since stayed away from the tour due to personal issues that he has kept private – although they are understood not to relate directly to his Crucible defeat. After his 4-2 loss to Brown, a close friend who is also from Antrim, Allen indicated he is set to take another long break from the sport – and could make it permanent.Inan emotional interview with TNT Sportsafter the match, Allen said he was “really overwhelmed”, adding: “I’m in a bad place at the minute, so even just to go out there and try was tough.”“I think if I wasn’t playing Jordan I wouldn’t have come back,” the former world No 1 said. “I felt like if I was going to play one last time, playing here at the Waterfront, where it all started in 2005, against one of my best mates – I thought that was a better way to sign out.”Asked if he was serious about his threat to retire from professional snooker, Allen confirmed his view and continued: “I’ve been flooded with support but the problems are within. I just don’t see a future with snooker in it, if I’m honest.“It’s sad to say, because it’s all I’ve loved to do since I was 12 but the last few months has been really difficult and it’s put snooker into perspective for me. At the minute I’m just trying to survive.”Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueIn a separate interview with BBC Sport NI, Allen said: “The last three months have been really, really difficult and I think even just being here today is an achievement. I am not going to announce [retirement] right now after a defeat, but it is something I have been contemplating for a while.”Allen, currently ranked No 12 in the world after his hiatus, has won 12 ranking tournaments in his career, including the 2022 UK Championship and two Northern Ireland Open titles. He has reached the world championship semi-finals three times, and lifted the Masters trophy in 2018.Brown, whose sole ranking title came at the 2021 Welsh Open, said: “First and foremost it’s just great to see Mark back playing. He obviously came through a tough time off the table and I’m with him every step of the way, like everybody is.“We’re all behind him. I miss him and I love him and we all just want to see him healthy and well and playing the game that he loves so much,” Brown added. “He’s a great player and a great guy.”Both the WorldSnookerTour and the sport’s governing body, the WPBSA, have provided support to Allen and have indicated their desire to continue helping him in any way they can.Allen is one of a number of high-profile players to exit this year’s Northern Ireland Open in the first round. Shaun Murphy was beaten 4-2 by Wales’ Liam Davies, with Mark Selby losing to Louis Heathcote by the same scoreline.The world No 1, Zhao Xintong, also lost 4-2 to Chinese compatriot Gao Yang while Neil Robertson went down 4-1 to Ricky Walden. Ronnie O’Sullivan also fell at the first hurdle, beaten 4-3 by Cheung Ka Wai of Hong Kong. The defending champion, Jack Lisowski, did advance to the last 32 with a 4-1 win over Huang Jiahao.Explore more on these topicsSnookerNorthern IrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Freer’ Red Roses resolve to come back stronger after Canada end epic run | England women's rugby union team | The Guardian
description: A first defeat in four years could be liberating for England after so long fighting to preserve their historic unbeaten run
Author: Sarah Rendell
Headline: A first defeat in four years could be liberating for England after so long fighting to preserve their historic unbeaten run
Content: The Red Roses’ world-record 41-match unbeaten run was broken by Canada in Toronto.Photograph: Ka Lok Ng/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Red Roses’ world-record 41-match unbeaten run was broken by Canada in Toronto.Photograph: Ka Lok Ng/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockThe Breakdown newsletterEngland women's rugby union team‘Freer’ Red Roses resolve to come back stronger after Canada end epic runA first defeat in four years could be liberating for England after so long fighting to preserve their historic unbeaten runSarah RendellTue 20 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland’s glittering unbeaten era is over.Canada defeated the Red Rosesto deal them a first defeat in four years after 40 wins and one draw. It was a landmark result for the Canadians, who will look to replicate the outcome this weekend when the two nations meet again. England must reset but they won’t panic; the Red Roses have been the standard bearers for the past seven years, which is why they have lost only twice in 73 matches. But while no team would ever aim to lose, falling to defeat is a good thing for England and the wider sport.Losing could actually make England a deadlier team to face. That is because they now need to find another level to their game with teams beginning to figure out ways to beat them. They have been pushed over the past few years by teams such as Canada, New Zealand and France, but they always had just enough to get the result over the line. Now they have been presented with a new challenge and John Mitchell, who lost his first game as Red Roses head coach, said post-defeat when his side “gets a setback, it generally learns quicker”.It is not just tactically and physically that the Red Roses may grow, but the mentality of the group may also shift. A defeat was inevitable at some stage, with everyone watching and waiting for the game in which it would come. Mitchell said his players may feel “freer” now that the unbeaten run is over.“The important thing is winning after winning is harder than before,” he said. “I guess what it does to everyone is it frees us up, which is cool. It allows us all to find more. I know this group has definitely got more in it but sometimes it requires the context that we have just received to dig deeper and push for something more.”Losing an international rugby game is a new experience for some of the players in the squad. Abi Burton and Maddie Feaunati are among those who have never tasted defeat for England. Jess Breach’s record is an incredible 59 wins and one loss. The defeat may make those players more versatile and adaptable, too.The England captain, Meg Jones, said of the initial reaction from the squad: “For us the biggest thing is that we stick together. Games are built on moments, it is not one individual moment, it is multiple. That is the beauty of it and we get to review it, we get to go again next weekend, we get to stick together.“I think it is good for us to reassess this and see where we are at. I think togetherness is the main message to come out of that because it’s how you respond when you have had a loss, I think that is the biggest test of character.“They are lessons at the end of the day, I don’t think a loss necessarily changes the way we approach things. You genuinely do learn from it. I spoke to Burts [Abi Burton] and we said: ‘How many games have we lost in our career?’ And we had a little chuckle, those are the ones that shape you the most at times. It’s the biggest lesson for sure. Teams are coming out to beat us, they are going to put their best foot forward. We need to make sure we have got our best foot forward as well.”View image in fullscreenEllie Kildunne (centre) tries to make ground without success during the match.Photograph: Phamai Techaphan/ShutterstockThe fact that England ended their unbeaten run away from home is also significant. Had the Red Roses lost one of their home games, which they almost did against the same opposition with that draw in Exeter, it would still have been a good thing for the team but the benefits would have been less impactful.It is rare for the Red Roses to play non-Six Nations teams away from home and the revamped WXV gives them more of those experiences, perfect preparation for the 2029 World Cup in Australia. England won’t have the cushion of home support and stadiums they are used to playing in when they attempt to defend their title in three years’ time, which is the ultimate goal of this cycle.If England get into a potentially similar situation in 2029 they won’t be in unfamiliar territory. They have now been away from home, in front of a hostile crowd and lost for the first timesince the 2022 World Cup final. In three years they may be able to weather the storm better and have more contingency plans.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMitchell had said before WXV began that the away part of these series of matches would be an “audition for 2029”. After the defeat against Canada, he was asked if this outcome and experience is what the team needed. “Definitely [it is],” he said. “I think even before that message we said: ‘Come and get us.’ We have been asking for someone to come and get us and they have done that. Not that we designed that to happen, far from it. We have to respond.”View image in fullscreenCanada’s victory is a sign of other teams stepping up to challenge England, according to John Mitchell.Photograph: Leonardo Ramirez/Eyepix Group/ShutterstockFor the sport more generally, this defeat may attract more fans or encourage those already watching to stick around and attend more matches. Rugby needs jeopardy and the thrill of a game comes when fans do not know who will be the winner on matchday. Of course this one loss won’t mean England’s dominance will disappear but when they play other top-five nations there will be more doubt over whether they will be the ones to come out on top.England’s unbeaten ticker may now stand at zero but no one will forget the run of 41 games. The Red Roses are written into history and their world record may never be beaten. They have forced other teams to raise their game and made many take notice of women’s rugby with millions now following. England are entering a new era and they have a chance for immediate revenge this weekend as they play Canada once again. They will see it as an opportunity to start a new unbeaten run.This is an extract from our weekly rugby union email, the Breakdown. title: Robinson sparks 23-0 run as Pistons stun Celtics in NBA season opener | NBA | The Guardian
description: Duncan Robinson inspired a stunning fourth-quarter comeback as Detroit overturned a 22-point deficit to beat Boston 121-113 in the NBA season opener
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Duncan Robinson inspired a stunning fourth-quarter comeback as Detroit overturned a 22-point deficit to beat Boston 121-113 in the NBA season opener
Content: Detroit Pistons forward Duncan Robinson shoots over Boston Celtics guard Derrick White during the second half of Tuesday’s NBA season opener in Detroit.Photograph: Paul Sancya/APView image in fullscreenDetroit Pistons forward Duncan Robinson shoots over Boston Celtics guard Derrick White during the second half of Tuesday’s NBA season opener in Detroit.Photograph: Paul Sancya/APNBARobinson sparks 23-0 run as Pistons stun Celtics in NBA season openerDetroit erase 22-point deficit to beat Boston 121-113Paul George scores 38 points on Celtics debut in defeatRobinson scores 15 of his 21 points in fourth quarterAgenciesTue 20 Oct 2026 18.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDuncan Robinson scored 15 of his 21 points in the fourth quarter as theDetroit Pistonsreeled off 23 unanswered points to beat the visiting Boston Celtics 121-113 in the NBA’s regular-season opener on Tuesday afternoon.Jalen Duren and Cade Cunningham scored 22 points apiece for the Pistons, who led the Eastern Conference with 60 wins last season.Javonte Green came off the bench to score 19 points in 18 minutes, while Ausar Thompson added 11 points, 11 rebounds and five assists.NBA 2026-27 season predictions: A Knicks repeat and LeBron’s villain arcRead morePaul George scored a game-high 38 points on his Celtics debut. Payton Pritchard and Derrick White scored 17 points apiece, but Jayson Tatum was held to 13 points on six-for-23 shooting, although he contributed 11 assists.The Celtics led by 13 at halftime thanks to a second-quarter surge. Detroit held a 39-35 advantage early in the quarter before Boston reeled off 15 unanswered points.George scored the Celtics’ final eight points of the half as Boston took a 58-45 lead into the break.George showed no signs of cooling off in the third quarter, hitting three three-pointers in a 52-second span to give Boston their biggest lead at 72-50.Green entered the game shortly afterward to slow George down. He not only did that but also gave Detroit an offensive spark, scoring 11 points in the quarter, including three three-pointers, as the Pistons pulled within three in the closing seconds.George opened the fourth quarter with a layup to give Boston a 90-82 lead. The Celtics soon stretched their advantage to 12 points, but Detroit began another comeback, sparked by a three-point play from Thompson.Robinson scored 11 straight points to pull the Pistons within one at 99-98. He then set up a three-pointer for Green before Duren converted a three-point play. Robinson hit another three-pointer with 5min 13sec remaining to put Detroit ahead 107-99.Green capped the 23-0 run with another three-pointer, extending the Pistons’ lead to 112-99 with 3min 33sec left.Boston rallied to within four points, but Green made two free throws with 6.7 seconds remaining to seal Detroit’s opening-day victory.Explore more on these topicsNBADetroit PistonsBoston CelticsBasketballUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: UK government failures led to Covid spreading ‘like wildfire’ in care homes, inquiry finds | Covid inquiry | The Guardian
description: Inquiry chair says failure to advise care homes to isolate people discharged from hospital was ‘significant oversight’
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: Inquiry chair says failure to advise care homes to isolate people discharged from hospital was ‘significant oversight’
Content: More than 43,000 people died from Covid-19 in UK care homes between March 2020 and July 2022.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenMore than 43,000 people died from Covid-19 in UK care homes between March 2020 and July 2022.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PACovid inquiryUK government failures led to Covid spreading ‘like wildfire’ in care homes, inquiry findsInquiry chair says failure to advise care homes to isolate people discharged from hospital was ‘significant oversight’Jessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentTue 20 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 15.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGovernment failures caused Covid-19 to spread “like wildfire” among vulnerable and elderly people, and Matt Hancock’s “protective ring” around care homes did not exist, a public inquiry has found.Heather Hallett, who is leading the Covid-19 inquiry, said the care sector was an “afterthought” and rejected the former health secretary’s long-held claim that he threw a “protective ring” around care homes from the start of the pandemic, saying it was “unfounded” and the “opposite was true”.She described the government’s failure to advise that patients discharged from hospitals into care homes should be isolated was a “significant omission”, which led the virus to spread rapidly among residents and staff.Lady Hallett also said preventing visits to care homes led to “immense emotional harm” for residents and left them with “profound isolation and a sense of abandonment”.“The adult social care sector as a whole appeared to be something of an afterthought, where the mantra of ‘protecting the NHS’ sometimes came at the expense of the users and providers of care,” she said.View image in fullscreenHeather Hallett is leading the inquiry.Photograph: UK Covid-19 Inquiry/PA“Care homes received insufficient protection at the time they most needed it. These failures created environments in care settings in which the virus could spread like wildfire.“Most distressingly, some people were not permitted to be with their dying loved ones. Many remain racked by a guilt that they do not deserve to carry.”Covid-19 Bereaved Families for Justice UK said Hancock’s claim about a protective ring had been a “cruel lie”.Speaking on behalf of the group, Jean Adamson – the daughter of the Windrush pioneer Aldrick Adamson, who died in a care home after contracting Covid – said the report was “a devastating account of one of the darkest episodes in our country’s history”.“It shows that the government knew the care sector was extremely vulnerable to a pandemic and yet did nothing – failing to act until it was too late,” she said.“The most at-risk people in our society, the sick, elderly – many of whom had a full and long life ahead of them – were failed by a government who abandoned them and left them to die.”‘Superficial damp squib’: Covid inquiry recommendations fail to impress bereaved familiesRead moreBut Adamson said the report “doesn’t go far enough” in its recommendations and the group felt “really let down in several places”.“We’re going to look at them in more detail, and aim to strengthen them, make them more robust. Because we don’t want to be standing in this place in 10 years’ time, trying to learn the same lessons all over again,” she said.More than 43,000 people died from Covid-19 in UK care homes between March 2020 and July 2022.Hallett’sreport, published on Tuesday, focuses specifically on adult social care and residential homes and is the sixth of 10 to be published by the inquiry.It is the most expensive public inquiry in the country’s history, costing more than £200m, and has so far made 55 recommendations on how the country can better prepare for pandemics.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe former health secretary Matt Hancock gave evidence to the inquiry in July 2025.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAHancock was called to give evidence in which he took responsibility for the government decision to discharge about 25,000 hospital patients into care homes to free up NHS bed space before mandatory testing was introduced on 15 April 2020. The policy waslater ruled unlawful by the high court.Hancock told the inquiry it was the “least worst decision to a terrible problem”. Hallett said the policy was necessary to free up hospital beds, but she criticised the government for not advising care homes to isolate discharged patients.The inquiry’s chair said it was “wholly unacceptable” that care staff were left without adequate personal protective equipment, describing how people resorted to using “festival waterproof ponchos, painters’ overalls and gloves purchased from DIY shops”, as well as making their own from fabric, bin bags and bed linen.She noted the emotional toll on staff, saying: “The scale of death and suffering witnessed by social care staff … was unlike anything they had seen before.” Hallett said this led to post-traumatic stress and suicidal thoughts, and that several care workers killed themselves.Hallett made eight key recommendations in the report, which included better pandemic planning, financial support to help social care staff to self-isolate, and guidance on visiting restrictions based on the principle that residents have the “right to in-person visitors, except in the most grave or exceptional of circumstances”.She also said there should be mandatory end-of-life care training for health and social care professionals, including on the use of do not resuscitate orders, after concerns that blanket policies based on age or disability were introduced during the pandemic.“The action taken by the UK government and devolved administrations to try to protect workers and users of adult social care came too late. My recommendations must be acted upon now before the next pandemic strikes,” she said.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the government was “committed to learning the lessons” from the report and pledged to use the findings to develop a plan for any future pandemic.Caroline Abrahams, the charity director of Age UK, said the report was “quietly devastating”.“It describes what in truth we already knew: that when Covid-19 took off, people using social care, and the staff and unpaid carers providing it, were left totally exposed,” she said.She said the report reinforced the need for “fundamental social care reform” but that many of its recommendations could be implemented before the conclusion ofLouise Casey’s review into the creation of a National Care Service.“It is tremendously important that government heeds this lesson and that work begins now,” she said.Explore more on these topicsCovid inquirySocial careCare workersConservativesCoronavirusOlder peopleHealth policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Two men re-arrested on suspicion of aiding Iran over RAF Fairford incident  | UK security and counter-terrorism | The Guardian
description: Counter-terrorism police say 24 and 25-year-old from central London detained under 2023 National Security Act
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Counter-terrorism police say 24 and 25-year-old from central London detained under 2023 National Security Act
Content: Police officers on guard at the perimeter fence of RAF Fairford last month.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APView image in fullscreenPolice officers on guard at the perimeter fence of RAF Fairford last month.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APUK security and counter-terrorismTwo men re-arrested on suspicion of aiding Iran over RAF Fairford incidentCounter-terrorism police say 24 and 25-year-old from central London detained under 2023 National Security ActDan SabbaghDefence and security editorTue 20 Oct 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 14.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCounter-terrorism police have re-arrested two men from central London accused of helping Iranian intelligence as part of the investigation into events at RAF Fairford last month.A 24-year-old UK national and a 25-year-old UK/Iranian national, both from Westminster, were detained on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service in breach of the 2023 National Security Act, police said.Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, the head of national counter-terrorism policing, said investigators considered it highly likely there was Iranian state involvement in the incident near the airbase last month.“Our investigators are continuing to examine what that level of involvement was and the ambition behind it,” he said.The two men were previously arrested on suspicion of terrorism offences and released on police bail. This time the arrests relate to section 3 of the National Security Act, which states that an offence is committed if a person engages in conduct “likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service”.Five men from London drove to Whelford, a village next to the Gloucestershire base used by the US Air Force, in three white vans shortly after midnight on 27 September, where they were arrested.They were picked up after calls from members of the public as they approached the village at about 12.45am, but were released on bail a day later after no bombs or explosive devices were found.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, told the Commons last week that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps was almost certainly behind the ambiguous episode, which led to the US withdrawing 12 B-1 bombers from the base.The US Air Force has long used RAF Fairford, and bombers involved in the US strikes on Iran during the spring and early summer took off from there.One of the five men who drove to Whelford, a 24-year-old British national, was one of those re-arrested on Tuesday. The other had been initially detained on 1 October and subsequently released on bail.Others who were involved in the late-night drive to Fairford may have not been aware what was going on, police believe, though investigations continue in an effort to establish a more definitive picture.“Due to their sensitive nature, national security investigations can take time to progress, and I’m grateful to everyone who has given my teams the time and space needed to pursue this work thoroughly and effectively,” Taylor said.“We know the public have unanswered questions. I want to be as transparent as possible and when we are in the position to share more, we will.”A seventh man was arrested during subsequent investigations. Both he and the other four who drove to Whelford last month remain on bail.Explore more on these topicsUK security and counter-terrorismIranDefence policyShareReuse this content

title: Google cloud failure hits millions as UK courts and banks knocked offline | Revolut | The Guardian
description: Services restored for most users, but power fault stalled hearings and left Revolut, Lloyds and HSBC customers unable to pay or move money
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Services restored for most users, but power fault stalled hearings and left Revolut, Lloyds and HSBC customers unable to pay or move money
Content: The Revolut outage could be linked to issues with Google’s cloud services.Photograph: Mateusz Słodkowski/Zuma Press Wire/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Revolut outage could be linked to issues with Google’s cloud services.Photograph: Mateusz Słodkowski/Zuma Press Wire/Rex/ShutterstockRevolutGoogle cloud failure hits millions as UK courts and banks knocked offlineServices restored for most users, but power fault stalled hearings and left Revolut, Lloyds and HSBC customers unable to pay or move moneyKalyeena MakortoffandJulia KolleweTue 20 Oct 2026 05.45 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn outage at Google’s cloud services in the UK has caused widespread disruption, hitting courts and leaving millions of customers unable to access or send cash at banks including Lloyds, HSBC andRevolut.Google blamed a “power event” for the failure at its London-based Cloud computing operations on Tuesday, which affected its “europe-west2-b zone”.The US tech company said services were starting to come back online as of 1pm London time, and were back online for most customers by 3pm, but not before critical financial transactions and legal proceedings were disrupted.That included the video system used by defendants, lawyers and other parties to attend court hearings remotely across England and Wales, which failed to work throughout the morning.The issue was believed to have delayed several hearings, as the system is often used for defendants who are in custody but need to attend court.Meanwhile, bank customers at high street lenders and leading digital bank Revolut were left in limbo as services including card payments, cash withdrawals and transfers were disrupted.By 5pm most Revolut services were still marked on its website as having problems, with only six out of 27 services listed, including support chat and internal transfers, said to be working.The City regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, confirmed it was in touch with Google and seeking more information about the outage. The Bank of England’s Prudential Regulation Authority is also understood to be speaking with the tech firm.Halifax, owned by Lloyds Bank, said on X that some of its customers had been unable to log in via the app and online.Revolut said its app was down because of a “service disruption” affecting several services, but insisted that customers’ funds and data were safe. The outage was affecting new and current customers, hitting its sign-up, sign-in, card payment, transfer, ATM withdrawal and cryptocurrency services.In a statement, Revolut said: “We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe. We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused.”A spokesperson for Lloyds originally said that customers were having issues with “certain online services” on Tuesday morning but that they were aware of “similar issues affecting other organisations”. By the afternoon, the banking group issued an update saying: “We understand the root issues have been resolved, so we expect to [have] all our services back to normal soon.”HSBC customers had also been complaining online that they were struggling to access their accounts. A spokesperson for the bank said: “Our services have returned to normal following earlier access issues. We continue to monitor the situation closely and thank customers for their patience.”This outage will be the first major test for the FCA and the Bank of England since the City watchdogs werehanded powers to regulate Google and other rival servicesthat have been supplying “critical” cloud services to UK financial firms this summer.Their response is already facing scrutiny by the influential Treasury committee of MPs, whose chair Meg Hillier wrote to the regulators asking for details about how they reacted and a sense of the total impact on the UK financial system. Hillier has asked for an initial response by 4 November.The property portal Rightmove was also reportedly affected by the Google cloud outage, and NewsThump, the satire and spoof news website, was struggling to load. Reports suggested Royal Mail and DPD had also suffered disruption.Google said: “We will publish an analysis of this incident once we have completed our internal investigation. We thank you for your patience while we’re working on resolving the issue.”An FCA spokesperson said:“We are aware of the incident affecting services provided by Google and are engaging with them and affected firms to understand the impact.“People need to be able to access their money and make payments, so we expect firms to fix issues quickly, keep their customers informed and ensure no one is left out of pocket.”Explore more on these topicsRevolutBankingGoogleFinancial sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ll make you famous’: court hears recording of Tommy Robinson threat to Daily Mail editor | UK news | The Guardian
description: Jurors in harassment trial told reporters who had written about far-right activist feared ‘vigilante attack’
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Jurors in harassment trial told reporters who had written about far-right activist feared ‘vigilante attack’
Content: Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, arrives at Southwark crown court, London on Tuesday.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAView image in fullscreenTommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, arrives at Southwark crown court, London on Tuesday.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAUK news‘I’ll make you famous’: court hears recording of Tommy Robinson threat to Daily Mail editorJurors in harassment trial told reporters who had written about far-right activist feared ‘vigilante attack’Ben QuinnTue 20 Oct 2026 13.16 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 16.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTommy Robinson told the Daily Mail’s editor he would make the paper’s journalists and their families “famous”, the harassment trial of the far-right activist has been told.The threat was made in a voicemail message left on the phone of Ted Verity as Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, allegedly waged a campaign of harassment against journalists from the newspaper.One of them was scared to go to their own house and left in fear of a potential “vigilante attack”, the trial was told on Tuesday. Another said they feared Robinson’s followers would “seek revenge” on them after reporting on his activities after the 2024 Southport killings and accusations he influenced subsequent riots.Jurors at Southwark crown court were played a recording of the message Robinson left on Verity’s phone in August 2024, saying: “I’ve already located every fucking one of you. I’ve got pictures of everyone here that can go in my story.”“I’m not threatening you with violence or anything like that. What I’m promising you is I’ll make you famous and your families because that’s what you’ve done to me.”He asked Verity to get in contact, saying that he was prepared to “come knocking”. Robinson said: “Now I know you wasn’t in your house yesterday … I don’t want to do it so please make sure you answer your phone so we can chat.”Robinson, 43, is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence in 2024 to two journalists who were working for the Mail, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber. He denies the charges.A recording of Young responding to Robinson’s call after the journalists had tracked him down to Cyprus was also played to Southwark crown court.View image in fullscreenTommy Robinson on his way into court.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockThe court heard that Young’s address had been published online by an anonymous X account and unknown men started appearing outside his home and that of another journalist working with him.“My main concern was that while he may not physically harm me, he had 800,000 followers on X at the time who might have been tempted to seek revenge on me or my home or my family for what I had written,” Young said in a statement read out in court.Robinson, who attended court with a large number of supporters, was said to have become enraged after the Mail published a story about him with the headline “Stoking race riots from his sunbed”.In another witness statement read to the court, Young’s daughter said that after Robinson’s X account posted pictures of her mother and sister with their faces cropped out, they felt “very worried about our safety”.She described watching a video of Robinson saying he had photos of the wives and daughters of “the journalists involved in the article”. She also told of seeing a “lone male” waiting in a vehicle parked outside the family home and seemingly taking pictures of her with his phone.Dirnhuber said it was the Mail’s view that Robinson was working in Cyprus, since posting on X was part of how he made money, and so they felt they could legitimately report on his activity. They did not publish any identifiable images of his children.Dirnhuber and his partner had to leave their home address after Robinson shared images of the journalist online and allegedly messaged him photographs of an unknown woman, the court was told.Dirnhuber said he felt he would be “looking over my shoulder for a long time”, adding: “I have the knowledge that Tommy Robinson knows my address and my last name is very identifiable.”The alleged harassment may have had an “adverse impact” on his “willingness” to cover certain stories, he added in his witness statement.Social media messages and direct messages sent to journalists by anonymous accounts and apparent followers of Robinson after statements by him on his X account were also read out in court. They ranged from comments about their appearance to more direct messages such as an email to Dirnhuber which said he would have cause to “regret when you are in hospital”.The trial opened on Monday, with prosecutor Ben Holt saying the case was about Robinson’s reaction to what he perceived to be “an unnecessary intrusion into his holiday”. Journalists and their family members had to flee their homes after “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics” were deployed against them, Holt said.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Prince Harry says he wants to reconcile with Charles and William | Prince Harry | The Guardian
description: Duke of Sussex says ‘there’s enough drama in the world’ without continuing to have issues with family
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Duke of Sussex says ‘there’s enough drama in the world’ without continuing to have issues with family
