Content: Prince Harry, seen visiting Nottingham last week, said he hoped sharing his experiences would help others.Photograph: ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPrince Harry, seen visiting Nottingham last week, said he hoped sharing his experiences would help others.Photograph: ShutterstockPrince HarryPrince Harry says he wants to reconcile with Charles and WilliamDuke of Sussex says ‘there’s enough drama in the world’ without continuing to have issues with familyCaroline DaviesTue 20 Oct 2026 12.26 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Duke of Sussex wants to repair his difficult relationship with his father and brother, he has said.Speakingto GQ magazine in New York, Prince Harry said of his complicated relationship with William and King Charles that from a family perspective it was a “massively relatable issue for so many people”.“There’s sibling disagreements, there’s broken relationships between kids and their parents, kids and one parent,” he said.“That continues to come up with me the whole time by people that I speak to, so I know how relatable it is.“That’s partly probably why there’s so much fascination … People maybe look at us and go: ‘How are you going to work it out?’ Then: ‘Maybe how I see you’re going to work it out, maybe that will help me work my stuff out.’“Some people don’t want it to work out. I want it to work out. With everything else that’s going on in the world, the most important thing is to reconcile. That’s the key point.”Asked if he thought he could repair “this wound”, Harry said: “Yeah, of course … look, scars stick around forever but … certainly letting go of the past, that’s something that I would encourage everybody to do.“If there’s certain things from the past that’s still affecting your everyday, that’s harder to let go of.“But yeah, for me, there’s enough drama in the world and enough drama in people’s lives than to continue with issues with family.”A spokesperson for the Sussexes later clarified that Harry’s comments were not intended as a swipe atPrince Williamor directed at any of the royal family in any way, but were made in a general context.The interview, conducted last month, was released on the GQ website as the royal family welcomed the Sultan of Oman to Windsor Castle for a state visit.Speaking of moving his family to the UK, Harry said they returned for “opportunities, for the family, being able to put the kids in British schools meant a lot to me”.He added: “I didn’t know how important it was to me. I always thought it was going to be something I would try and do or that we would try and do, but now they’ve been in school for two weeks they’re loving it and it’s just giving them a whole different experience. Don’t worry, I’m not criticising American schools.”He added it was “so important” for his children, Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five, to have two “completely different cultural experiences”.Harry, who spoke about dealing with grief and trauma after his mother’s death, said he hoped sharing his experience would help others rather than garnering public sympathy for himself.“I certainly don’t want any sympathy. Why? Because I’m a prince. I’ve got a support network around me, I’ve done different forms of therapy, and I put in the work. I wonder where I would be if I didn’t – it could be a very different situation,” he said.Explore more on these topicsPrince HarryKing Charles IIIPrince WilliamMonarchynewsShareReuse this content

title: Why have countries been pushing for a vital global climate report to be delayed? | Environment | The Guardian
description: Saudi Arabia, Russia and China among those claiming developed countries have skewed findings of IPCC review
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: Saudi Arabia, Russia and China among those claiming developed countries have skewed findings of IPCC review
Content: Storm waves crash into homes in Long Beach, California, 11 October. Scientists are concerned that delay to the IPCC assessment report 7 will mean it won’t inform the next round of pledges of emissions cuts, due to be discussed in 2028.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenStorm waves crash into homes in Long Beach, California, 11 October. Scientists are concerned that delay to the IPCC assessment report 7 will mean it won’t inform the next round of pledges of emissions cuts, due to be discussed in 2028.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesEnvironmentExplainerWhy have countries been pushing for a vital global climate report to be delayed?Saudi Arabia, Russia and China among those claiming developed countries have skewed findings of IPCC reviewFiona HarveyEnvironment editorTue 20 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 04.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change suspended an important meeting on Friday in Addis Ababa without setting out a firm timetable for its next report. The world’s governments are due to meet in less than a month for the Cop31 climate summit, and this leaves thefuture of scientific advice to governments on the climate in doubt.What has happened?The IPCC –the UN-convened body of the world’s leading climate scientists– met for a week but, despite progress in many areas, was unable to come to agreement on the substantive issue of setting a launch date for its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of climate science. The seventh assessment report, known as AR7, was expected to be published in 2028, seven years after thelast report in 2021. But some want this timetable to be delayed to 2029, or later.Who wants a delay and why?A loose group of governments led by Saudi Arabia, Russia and India, and also including China and Kenya, have raised objections to publishing the report in 2028, arguing that climate science is dominated by developed countries, which they say has skewed its findings.But many scientists, and experts, worry that a delay would prevent AR7 being used to inform the next round of pledges of emissions cuts, due to be discussed by governments at the Cop33 climate summit in late 2028. Under the timetable set out by the2015 Paris agreement, 2028 is a crucial year as it will be the second“global stocktake”, by which governments’ pledges on emissions are scrutinised to ensure they are in line with the goal of holding temperature rises to 1.5C above preindustrial levels.Saudi Arabia has a long history of obstructing climate action, including seeking to water down previous IPCC reports, and hasemployees of its oil company and scientists with oil links on the IPCC committees.Would a delay enable more science from developing countries?Most of the science that will be in AR7 has already been published and is now under review. IPCC reports take years to compile, combing nearly every possible source of data, and that is done at an early point in its reporting cycle. Establishing new sources at this late point is more difficult.The IPCC argues that it already takes pains to include scientists from around the world and keeps a critical eye on equity to ensure against developed country bias. Much of the basic science it relies on is based on theglobal workings of the climate system, and understanding the underlying physics and chemistry, which do not differ from developed to developing countries.Critics also point out that Saudi Arabia, Russia, China and India are all powerful economies with well-established scientific institutions and research bases – if they wanted to produce scientific models themselves, they could have done so by now, or could have provided financial assistance to other developing countries to do so.One possible compromise is for the IPCC to start working now on new ways to bring in more science from the developing world, and undertake a critique of its processes to that end, while keeping to the 2028 timetable for the first part of its four-part report, which deals with the underlying physical science, and allowing the other parts – which cover theimpacts of climate breakdown around the world, and solutions to it – to be delayed.What do civil society activists think?They are divided. Some are against a delay and view it as a danger to progress on cutting emissions. Some leading figuressupport it, arguing that whose research informs the science, and whether scientists from developing countries can participate meaningfully, is as important as speed. Others have issued statements deploring the row while carefully not taking sides.Mohamed Adow, director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank, said: “It is deeply frustrating that governments have failed to agree a way forward. Developing countries must have a meaningful voice in shaping that science, and wealthy nations must provide the funding needed to make that possible. But legitimate concerns about fairness cannot become an excuse for endless delays.”Oscar Soria, director at the Common Initiative group, said: “The failure to agree the timeline is not a procedural detail, it has real consequences.. The answer is not to choose between urgency and equity, but to provide the resources and support needed to achieve both.”What happens now?A group of 117 scientists, many of them from developing countries, including several from China and one from India, have written anopen letter vowing to push ahead with their work. “Our message to governments and to the world is simple: we will keep working,” they wrote. “Equity is built into how our assessment is being drafted. Author teams are working from a far wider evidence base than in AR6. It includes literature from the global south, non-English sources, grey literature and Indigenous knowledge and local knowledge.”The IPCC’s chair, Jim Skea, has alsopledged to reconvene as soon as possible.The issue is certain to come up at theCop31 talks in Turkey next month, where governments will be asked what they are doing to show a sense of urgency in tackling the climate crisis, in the face of what is likely to be thestrongest El Niño in decades,supercharged by global heating, and likely to cause huge amounts of damage – in developed and developing countries.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentCop31Climate crisisGreenhouse gas emissionsIntergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)Climate scienceGlobal climate talksexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Baby who died from meningitis may have been saved if tested sooner, inquest finds | NHS | The Guardian
description: Five-month-old Esta High died at Leeds General Infirmary in November 2023 after doctors put her symptoms down to Covid-19
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Five-month-old Esta High died at Leeds General Infirmary in November 2023 after doctors put her symptoms down to Covid-19
Content: Baby Esta High with her mother Lynsey Carr.Photograph: Family Handout/PAView image in fullscreenBaby Esta High with her mother Lynsey Carr.Photograph: Family Handout/PANHSBaby who died from meningitis may have been saved if tested sooner, inquest findsFive-month-old Esta High died at Leeds General Infirmary in November 2023 after doctors put her symptoms down to Covid-19Hannah Al-Othman, North of England CorrespondentTue 20 Oct 2026 13.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 14.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA baby girl who died from meningitis may have been saved if doctors had tested her for the infection sooner, rather than putting her symptoms down to Covid, an inquest jury has found.Five-month-old Esta High died atLeedsGeneral Infirmary in November 2023, days after she was taken into the emergency department with a high temperature and vomiting.She had tested positive for coronavirus, and so opportunities were missed when doctors stuck with a diagnosis of Covid, the inquest found.Esta died from streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis, and her parents Lynsey Carr and Leon High told the inquest that doctors had missed vital chances to test for a bacterial infection and start vital antibiotic treatment.Carr told the inquest, at Wakefield coroner’s court, that their concerns were ignored until it was too late.On Tuesday, an inquest jury of five women and six men concluded: “Esta died of natural causes which was contributed to by neglect. Had Esta received required care, based on the balance of probabilities, it would have probably saved or prolonged her life.”Carr said she and her partner had refused advice from doctors to take Esta home, as she would not stop vomiting and had a temperature of over 40C.She said her daughter developed a rash and her arm started shaking, which she feared was a seizure. She told the jury “we were extremely worried” and “kept asking for help”, but “staff were rude and don’t listen to our concerns”.View image in fullscreenEsta High’s parents Leon High and Lynsey Carr as they listen to their solicitor reading their statement outside Wakefield coroners court.Photograph: Dave Higgens/PACarr told the inquest that the family, from Leeds, were put into a side room at the hospital’s children’s assessment and treatment (CAT) unit, adding that she believed staff were more concerned with isolating Esta due to the Covid risk than listening to her parents.She described Esta’s time on the CAT unit as “15 hours that were filled with missed opportunities”.By late afternoon on 2 November, Esta was unresponsive, and the jury heard how scans and other tests showed evidence of meningoencephalitis and streptococcus pneumoniae.She was taken to intensive care and attempts were made to save her life, but she died on 6 November.“Unfortunately, as our daughter had been left untreated for 55 hours, it was too late to save our darling girl,” Carr told the inquest, describing her daughter as “bright, beautiful and perfect from the first moment”.In a statement read by her solicitor outside court on Tuesday, Carr said: “Making the decision on the advice of the intensive care staff to withdraw Esta’s life support broke us. Esta passed away lying between me and Leon – something no parent should ever have to go through.“We felt so blessed that Esta was our daughter, and for her to be taken away so cruelly is something we’ll never get over.”She added: “Parents know their children better than anyone, and when they say something isn’t right they need to be listened to and taken seriously.”Solicitor Joe Haley, of Irwin Mitchell, said: “It’s now vital that lessons are learned to help improve patient safety and prevent others from going through the terrible suffering Esta’s family has endured.”Dr Elizabeth Garthwaite, the chief medical officer at Leeds teaching hospitalsNHStrust, said: “We are deeply sorry that we failed Esta and her family, and offer our sincere and heartfelt condolences to Lynsey and Leon following the tragic death of their daughter.”She added: “We recognise that serious failures occurred in the care provided to Esta and that these failures had devastating consequences.“We take the concerns raised by the coroner extremely seriously and will carefully consider the report’s findings and recommendations.“We are committed to responding openly and fully, and to taking any further action necessary to improve patient safety.”Explore more on these topicsNHSLeedsHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC Three and BBC Scotland TV channels to be shut down next year  | BBC | The Guardian
description: Corporation announces broadcast closures and job losses in effort to find savings of £500m
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Corporation announces broadcast closures and job losses in effort to find savings of £500m
Content: Killing Eve and Fleabag were both launched on BBC3.Composite: BBCView image in fullscreenKilling Eve and Fleabag were both launched on BBC3.Composite: BBCBBCBBC Three and BBC Scotland TV channels to be shut down next yearCorporation announces broadcast closures and job losses in effort to find savings of £500mUK politics live – latest updatesMichael SavageMedia editorTue 20 Oct 2026 10.54 EDTFirst published on Tue 20 Oct 2026 09.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTelevision channels BBC Three and BBC Scotland are to close and theRadio 4 Extraradio station will be scrapped, as part of the corporation’s drive to cut £500m in costs.Both TV channels are to move online as executives try to plug a funding crisis and adapt the broadcaster’s output for audiences that increasingly watch content on demand. All three outlets will close in the spring.Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, said the corporation needed to “make every pound work harder for audiences as we respond to the immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world”. He added: “We all know that means tough choices.”A further 100 jobs will also be cut atBBCNews to save £5.5m. However, thedepartment’s new director, Rachel Jupp, warned staff that its £51m cuts target could yet increase as a result of the broadcaster’s funding crisis.Even with the channel closures, which come on top of other cuts already announced, BBC insiders said the corporation was not even half way to meeting its £500m target.Only about £200m has been cut so far, suggesting even more controversial cuts will have to be made over the next year to plug the funding gap.It marks the second time that BBC Three’s linear TV channel has been closed, having beenmoved online in 2016but brought back in 2022.View image in fullscreenA scene from Gavin and Stacey: The Finale. The hit show was launched on BBC3.Photograph: Toffee International Ltd/PAThe Guardianrevealed this monththat the channels were likely to be axed.BBC Three, which is aimed at young audiences, launched shows including Gavin and Stacey, Fleabag and Killing Eve. However, it was an obvious candidate to move online and have more of its content placed on YouTube, where younger audiences have migrated. Typically, about 4% of the UK population watch the channel live in a week.The BBC promised there would be increased investment in content for younger audiences. It has already cancelled the high-profile BBC Three showRuPaul’s Drag Race UK.BBC Scotland’s viewership was seen as too low to justify the cost of keeping it on air, with its digital audience increasing via the BBC’s iPlayer. Its content will also be available on BBC One and BBC Two inScotland.The decision to close Radio 4 Extra came after it was decided much of its content could be accessed digitally, via the BBC Sounds app. The station reached an audience of 1.4 million a week, according to the most recent Rajar data.There has already been severe internal criticism from BBC staff over where the cuts are being made.View image in fullscreenBBC Scotland’s headquarters and studios at Pacific Quay in Glasgow.Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The GuardianBBC executives have said they planned to safeguard content that fulfilled its duty to produce programming for everyone. However, many staff now fear that the BBC is targeting public service content that commercial rivals would never replicate.There has been increasing disquiet over the decision toaxe BBC Radio 4’s The World Tonightafter more than 50 years. Consumer affairs showYou and Yoursis one of a number of fellow Radio 4 shows going, to be replaced by a new format.Some of the BBC’s freelance foreign correspondents have also been cut, while the number of local correspondents across Britain is being reduced, with those still in post asked to becomegeneral reporters rather than specialists. Meanwhile, the BBC’s local radio output is being made more regional.The BBC has also faced a backlash from politicians, as well as from the staff and crew of its flagship radio drama The Archers, after a decision not to build a planned radio drama studio for the show in its new Birmingham headquarters.The vast majority of staff accept that the corporation is under financial strain and needs to modernise in an age of streaming and digital platforms consumed over a smartphone.However, morale has been hit by the time it has taken to drip out the cuts, while others believe the cuts will result in the BBC replicating too much content similar to that on commercial networks.In a note to staff, Brittin said: “We would all prefer immediate certainty. However, it unfortunately takes time to develop proposals that ensure we focus scarcer resources on the shows, stories and services that can have the biggest impact.”Further major changes to BBC News are still to come, but have been delayed to allowJuppto draw up her strategy for the newsroom. She has been tasked with boosting BBC News on digital platforms such as YouTube and TikTok, as well as the BBC’s own apps and iPlayer.Philippa Childs, the head of the Bectu union, said the latest cuts and channel closures were “in danger of causing irreparable damage to the BBC and will do yet more harm to the morale of its employees”.“The continued drip-feed of planned job and output cuts is putting increasing pressure on an already bruised workforce at the BBC,” she said.The BBC is having to make the cuts as a result of its serious financial challenges, with itscash revenues falling at an alarming rateover the last year. Brittin has said he was not fully aware of the pressures when he took the job earlier this year.One BBC insider said the corporation was “taking an axe to so much content that is unmatched by the commercial sector”.“The pace of this change appears to be accelerating,” they said. “I think there is a very credible threat that there will be an increase in people choosing to opt out of the licence fee because it no longer does them a service. The doom spiral continues.”Explore more on these topicsBBCScotlandRadio 4 ExtraBBC ThreeMatt BrittinPublic service broadcastingTV streamingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Storm Austen forecast to hit southern UK | UK weather | The Guardian
description: Yellow severe weather warning issued for first named storm of season with gusts of up to 60mph expected
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Yellow severe weather warning issued for first named storm of season with gusts of up to 60mph expected
Content: The effects of Storm Amy in Porthcawl, Wales, in October last year.Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe effects of Storm Amy in Porthcawl, Wales, in October last year.Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty ImagesUK weatherStorm Austen forecast to hit southern UKYellow severe weather warning issued for first named storm of season with gusts of up to 60mph expectedJamie GriersonTue 20 Oct 2026 10.04 EDTFirst published on Tue 20 Oct 2026 07.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first named storm of the season, Austen, is expected to bring gusts of up to 60mph to southern areas of the UK at the end of the week, forecasters said.While there would be spells of rain and showers for many on Tuesday and Wednesday, by Thursday, Storm Austen would be approaching the south-west of the UK, the Met Office said.An area of low pressure in the Atlantic would deepen rapidly as it was invigorated by the jet stream, the forecaster added.A storm in the UK is named when it has the potential to cause disruption or damage that could result in an amber or red warning. The Met Office issued a yellow severe weather warning for strong wind from midnight to midday on Friday which covers most of south-westEnglandand southern Wales. Parts of the south coast as far east as Brighton were also expected to be affected.Shaun the Sheep hailed on latest list of storm namesRead moreThe Met Office deputy chief forecaster, Tom Crabtree, said: “While the exact track and position of Storm Austen is still being determined, what’s clear is that we have an impactful period of weather on the way and the potential for disruption in places, which has resulted in the system being named.“Peak gusts in excess of 70mph are possible on the most exposed coastal areas, while 50-60mph are likely more widely within the warning area. Weather warnings are under constant review and could be updated as confidence increases, so it’s important to stay up to date with the forecast in the coming days.”Storm Austen would move from west to east through Friday, with winds diminishing later in the day. About 20mm-30mm of rain was expected in many places.The storm would move toward the North Sea late on Friday, but more wind and rain was probable throughout the weekend and into the start of next week, with the heaviest rain expected to be in western areas, the forecaster said.View image in fullscreenA walker contends with the rain in Dunsden, Oxfordshire, on Tuesday.Photograph: Geoffrey Swaine/ShutterstockThe Met Office storm year runs from September to August, with each 12-month period having its own alphabetical list of names that are used to label successive storms.This year’s listbegins with Austen and continues with Boelo, Chloe, Dano and Evelyn, ending at W with Wende.The letters Q, U, X, Y and Z are not used, in line with international storm naming conventions. The names are decided by the Met Office in conjunction with Met Éireann and KNMI, which are the Irish and Dutch national meteorological services respectively.Austen was selected by Met Éireann in honour of Austen Nagle, the first director of the service. Other names are chosen from suggestions submitted by the public, with Chloe having been nominated more than 130 times.The Met Office began naming storms in 2015, since when the furthest letter of the alphabet reached within any 12-month period was L, in 2023-24. Only four storms were named in 2025-26: Amy, Bram, Chandra and Dave.Holly Clements, the Met Office head of warnings and guidance, said: “For more than a decade, storm naming has helped us communicate the risks from severe weather more effectively.“A named storm provides a clear focus for forecasts and warnings, helping more people understand the potential impacts and take action to protect themselves, their families and their property.”Explore more on these topicsUK weatherEnglandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Vast Beatles museum, hailed as ‘extraordinary’ by Paul McCartney, to open in Liverpool in 2028 | Music | The Guardian
description: City’s Beatles Story museum to move to 100,000 sq ft new home and official ownership, along with Yellow Submarine makeover of Liverpool’s second-tallest building
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: City’s Beatles Story museum to move to 100,000 sq ft new home and official ownership, along with Yellow Submarine makeover of Liverpool’s second-tallest building
Content: ‘Liverpool was, and still is, a music city’ … the Beatles in 1962.View image in fullscreen‘Liverpool was, and still is, a music city’ … the Beatles in 1962.MusicVast Beatles museum, hailed as ‘extraordinary’ by Paul McCartney, to open in Liverpool in 2028City’s Beatles Story museum to move to 100,000 sq ft new home and official ownership, along with Yellow Submarine makeover of Liverpool’s second-tallest buildingBen Beaumont-ThomasTue 20 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLiverpool is to unveil a new 100,000 sq ft visitor attraction about the Beatles, in plans hailed as “extraordinary” byPaul McCartney, and by Andy Burnham as having “the kind of ambition I want to see more of across Britain”.Opening in 2028, the project is a huge upgrade for the Beatles Story, a museum which opened in Liverpool’s Royal Albert Dock in 1990. Ownership will now pass to the Beatles company Apple Corps, making the Beatles Story the band’s first official fan experience in their home city.It will also move across the city to the former shopping centre St John’s Market, close to Liverpool’s Lime Street railway station, which has lain unused since closing in 2024. The new site will allow the museum to become four times bigger than its current home.Apple Corps has also announced it will take over and renovate Liverpool’s second-tallest building: St Johns Beacon, a 450ft tower that has also remained unused since 2024, when its viewing gallery closed and its radio station tenants vacated. Neighbouring the redeveloped museum, the tower will become a separate attraction themed around the Beatles’ whimsical and psychedelic animated film Yellow Submarine.View image in fullscreenSt Johns Beacon pictured earlier this year.Photograph: Chris Chambers/AlamyThe new iteration of the Beatles Story is being billed as a “multi-hour experience” which will recreate settings from the group’s history, from their childhood homes in Liverpool to the city’s Cavern venue and the nightclubs where they cut their teeth in Hamburg, and on to Abbey Road, New York’s Shea Stadium – where Beatlemania provoked such fevered screaming that the band couldn’t hear themselves play – and the building on London’s Savile Row where they played their final rooftop concert in 1969.McCartney said: “I find it incredible and humbling that people are still interested in our story and it’s very exciting to me that the Beatles Story and the Beacon are being transformed in such an exciting way in the heart of Liverpool city. I love Liverpool. It’s part of who I am, it’s part of who the Beatles are. If you’d told us this was going to happen when we were hanging out and getting started, we’d never have believed it.”Ringo Starr also celebrated the plans, saying: “It is great to be part of this – deep down I am still a scouser.“Liverpool was, and still is, a music city. And now we are expanding the Beatles Story … how far out. The beat goes on.”A new charity, the Apple Corps Liverpool Trust, has also been founded. It will receive a portion of every ticket sold, and use that revenue to fund initiatives for local musicians.Andy Burnham praised the Liverpool plans as having “the kind of ambition I want to see more of across Britain: backing the things our great cities do best and turning that global reputation into jobs, opportunity and growth”. He hailed the charitable arm as helping “the next generation of young artists, wherever they grow up, to believe there is a route from their bedroom, rehearsal room or local venue to the very top of the world.”View image in fullscreenSt John’s shopping centre pictured in 2019, part of which will house the new Beatles Story museum.Photograph: Greg Balfour Evans/AlamyLiverpool’s mayor Steve Rotheram said: “People already travel halfway around the globe to visit the birthplace of four lads that shook the earth. These plans take that extraordinary pull to another level – creating a world-class destination that will give millions more fans a reason to make the pilgrimage to their spiritual home and experience the city, its music and its culture for themselves.”The project is being helmed by Apple Corps in tandem with Liverpool city council and Liverpool City Region Combined Authority, with UK government support. Financial details of the project and its partnerships have not been disclosed.Apple Corps’ chief executive Tom Greene compared the plans with Elvis Presley’s Graceland in Memphis or Dolly Parton’s Dollywood in Tennessee: “A world-class destination for fans to visit in the centre of the city where the story started.”Greene is already overseeing the development of another official Beatles attraction: a renovation of 3 Savile Row where that final rooftop concert took place. The seven-floor museum, due to open in 2027, will allow visitors to access the rooftop and will also recreate the building’s in-house studio where they recorded the Let It Be album, alongside showcases of Apple Corps’ archive and temporary exhibitions.The plans come amid sustained and varied efforts to carry the Beatles’ legacy forward, not least with an ambitiousfour-film biopic project helmed by director Sam Mendes, telling the stories of each band member. Currently in production, those films will also arrive in 2028, and sets and props will be reused for the recreated environments in the new iteration of the Beatles Story.The band’s Hamburg era is being separately told in Hamburg Days, a forthcoming BBC drama scripted by Succession writer Jamie Carragher, and a reissue programme of the Beatles’ catalogue continues: an expanded version of 1965’s Rubber Soul reached No 2 in the UK charts earlier this month.View image in fullscreenThe current iteration of The Beatles Story, in Liverpool’s Albert Dock.Photograph: David A Eastley/AlamyThe Beatles are a big tourism draw in Liverpool, with a 2016 study suggesting the band added £82m to the local economy each year.The current iteration of the Beatles Story has helped to drive that success, with exhibits such as George Harrison’s first guitar and John Lennon’s glasses. The museum has won VisitEngland awards for excellence in each of the last two years.Explore more on these topicsMusicThe BeatlesLiverpoolMerseysidePop and rockPaul McCartneyRingo StarrnewsShareReuse this content

title: Michael Bloomberg spends $80m on Democrats as Trump moves $400m to Republican candidates | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Billionaire ex-mayor of New York City is focusing funds on House races to help Democrats retake majority in midterms
Author: Chris Stein
Headline: Billionaire ex-mayor of New York City is focusing funds on House races to help Democrats retake majority in midterms
Content: Michael Bloomberg on 28 April 2026 in Madrid, Spain.Photograph: Europa Press News/Europa Press/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMichael Bloomberg on 28 April 2026 in Madrid, Spain.Photograph: Europa Press News/Europa Press/Getty ImagesUS midterm elections 2026Michael Bloomberg spends $80m on Democrats as Trump moves $400m to Republican candidatesBillionaire ex-mayor of New York City is focusing funds on House races to help Democrats retake majority in midtermsUS politics live – latest updatesChris Steinin WashingtonTue 20 Oct 2026 18.07 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 20.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe billionaireMichael Bloombergwill spend $80m to help Democratic candidates in themidterm elections, US media reported on Tuesday, a significant infusion of cash for a party that has recently struggled with fundraising as it seeks to win control ofCongress.The reported donations came asDonald Trumpannounced on Tuesday he intended to spend a total of $400m to aid Republican candidates, with $300m already disbursed.The New York Times reportsthat Bloomberg made the contributions in September and October, and is particularly focused on Democrats running to flip the US House of Representatives, which Republicans currently control by a historically small margin. The goal, Bloomberg’s political adviser Howard Wolfson told the Times, is to ensure that a Democratic majority is greater than just the 218 seats needed to win control of the chamber.Ohio Democrat’s family criticizes Vivek Ramaswamy for bringing up estranged mother in gubernatorial adRead more“The difference between 221 and 230, in terms of the House majority, really matters,” Wolfson said.One of the world’s richest men, Bloomberg, 84, served three terms as mayor of New York City, from 2002 to 2013. He was an independent then, but later registered as a Democrat, spending $80m to help the party in the 2018 midterms, during Trump’s first term, then made a well-funded butunsuccessfulbid for the party’s presidential nomination in 2020.Among his donations this year are $24m to Everytown for Gun Safety, a group he cofounded that is spending on Democratic candidates in the lower chamber, and $16m to the House Majority Pac, which is connected to the House minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries.Democrats believe they are favored to take back the House this year, though they’veacknowledgedtrailing Republicans in fundraising. Besides Trump’s money, Republicans are being aided by the president’s ally Elon Musk, who hasspent $366mon conservative groups and campaigns so far.Democrats also believe they have a shot at netting the four seats necessary to retake control of the Senate, though analysts believe it could go either way.Control of either chamber would allow Democrats to block Trump’s legislative agenda and more effectively investigate his administration. If they win a majority in the Senate, the party’s lawmakers could also reject his nominees for the supreme court and other federal judicial positions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, plus breaking news alertsSign up toThe Stakes 2026A weekly guide to what really matters in the US midterms, plus breaking news alerts.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBloomberg has donated $2.5m to a Super Pac backing James Talarico, the Democratic candidate in Texas’s US Senate race, as well as a Super Pac backing the re-election campaign of theNew Yorkgovernor, Kathy Hochul, and the campaigns of several Democratic gubernatorial candidates, the Times reported.Asked how effective Bloomberg believed the money would be, Wolfson said: “He is of the view that resources matter in campaigns.” He added that the billionaire “expects a result”.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026Mike BloombergDonald TrumpDemocratsRepublicansHouse of RepresentativesUS CongressnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK to deploy fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks | Defence policy | The Guardian
description: RAF Typhoon fighters to fly defensive missions over cities and infrastructure in extension of UK support for Riyadh
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: RAF Typhoon fighters to fly defensive missions over cities and infrastructure in extension of UK support for Riyadh
Content: The Ministry of Defence said the aircraft would not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis.Photograph: Simon Maycock/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Ministry of Defence said the aircraft would not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis.Photograph: Simon Maycock/AlamyDefence policyUK to deploy fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacksRAF Typhoon fighters to fly defensive missions over cities and infrastructure in extension of UK support for RiyadhDan SabbaghDefence and security editorTue 20 Oct 2026 14.30 EDTFirst published on Tue 20 Oct 2026 07.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRAF Typhoon fighters are to be used in efforts to protectSaudi Arabiafrom attack by Yemen’s Houthis, flying protective missions over the country’s cities and critical infrastructure as western allies increase their intervention in the escalating conflict.The operation – the most significant military mission signed off by Andy Burnham as prime minister – will involve RAF pilots attempting to shoot down Houthi missiles and drones, which attacked Saudi airports and oil facilities.The Ministry of Defence emphasised that the role of the fighters – whose number was not stated – would be limited. “These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against theHouthis,” it said.An offensive by the Iran-aligned Houthis inYementhat began in September has gradually escalated into a deadly regional conflict. This month the Houthis have attacked Saudi Arabia, the backer of Yemen’s officially recognised government.Thirteen people were killed when a missile hit King Khalid international airport in Riyadh, the deadliest incident since September in a war that has claimed 19 lives in Saudi Arabia so far.Dozens more have been killed in Yemen by the surge in fighting. The death toll from Monday’sHouthi missile strike on a Yemeni government training camphas risen to 73, a brutal demonstration of the rebel group’s military effectiveness.Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said in a TV interview the UK had agreed to help Saudi Arabia to counter the “outrageous Houthi escalation that we’ve seen in recent weeks” and said the UK was “responding to protect civilians” from attack.HA Hellyer, a Middle East expert with the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, speculated that the UK could get drawn further into the conflict in the future, asking: “What does defensive mean?”He asked what the RAF would do if a Houthi attack happened on a Saudi ship in the Red Sea and the British were in a position to stop it. “The UK might say it was defensive but the Houthis would see it as offensive,” he said.Streeting, however, said that the fighter jets’ remit was narrow. “RAF Typhoons will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles,” he said.Military advisers said the UK would also provide an Atlas A400M transport aircraft capable of transporting heavy equipment, in addition toan existing commitment to supply air-to-air refuelling for Saudi fighter jetswith an RAF Voyager. The refuelling mission has been extended by 90 days.The UK has long been a military ally of Saudi Arabia: BAE Systems has supplied it with 72 Typhoons in a deal originally worth £4.4bn. Riyadh has been considering buying another 48 in a negotiation that has dragged on for years.Though the UK only had a limited involvement in the US-Israel war against Iran, Typhoons from the RAF airbase in Akrotiri, Cyprus, and in Qatar, flew defensive missions in the spring and summer to shoot down missiles and drones launched by Iran and other proxies against Gulf states.View image in fullscreenThe UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, met his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, last week.Photograph: Finn Gomez/Getty ImagesBritain’s announcement came a few days after Streeting visited his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon, where they discussed how to respond to the Houthi escalation amongst other issues.The US has so far stepped up its intelligence support and sent more than 100 military advisers to help the Saudis with targeting, but it has been cautious about providing more direct military support. Donald Trump urged Riyadh on Friday to accept help from Israel, though it was unclear what was on offer.The White House has been trying to de-escalate against Iran and in the Middle Eastbefore US midterm elections in November and with the oil price over $100 a barrel. The US envoy to Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack, told a conference in Qatar that sending in ground troops against the Houthis “seems fruitless”.The Saudi strategy for dealing with the Houthis, who have been gaining territory along the Red Sea coast, remains unclear. “Allies would be happy to help the Saudis, but they have not been very good at explaining what they want,” said Hellyer.He suggested UK military support could help free up the Saudi military to step up direct attacks on the Houthis, though in the past the Saudi air force has been accused ofusing UK- and US-made weaponsin indiscriminate bombing.Amid some concern that the UK risks being seen as closely aligned to the unpopular US war on Iran, the military intervention was partly justified because instability in the Middle East was driving up energy prices and affecting the cost of living.Explore more on these topicsDefence policyRoyal Air ForceMilitarySaudi ArabiaHouthisYemenMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Flavio Bolsonaro’s ‘corrupto’ stunt sparks viral meme before Brazil election runoff | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Far-right presidential candidate’s TV debate swipe at rival backfires as people take to social media to parody it
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Far-right presidential candidate’s TV debate swipe at rival backfires as people take to social media to parody it
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro during last Sunday’s televised presidential debate.Photograph: Allison Sales/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro during last Sunday’s televised presidential debate.Photograph: Allison Sales/NurPhoto/ShutterstockBrazilFlavio Bolsonaro’s ‘corrupto’ stunt sparks viral meme before Brazil election runoffFar-right presidential candidate’s TV debate swipe at rival backfires as people take to social media to parody itTom PhillipsLatin America correspondentTue 20 Oct 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 11.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleToFlávio Bolsonaroand his publicists, it must have seemed an ingenious idea that would expose his rival’s supposed crookedness on the eve of Brazil’s presidential election.But the far-right politician’s decision to attend a primetime television debate against his leftwing opponent,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, with the word “corrupto” (corrupt) written on the palm of his hand has backfired.Rather than drawing attention to the incumbent’s alleged misdeeds, many of the programme’s millions of viewers sarcastically took Bolsonaro’s hand-written message as an admission of his own guilt.Following Sunday night’s debate, Lula supporters from all walks of life have flooded social media with photographs of their own self-descriptions inked on their palms.John Ulhoa, the guitarist from a pop rock band called Pato Fu, jokinglydescribed himselfas a “musician (and a hunk)”.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThe Emmy-winning comedian Antonio Tabetintroduced himselfto his 2.8 million followers on X as an artist.Carlos Marcio used both palms to portray himself as a cellist and author.Carla Emanuela Sacramento, an obstetric nurse,posted a photographof herself clad in personal protective equipment and with the words “primary health care nurse” proudly written on her right palm.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueProminent politicians also jumped on the trend, including Lula’s health minister, the infectious disease specialist Alexandre Padilha,whose palm noted he was a doctor, and Tabata Amaral, whoidentifiedas a political scientist and astrophysicist.All across the country, librarians, oil workers, engineers, journalists, architects, pilots, psychologists, seamstresses, street cleaners, teachers, influencers, and police officers used ballpoint pens to inscribe their professions on to their skin.Writing on Substack, the Latin America expert James Bosworth called Bolsonaro’s stunt a “critical error” in his bid for power.“It may have seemed like an inspired pre-debate gimmick. Instead, he gave the world a meme image that will stick with him for the rest of his political career,” Bosworth said, offering politicians a word of advice.“Don’t write the word ‘corrupto’ on your hand and show it to the audience,” Bosworth suggested.Bolsonaro, who is the son of the jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, is a professional politician who has long faced corruption accusations, although he denies them and has never been convicted. The 45-year-old senator also haswell-documented tiesto members of Rio’s mafia underworld andonce employedthe relatives of the city’s most notorious contract killer, Adriano da Nóbrega. Last week two allies were arrested for alleged involvement with the Red Command drug faction, which Donald Trumprecently designateda foreign terrorist organisation. Bolsonarovoiced surpriseat those arrests and said the men had the right to prove their innocence.On Monday, Brazilian media reported that Bolsonaro was being investigated by the federal police as part of a money-laundering inquiry.Lula, whose Worker’s party (PT) has also been involved in major corruption scandals, used Sunday’s debate to throw down the gauntlet to Bolsonaro.The leftwing incumbent said he would give electoral authorities access to his banking and phone recordings, and those of close relatives, in order to prove he was not corrupt – if Bolsonaro agreed to do the same.Bolsonaro, who, polls suggest, holds a slender advantage ahead of Sunday’s second-round runoff, has yet to respond to Lula’s challenge. The rightwingerwon the 4 October first roundby more than 2m votes.Explore more on these topicsBrazilFlávio BolsonaroLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmericasThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brendan Nugent facing three charges over alleged attack on MP Helen Haines | Helen Haines | The Guardian
description: Victoria police arrested the 43-year-old Tarrawingee man on Monday afternoon after the incident in Wangaratta
Author: Nino Bucci
Headline: Victoria police arrested the 43-year-old Tarrawingee man on Monday afternoon after the incident in Wangaratta
Content: Brendan Nugent has been charged after an alleged attack on Helen Haines outside her electorate office in Wangaratta in northern Victoria.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/EPAView image in fullscreenBrendan Nugent has been charged after an alleged attack on Helen Haines outside her electorate office in Wangaratta in northern Victoria.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/EPAHelen HainesBrendan Nugent facing three charges over alleged attack on MP Helen HainesVictoria police arrested the 43-year-old Tarrawingee man on Monday afternoon after the incident in WangarattaWho is Helen Haines, the MP allegedly attacked in Victoria?Brendan Nugent’s family say Haines has been their friend for more than 20 yearsGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastNino BucciTue 20 Oct 2026 05.18 EDTFirst published on Tue 20 Oct 2026 04.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHelen Haines’ alleged attacker, Brendan Nugent, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official.He will be held overnight to appear at Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday, Victoria police confirmed in a statement, adding that it would be alleged the attack was targeted.Victoria police arrested the 43-year-old Tarrawingee man on Monday afternoon after he allegedly struck the independent MP for Indi with a Toyota LandCruiser outside her electorate office in Wangaratta in northernVictoria.Haines remains in a critical but stable condition after being airlifted to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital for emergency surgery. She has lost one leg and surgeons were fighting on Tuesday to save the other leg.Police also said in the statement released late on Tuesday that one of its highway patrol officers responded to the incident only eight seconds after emergency services were called.They confirmed that a search warrant had been executed that morning at Nugent’s Great Alpine Road property.“Victoria Police will continue to maintain an enhanced presence in Wangaratta, including members from the Public Order Response Team who have deployed to the area.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“At this stage it appears this is an isolated incident, and there are currently no other known threats connected to this matter.”Explore more on these topicsHelen HainesVictoriaAustralian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: NatWest cracks down on 13,000 staff attending office two days a month | Banking | The Guardian
description: Union furious as bank scraps remote-first policy from February 2027, forcing all UK employees to come in at least twice a week
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Union furious as bank scraps remote-first policy from February 2027, forcing all UK employees to come in at least twice a week
Content: NatWest’s work policy changes will hit lowest paid workers hardest, Unite has warned.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenNatWest’s work policy changes will hit lowest paid workers hardest, Unite has warned.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPABankingNatWest cracks down on 13,000 staff attending office two days a monthUnion furious as bank scraps remote-first policy from February 2027, forcing all UK employees to come in at least twice a weekKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentTue 20 Oct 2026 12.45 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNatWest has ordered 13,000 staff to increase their in-office days from two days a month to two days a week, angering its staff union.The banking group, which serves customers under the Royal Bank of Scotland, NatWest, Ulster Bank and Coutts brands, will require all of its nearly 40,000 UK staff to follow a strict two days a week office schedule from February 2027, abolishing a remote-first policy for thousands of employees.Unite said it was a “kick in the teeth” for the 13,000 employees who attend the office only two days a month, and accounted for some of NatWest’s lowest-paid workers, including staff involved in technology, security, data analytics and human resources.The union said the change would pile additional financial pressure on staff already struggling with rising living costs, while undermining flexible arrangements for those with caring responsibilities or disabilities. Many had also structured their lives around flexible working agreements that were expanded during the Covid pandemic, it said.“This is yet another kick in the teeth for workers who have suffered years of real-terms pay cuts and who are struggling to make ends meet,” said the Unite general secretary, Sharon Graham.“NatWest’s decision is completely out of touch with the realities facing its workforce,” she added, noting that thousands of staff would face higher travel and childcare costs as a result.“For NatWest to impose these changes while reneging on existing agreements shows complete contempt for its workforce. NatWest must ditch these proposals and engage properly with its workers.”The bank said its policy was meant to “help teams collaborate,” echoing arguments made by other banks ranging from JP Morgan toRevolut, which clamped down on remote working,saying it harms the training of younger staff.Last month Barclays was forced to push back its return-to-office plans after astaff backlash, backed by Unite. It had ordered staff to come in at least three days a week from early October, up from two days a week. The bank eventually softened its stance and allowed some staff to delay the requirement until next year.Some staff at NatWest – including traders, branch workers and relationship managers – are already required to be in the office four days a week. Others, including its communications, administrative and analytics staff, work a hybrid schedule where they are in six times a month.A NatWest spokesperson said: “Flexible working remains an important part of how we work but we’ve also learned more about the value that spending time together brings for our colleagues and customers – helping teams collaborate, share ideas, build relationships and learn from one another.”The bank added: “We recognise this will be a change for some colleagues and we’re giving them time to plan ahead and will support them through the transition.”Explore more on these topicsBankingNatWest GroupWork & careersTrade unionsWork-life balanceWorking from homeFinancial sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: European air fares could rise by as much as 20% in 2027, Ryanair boss predicts | Airline industry | The Guardian
description: Conflict in Middle East is pushing jet fuel costs higher and many carriers are not hedged against such increases, Michael O’Leary says
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Conflict in Middle East is pushing jet fuel costs higher and many carriers are not hedged against such increases, Michael O’Leary says
Content: Ryanair and many other European airlines had hedged their jet fuel requirements for 2026, O’Leary said.Photograph: Alexandros Avramidis/ReutersView image in fullscreenRyanair and many other European airlines had hedged their jet fuel requirements for 2026, O’Leary said.Photograph: Alexandros Avramidis/ReutersAirline industryEuropean air fares could rise by as much as 20% in 2027, Ryanair boss predictsConflict in Middle East is pushing jet fuel costs higher and many carriers are not hedged against such increases, Michael O’Leary saysJoanna PartridgeTue 20 Oct 2026 10.28 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 10.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRyanair’s chief executive has predicted a record increase in European air fares next year, as airlines grapple with fuel bills pushed higher by the Middle East conflict.Many carriers are not hedged against rising jet fuel costs, Michael O’Leary said, which he predicted would lead to airline bankruptcies and takeovers. He forecast these pressures would result in the price of plane tickets rising by as much as 20%.“You’re going to see air fares rise next year inEurope, I think by 10, 15, maybe 20%. You’re going to see ⁠the biggest increase in air fares, I would say, in history in Europe for the next 12 ​months,” O’Leary told a news conference ‌in Brussels.Jet fuel prices have soared in recent months, as the war on Iran has choked off fuel supplies. Jet fuel accounts for a large portion of carriers’ costs. The airlines body IATA previously predicted jet fuel prices would be70% higher across 2026– estimated toaverage $152 (£114) a barrel for the year, compared with $90 in 2025 – slashing airlines’ profits.Ryanair and many other European airlines had hedged their jet fuel requirements for 2026, O’Leary said, adding that Ryanair was 80% hedged at $67 a barrel at the time the Iran conflict began in late February.However, the boss of Europe’s largest airline said most European carriers, including Ryanair, do not have significant hedging in place from April 2027 onwards to protect them if oil prices remain high.“We’re 85% unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” O’Leary said.Ryanair’s hedging contract for 2027 covered 15% of its fuel costs at $85 a barrel, he added, whereas spot rates are currently hovering at about double that level.View image in fullscreenDuring his visit to Brussels, O’Leary announced he was cutting 20 of Ryanair’s routes and more than one million seats from Belgium from the airline’s winter schedule.Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPAEasyJet reported a £105m annual rise in fuel costs in July, adding it had hedged 62% of its fuel requirements for the first half of 2027 and 37% for the second half of the year. The airline announced in October it was cutting 700,000 seats from its winter schedule in an attempt to save fuel.During his visit to Brussels, O’Leary announced he was cutting 20 of Ryanair’s routes and more than one million seats from Belgium from the airline’s winter schedule, after the federal government’s decision to increase its aviation tax from €2 to €7 in January.O’Leary is the latest executive to warn of thedownbeat outlook for aviation. Industry leaders have said some carriers will struggle to survive the fuel price shock. Passenger surveys have shown travellers arebraced for higher faresand are prepared to spend more, but airlines do not know how long consumers will be able to afford pricier tickets.Explore more on these topicsAirline industryAir transportEuropeRyanaireasyJetUS-Israel war on IranMichael O'LearynewsShareReuse this content

title: Paddy Power owner blames tax rises for plan to shed up to 1,400 jobs | Gambling | The Guardian
description: Flutter says one in 10 UK and Ireland workers at risk of redundancy because of a ‘material increase in betting and gaming duties’
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Flutter says one in 10 UK and Ireland workers at risk of redundancy because of a ‘material increase in betting and gaming duties’
Content: John Healey, the chancellor, is considering an increase in the tax on betting machines.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJohn Healey, the chancellor, is considering an increase in the tax on betting machines.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesGamblingPaddy Power owner blames tax rises for plan to shed up to 1,400 jobsFlutter says one in 10 UK and Ireland workers at risk of redundancy because of a ‘material increase in betting and gaming duties’Rob DaviesTue 20 Oct 2026 10.24 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 18.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe gambling company behind Paddy Power and Sky Bet has announced up to 1,400 job cuts, blaming tax rises imposed byRachel Reeves.Flutter Entertainment revealed plans on Tuesday to restructure its UK and Ireland division, affecting staff in Leeds, Dublin and Sunderland. Redundancies are also expected to hit offices in Porto in Portugal and Cluj-Napoca in Romania.But Flutter’s domestic market, where it employs 8,960 people, is expected to bear the brunt of the cuts, indicating that more than 10% of its UK and Ireland workforce could lose their jobs.The announcement is likely to echo loudly in the Treasury a week before John Healey’s first budget. The chancellor is considering an increase in machine games duty (MGD), a tax levied on slot machines. Industry figures warn this would trigger thousands of job losses.Flutter’s bombshell will heat up thedebate over whether tax rises are wholly to blamefor job losses in the sector, or whether companies are using government policy as cover for strategic cost-cutting, amid lacklustre conditions in the UK market.Paddy Power’s founder, Stewart Kenny, has accused the industry of “scaremongering” about jobs to avoid paying more tax.But Flutter pinned the blame squarely on the “significant” increase in gaming duties announced by Reeves in the 2025 autumn budget.The then chancellor increased remote gaming duty – levied on online casino games – from 21% to 40%. She also raised duty on online sports bets from 15% to 25%.Several major gambling companies, including Ladbrokes owner, Entain, and Evoke, which is owned byWilliam Hill, have blamed Reeves for poor financial results or job cuts.One industry insider, who asked not to be named, said Flutter’s absorption of Sky Bet, which it bought in 2020, was likely to be a contributing factor. “Government policy changes ran alongside existing integration of its [Flutter’s] brands with inevitable job cuts,” they said.Many of the job cuts are expected to fall in Leeds, which was Sky Bet’s key centre of operations. Flutter said it expected to take a one-off hit of $90m (£67.3m) from the redundancy round. Its shares rose more than 2% in early trading in the US as investors looked forward to the prospect of a leaner business with fewer employees.“The material increase in betting and gaming duties announced in the UK budget last year has fundamentally changed the economic model of the regulated betting and gaming industry in the UK while helping to fuel the unlicensed, unregulated market,” said Kevin Harrington, Flutter’s UK and Ireland chief executive.“As we warned a year ago, we cannot fully absorb a rise of this magnitude without reducing our fixed-cost base and therefore must restructure our business so that we can best position ourselves for the future. We remain confident that we are well placed to benefit from share gains given our position as the largest scale operator in the UK.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLeading figures in the gambling industry, which takes £13bn from British punters every year, have warned Healey to expect further contraction among the major operators if he goes ahead with plans to increase MGD.The Social Market Foundation, a cross-party thinktank, has called for a doubling of the levy from 20% to 40%, saying this could raise up to £460m.Adult gaming centres, slot machine venues that can be open 24 hours a day on high streets, are understood to be one of the main targets for any such rise. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been a vocal critic of the centres.The Guardian has exposed exploitative practices in the sector, whichdisproportionately clusters its shops in deprived areas.Some industry insiders say that gaming centres, which have lower overheads than bookies, could survive a tax rise relatively unscathed, whereas betting shops and casinos would face closures.Explore more on these topicsGamblingSport bettingPaddy PowerWilliam HillBudget 2026John HealeyRachel ReevesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Explosive births, talking foxes and the devil in a trenchcoat – the Sitges fantastic film festival in all its creepy glory | Movies | The Guardian
description: Olivia Colman goes vulpine, Rupert Grint’s newborn is a monster and Joko Anwar makes a warmhearted violent ghost story set in an Indonesian prison
Author: Anne Billson
Headline: Olivia Colman goes vulpine, Rupert Grint’s newborn is a monster and Joko Anwar makes a warmhearted violent ghost story set in an Indonesian prison
Content: Indecently entertaining … (l-r) Andrea Genovese, Adriano Giannini, Jasmine Trinca and Gabriella Telegrafo in The Spiral.Photograph: Andrea MiconiView image in fullscreenIndecently entertaining … (l-r) Andrea Genovese, Adriano Giannini, Jasmine Trinca and Gabriella Telegrafo in The Spiral.Photograph: Andrea MiconiMoviesExplosive births, talking foxes and the devil in a trenchcoat – the Sitges fantastic film festival in all its creepy gloryOlivia Colman goes vulpine, Rupert Grint’s newborn is a monster and Joko Anwar makes a warmhearted violent ghost story set in an Indonesian prisonAnne BillsonTue 20 Oct 2026 10.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 10.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf I’d ever wanted children, the films showing at the 59th edition of the International Fantastic film festival of Catalonia in the coastal town of Sitges, south of Barcelona, would have soon set me straight. This year’s recurring themes were explosive parturition, chewed-up nipples and the fruit of the womb turning out to be at best sociopathic, at worst inhuman.The theme was celebrated in an evil-kiddy exhibition at the Miramar Cultural Centre, marking the 50th anniversary ofNarciso Ibáñez Serrador’s “fantaterror” classic Who Can Kill a Child?, some of which was filmed in Sitges itself. The expo traced the subgenre from 1956’s The Bad Seed, via Rosemary’s Baby and The Exorcist, tothis year’s Nightborn, in which poor Rupert Grint, as the hapless husband, is no match for the developing folk-horror bond between his depressed wife, their newborn “child”, and the spooky forest surrounding their house. Finnish director Hanna Bergholm, in her introduction, confessed it was inspired by her experiences of motherhood. Only up to a point, one hopes.Postpartum depression reared its head again in Mutter: The Diary of a Mother from Turkish director Alphan Eşeli, which begins with a father taking one look at his newborn offspring and fleeing into the woods. Hazar Ergüçlü’s terrific central performance keeps the focus on the social and economic plight of being a single parent, even when your baby resembles the one in Eraserhead.View image in fullscreenSpooky … Seidi Haarla and Rupert Grint in Nightborn.Photograph: Pietari PeltolaAs usual, a third of the titles in competition here were directed by women. Indeed, winner of this year’s best feature film award was Marion Le Coroller’s Sanguine (AKA Species), which followed in the gloopy French body horror footsteps of Julia Ducournau (Raw) and Coralie Fargeat (The Substance) with a medical intern developing a disfiguring skin condition that will have anyone who ever squeezed a pimple squirming in sympathy. The festival’s award for best female performance went to Jasmine Trinca as a mother who enters into a diabolical pact in Paolo Strippoli’s indecently entertaining The Spiral, though it is supporting actor Valeria Bruni Tedeschi who steals all her scenes as a soigné Mephistopheles in a trenchcoat.Meanwhile, best actor went to Benoît Magimel, oozing menace in one of his sleazy white suits in Léa Mysius’s The Birthday Party, a finely wrought home invasion thriller, and another of the films pivoting on a fraught mother-child relationship. It was heartening to see so many female protagonists in genre films, even ones by male directors such as Casey Affleck, whoseCompany, with its Russian doll structure, slowly morphs from a frontier western into a spine-tingling tale of the supernatural.Elsewhere, young women train as mermaids (Titanic Ocean, which teases the possibility of a mermaid-shark face-off, but fails to deliver), or bond with their abductors (The Daughters), or face off against a sociopathic youngster who infiltrates her snowed-in scout troop (11).Warmhearted …Ghost in the Cell.Photograph: Come and See PicturesAlas, I was so busy watching these that I missedthe 4K restoration of Jimmy Wang Yu’s Master of the Flying Guillotinefrom 1976 with its glorious krautrock soundtrack. But I did get to pay my respects to the late, great Sam Neill, who provided the voice of a magpie in Dario Russo’s bawdy, unabashedly full-frontalAustralian folk yarn The Fox. The stacked cast includes Jai Courtney and Olivia Colman as the voice of a wily talking fox.My favourite films of the festival included Javier Ruiz Caldera’s 5 More Minutes, which manages to put a new spin on the time-loop subgenre, its early lighthearted tone sliding into darker Timecrimes territory. Then there was The Mouths, about a cursed tree, a return to J-horror form from Takashi Shimizu (The Grudge) that gets more sinister and disorientating as it goes on, plus Sabu’s Taiwanese-Japanese co-production Arrested Memory, in which a traumatised Taipei cop suffering from Guy-Pearce-in-Memento syndrome bumbles his way through kidnapping, drug deals and car chases, to deadpan but ultimately hilarious effect.But best of all was Joko Anwar’s Ghost in the Cell, in which all the usual prison tropes – rioting, brutal guards, shivs, the threat of sexual violence – are supplemented by a supernatural curse, arty splatter, interpretative dance, a commentary on Indonesian corruption, and – best of all – an unexpectedly warmhearted vibe. Fortunately for everyone, it hasa UK release on digital platforms from 26 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmScience fiction and fantasy filmsHorror filmsThrillersSpainEuropeOlivia ColmanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I had no plan. Just total scorched earth’: how Kiran Leonard survived teen success to make songs of full-body joy | Experimental music | The Guardian
description: Hailed as a prodigy at 16, the Saddleworth singer-songwriter was patronised in the press and lost his musical path. Now courted by imaginative new bands, he explains his route back
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: Hailed as a prodigy at 16, the Saddleworth singer-songwriter was patronised in the press and lost his musical path. Now courted by imaginative new bands, he explains his route back
Content: ‘I couldn’t really find another manager – never have since, actually’ … Kiran Leonard.Photograph: Ben BeauvalletView image in fullscreen‘I couldn’t really find another manager – never have since, actually’ … Kiran Leonard.Photograph: Ben BeauvalletExperimental musicInterview‘I had no plan. Just total scorched earth’: how Kiran Leonard survived teen success to make songs of full-body joyShaad D'SouzaHailed as a prodigy at 16, the Saddleworth singer-songwriter was patronised in the press and lost his musical path. Now courted by imaginative new bands, he explains his route backTue 20 Oct 2026 09.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 09.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKiran Leonard presses the tips of his fingers together and looks at me solemnly across the table. “I don’t know if I’m doing a very good job,” he says, “But I’m trying really,reallyhard not to swear.”A decade ago, he explains,he was interviewed by the Guardian, got too drunk, and “swore all the way through the interview”. When the piece came out, his grandfather was thrilled. “But he couldn’t show any of his friends because I just sounded really aggressive,” he tells me sheepishly.It’s true that, the last time Leonard had a profile in this paper, he sounded a lot like a twentysomething trying hard to shed the preciousness of his former status as a teenage wunderkind. Hailed as a prodigy at age 16, upon the release of baroque, bonkers 2012 debut Bowler Hat Soup, a lot of Leonard’s early press plays up his age in a way that now reads as embarrassingly trite. “I think, unconsciously, I was probably quite defensive about how I was written about,” he says. “It’s not nice for journalists to fetishise the density or the ambitiousness of the music – it [was] obviously meant in a slightly patronising way.”The Leonard sitting across from me at a pub near his home in south-east London speaks calmly and carefully, like someone with nothing to prove – because, perhaps, he has so thoroughly proved himself over the interceding decade. In the past five or so years, Leonard has emerged as one of Britain’s most consistently fascinating experimental musicians. His recent slate includes 2024’s Real Home, a rangy pop record that touches on ramshackle country, menacing prog and Jonathan Richman-esque romanticism; last year’s Small Brown Bed/With You Waltz, a surrealist album of live takes recorded at notable DIY venues such as the Golden Lion in Todmorden and Delicious Clam in Sheffield with a group of musicians he calls No Tailgate; and credits on acclaimed records by Eli Winter, Caroline and My New Band Believe.His music is certainly far less wordy these days, far less likely to garner comparisons to Captain Beefheart or Joanna Newsom. But that’s because at this point, he says, he’s searching more for a sense of pure feeling: “I’m strongly driven by a very physical thing – which might seem quite broad, but it’s what distinguishes what I’m interested in and what I’m not.”Leonard was born and raised in Saddleworth, near Manchester, the son of a community midwife and John Leonard, a folk musician who worked for BBC Radio 1 and 2 in Manchester in the 80s and 90s. Although it’s clear he was making music from a young age, it’s less clear how he ended up signed, with a manager and booking agent, before he could legally drink. “The short answer is: I don’t know,” he says. “I was very ignorant and sheltered from a lot of it. I made Bowler Hat Soup and put it on Bandcamp. I think I sent it to a load of blogs, and a blog wrote about it, which was then read by [the people who ran the label] Hand of Glory. I didn’t really come up through like, gigging.”From there, Leonard was set up with that dreaded industry mechanism: a team. He got a publicist and a radio plugger and, through his management, a band, thankfully comprised of Manchester musicians who were at least making music that felt aligned with Leonard’s own. “I was fortunate to work with really good people and great musicians and have all this support, but the context was wrong,” he says.View image in fullscreenFinding his groove, Leonard performing in 2024.Photograph: Ben BeauvalletDuring that period, he made and released four albums, but increasingly felt as if he wasn’t in the right zone. Enamoured by fuck-the-industry icons such as Steve Albini, he began tanking his commitments because the music was the one thing he had control over. He moved to London and then, one day, ditched his entire team. “It was a disaster – just total scorched earth,” he says with a sheepish smile. “I had no plan, had no idea what I was doing.”Leonard found London “really alienating and difficult”, a feeling that was compounded by the fact that, he soon realised, he didn’t really know how much his team had sheltered him. “I couldn’t really find another manager – never have since, actually. And couldn’t get gigs,” he says.Leonard “gradually found a groove in London, found a way to find it really stimulating and engaging”. That came through booking more shows and from befriending the post-rock band Caroline, who are the nexus of some of the country’s most vital experimental music. “I’m sure many people in this community would say the same thing,” he says. The band have become “a centre of activity in a lot of the work that I do because there’s so many of them, the quality of what they do is such a high standard and they’re operating at a level that everyone is very proud of and impressed by.”Leonard quickly realised that his work could comprise “different investigations” – that he didn’t have to feel pinned down by one style, and that he didn’t have to be haunted by the music he made as a teenager. “I wanted to articulate myself more clearly and with less pomposity, less adolescent over-the-top-ness,” he says. “With the teenagery records, a lot of them were coming out much later than they’d been made. The difference between 15 and 18 is really massive, so playing those songs, I’d feel a bit of a dissonance, which made me more conscious of wanting to move past [them].”Leonard says that most of his work now is extremely solitary, although he occasionally plays in Caroline, and enjoys playing in a project where he doesn’t have to add his own compositional voice to the mix. An exception to that solitary work is Or Sobre Blau, Leonard’s duo with Catalan guitarist Andreu G Serra. Their remarkable second album, Making Friends, released earlier this year, is a heady mix of ambient guitar primitivism, oddball samples and scratched-up found sound. “Or Sobre Blau is really thrilling because it’s in a totally different voice,” he says. “It’s the voice of that friendship, which is really thrilling because for my stuff, I’m just in my head, which is sometimes horrible.”My New Band Believe review – beautiful ideas burst from ex-Black Midi man’s lovable debut albumRead moreIf there’s a common link between all Leonard’s work now, it’s that it often comes from a desire to make sounds that conjure full-body sensations. He often gets there. “I remember having a conversation with someone about the Caroline song Total Euphoria,” says Leonard. “They were like, I don’t know how often I feel total euphoria. I’m like: ‘I feel it quite a lot.’”Kiran Leonard istouring the UK, Europe and US, including dates as Or Sobre Blau, into January 2027Explore more on these topicsExperimental musicinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Spielberg’s War of the Worlds forced Americans to look in the mirror – and see the real monster | War of the Worlds | The Guardian
description: Starring a smooth-sprinting Tom Cruise at the top of his game, Steven Spielberg’s sci-fi thriller shows the scales falling from his own country’s eyes
Author: Tim Byrne
Headline: Starring a smooth-sprinting Tom Cruise at the top of his game, Steven Spielberg’s sci-fi thriller shows the scales falling from his own country’s eyes
Content: (L-R) Tim Robbins, Tom Cruise and Dakota Fanning in Steven Spielberg’s 2005 film War of the Worlds.Photograph: Moviestore/RexView image in fullscreen(L-R) Tim Robbins, Tom Cruise and Dakota Fanning in Steven Spielberg’s 2005 film War of the Worlds.Photograph: Moviestore/RexStream teamWar of the WorldsSpielberg’s War of the Worlds forced Americans to look in the mirror – and see the real monsterStarring a smooth-sprinting Tom Cruise at the top of his game, Steven Spielberg’s sci-fi thriller shows the scales falling from his own country’s eyesTim ByrneTue 20 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 19.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIknow, I know. There have been so many adaptations of HG Wells’ classic 1898 science fiction novel of planetary invasion, both before and since Steven Spielberg took his swipe at the story in 2005, with a Tom Cruise still at the top of his box office game. Some versions ofWar of the Worldshave been dire, while others – the 2019 TV adaptation starring Gabriel Byrne, or Jeff Wayne’s 1978 concept album featuring Richard Burton – have been expertly realised, refracting the story through their own contemporary lenses. But Spielberg’s is the best.While it was a financial hit, Spielberg’s version was not universally loved.
