Peter Bradshaw, in his review for this masthead, called it “fundamentally unambitious and often quite dull”. So there! One of his strongest gripes was the design of the aliens themselves, which were “just Area 51 cliches”. But, at risk of raising the ire of one of the great film critics of our time, I think Bradshaw missed the point. Spielberg’s aliens were designed to be cliches, cobbled from the fears of previous generations. They were supposed to be familiar because we’d invented them.Thunderbirds was far more than puppets on strings – it was a strikingly optimistic view of humanityRead moreCruise plays Ray Ferrier, a Brooklyn longshoreman who is also something of a deadbeat dad; the hostility coming from his kids, Robbie (Justin Chatwin) and Rachel (Dakota Fanning), feels deserved and longstanding. The opening scenes – as heavily pregnant ex-wife Mary Ann (Miranda Otto) reluctantly drops them off with their father – speak of years of disappointment, resentment and the slow curdling of familial love. Spielberg of course is a master of the subtexts of divorce, from as far back as ET.When threatening storm clouds and uncanny lightning strikes hit the local area, Ray goes to investigate, only to come face to face with deadly tripod-like machines emerging from underground, who unceremoniously eviscerate those around him. This scene is monstrously effective, Cruise doing his famousTom Cruisesprint towards camera as clouds of human ashes rain down.From then on, Ray and his kids are on the run, first to Mary Ann’s infinitely swankier house – soon destroyed by a falling passenger jet – then through an increasingly ghastly landscape of blight and ruin (the unnatural reds and greens in Rick Carter’s eerie production design are brilliantly unnerving). It becomes clear that these attacks are indiscriminate, that money and status are no longer a protection against the forces of destruction. The US finally becomes egalitarian: everyone is reduced to insect-like prey. Even having a working car puts you in danger from the desperation of the mob.The top 20 Tom Cruise movies – ranked!Read moreIt’s fascinating to watch Spielberg undermine and critique the military triumphalism of previous alien invasion narratives likeIndependence Day.Here, uniformed soldiers are utterly useless against an unstoppable enemy not through any lack of fire power or command control, but sheer inadequacy. It’s hard not to read this as political commentary about the conflict in Afghanistan and the futility of the conventional warfare in which the US was mired at the time.The film’s ending was highly criticised as anti-climactic, but I’d argue it reinforces the point made above. This existential threat, “vast and cool and unsympathetic”, can’t be fought in any traditional sense; it must be expurgated by nature itself in the form of microbial bacteria. As Rachel says of a splinter she gets at the beginning of the film: “When it’s ready, my body will just push it out.” The invaders (no longer from Mars because thatwouldbe silly) are endured rather than vanquished, depriving humanity of any moral victory but also saving it from its own hubris.View image in fullscreenDakota Fanning and Tom Cruise as Rachel and Ray Ferrier in War of the Worlds.Photograph: Paramount/AllstarLooking back at the film now, it seems astonishing that its critics seemed to view it solely through the lens of the commercial blockbuster. Few reviews made any mention of Spielberg’s primary target, the “infinite complacency” that leads Americans to feel immune from the displacement, forced migration and environmental catastrophe it happily inflicts on other parts of the globe.In his novel, which was inspired by the atrocities committed on Aboriginal Tasmania by British settlers, Wells calls the aliens attack “the great disillusionment”. Spielberg’s vision shows the scales falling from his own country’s eyes, capturing the horrifying realisation that the monster has been on Earth with us all along.War of the Worlds is available to stream on Stan in Australia, Paramount+ in the UK and Paramount+ and Peacock in the US.Explore more on these topicsWar of the WorldsStream teamSteven SpielbergTom CruiseScience fiction and fantasy filmsThrillersAction and adventure filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Children of the Wicker Man review – how the folk-horror classic haunted the family that made it | Movies | The Guardian
description: Director Robin Hardy’s children lay bare the sometimes agonised family background to a movie that went from ruinous flop to cult favourite
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Director Robin Hardy’s children lay bare the sometimes agonised family background to a movie that went from ruinous flop to cult favourite
Content: Spawning a monster hit … Children of the Wicker Man.Photograph: Courtesy of Hardy PicturesView image in fullscreenSpawning a monster hit … Children of the Wicker Man.Photograph: Courtesy of Hardy PicturesMoviesReviewChildren of the Wicker Man review – how the folk-horror classic haunted the family that made itDirector Robin Hardy’s children lay bare the sometimes agonised family background to a movie that went from ruinous flop to cult favouriteLeslie FelperinTue 20 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 08.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis documentary is a collaboration between Justin Hardy and Dominic Hardy, two of film director Robin Hardy’s children (he had seven in all, and was married five times), and it delves into the legacy of both their father and his most enduring work, 1973 folk-horror classicThe Wicker Man. The latter still stands today, for all its imperfections and peculiarities, as one of the most unsettling and paradoxically influential British films of all time, despite being a box-office flop on its initial release. This latest work is partly an account of The Wicker Man’s troubled production – a story that’s been told in books and journalism a fair few times already – and its strange reemergence as a cult movie-cum-fetish object, and partly a therapeutic exercise for the brothers themselves, full of raw feeling that’s sometimes painful to watch.However, while the brothers’ willingness to share their pain remains admirable, their film feels hampered by omissions and silences. On some level it is haunted by the ghosts of significant players in the story who have passed away, including Hardy himself and screenwriter Anthony Shaffer, as well as other key figures who are alive but aren’t interviewed here. Where, for example, are the brothers’ other siblings? Allan Brown, author of Inside The Wicker Man: How Not to Make a Cult Classic, is mentioned in several juicy anecdotes but is also absent, while somewhat bafflingly there’s a fair amount of an interview with Scottish actor Bill Paterson, who was almost cast in the original film but wasn’t.Of the two brothers, Justin’s is the more prominent voice;he died in Augustjust before the festival premiere of Wrath of the Gods, a long-nurtured semi-sequel to The Wicker Man he made with Dominic. Justin comes across as a choleric, clenched figure, understandably simmering with rage at a father who walked out of his life when he was still a child, leaving him and his sister in the care of their alcoholic mother, who was effectively bankrupted by the financial failure of The Wicker Man. Dominic, born to a different mother and raised in Canada, comes across as more tender-hearted, more forgiving of his father, thanks perhaps to both physical distance and the detachment of his training as an art historian.There’s a little, possibly unintentional, comedy to be had at one point when Dominic goes missing during filming and we see Justin raging over it to the film’s producers. The vignette stands as a salutary reminder that film-making is bloody hard work and it’s almost a miracle anything ever gets made, let alone an accidental masterpiece like The Wicker Man.Children of the Wicker Man is in UK cinemas from 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsThe Wicker ManHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea review – stirring portrait of fishers driven to eco-activism | Movies | The Guardian
description: With catches down 80%, dead crabs and lobsters washed up on beaches and officials denying any responsibility, Hartlepool seafarers have taken a stand
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: With catches down 80%, dead crabs and lobsters washed up on beaches and officials denying any responsibility, Hartlepool seafarers have taken a stand
Content: Brewing up trouble … Stan Rennie in  All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea.Photograph: Courtesy of Jeanie FinlayView image in fullscreenBrewing up trouble … Stan Rennie in  All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea.Photograph: Courtesy of Jeanie FinlayMoviesReviewAll Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea review – stirring portrait of fishers driven to eco-activismWith catches down 80%, dead crabs and lobsters washed up on beaches and officials denying any responsibility, Hartlepool seafarers have taken a standCath ClarkeTue 20 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHartlepool fisherman Stan Rennie has been calledthe next Mr Bates. For nearly 50 years Rennie has fished the same stretch of northeast coastline – then in October 2021, thousands of crabs, starfish and lobsters washed up dead and dying on the beaches. “It was like something out of a horror film,” says one local. Rennie and other fishermen suspected industrial pollution, but an investigation by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs concluded that the most likely cause of the die-off was “algal bloom”. For Rennie and the other fisherman, it didn’t add up. So, they crowdfunded their own independent scientific study.This documentary from Jeanie Finlay (Your Fat Friend)tells the story, and it’s maddening. The fishermen are close to bankruptcy, they’ve got mortgages and kids, catches are down 80%. The cost of diesel is higher than the price of a haul, and most put their boats up for sale. “Any jobs in Lidl?” reads one placard as they protest through town. What the fishermen suspect is that toxic sediment dredged from the River Tees and dumped in the sea is to blame. Their investigation finds evidence of a link to the chemicalpyridine, a byproduct of steelmaking.The reason for the dredging is the development of the then Conservative government’s flagship freeport (a zone with tax and customs breaks to attract investment) in the Tees Valley. The freeport was seen as key to the Tories’ “levelling-up” agenda after Brexit – and there’s footage of Boris Johnson at the site in his favourite dressing-up costume, a hi-vis vest. The gaslighting of fishermen and their concerns by public officials is enraging.Tees Valley mayor Ben Houchenbrushes them off as conspiracy theorists, crackpots and – a word he delivers with a sneer – activists. But, like Alan Bates, Rennie refuses to give up. “If an activist is someone who is trying to stop the ecosystem being killed, I’m an activist.”All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea is in UK and Irish cinemas from 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsPollutionFishingFishing industryAnimalsConservationreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Monster Mia review – kooky kid discovers school of beastly besties in wholesome Halloween fun | Movies | The Guardian
description: A scrappy girl discovers her tribe – which includes a vegan vampire – at a school for top scarers in this entertaining pre-teen animation
Author: Catherine Bray
Headline: A scrappy girl discovers her tribe – which includes a vegan vampire – at a school for top scarers in this entertaining pre-teen animation
Content: Motley crew … Monster Mia.Photograph: Kazoo FilmsView image in fullscreenMotley crew … Monster Mia.Photograph: Kazoo FilmsMoviesReviewMonster Mia review – kooky kid discovers school of beastly besties in wholesome Halloween funA scrappy girl discovers her tribe – which includes a vegan vampire – at a school for top scarers in this entertaining pre-teen animationCatherine BrayTue 20 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn films, twins are usually written as either identical personalities or complete and total opposites, and it’s the latter dynamic that’s at work in this pre-teen animation. One twin is a popular straight-A student heavily invested in fitting in and doing well at ballet, while her sister Mia is a chaotic kook. They both live in Primrose, an appropriately named community that apparently used to be infested with monsters, but can now claim to be proudly monster-free for the last 500 years. The twins’ parents are supportive of their golden child and try their best to understand Mia too, but it is easier for them to praise the kid bringing home the perfect behaviour reports than the one exasperating her teachers with her determination to discover monsters, by hook or by crook.Scrappy Mia is, naturally, the protagonist of this film, and it’s not too long before she finds herself accidentally enrolled in Rotwood Academy, a school for monsters who would be shocked to discover a human in their midst; from their point of view, humans are brutal, cold-blooded creatures, best avoided, who prefer – ugh! – cupcakes to grave-worms. Mia quickly buddies up with some misfits including a vegan vampire, and the stage is thus set for some Addams Family Lite hijinks, with culture clash comedy highlighting the difference between monster norms and human ways providing much of the humour.The underlying message that we shouldn’t be scared of difference is swiftly established as the major moral theme and while this is not exactly totally original, it proves distinctive enough to entertain its target audience. The message might be hammered home with all the subtlety of a croquet mallet to the head, but – what the hell – it is at least a wholesome philosophy, wrapped in palatable packaging. TheHalloweentiming of the release should help it connect enjoyably enough with younger spooky-season thrill-seekers.Monster Mia is in UK and Irish cinemas from 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmFamily filmsAnimation in filmComedy filmsComedyHalloweenreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Taylor Swift tells us to take the lead!’ Could highly organised pop fans clinch victory for Brazil’s Lula? | Music | The Guardian
description: Brazil’s famously outspoken fandoms have near-unanimously rallied behind the leftwing presidential candidate. On the streets of São Paulo, they explain their mission
Author: Felipe Maia
Headline: Brazil’s famously outspoken fandoms have near-unanimously rallied behind the leftwing presidential candidate. On the streets of São Paulo, they explain their mission
Content: Two pop fans at a pro-Lula demonstration in São Paulo.Photograph: Felipe MaiaView image in fullscreenTwo pop fans at a pro-Lula demonstration in São Paulo.Photograph: Felipe MaiaMusic‘Taylor Swift tells us to take the lead!’ Could highly organised pop fans clinch victory for Brazil’s Lula?Brazil’s famously outspoken fandoms have near-unanimously rallied behind the leftwing presidential candidate. On the streets of São Paulo, they explain their missionFelipe MaiaTue 20 Oct 2026 06.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 06.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier this month, Brazil’s presidentLuiz Inácio Lula da Silvaled a rally in São Paulo, as he aims to be re-elected to a fourth presidential term, and faces serious opposition from right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro. Taking the mic before a crowd on Avenida Paulista that organisers put at more than a million, the former union leader began: “I’m not sure whether to open this speech with ‘comrades’ or ‘fandoms from all over Brazil’.” The rally was organised by Lula’s Workers’ party (PT) and a string of other leftwing groups – but the spark came from pop music fandoms.More than 600 Brazilian fanbase groups forBillie Eilish, Lady Gaga, Katseye, Demi Lovato, Harry Styles, Katy Perry, Selena Gomez, as well as Brazilian stars such as Anitta, Marina Sena and Ludmilla among others, all came together to back Lula, waging an intense online campaign as soon as Lula’s rival, son of imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro, came out on top in the first round on 4 October. Neither candidate earned more than 50% of the vote, so a runoff is now scheduled for 25 October to decide between the two.When the first round results came in, “I had this feeling I’d seen it all before with Jair Bolsonaro, and that was really frustrating,” says V, a Billie Eilish fan who helps run Info Billie Brasil, one of the country’s biggest fan communities dedicated to the US singer. “So my first reaction was to use the only communication tool we have and get our community to embrace the cause: Lula’s re-election.”View image in fullscreenAnother pro-Lula demonstrator.Photograph: V-Info Billie BrasilThe account posted a short open letter to Lula on X and Instagram: “Our social media pages are open for you and your team”. Within hours, a wave of fan accounts had shared the same message. “We knew social media had always been a weak spot for his campaign, so for the second round we’ll do everything we can to get the word out about Lula’s government,” says V (their name, and others in this report, have been anonymised). The initiative eventually grew into Fandoms Pelo Brasil, a website explaining to pop music fans how to mobilise for Lula. “Our frustration with the election turned into something massive, uncontrollable.”Amid the crowd on Paulista, São Paulo’s main avenue, supporters carried the familiar symbols of the left, from the hammer and sickle to Palestinian flags, but there were newcomers too: Beyhive T-shirts, BTS merch andTaylor Swiftmotifs.“We’re inspired by these artists, and Taylor is always talking about how young people should take the lead,” said Josiane, a Swiftie. Her friend Giovanna, a member of the Army fandom for K-poppersBTS, agrees: “We need to step up and make ourselves heard.”“A lot of people don’t keep up with politics, but they do follow fanclubs and fan accounts, so I think fandoms can bring this kind of discussion to more people,” said Raissa, a Beyoncé fan. “She’s a pop diva who talks about LGBTQ+ freedom and freedom of speech, and that matters to us too.”Pop stars’ mostly progressive politics, however tempered by the commercial interests of the music industry, are the main convergence point for these fandoms. And the influence can run the other way, too. After Info Billie Brasil reached out to him, Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and collaborator, endorsed the movement with a story on his Instagram account.“Our views clearly line up with those of the Blackpink members,” says W, one of the people who run a leading Blackpink fan account inBrazil. “Some of them are ambassadors for Unicef or the UN, and they stand up for the environment and women’s rights. We can’t speak for them, but our ideas are aligned.”Pop music is a huge business in Brazil, and the country’s fans are globally famed – even notorious – for the intensity of their fandom, imploring artists to tour from overseas via hundreds of comments on their social media pages.View image in fullscreenA fan with a bag featuring bespoke BTS stickers.Photograph: Felipe MaiaLula’s government has cannily courted these vociferous, campaign-minded fans. In August, he signed a “fan decree” cracking down on ticket-scalping bots and requiring free drinking water at all large public events. Some fandom representatives attended a meeting with the president. “There was no political coordination in regards to the election on our side back then, but ticketing is a huge part of fan life,” says W.Fandoms aren’t unanimously leftwing.NJZ Brasil, a fan page for the K-pop group NewJeans, is openly pro-Bolsonaro; W says they have “noticed comments and messages from rightwing voters in the Blackpink fan community”.Shakira Brasilhas stayed out of political campaigns, following an earlier instruction from Shakira’s team restricting the use of the singer’s image in political content online.But V rejects that stance: “I remember congresswoman Erika Hilton once saying that everything is political, so a party or a concert can be political too.” Hilton, who was re-elected this month as the most-voted woman in the history of Brazil’s lower house, joined forces with fandoms in 2024 to campaign against a bill that would have equated abortion after 22 weeks of pregnancy with homicide, even in cases of rape. The bill stalled after a public backlash.“We’ll wage a digital guerrilla campaign, but we’ll be on the streets as well,” Hilton said in avoice notesent to the fandoms the day after the first round. “Lula will be president again. That’s our mission, and we’re in this together – count on me.”The Info Billie Brasil team has told its followers that, until the runoff, politics will take priority over Billie Eilish news, “because we can get our issues seen,” says V. “We want to win rightwing voters over to the left. We won’t stop.”Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaFlávio BolsonaroAmericasTaylor SwiftfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Alonetimes review – frenetic, funny and exhilarating music theatre | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Six performers navigate a disjointed world of online slang, loneliness and absurdity in the UK premiere of Jennifer Walshe and Philip Venables’ thrillingly original collaboration
Author: Flora Willson
Headline: Six performers navigate a disjointed world of online slang, loneliness and absurdity in the UK premiere of Jennifer Walshe and Philip Venables’ thrillingly original collaboration
Content: Fleetingly poetic … The Alonetimes at Schwarzman Centre, Oxford.Photograph: Cyril MarcilhacyView image in fullscreenFleetingly poetic … The Alonetimes at Schwarzman Centre, Oxford.Photograph: Cyril MarcilhacyClassical musicReviewThe Alonetimes review – frenetic, funny and exhilarating music theatreSohmen Concert Hall, Schwarzman Centre, OxfordSix performers navigate a disjointed world of online slang, loneliness and absurdity in the UK premiere of Jennifer Walshe and Philip Venables’ thrillingly original collaborationFlora WillsonTue 20 Oct 2026 06.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 06.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs we found our seats, a druidic figure wearing a string of vapes as a necklace sat on stage swathed in white fabric and smoke, emitting close-miked mouth noises amid a rising chorus of percussive hisses and rattles. Then dancing flashlights, reverb and thunderous drum rolls. Later came monologues delivered with quiet, skin-crawling sincerity or pounded out as a kind of manic rap and comically dysfunctional text chats projected on the backcloth. Not to mention the dance breaks. There was an angular, hyper-controlled trio fluent in the language of modern ballet and a hands-on-hips traditional number as faux-folk lyrics scrolled in gothic script and a hefty synthetic beat throbbed below.The first collaboration betweenJennifer WalsheandPhilip Venables– two of the most distinctive creators in music theatre today – The Alonetimes was never likely to adhere to the conventional playbook of opera. Theprogramme for its UK premieredescribes the work as “a fragmented archaeology of personal stories”. Alternatively: there is no single linear plot but instead six performers, who step constantly in and out of unnamed roles, switch between playing instruments and singing, form a taut Greek chorus and stand alone in the spotlights.View image in fullscreenCare and conviction … Vanessa Porter in The Alonetimes.Photograph: Cyril MarcilhacyThe text is at once very online (hello, “soft looksmaxxing”) and very sweary – “super-fucking awkward!” intones the Greek chorus in one scene – but also fleetingly poetic in its observations on life, love and loneliness. The music obsesses over short loops (frantic violin lines, for instance, that might have escaped from one of Bartók’s folksier scores) and hammers away rhythmically like a sonic answer to strobe lighting. There are moments of ethereal beauty, too: quiet drones, gentle humming, disjointed suspensions on the accordion, timpani sliding in unison with a single voice, a brief six-part chorale.Above all, though, The Alonetimes is funny. Not because of the contemporary references and the jokes about dating apps – but because these six performers brought to life people we’ve all been or met with absolute care and conviction. Oskar McCarthy’s turn as the instructor of an over-65s aerobics class – “hi everyone”, he murmured, the swerve into slippers-and-Ovaltine provoking gales of laughter – was one comic highlight. But Andreas Borregaard, Diamanda La Berge Dramm, Loré Lixenberg, Vanessa Porter and Adam Starkie were every bit as virtuosic as they negotiated the work’s hyperactive tragicomedy. Sometimes baffling and often bonkers, this was also an exhilaratingly enjoyable piece of contemporary music theatre.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicPhilip VenablesOxfordExperimental musicTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It speaks very poorly of us as a society’: Lawrence Wright on his book on death row and redemption | Books | The Guardian
description: The Pulitzer prize-winning writer’s new book looks at the women on death row in Texas and the nuns who have been trying to help them
Author: Martin Pengelly
Headline: The Pulitzer prize-winning writer’s new book looks at the women on death row in Texas and the nuns who have been trying to help them
Content: Supporters of the death row inmate Melissa Lucio.Photograph: Jay Janner/APView image in fullscreenSupporters of the death row inmate Melissa Lucio.Photograph: Jay Janner/APBooksInterview‘It speaks very poorly of us as a society’: Lawrence Wright on his book on death row and redemptionMartin PengellyThe Pulitzer prize-winning writer’s new book looks at the women on death row in Texas and the nuns who have been trying to help themTue 20 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is “stunning”, the Pulitzer-winning reporter Lawrence Wright said, that Redemption, his new book about women on death row inTexasand the nuns who minister to them, turns out to be published at a time of intense focus on capital punishment.Christa Pike’s botched execution is a reminder of the horror of the death penalty | Moira DoneganRead moreTwo cases dominate headlines: the Trump administration’sabandonedplan to livestream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, and Tennessee’sfailureto kill the convicted murderer Christa Pike by lethal injection. Away from the headlines, inTexasand elsewhere, executionscontinue.From his study in Austin, Wright said: “In Texas, capital punishment is too frequently a subject of discussion, so people are inured to it. I think we killed somebodya couple of days ago, and that I guess was not mentioned in the paper at all.“On Nidal Hasan, to roll this guy in a wheelchair before a firing squad and televise it [would have been] al-Qaida’s dream, and I can speak with some authority on that.” Wright wrote The Looming Tower: al-Qaeda and the Road to 9/11,a Pulitzer winner in 2007, the basis for a hitTV drama. “A person would have to be totally ignorant of the nature of al-Qaida and Isis. The goal of martyrdom against the west is such a powerful inducement for so many people to join those organizations, and this is like a recruitment ad.”In the case of Christa Pike, Wright said: “The evidence of the execution chamber is that occasionally something goes really badly wrong, and it’s very embarrassing and inhumane, and then everybody is awakened to it, especially when a woman’s involved.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alfred A KnopfRedemption is about two groups of women: the seven who sit on death row in Texas and theSisters of Mary Morning Star, a contemplative order in Waco. In 2014, a deacon, Ronnie Lastovica, asked the nuns to meet the prisoners. Wright, who first wrote about Lastovica and the sistersfor the New Yorker, describes that remarkable first meeting, and how each group then changed the lives of the other. The result is a book as much about the spiritual life as the American way of death.“I didn’t write it for it to be a book about capital punishment,” Wright said. “What I was interested in was the possibility of redemption. I wasn’t interested when I started about, you know, finding an innocent person and trying to free them. Although I’m now in that spot.”Melissa Lucio, from Harlingen in south Texas, was sentenced to die for beating her two-year-old daughter to death. Death row moves slow. The appeals process is torturous. Convicted in 2008, due to die in 2022, Lucio was granted alast-minute reprievegiven evidence her daughter, Mariah, died from a fall and Lucio’s confession was coerced, a case the film-maker Sabrina Van Tassel made powerfully withThe State of Texas vs Melissa. Lucio’s other children proclaim her innocence. In 2024, a judgepronouncedLucio “actually innocent”. But this is Texas. Last month, an appeals courtsaidLucio should be killed regardless.After our interview, Wright has a meeting “to talk about Melissa’s case”. It has become personal, but so is his engagement with all the women on death row.“I would just assume that all seven women on the row are guilty, and they did heinous things,” he said, of how he started work. “What I wanted to know is, could someone like that be redeemed? And if so, then what do we do with them? As a society, are we at a point where we’re killing people on principle, whether or not they are no longer the person that committed that crime 20, 30 years ago? Is it redemptive, is vengeance suitable when all the victim’s family have passed on, of old age? There is a creepiness about it. Aside from the absence of justification, it speaks very poorly of us as a society.”Now 79, Wright haswritten12 books of nonfiction, four novels, plays and screenplays. “My first book was about the Amish,” he said. “I’ve written about the Mormons and Scientology and Jonestown and Branch Davidians and Satanists. There’s some kind of mania going on there. Now I look back at it, I think what was happening to me was that I was so interested in religion but not being religious myself. I’m just interested in the fact that you can be political, and it won’t change your behavior at all … but if you’re intensely religious, it dictates every part of your life.”View image in fullscreenMelissa Lucio.Photograph: The GuardianIn Redemption, other factors are in play: race and class. Wright examines the case of Walker Railey. A well-off white pastor, Railey was acquitted of killing his wife, left Texas to start anew in California. Wright knew him, haswritten about him, and is convinced of his guilt. But the main focus of Redemption is religion. As law professorMark Oslerputs it: “Without the support of Christians, we wouldn’t have the death penalty.”Wright said: “As reporters, we rarely investigate people’s religious beliefs. In a way, speaking as a skeptic, you feel kind of sorry for anybody that is captive to these intense religious beliefs. On the other hand, it’s transformative, and I’ve seen it before I got into this project, in other prisons, with other individuals who had done horrible things, and yet when exposed to faith of one sort or another have had a chance to climb out of that personality that was so deformed by whatever life they might have had in the past, and turned into someone who seems to me totally redeemed.”Some of the crimes described in Redemption might seem irredeemable. Brittany Holberg was convicted in 1998 for the brutal murder of AB Towery Sr, an 80-year-old man from Amarillo. Wright’s account of the killing is unsparing. Holberg, a sex worker and crack addict, claimed self-defense. A paid police informant said she confessed to enjoying the killing and said she would do it again. Holberg was sentenced to death.Writing about “wildly incompetent homicides”, Wright knew he’d “be dealing with extreme violence” but “owed it to the families of the victims, I couldn’t write about this without looking at the damage that these women left behind them, and even as much as I oppose lethal injection and so on, it is a bitter death that they gave to their victims, and so I can understand the wrath of the families. But after 30 years or something like that, you know, when basically they’ve served a life sentence, It seems cruel and pointless to execute them. The arbitrariness of it is.”Law enforcement malpractice is also common: brutal police railroading women into false confessions, ambitious prosecutors out to secure a conviction.“I have to confess that this book has been very disillusioning in terms of our justice system,” Wright said. “It’s a small pool that I’m looking at, but you know you have the DA framing Brittany Holberg. He put a snitch in her jail cell, and wrote a script for her to testify to. And later, this woman recanted. But you know, [the DA] wanted not just a homicide conviction; he wanted capital murder. And so he made sure he would get it.”View image in fullscreenLinda Carty.Photograph: Michael Graczyk/APLast year, Holberg was tried again. Her conviction wasupheld. Other cases examined by Wright include that of Linda Carty, a British citizenconvictedof murder despite a complete lack of forensic evidence and “whose defense attorney had lost more than 30 capital cases”. Kimberly Cargill wasconvictedof murdering her children’s babysitter, but the medical examiner could find no cause of death, and so it was described as ‘homicide of unknown cause’, and you wonder what that could even mean.Redemption is 250 pages long but contains multitudes. The remarkable, in places dark story of the Sisters of Mary Morning Star, how they came to Texas from France, would make a book of its own. With Wright due to turn back to Melissa Lucio and attempts to stop her state killing her, a last question turned to present-day Texas headlines, to Democrats Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico challenging hard-right Republicans for the governorship and a Senate seat, election day two weeks from now. Many liberals hope Texas might yet turn from its hardline path. Does Wright think redemption is near?“I guess what I should say about this is there’s cause for prayer,” he said, with a rueful laugh. “I don’t know what’s going to happen, butfor 32 yearswe haven’t elected a Democratic candidate statewide. It’s like we’ve been living in an enchanted forest, and the witch controlling it has cursed us. So will the wicked witch be dead at the end of November? I don’t know. It’s a time of great promise, but we’ll see if that promise is kept.”Redemption isout nowExplore more on these topicsBooksTexasCapital punishment (US news)Capital punishment (World news)interviewsShareReuse this content

title: Alone With a Book by Tessa Hadley review – an acclaimed writer’s cultural prescription | Tessa Hadley | The Guardian
description: This collection of essays from the beloved novelist is full of gem-like insights on art and books
Author: Chloë Ashby
Headline: This collection of essays from the beloved novelist is full of gem-like insights on art and books
Content: Tessa HadleyPhotograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTessa HadleyPhotograph: David Levene/The GuardianTessa HadleyReviewAlone With a Book by Tessa Hadley review – an acclaimed writer’s cultural prescriptionThis collection of essays from the beloved novelist is full of gem-like insights on art and booksChloë AshbyTue 20 Oct 2026 04.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenTessa Hadleywas a child, someone gave her a copy of Lois Lenski’s Papa Small, which follows Mr Small and his family through a typical week. Papa Small goes to work, Mama Small cooks the supper, and the small Smalls dry and put away the dishes. “I thrilled to its ordinariness,” writes Hadley, a novelist known for her depictions of the ordinary that are anything but. In all her novels and short stories, she’s spectacularly alive to the everyday, both the seemingly humdrum surfaces and the darkest emotional depths.So you know what you’re in for when you reach for a book by Hadley, which is why I was in equal parts excited and apprehensive about her first foray into nonfiction. At least, it’s her first in bound form: Alone With a Book comprises published essays written since 2000. A nimble mix of biography, cultural criticism and personal reflection, it traces her development as both a reader and a writer, and burrows into the literary and artistic works that have kept her company along the way. For fans, it’s a fascinating insight into how and why she became the beloved author she is. For the rest, it’s a first-class reading (and picture) list.Hadley was a bookish child. Plain and “physically inept”, she felt more at home curled up in the corner of a library than hanging off the bars of a climbing frame. Her father was a teacher and jazz trumpeter, her mother a housewife and occasional dressmaker. On the walls of her childhood home were prints by Amedeo Modigliani, Pablo Picasso, Maurice Utrillo. Hadley’s brother, Tom, went on to become a scholar of Renaissance art, forever squabbling with their mother, who at art school had learned to think of everything pre-impressionist as “academic and stuffy”. “Mum and Dad’s feeling for books trailed well behind their interests in music and the visual arts, so that I never felt the burden of their judgment, for which I’m grateful.”double quotation markThere’s comfort to be found in seeing a writer so seasoned, so talented, still reading, still learningFor a long time, writing felt to Hadley like a form of failure: “I was a slow developer and too impressionable, too ready to take on the colouration of whatever I was absorbed in.” It was only when she found Alice Munro in the late 1980s, by which point she was in her early 30s, a wife and a mother, that she began to understand there might be ways to write about “the small ordinary things I was expert in, instead of trying to know what other people knew”.There are two essays on Munro in Alone With a Book, and more on other writers Hadley considers her “intimates” – Anne Tyler (“indefatigably inventive”), Elizabeth Bowen (“better than Woolf”), Anita Brookner (“What a confessional writer she is!”). Hadley as critic is as passionate as she is shrewd: her only quibble with Ferdinand Mount’s excellent English Voices is directed at his essay on Germaine Greer “not because he isn’t right about some of her contradictions, but because he can’t quite keep ‘Calm down dear’ out of his tone”; Margaret Drabble’s The Millstoneis “the seminal 1960s feminist novel that Doris Lessing’s The Golden Notebook is always supposed to be”.Now and then I found myself yearning to be nose-deep in a Hadley novel, rather than reading her thoughts on others’ work. But there’s comfort to be found in seeing a writer so seasoned, so talented, still reading, still learning. The section on art is brilliant, albeit brief, and although Hadley doubts herself – she’s aware “how my eye is untrained, careless of the visual construction, too quick to move to the contents of what’s narrated” – her way of looking at paintings is witty and fresh. Here she is on Félix Vallotton’s portrait of his wife Gabrielle sitting calmly in a chair while her baby niece rips up a piece of paper on the floor: “Is Vallotton perturbed by how his wife is smiling and fatalistic, overseeing the destruction of something so closely resembling his own work?”It’s curious that two of the four artworks she writes about are religious in theme – and yet, as she points out, Christian stories have “shaped our aesthetic and moral imagination at levels so deep we’re mostly unconscious of it”. During the pandemic, when she was sheltering apart from her sons (she has three, as well as three stepsons), she found herself drawn to The Coronation of the Virgin by Jacopo di Cione, “a grave and golden reverberation in my thought”. In this political moment, she finds herself “seeking out certain images of cruelty in art, as if I need to look straight at it and into it”. Cue Giovanni Bellini’s The Assassination of Saint Peter Martyr.As a child, Hadley shunned certain of Grimms’ fairytales because “they were too terrible”. Terrible things happen in her stories too – things to do with thwarted ambitions, adultery and ageing – amid the gentle, persistent patterns of daily life. Here, she makes a compelling case for keeping books and art close in both good times and bad, and (in the right hands) for the “powerful magic” of domestic realism.Alone With a Book: On Reading, Writing and Looking by Tessa Hadley is published by Jonathan Cape (£22). title: Gilgamesh by Simon Armitage review – an ancient epic is brilliantly translated for our times | Poetry | The Guardian
description: The poet laureate’s visceral take on the legendary Mesopotamian hero’s wild adventures is a tour de force
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The poet laureate’s visceral take on the legendary Mesopotamian hero’s wild adventures is a tour de force
Content: An orthostate depicting Gilgamesh between two minotaur demigods holding up a sun disc.Photograph: Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn orthostate depicting Gilgamesh between two minotaur demigods holding up a sun disc.Photograph: Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/Getty ImagesBook of the dayPoetryReviewGilgamesh by Simon Armitage review – an ancient epic is brilliantly translated for our timesThe poet laureate’s visceral take on the legendary Mesopotamian hero’s wild adventures is a tour de forcePhilip TerryTue 20 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 02.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe poet laureate is paid a salary of £5,750 per annum plus a barrel of sherry. No specific duties are attached to the role, but there is an expectation that poets will write verse for public occasions and royal events, a duty that Simon Armitage has fulfilled by writing a poem on the death of Elizabeth II, Floral Tribute, and another to mark the coronation of Charles and Camilla in 2023. Though it’s an awkward time for the royals, no laureate is going to write about them behaving badly (it wasn’t John Dryden, the first laureate, who wrote about Charles II’s bedroom habits, but John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester). And yet with Gilgamesh, Armitage does deliver a poem about royalty’s misdeeds, at least in part.The epic originated in ancient Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq) at least 4,000 years ago, and it begins with the eponymous demigod, king of Uruk, lording it over his subjects. Among other bad habits, he exercises the “right of the first night”, which allows him to bed newlywed brides before their husbands. To check his powers, the gods create his counterpart, the wild man Enkidu, who confronts Gilgamesh outside the house of one of these brides. The two rivals turned comrades then embark on a series of extraordinary adventures, including battles with Humbaba, guardian of the Cedar Forest, and with the winged Bull of Heaven, sent by the goddess Ishtar in revenge after Gilgamesh rejects her marriage proposal. Following Enkidu’s death, Gilgamesh sets out alone on a desperate quest for immortality that leads him to the very edge of the world.In his introduction Armitage draws our attention to the poem’s rich modern resonance, including its frankness about sex workers, who play a key role in bringing Enkidu to Uruk, its ecological dimension – Enkidu’s death is a punishment for cutting down the forest guarded by Humbaba – and the way the relationship of Gilgamesh and Enkidu can be seen as a celebration of same-sex physical love (Gilgamesh loves his companion “like a wife”). Most striking of all is the way the heroes’ fight with Humbaba echoes modern resource wars. The Gulf wars took place in the same geographical region, though the commodity in question was not timber – the prime building material at the time of the poem – but oil.double quotation markSome of the finest passages have a sumptuousness you can almost taste and touchThe poem’s uniquely fragmented history makes it both ancient and modern. Sumerian sources date back to 2000BC, but it remained lost until fragments of cuneiform tablets in a later Akkadian form were discovered by archaeologists in the 19th century. A tablet on display in the British Museum drew the attention of George Smith, employed by a firm that designed bank notes, and he repeatedly visited the museum in his lunch hour to gaze at it. When the keeper of Babylonian antiquities asked him what he was doing, Smith replied that he was reading it. Later, now in the employ of the British Museum, Smith was excited to discover a tablet describing a great flood. Crying “I am the first person to read that after 2000 years of oblivion,” he rushed about the room in a state of great excitation, and to the astonishment of those present began to undress. The passage Smith had deciphered comes towards the end of the poem, where Gilgamesh visits the now-immortal flood survivor Uta-napishtim – the poem’s Noah character – in an attempt to find immortality himself. It caused a sensation in Victorian England because of its similarity to the flood story in the Book of Genesis: here perhaps was evidence of the historical veracity of the event.This fragmented history of the poem is reflected in the way it has come down to us in broken tablet form, which Armitage compares to a vast jigsaw with pieces still missing. Readers who see this fragmentation as integral to the poem may be disappointed with Armitage’s approach, which is generally to paper over the cracks, as he puts it (though he does present passages that have been restored from later sources in prose, and occasionally leaves gaps whose contents he speculates on in detailed footnotes). One feature Armitage is very faithful to is the incantatory use of repetition, as in the journey to meet Humbaba – “After forty leagues they stopped and broke bread. / After sixty leagues they stopped and pitched camp” – which he says “enacts the mundane regularity of a long slog across featureless terrain”. Generally, the results are fresh and impressive, as in the poem’s opening lines, as solid as the rock they were once carved on:He witnessed great depths, saw the land’s bedrock.Astute in all subjects, wise in every matter,Gilgamesh glimpsed the foundations of life.Nothing escaped him; he possessed all knowledge,had learned each discipline in equal measure,understood completely the ways of the world.He uncovered secrets, revealed what was hidden,brought back word from before the Great Flood,trudged distant paths, earned his rest.He carved his trials and travails in a stone.Armitage wisely avoids rhyme, unlike some recent versions – there is no evidence of rhyme in the original text – but he knits his poem together tightly with a standard four-beat line, a fine-spun mixture of the modern and the archaic, and a smattering of the alliteration he employed inhis translation of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. Some of the finest passages have a sumptuousness you can almost taste and touch – Gilgamesh’s mother Ninsun, “She-Wild-Cow”, purifies herself with “tamarisk and soapwort”. Others have a delicious contemporaneity, as Humbaba calls Enkidu, created by the gods out of a lump of clay, a “half-wit”, a “crossbred freak” who “never sucked milk from his mother’s tit”. Of all the scenes, it is those in the forest, as the heroes make their way towards the home of Humbaba, that bring out Armitage’s best poetry, which sings and clatters its way through the undergrowth:The canopy was knitted and knotted with creepers;sap and resin came raining downand flowed away through channels and gorges.A bird called out, then the forest echoedwith the racket of more birds calling in answer.A lone cicada sounded its note,triggering a chorus of piping and hymning.A turtle dove answered the cries of a pigeon.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe register of Gilgamesh remains one of the great unknowns of the poem. Given the nature of its content – often violent, mocking and sexually explicit – there is no reason to assume it should, as it generally is, be translated into elevated language. Armitage tackles this head on by mixing different registers and idiolects. His tactile, visceral version is a tour de force, combining careful scholarship with poetic verve and deft linguistic meldings, and it is likely to become one of the standard renditions in English. It cannot, though, be the last word on this continuingly resonant poem, whose fragments are still coming to light in museum collections, fresh excavations and accidental finds.Philip Terry is the author of Dictator: A Free Version of the Epic of Gilgamesh in Globish (Carcanet, £12.99). Gilgamesh: A New Verse Translation by Simon Armitage is published by Faber (£14.99).To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Listen out for Lanny: can Max Porter’s mythic tale of a mulch-guzzler really be heard in this woodland? | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Every sun-dappled object is an instrument as composer Dom Coyote and sound designers Elena Peña and Dave Price conjure trip-hop-inspired rhythms in the Mendips for a new stage adaptation
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: Every sun-dappled object is an instrument as composer Dom Coyote and sound designers Elena Peña and Dave Price conjure trip-hop-inspired rhythms in the Mendips for a new stage adaptation
Content: A microphone placed in Stockhill Wood on the Mendip Hills.Photograph: Courtesy Dom CoyoteView image in fullscreenA microphone placed in Stockhill Wood on the Mendip Hills.Photograph: Courtesy Dom CoyoteTheatreListen out for Lanny: can Max Porter’s mythic tale of a mulch-guzzler really be heard in this woodland?Every sun-dappled object is an instrument as composer Dom Coyote and sound designers Elena Peña and Dave Price conjure trip-hop-inspired rhythms in the Mendips for a new stage adaptationKate WyverTue 20 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 02.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe woodland is stuck to our skin. Sound designers Elena Peña and Dave Price are hunched next to me, burying a microphone into mossy ground. Composer Dom Coyote is listening on headphones, crunching out a rhythm with his boot before shucking his shoes for a subtler sound. “It’s got to be socks off, Dom,” says Price. Coyote obliges, the balls of his feet soon covered in dead conifer needles. “Do you wish you’d had a pedicure now?” Peña asks.It’s a short drive from Bristol to this patch on the Mendip Hills, where pine cones and rowan berries scatter at the entrance to the trees. We’re on the hunt for sounds to orchestrate a staging of Max Porter’s novelLanny. The adaptation by Somerset-based Bea Roberts moves the spectral story of a lost boy and a mulch-guzzling creature from commuting-distance-to-London to commuting-distance-to-Bristol, with director Nancy Medina wanting the show’s sound to exist within the city’s historical music scene. “A kind of trip-hop world,” says Coyote, who is exploring this idea by replacing electronic beats with those of the natural world. “So we need to go and play the forest.” Every sun-dappled object becomes an instrument. Up on his feet, Price tests out a rhythm on a deep-timbred trunk. He points to the tree. “Any notes for the snare drum department?”View image in fullscreenElena Peña, Dave Price and Kate Wyver attempt to make the sound of deer running.Photograph: Courtesy Dom CoyoteLanny is a story that lends itself to the ear. On the page, which uses experimental typography, Porter’s text curls as Dead Papa Toothwort – an ancient creature who is myth, fable, scapegoat and threat – inhales the sounds of the village. “Music is so part of the book,” says Coyote, who describes the novel as like a spell. “You can already hear this village voice, where Dead Papa Toothwort is almost feeding off the language and culture and thoughts.” The team shake and rustle the trees, listening for sounds to bring the audience into Dead Papa Toothwort’s mystical world. Coyote’s aim is for the audience to ask: “Is the world making music, or am I just making sense of it?” As he and Peña are changing a microphone’s settings, Price appears with a blackberry plucked for each of us. “To enter the other realm,” he smiles.The human world is hard to escape. They worry the road is too close. A little further in, we come to a contained ring of spruce trees, where Peña places a stethoscope-like contact mic – so called because they only record what they’re in contact with – against a trunk. Every angle she taps and twists gives a different quality of sound. “Infinity,” she whispers. One tree sounds remarkably like bongos. “Too cheery,” Coyote frowns. Lanny is a tale of warning: a boy is lost, a village turns against itself and a family is torn apart. “When we do our job well, people don’t notice it,” says Coyote. “But it’s drawing you in, sharpening the lens.” He hopes this show’s music will “give the audience wonder”, he says, “to counteract the absolute tragedy of the tale”.A folk song laces through Roberts’ adaptation, which Coyote has put to the tune ofSumer Is Icumen In. “Dead Papa Toothwort is living outside of our human arrow of time,” he says. “He’s in the past, present and future.” Coyote is hoping to capture the natural, folkloric feel, which runs stream-like through Porter’s story, within his compositions. “I’m not particularly interested in a trained voice,” he says. “I like rawness. Rough magic.”View image in fullscreenRough magic … Dom Coyote in rehearsals for Lanny.Photograph: Helen MurrayCoyote never officially studied music. Instead, he learned guitar and acted, made anarchic music with Kneehigh in Cornwall, then continued doing theatre. Cracking open his laptop, he gives us a taste of his work-in-progress, made from recording sounds at home, in his garden and using the rattles of his child’s toys. “I used to feel very self-conscious about the fact that I couldn’t read music,” he says, “but now I see people want something more. For it to be led by ear. To feel really human.”Tilting back his head, Coyote begins to sing. It’s a song about a mother calling to her lost son, which the composer has been teaching to the cast in a round. Peña and Price start tapping and crunching out rhythms in the leaves. Even in this rough form, the raw folk song and cathedral-like synths from his laptop sound like the breath of the woodland. The treetops seem to sing it back and pass it on, starting a round of their own. “It’s a temple,” Coyote says, “isn’t it?” Now their job is to bottle this rough magic and bring it back inside.Lanny is atBristol Old Vicuntil 7 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreBristol Old VicMax PorterExperimental musicBristolSomersetMassive AttackfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TS Eliot’s Murder in the Cathedral review – gather in wonder at David Suchet’s excellent archbishop | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The poet’s 1935 verse drama has its eccentricities but the meticulous star plays Thomas Becket with a Shakespearean relish
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: The poet’s 1935 verse drama has its eccentricities but the meticulous star plays Thomas Becket with a Shakespearean relish
Content: Mass appeal … David Suchet as Thomas Becket in Murder in the Cathedral at St John the Divine church.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenMass appeal … David Suchet as Thomas Becket in Murder in the Cathedral at St John the Divine church.Photograph: Marc BrennerTheatreReviewTS Eliot’s Murder in the Cathedral review – gather in wonder at David Suchet’s excellent archbishopSt John the Divine church, LondonThe poet’s 1935 verse drama has its eccentricities but the meticulous star plays Thomas Becket with a Shakespearean relishMark LawsonTue 20 Oct 2026 07.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 15.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAstriking example of site-specific theatre, TS Eliot’sMurder in the Cathedralwas first performed in 1935 at Canterbury Cathedral. This was the location, in 1170, for its pivotal event: the killing by Henry II’s knights of Archbishop Thomas Becket during a dispute over the powers of church and state.Subsequently, audiences have been more likely to enter a production via a church nave than a theatre aisle. The latest host venue is St John the Divine, opposite theOrange Tree theatre, whose boss, Tom Littler, co-directs with Francesca Ellis.David Suchet’s Becket, in gilded vestments, preaches from the pulpit. Dozens of candles on the altar and lining a marbled walkway between pews (design by Rob Jones, lighting by Peter Mumford) cast shadows on the walls around stained glass windows.The overall classiness of the show is extended by a programme essay by an actual former archbishop of Canterbury,Rowan Williams, covering Eliot’s concern with whether priests, in 1930s England and Germany, served or resisted politicians.View image in fullscreenHard lesson … (from left) David Yelland, Ben Caplan, David Suchet, Nick Sampson and Jyuddah Jaymes.Photograph: Marc BrennerNo staging can disguise the eccentricities of a text that begins classically with a Greek-like chorus of Canterbury women (Eliot’s four swollen to a dozen by a community ensemble) but concludes with a precociously postmodern coda where the slaughtering quartet engage the audience in an emergency seminar about whether the churchman deserved it.Like Pinter heavies in black leather jackets and polo sweaters, Jyuddah Jaymes, Ben Caplan, Nick Sampson and David Yelland memorably double the murderous knights with the four tempters who offer Becket varieties of earthly and heavenly riches. Less successfully, the women’s choruses are musicalised (composer Orlando Gough) more than Eliot indicated, muffling some of the poetry in a piece with lines (“Human kind cannot bear very much reality”) directly rehearsing Eliot’s Four Quartets.His verse dramas often feel more written for page than stage; of seven plays, only this one is regularly revived and his biggest theatrical hit was, inadvertently, the musical Cats. Becket is a role with difficult rhythms for an actor. Initially listening to lengthy speeches by women, priests and tempters with minimal responses, the character then speaks unbroken for six pages.Listen out for Lanny: can Max Porter’s mythic tale of a mulch-guzzler really be heard in this woodland?Read moreAlways a meticulous actor, Suchet makes each gesture and syllable precise and shows the making up of Becket’s mind in the responsive phase and then brings the clarity and verbal relish of the best Shakespearean soliloquies to the Christmas Day sermon in which the turbulent priest accepts that he must be killed.Eliot, raised in the austere Unitarian church in St Louis, seems, on converting to Anglo-Catholicism in 1927, to have been enthralled by its tradition of martyrs and the play challenges each age with the balance between conviction and fanaticism, belief and futile sacrifice. If everything in churches were as dramatic and atmospheric as this, Becket’s current successor would not have to worry about declining congregations.AtSt John the Divine church,London, until 7 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreOrange Tree theatreDavid SuchetTS EliotReligionPoetryAnglicanismreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Getting Ziggy with it: David Bowie’s alter egos inspire dance show that will transform his songs | Stage | The Guardian
description: Subject to Change: A Dance for David Bowie will explore how the musician ‘practised a form of artistic reincarnation’, says choreographer Marcos Morau
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Subject to Change: A Dance for David Bowie will explore how the musician ‘practised a form of artistic reincarnation’, says choreographer Marcos Morau
Content: Not a ‘nostalgic tribute’ … David Bowie as Ziggy Stardust in 1973.Photograph: Ilpo Musto/AlamyView image in fullscreenNot a ‘nostalgic tribute’ … David Bowie as Ziggy Stardust in 1973.Photograph: Ilpo Musto/AlamyStageGetting Ziggy with it: David Bowie’s alter egos inspire dance show that will transform his songsSubject to Change: A Dance for David Bowie will explore how the musician ‘practised a form of artistic reincarnation’, says choreographer Marcos MorauChris WiegandStage editorTue 20 Oct 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Let’s dance,” sangDavid Bowiein 1983, commanding: “Put on your red shoes and dance the blues.” That call is to be answered – with footwear TBC – by an international dance production featuring new choral arrangements of songs from throughout his career.Subject to Change: A Dance for David Bowiewill be staged at Sadler’s Wells in London in autumn 2028 after a world premiere in Luxembourg. It will visit Tokyo in 2029. The show will explore how Bowie “practised a form of artistic reincarnation” according to Spanish choreographer Marcos Morau who is taking inspiration from the superstar’s transformations into personas such as Aladdin Sane and the Thin White Duke.“One of the greatest dangers for an artist is ending up resembling themselves too much,” said Morau. “Bowie turned change into a way of remaining true to himself. That inspires me deeply. I believe every new work should force us to let go of some certainty. Art shouldn’t serve to confirm who we are, but rather to accept that life transforms us, that we change over time, and that our own contradictions help us grow.”View image in fullscreen‘What happens when his songs leave behind the voice we all know?’ … Bowie in his Thin White Duke era in 1976.Photograph: Jorgen Angel/RedfernsOrchestrations of pop and rock classics have powered recent hit dance productions such asBlack Sabbath: The Balletanda reworking of The Who’s Quadrophenia, bringing in new audiences. In Subject to Change, Bowie’s songs will be interwoven with choral sounds from around the world and the voice of Spanish singer Maria Arnal. “I’m not interested in reproducing Bowie or creating a nostalgic tribute,” said Morau, who wants to explore “what happens when his songs leave behind the voice we all know and travel towards other voices, other cultures and other generations”. By employing different choral traditions, he hopes to “transform something deeply individual into a collective experience. I like to think that a work of art remains alive as long as we are able to transform it, and that perhaps the best way to remain faithful to Bowie is to dare to change him.”Over his career, Bowie collaborated with significant choreographers including Édouard Lock and Annie-B Parson. He was taught dance by the great mime Lindsay Kemp who recalled him taking part in improvisations such as sailors drowning at sea. Kemp directed Bowie in a 1967 theatre show, Pierrot in Turquoise, and tried – but failed –to get him to play Puss in Boots.The pierrot became one of Bowie’s alter egos – others included Halloween Jack from his Diamond Dogs era and, most famously, Ziggy Stardust, the intergalactic rockstar who “took it all too far but, boy, could he play guitar”. A black vinyl jumpsuit with stripes known asTokyo Pop, designed by Kansai Yamamoto for Bowie to wear as Ziggy in 1973, is used in the promotional image for Subject to Change.View image in fullscreenThe Subject to Change promotional image featuring the Tokyo Pop costume designed by Kansai YamamotoPhotograph: Kazuyoshi ShimomuraEach of his alter egos ushered in a new musical direction and a fresh look for Bowie but also brought out a different physicality, said Morau. “For Bowie, the body was just as important as the music or the costumes. It wasn’t simply a matter of appearance, but of how he inhabited space. What fascinates me is that he managed to turn his own body into a territory of fiction, allowing those fictions to become part of reality. When you can transform yourself with that kind of freedom, you can also find new ways of living. In a world obsessed with categorising us and making us follow certain patterns, Bowie turned his body into an act of defiance.”View image in fullscreen‘Perhaps the best way to remain faithful to Bowie is to dare to change him’ … Marcos Morau.Photograph: Kazuyoshi ShimomuraMorau is an in-demand choreographer whose works includeHorses(2024), created for Nederlands Dans Theater, which featured animalistic dancers prowling around mean streets to music by contemporary classical composer Caroline Shaw.Étude, performed earlier this year by the Paris Opera Ballet, upended the conventions of ballet. The former piece featured dancers wielding giant lamp posts; the latter used a swinging replica of the chandelier in the auditorium of Paris’s Palais Garnier. Both sets were designed by Max Glaenzel who will work on Subject to Change. The costumes will be by another of Morau’s regular collaborators, Silvia Delagneau, and the musical direction is by Alex Röser Vatiché and Ben Meerwein. It is co-produced by Sadler’s Wells, Bunkamura in Japan and Morau’s company La Veronal.Ten years after Bowie’s death, the musician continues to fascinate. Earlier this year, a3D documentaryabout him was unveiled at the Venice film festival.David Bowie: You’re Not Alone, an hour-long immersive portrait, is running at Lightroom in London and the V&A’s Bowie archive, featuring Yamamoto’s costumes for Ziggy Stardust,goes on tour next month.Last weekend, Let’s Dance inspireda paso doble on Strictly. What is Morau’s favourite Bowie song to dance to? “Space Oddity – it’s probably not the most obvious choice for dancing, but that’s precisely why I like it,” he said. “There’s something profoundly choreographic about imagining a body losing gravity and drifting away from everything familiar.”Explore more on these topicsStageDanceTheatreDavid BowieSadler's WellsJapanLuxembourgnewsShareReuse this content

title: The little-known friendship between Nina Simone and Langston Hughes | Black US culture | The Guardian
description: A new book charts how a 1949 meeting between the renowned poet and the legendary musician, then a 16-year-old girl, sparked enduring ties and fruitful collaboration
Author: Adria R Walker
Headline: A new book charts how a 1949 meeting between the renowned poet and the legendary musician, then a 16-year-old girl, sparked enduring ties and fruitful collaboration
Content: Left: Nina Simone. Right: Langston Hughes.Composite: Getty Images, CorbisView image in fullscreenLeft: Nina Simone. Right: Langston Hughes.Composite: Getty Images, CorbisBlack US cultureInterviewThe little-known friendship between Nina Simone and Langston HughesAdria R WalkerA new book charts how a 1949 meeting between the renowned poet and the legendary musician, then a 16-year-old girl, sparked enduring ties and fruitful collaborationTue 20 Oct 2026 11.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 12.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1949, the poet and writerLangston Hugheswas already a towering figure – he toured the country reading his poems and lecturing, drawing crowds that filled auditoriums. That year, at a lecture in Asheville, North Carolina, Hughes met a 16-year-old girl, Eunice Waymon, who would go on to make history in her own right using her stage name,Nina Simone.Hughes and Simone became friends and collaborators, working together on songs such as Backlash Blues, which soundtracked what was then a nascent Black Power movement. The song influenced Kwame Ture, the activist and Black revolutionary who was then known as Stokely Carmichael, who popularized the phrase “Black power”.“Nina Simone refined the strategies of resistanceLangston Hughespioneered during the Harlem Renaissance to create the soundtrack to the civil rights movement and inaugurate the birth of Black Power,” writes W Jason Miller, author of Don’t Let Me Be Misunderstood: Nina Simone, Langston Hughes, and the Birth of Black Power, a new book that explores the previously underacknowledged relationship between Hughes and Simone.Using new first-hand accounts and archives, Miller, a distinguished professor of English at North Carolina State University, writes a history of the friendship between two American heavyweights. The Guardian spoke to Miller about Langston Hughes,Nina Simoneand their relationship.This interview has been lightly edited for clarity.How did you settle on writing about Langston Hughes and Nina Simone’s relationship?I’ve been a Langston Hughes scholar for about 22 years. At a book event in Raleigh, I told the audience that Hughes was approached by a singer to write the liner notes for her album. And Langston Hughes’ response was, “Why, Nina, I’d be happy to.”The audience gasped at the thought of their Nina Simone, North Carolina icon, being in connection with Langston Hughes. I knew immediately that I had to find out everything about these two. I found one single sentence that even mentioned Nina Simone in seven biographies about Hughes.For the last six years, I tracked down every letter they exchanged, every time they were together and located one of Nina’s roommates, a woman who, at 91 years old, remembered the day that Langston Hughes came to their high school and first met Nina.I don’t think that either Hughes or Simone receive as much credit as they should for their role in the Black Power movement. Can you talk a bit about that?Langston Hughes is often introduced as a figure of the Harlem Renaissance of the 1920s, of which he was of course a leading figure. But Hughes died in May of 1967 – less than 11 months before Dr King’s assassination. He was active, involved and productive up until the very end.In terms of Nina Simone, her oeuvre and her musical career were wide and far-reaching. When folks think about the civil rights movement and reduce it to nonviolence, they miss Nina’s key role. If Nina were a figure of the civil rights movement leadership, she’s more like [Kwame Ture] than she is like Malcolm X or Martin Luther King. She’s a fiery young figure that can get overlooked by people that don’t know, but the people that latch on to her know her iconic songs and her protest music. Their ability together created the soundtrack to the civil rights movement.What was most surprising to you about their relationship?Langston Hughes really wanted to have a hit song written. He’d been trying since 1949 to break through in music. He had this desire to have Nina Simone sing one of his songs. The last poem that Hughes ever sent out for publication was called Backlash Blues. It’s the poem he gave to Nina to sing that became her iconic song.‘They were brilliant people’: fascinating film reveals a Harlem Renaissance reunionRead moreThis book is a biography of their friendship, which involves strategies for how two figures go through the practice of mentoring, building a relationship and collaborating. Nina sat in the third row at the 1960 Newport jazz festival while Hughes led a blues session in which he was directing Muddy Waters and John Lee Hooker for two and a half hours. Nina saw Hughes not just as an important cultural icon, she recognized him as a music lover that she could trust.Leonard Bernstein and Walt Disney are generally more associated with making classical music accessible to a wider audience. But you argue that Simone did something similar with her interpolation of Bach in Love Me or Leave Me and a few other pieces.Nina Simone grows up in Tryon, is educated in Asheville, North Carolina, with the goal of becoming a classical pianist. Her icon is Hazel Scott and her favorite musician of all time was Bach. What she was able to do in the very end of her career is combine popular music with classical music. She hides classical music inside of these popular songs. Unconsciously, audience members that listened to the vinyl or saw her in concert were being exposed to classical music.For her first concert at Carnegie Hall, Andy Stroud, her manager husband, puts up a great deal of money, hires a big promoter, and they’re worried about being able to sell out. The first half of that entire concert is filled with classical instrumental music, not her singing. Langston Hughes had written promotional materials, so posters and newspaper ads had blurbs of support from Hughes.What about their upbringing assoutherners influenced their relationship and their wider reputations?Nina Simone’s education in western North Carolina shapes her a great deal. She starts playing in the church. That area of the country gives us the incredible song Sinner Man, one she heard and performed. In late 1965, at the prompting of Langston Hughes, she records it, and it becomes a way to retell history. We’re not just thinking about God, the devil and the sinner. We’re thinking about student ambassadors who are trying to fight for change, white Klan members and the role of prayer in the civil rights movement.Hughes’ grandmother spent time here in North Carolina with the Lumbee people. Right before he met Nina Simone, Langston Hughes gave a newspaper interview where he talked about his grandmother being part Lumbee and being part of the North Carolina tradition.Hughes was condemned for his leftist politics and Simone faced similar condemnation. Do you think that their relationship informed their ability to use art to convey their political messages?Langston Hughes not only recognized the talent that Nina Simone had, he not only had this desire to have his music performed, and he not only had a genuine interest in supporting the next generation, but he recognized that she could use the same strategies he had pioneered in the Harlem Renaissance. If you’re an academic, we call this signifying. If you’re a high school teacher, we call it allusion. But all people today know this as sampling.Nina learned she could sample old music and update it. When she sang songs like Tomorrow Is My Turn, she turned a love song into a statement that tomorrow I’m going to get a chance. When she took songs like Go to Hell, Nina writes a new last verse. She says: we are in hell.She brought this to her work in Sinner Man, especially. Nina activated those characters by thinking about Jimmy Lee Jackson and what started the march from Selma to Montgomery. When Nina used strategies to seem to be talking about something and slip it in, that’s when she was tuning her soul to the wavelength of Langston Hughes.What made their relationship special?It starts with Langston Hughes’ spirit. The list of people he welcomed into his orbit and deliberately mentored is unbelievable. It includesGwendolyn Brooks,Margaret Walkerand he was very supportive of Amiri Baraka. I met a woman in Oxford, North Carolina – Mary “Pee Wee” Lindsay. She talked about meeting Hughes in the early 1950s, walking up to him with a couple pages of poems. She said that Hughes sat down with her for 30 minutes and went through those poems, even though she had no international-level talent, never published a book.Simone and Hughes connected because, in so many ways, they were moving in the same direction. When Langston Hughes dies in 1967, Nina has Backlash Blues ready, but she hasn’t recorded or released it. After he dies, she writes a new verse. She includes their relationship. That leads her to understand one of Hughes’ key lessons, which is how to incorporate great people into music and art. One year later, she recognizes Martin Luther King’s assassination. Nina composed and thought of the song To Be Young, Gifted and Black in 1969. Hughes’ relationship sent her on this course of making music like Backlash Blues, Why the King of Love Is Dead, To Be Young, Gifted and Black that would stand as symbols of these great people.Explore more on these topicsBlack US cultureNina SimoneLangston HughesBlack power movementCivil rights movementRacePoetryinterviewsShareReuse this content
