title: The CO2-absorbing building made of old sinks, windscreens and toilets: Ghent’s £17m design museum is a green marvel | Architecture | The Guardian
description: Inspired by a gothic cathedral partly built using human bones, this gleaming monument to recycling boasts 82,000 bricks derived from construction waste – following a two-day brick-making festival
Author: Oliver Wainwright
Headline: Inspired by a gothic cathedral partly built using human bones, this gleaming monument to recycling boasts 82,000 bricks derived from construction waste – following a two-day brick-making festival
Content: Even its loos have QR codes … the building lit up for its opening party.Photograph: Behangmotief for Design Museum GentView image in fullscreenEven its loos have QR codes … the building lit up for its opening party.Photograph: Behangmotief for Design Museum GentArchitectureThe CO2-absorbing building made of old sinks, windscreens and toilets: Ghent’s £17m design museum is a green marvelInspired by a gothic cathedral partly built using human bones, this gleaming monument to recycling boasts 82,000 bricks derived from construction waste – following a two-day brick-making festivalOliver WainwrightTue 20 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMuseums often try to reflect the world around them, but rarely are they made so literally of their surroundings as thenew design museum in Ghent. Rising above the Belgian city’s medieval tiled rooftops like an angular white watchtower, the new building has vacuumed up the city’s condemned concrete frames, windows, car windscreens, sinks and old toilets, and transformed them, phoenix-like, into a gleaming monument to recycling.“There’s nothing new about reuse,” says Andy Groarke, co-founder ofCarmody Groarke, the London-based architects who designed the €20m (£17m) project with local firmsAtamaandRe-st. “We’ve just forgotten how to do it.”double quotation markFor €10, you can take a brick home from the museum shopHe says the team drew inspiration from Ghent’s 16th-century gothic cathedral, Saint Bavo’s, which was partly built using the white limestone blocks of the 10th-century romanesque basilica that had stood on the same site (recent renovations also ghoulishly uncoveredwalls made of human bones, femurs and tibias apparently having particularly useful structural properties, with crushed skulls for infill).View image in fullscreenEarthy layers of rubble … Design Museum Ghent.Photograph: Oliver WainwrightThe new design museum doesn’t quite go that far in its nose-to-tail approach, but almost. The toilet cubicles are a smorgasbord of “biomaterials”, each featuring different tiles made of seaweed, flax, wood terrazzo and volcanic ash (you can scan a QR code for more info while you’re sitting on the loo). Some walls are plastered with local clay, while a chunky column in the entrance hall revels in its earthy layers of rubble dug straight from the building site.But thereal innovation is the brick, which was specially developed, tested and certified for the project (funded by a grant from Circular Flanders and Sogent, the city’s development agency). Each brick is made of 63% construction waste, sourced from within 8km of the museum, pulverised and compressed with hydrated lime, saving two-thirds of the embodied carbon of a regular fired clay brick. And the lime will continue to absorb CO2 from the atmosphere as it cures over the coming months and years.“We’re not claiming this is a panacea, or a solution to the climate crisis,” says architect Sian Ricketts, Carmody Groarke’s sustainability lead. “But it is a sort of 82,000-brick proof of concept that you can do something different, with the right collaborators and the right clients.” Developed by East Sussex firmLocal Works Studioand Brussels groupBC Materials, the bricks were made in a former railway depot nearby, with the public invited to mix the ingredients and press their own blocks during a two-day festival of brickmaking. For €10, you can take one home from the museum shop.Public participation extended to defining the very essence of the museum, too. In keeping with Belgium’s democratic traditions, a“citizens’ panel”of 40 people, drawn from a wide variety of Ghent residents, was established to inform what the museum should be. Their 100+ recommendations ranged from incorporating unticketed areas, to being able to see work-in-progress, and having plenty of seating, as well as ensuring that the “chic” building didn’t put people off. The result is as locally sourced and collaboratively created as big civic buildings come. “This expansion and renovation are not about creating more museum,” says the outgoing director, Katrien Laporte, “but about creating more than a museum: a community sense-making museum with real social relevance.”View image in fullscreenAngular geometries … Design Museum Ghent.Photograph: Johan DehlinThe extension fills a leftover plot on the museum’s site, uniting the galleries that were previously spread between an 18th-century rococo mansion, called the Hotel de Coninck, and a troublesome 1990s addition – designed with a moving glass floor that rarely moved, now thankfully banished. The new building stands with the presence of a grand Ghent house, rising in five large storeys, and turning as it climbs to face the city centre, with big picture windows looking out in different directions on each floor. “We wanted it to feel domestic, industrial and civic at once,” says Groarke. It certainly has a bold presence.Not everyone has welcomed its industrial bulk. Concerns have been raised about how the boxy white mass lumbers into view from the city’s quaint historical centre, and there is something slightly clumsy about the form on the skyline, topped with multiple roofs angled in different directions. Silicone joints between stretches of brick don’t help either, reading as unsightly seams from a distance. The museum defended the height as providing never-before-seen views of the city, and it’s true: when you’re on the top floor – a freely accessible public loft – or the roof terrace below, the panoramic vistas of Ghent’s castle and church spires are a treat.View image in fullscreenLumbers into view … Design Museum Ghent.Photograph: Michiel De Cleene/Design Museum GhentSkyline concerns also fade away as you approach the museum at street level. Agate in the form of a billowing metallic curtain, frozen in motion, signals the new entrance in a delightfully surreal touch. Designed by Antwerp studio Unfold and 3D-printed in aluminium, it is a welcome change from the previously off-putting carriage entrance of the historical hotel down the sidestreet. The striking gate is one of a series ofspecial projectscommissioned by curator Siegrid Demyttenaere that have been dotted throughout the building, from a cast street number to a reception desk and lockers, making functional parts of the museum exhibits in themselves.A lobby lined with timber salvaged from a tobacco factory in Brussels leads into thestadskamer, or city room, opening through big sliding windows on to the museum courtyard on one side, and the street on the other. It was thronging with visitors during the opening weekend, with the feeling of a true public square. The chubby earthen column (a commission byGrond Studio) rises to support an intersection of the deep wooden beams that crisscross the ceiling, the first glimpse of the building’s sculptural timber frame. The architects say it is the biggest mass timber public building in Belgium, featuring walls and floors of spruce CLT (cross-laminated timber) and chunky beams of beech LVL (laminated veneer lumber), imported from Austria. A beautiful oak staircase connects the floors, with joinery details in darker walnut, its angular geometries lending a Piranesian air.View image in fullscreen‘The feeling of a true public square’ … the stadskamer (city room).Photograph: Johan DehlinThe new building is “a stack of five rooms”, says Groarke, “each with a particular identity”. The stairs lead to the Forum, for lectures and events; the Atelier, a light-flooded studio for education workshops; and the Vitrine for temporary exhibitions – before arriving at the Loft, a grand event space with spectacular views. Its balcony became an urban-scale DJ booth for the opening party, when local duo2manydjsperformed above the rooftops to 5,000 revellers dancing in the streets below.Spectacle aside, one of the building’s most useful achievements is connecting the museum’s pre-existing wings in a continuous, accessible loop for the first time. Visitors can now move from the chandelier-bedecked suites of the Hotel de Coninck, through to the 90s wing – from which 60% of the columns have been removed and voids filled in to create more display space for the permanent collection – to the light, woody world of the new tower. It was made possible by a wise use of funds: while competing architects proposed taller towers and deeper basement levels, the winning team suggested a better use of some of the tight budget would be to refurbish and renew what was already there.View image in fullscreen‘Functional parts of the museum are exhibits in themselves’ … the entrance gate by Unfold.Photograph: Johan Dehlin“The competition was such a great process,” says Groarke, singing the praises of the renownedFlemish Open Callrun by the Vlaams Bouwmeester (the government architect), with a jury that included five international museum directors alongside architects and planners. You can stillsee all the entries online. “Architecture is in the public consciousness here in a way that it’s not in the UK,” Groarke continues. “Back home, it’s seen as an extension of the property industry, with a pyramid scheme of mediocrity in the way.”He’s got a point. It would be hard to imagine a building of such quality and imagination being realised on British shores, where contractors rule all and architects are forced to compete on fees in a self-sabotaging race to the bottom. Public procurement rules also mean architects generally have to have built several buildings of the type they are bidding for before they can even qualify to compete, meaning few opportunities for young practices.Our bureaucrats might do well to spend some time in the museum’s opening exhibition,Public Matter(s): Design and Democracy. Curated by Amelie Klein and Vera Sacchetti, it is a fascinating exploration of the design of democratic decision-making, examining everything from ballot papers to the layout of parliament buildings, to how nature might be given a seat at the table. One particularly revealing project,The Flemish Scrollersby artist Dries Depoorter, uses AI to track distracted politicians scrolling on their phones during parliamentary sessions, and automatically posts screenshots of the live stream to social media, asking the elected officials to do better.Perhaps a similar algorithm could be used to name and shame each time a public tender is awarded to the same old suspects, with dismal results for our built environment. Once again, the Flems are leading the way.Explore more on these topicsArchitectureBelgiumMuseumsDesignGreen buildingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘How green are our valleys?’: in the footsteps of miners on south Wales’s new forest trail | Wales holidays | The Guardian
description: The first stage of an ambitious new hiking route that will link woodlands across Wales takes walkers into the wild hills above the valleys’ old mining villages
Author: Rhiannon Batten
Headline: The first stage of an ambitious new hiking route that will link woodlands across Wales takes walkers into the wild hills above the valleys’ old mining villages
Content: On the climb up to Tarren y Fforch plateau, looking back to Nant-y-Moel.Photograph: Rhiannon BattenView image in fullscreenOn the climb up to Tarren y Fforch plateau, looking back to Nant-y-Moel.Photograph: Rhiannon BattenWales holidays‘How green are our valleys?’: in the footsteps of miners on south Wales’s new forest trailThe first stage of an ambitious new hiking route that will link woodlands across Wales takes walkers into the wild hills above the valleys’ old mining villagesRhiannon BattenTue 20 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 02.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBracken and heather ripple across the plateau. I exhale into the chill autumn air and my breath mists a view that reaches all the way to Gower and the ochre peaks of Bannau Brycheiniog (formerly the Brecon Beacons). Far below, the Ogmore valley’s terrace houses look like tiny constellations but up here on Tarren y Fforch, it’s just me and a few sheep taking springy steps between tufts of bilberries. If this corner of the south Wales valleys feels a long way from its coal mining past, that is, partly, the point.I’m hiking the newLlwybr Coedwig Cymru Trail, or Wales Forest Trail. Running from Porthkerry Park, near Barry, to Pont Walby, close to Glynneath, this 50-mile (80km) pilot route is the first section of what theNational Forest for Waleshopes will eventually be a trail linking woodlands across the length and breadth of Wales: a sylvan counterpart to theWales Coast Path.My father grew up in one of the valleys’ mining villages and, when I visited relatives there as a child, the disconnection of those post-industrial communities from the wild hills that loomed above them was striking. Mountain bikers have long discovered the region’s potential, but walkers still tend to head for the more obvious trails that wind through thenational parksor along the coast. This pilot trail seems a good excuse to explore untapped footpaths.View image in fullscreenThe trail starts near the viaduct in Porthkerry Park.Photograph: Freespiritarchitecture/AlamyWith the sea behind me, I set off from the oak leaf sculpture that marks the trail’s start. The viaduct ahead once carried coal to Barry docks, but today it stands overCaffe Matteo, busy with dog walkers sipping cappuccinos. Leaving them behind, I cross the park between the soft greens of birch and oak trees.I swerve on to a fern-fringed path and follow a stream to the outskirts of Barry. The next section is less lovely – a long stretch of roadside pavement until I enterHensol Forest. The sunshine splinters through ancient pine trees and their needles cushion the ground. Weaving in and out of forest and fields, I soak up all the calm this long-distance forest-bathing exercise can offer until theVale Resortcomes into sight.This vast hotel is popular with golfers, but also holds two trump cards for walkers: aspawhere weary hikers can swim, sauna and steam their muscles limber again, and abarserving energy-boosting Welsh rarebit spiked with ale mustard, Dragon cheddar and charred leeks.Restored, I rejoin the trail the next morning, dipping along leafy lanes and footpaths as the roar of the M4 gets louder. I cross beneath it to enter Coedwig Gellihir, a small broadleaf woodland, then continue north into Pontyclun, before clambering down to the river at Ynysmaerdy Forest to pick up an old railway path to Coedely.double quotation markParts of the trail follow the paths miners took. I’m glad they had this antidote to the darkness and danger undergroundThe trail has been designed to offer stretches for cyclists, pushchair users and horse riders, with more pavement-pounding and, in Thomastown, a reminder of the challenges faced by post-industrial communities. Leaving the village behind, the trail opens out again on to a little rocky path with soaring views of Ogwr Fach Valley.One of the National Forest for Wales’s aims is to help communities connect with nearby woodlands. In Blackmill, the next village I come to, the trail passes Coed Bach Dimbath, a small community woodland where local groups have come together to build an otter hide, outdoor classroom and accessible paths.“The woodland there had been inaccessible for decades, and now people can access it,” says Rhodri Hewitt of Natural Resources Wales, the trail’s project lead. “The valleys can feel desperately poor in places, but the River Ogmore is another world entirely.”Continuing north to Nant-y-Moel, I come to Blaenogwr Farm, a Georgian farmstead marooned in the village, where I’m staying in ahomely holiday cottage. I drop off my backpackand head across the road for fish with buttery potatoes and laverbread (made from edible seaweed) and cockle sauce at theBlaenogwr Hotel.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe holiday cottage at Blaenogwr Farm.Photograph: Rhiannon BattenMy final day’s walking starts with a climb up to that extraordinary plateau on Tarren y Fforch. Hewitt tells me that parts of the trail follow the paths miners took across these hills to work in pits in neighbouring valleys. I’m glad they had this antidote to the darkness and danger underground. Today’s route feels uplifting. I slip through an ancient gate on to open moorland and pick my way up the escarpment, meadow pipits chirruping around me.Crossing the plateau, I enterAfan Forest park, a large commercial woodland that’s also home to a forest of wind turbines, a peat restoration project and a network ofmountain-biking trails. I have an urge to be inside the forest rather than tracing its edges and detour on to a footpath leading up to the trig point at Craig y Llyn, the highest point of the valleys at 600m.Continuing beneath branches dripping velvety lichen, I come to another spectacular viewpoint, as the land drops away to the waters of Llyn Fach and Llyn Fawr, with the peaks ofCorn Du and Pen y Fan shrouded in soft-focus drizzle behind them. Soon I dip into the loveliest stretch of forest along the whole trail.The valley of Cwm Gwrelych is a designated geological site of special scientific interest because of the near complete 300m-year-old strata exposed here. But it’s also rainforest-like, cut through with waterfalls, a dark, glossy river and dense, broadleaf woodland. I feel completely enveloped in green as I hike the last couple of miles to the trail’s current end, the Isambard Kingdom Brunel-designed viaduct at Pont Walby. As I continue toSgwd Gwladyspub with rooms in nearby Pontneddfechan, I remind myself that this is not a finished trail but the beginning of one.View image in fullscreenSgwd Gwladys waterfall.Photograph: Liquid Light/AlamyThe next morning, I pull on my boots one last time and set out in search of the waterfall the pub is named after. Mist rises from the river, shafts of sunlight turn the leaves amber and a heron glides past in cinematic slow-mo. When we spoke about the trail, Hewitt mentioned an old Welsh proverb:Dod yn ôl at fy nghoed, meaning “To return to my trees”, or finding your way back to a balanced state of mind. As I sit and admire SgwdGwladys’ thundering cascade, I realise this leafy trail has delivered exactly that.The trip wasprovided by theNational Forest for WalesandNatural Resources Wales.Vale Resorthasdoubles from£104room-only. The Airbnb cottage costs from£87 a night.Sgwd Gwladyshasdoubles from£65.55, room only. Fortrail information, visitgov.wales/llwybr-coedwig-cymru-trailandfor region informationVisitwales.comExplore more on these topicsWales holidaysWalkingWalking holidaysUnited Kingdom holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fridge or not? What’s the best way to store bread? | Chefs | The Guardian
description: Our experts have some airtight advice to stop your loaf from going stale
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: Our experts have some airtight advice to stop your loaf from going stale
Content: That greaseproof paper your loaf came in is the best way to store it.Photograph: Nazgul Anarbekova/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThat greaseproof paper your loaf came in is the best way to store it.Photograph: Nazgul Anarbekova/Getty ImagesKitchen aideChefsFridge or not? What’s the best way to store bread?Our experts have some airtight advice on stopping your loaf from going stale – and even freshening it up again – but whatever you do, keep it out of the fridgeAnna BerrillTue 20 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat’s the best way to store bread? Beeswax wraps, plastic bags, fridge – I’ve tried everything except a bread bin.Nancy, by email“When bread is baked, what happens is that all the starch in the flour expands and takes in all the water,” saysSophia Handschuh, co-founder ofSourdough Sophiain London. That’s why the crumb turns all soft and fluffy. “When you pull the bread out of the oven, as soon as it touches any surface it will start to dry up, which is why bread goes stale; the starch doesn’t like being kept in the air.”To combat this, Handschuh stores her loaf at room temperature in a greaseproof paper bag (ie, the one you bring it home in): “That’s probably the best way – no plastic. And, yes, you can use beeswax wrap, but that’s expensive and you shouldn’t have to go and buy some just for storing bread.”A paper bag is also Rachel Morgan’s preference: “I’d avoid a bread bin, though,” says the co-founder ofTwelve Trianglesin Edinburgh. “That can trap moisture, so the bread gets a bit sweaty, which softens the crust and encourages mould.”As for the fridge, that’s a hard no, says Florin Grama ofTarn Bakeryin north London: “It’s the worst thing you can do,” he says. “Your bread will go stale in about a day.” (As Harold McGee discovered in an experiment for his masterworkOn Food & Cooking, “bread stored in the refrigerator at 46F/7C staled as much in one day as bread held at 86F/30C did in six days”.)Reheating is your gateway to regaining freshness: “Warming bread enables the water to evaporate and for the starch to reactivate,” Handschuh says. So, if your bread is a couple of days’ old, “stick it in the oven for five to 10 minutes, and it should stay fresh for a day or two longer”.If you’re not planning to eat that loaf within a few days of buying it, meanwhile, freezing is by far the best option, Grama says – especially if you’re planning to toast it anyway. “Slice it, so you can later take out only what you need, then wrap tightly, freeze and toast from frozen.” Alternatively, freeze the loaf whole and intact, Handschuh says: “Let that defrost, then stick it in the oven at a low temperature [about 160C] to warm through.”If your bread’s almost on the turn, however, Handschuh recommends tearing it into pieces, and tossing it with “loads” of olive oil, flaky sea salt, a bit of garlic and fresh thyme. “Whack that in the oven for 10-20 minutes, until browned, and you’ll have a batch of chunky croutons for salads.”Equally worthy of consideration are sourdough crisps, especially as we head into soup season, Handschuh adds: “Slice the bread really thinly, drizzle with olive oil and pop in the oven to dry out completely.” Morgan, meanwhile, keeps a bag of stale ends knocking about to turn into breadcrumbs, which will improve all manner of meals: fried in olive oil and used to top pasta; to coat chicken breasts for schnitzels; or to mix into fritters, meatballs and cakes. Alternatively, says Grama, simply refresh an old loaf with a sprinkle of water, then slice it and stuff with “loads of herby, garlic butter, maybe some cheese, too – that will give more life to your bread”. And probably to Nancy, too.Got a culinary dilemma? Emailfeast@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsChefsKitchen aideBreadFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sami Tamimi’s recipes for lamb meatballs with spinach and chickpea stew, and red rice | Food | The Guardian
description: A comforting stew that’s made to be shared
Author: Sami Tamimi
Headline: A comforting stew that’s made to be shared
Content: Sami Tamimi’s lamb meatballs with spinach and chickpea stew and red rice.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Emma Cantlay. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.View image in fullscreenSami Tamimi’s lamb meatballs with spinach and chickpea stew and red rice.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Emma Cantlay. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.FoodSami Tamimi’s recipes for lamb meatballs with spinach and chickpea stew, and red riceServe this warm and juicy meatballsabanekhwith Iraqi tomato rice for a comforting meal that’s made to be sharedSami TamimiTue 20 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is the kind of meal I love for its generosity and simplicity. A comforting spinach and chickpea stew (sabanekh), scattered with tender lamb meatballs and finished with a bright squeeze of lemon. And, alongside, Iraqi red rice (timman ahmar) brings warmth, colour and a gentle sweetness from the tomato, and soaks up the rich, savoury juices of the stew. Together, they form a hearty meal made for sharing.Lamb meatballs, spinach and chickpea stew (sabanekh)View image in fullscreenSami Tamimi’s lamb meatballs with spinach and chickpea stew.Sabanekh is a beloved spinach stew across the Levant, and here I’ve added lamb meatballs to make it a more substantial meal. The combination of cumin, coriander and garlic gives warmth and depth, while a generous squeeze of lemon brightens everything. Serve with rice or warm flatbread to soak up the delicious, fragrant sauce.Prep10 minCook1 hrServes4-6500glamb minceSalt and black pepper1 tspbaharatmix4 tbsp olive oil30g pine nuts1 large onion, peeled and finely chopped (180g)600g frozen whole-leaf spinach400g tin chickpeas, drained and rinsed500ml water or chicken stockRice and/or flatbread, to serve2 tbsp lemon juice, plus lemon wedges, to serveFor theadhagarnish60ml olive oil5 garlic cloves,peeled and crushed20g fresh coriander, finely chopped½ tspaleppo chilli flakesPut the mince in a medium bowl, add a teaspoon of salt, half a teaspoon ofbaharatand a third of a teaspoon of black pepper, and mix well. Shape the meat into 25 balls (about 20g each) and set aside.Heat two tablespoons of olive oil in a large saucepan on a medium heat. Add the pine nuts and cook, stirring constantly, for three to four minutes, until golden brown. Spoon the pine nuts into a bowl.Add the meatballs to the pan in two batches and cook until brown all over. Remove the meat from the pan and add the remaining two tablespoons of oil and the onion, and cook, stirring occasionally, for seven minutes, until soft and translucent. Add the spinach, chickpeas, water/stock, lemon juice, one teaspoon of salt, a good grind of black pepper, and the remaining half-teaspoon of baharat. Bring to a boil and cook for five minutes, until the spinach is soft. Return the meatballs to the pan, cover and cook on a low heat, stirring occasionally, for 20 minutes, until the stew has thickened slightly.To make the adha garnish, put the oil and garlic in a small frying pan on a medium heat. Cook, stirring often, for two to three minutes, until the garlic is lightly golden, then take off the heat and stir in the coriander and chilli. Pour the adha over the stew, cover and leave for five minutes.Scatter over the toasted pine nuts and serve hot with the red rice below, or plain steamed rice, and lots of lemon wedges.Red rice (timman ahmar)View image in fullscreenSami Tamimi’s red rice.A simple and deeply comforting rice dish, known for its rich colour and savoury flavour. Traditionally made by cooking rice with tomato, onion and spices, it’s the kind of everyday dish that sits naturally at the centre of the Iraqi table. The gentle sweetness of the tomato is balanced by warm spices, while the rice remains light and fluffy. Serve alongside stews, grilled meats or vegetables.Prep15 minSoak20 minCook50 minServes4–6300g basmati rice3 tbsp vegetable oil120g vermicelli, broken into small pieces1 medium onion, peeled and finely chopped (120g)3 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed1 green chilli, finely chopped (seeds removed if you want less heat)2 tbsp tomato puree1½ tbsp pomegranate molasses1½ tsp ground cumin¾ tsp ground allspice½ tsp ground cinnamon1 large tomato(140g), finely chopped1 green pepper, stalk, pith and seeds removed, fleshfinely chopped (160g)600mlhot vegetable stock25g unsalted butterSalt and black pepperRinse the rice under cold running water several times, until the water runs clear. Leave the rice to soak in fresh water for 20 minutes, then drain well.Heat a tablespoon of the oil in a medium saucepan on a medium heat. Add the vermicelli, cook, stirring, for five minutes, until golden brown, then tip on to a plate.Add the remaining two tablespoons of oil and the onion to the pan, and cook, stirring occasionally, for seven minutes, until soft and lightly golden. Stir in the garlic and chilli, and cook for a minute. Add the tomato puree, pomegranate molasses and spices, and cook for another minute, until fragrant.Stir in the tomato and green pepper, and cook for three minutes. Add the drained rice and toasted vermicelli, and stir gently for a minute, making sure all of the grains are coated in the tomato sauce.Pour in the hot stock and add the butter, one and a quarter teaspoons of salt and a good grind of black pepper. Bring to a boil, then cover the pan and leave to cook on a very low heat for 15 minutes. Take off the heat and leave covered for 10 minutes. Gently fluff the rice with a fork, then serve.Explore more on these topicsFoodMiddle Eastern food and drinkRiceMain courseHerbs and spicesMeatStewfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘No real sense of appeal’: Vinted sellers complain of unfair account ‘bans’ | Consumer affairs | The Guardian
description: Some users claim online marketplace’s automated systems stack odds against them when sales go wrong
Author: Sarah Marsh
Headline: Some users claim online marketplace’s automated systems stack odds against them when sales go wrong
Content: Using the Vinted app is simple enough – but some sellers claim it is not so easy to resolve problems that crop up with sales.Photograph: ShutterstockView image in fullscreenUsing the Vinted app is simple enough – but some sellers claim it is not so easy to resolve problems that crop up with sales.Photograph: ShutterstockConsumer affairs‘No real sense of appeal’: Vinted sellers complain of unfair account ‘bans’Some users claim online marketplace’s automated systems stack odds against them when sales go wrongSarah MarshConsumer affairs correspondentTue 20 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter Catherine Warrilow sold a Zara necklace for £6 on Vinted, she packed it up and posted it off, just as she had done with many things before. Only this time the buyer claimed the parcel arrived empty.Warrilow, 47, from Oxford, provided Vinted with photos and videos of the package, including date-stamped Ring doorbell footage of her leaving the house to post it. But she says the resale platform refunded the buyer and left her out of pocket.“I challenged Vinted on what evidence they had and asked them to supply it, but they simply said ‘based on our evidence’ and ‘our evidence suggests’ and could not explain what that was,” she says. “The photos from the buyer showed that all of the parcel tape I’d used had been removed.”Vinted has become a giant of the secondhand economy. In 2025, users traded €10.8bn (£9.1bn) worth of goods through the platform – a47% increaseon the previous year.It generated €1.1bn in revenue and made a €62m profit. It now operates across 26 markets and has expanded beyond clothes into books, toys, sports goods and collectibles, as well as building its own shipping and payments businesses.It is a success story, but some sellers feel that the odds are stacked against them.Warrilow had used the app for five years, usually selling items her children had outgrown or things she had “fallen out of love with”. After having problems as a buyer, too, she had had enough.In both cases, “small amounts” of money were lost, Warrilow says. “But the principle of the lack of support led me to start a survey.”She did this on the website she set up calledSad Vinted Faces.Within two days, hundreds of people had responded. Since then, she says, more than 6,400 cases have been collected.View image in fullscreenCatherine Warrilow of the Sad Vinted Faces campaign.Photograph: HandoutOne of the users who claimed, via Warrilow’s website, that she had had a bad experience, was Maggie, who did not want to give her last name. She says she sold a pair of Birkenstock Boston clogs for £72. When the buyer disputed their authenticity, she provided photographs of the shoes, and a bank statement showing she had bought them from Office.But Vinted decided the shoes were counterfeit, she says. The buyer was refunded and kept them, and Maggie permanently lost her account.“What upset me the most was not just the financial loss, but the feeling that my evidence was never properly considered,” Maggie says. “I had no meaningful opportunity to explain my case, or have it reviewed by a real person.”The consumer expert Martyn James says he has been “flooded” with messages from people who say they were accused of selling counterfeit goods and then had their Vinted accounts, and their money, frozen.“This problem has been bubbling away for a while,” he says.Part of the issue, he says, appears to be the use of automated systems in dealing with disputes.“AI is all well and good as a first line of investigation,” he says. “It is fine to use it to speed things up. But a service cannot exist without the service part, and that has to involve a human being.”He adds: “There seems to be no real sense of appeal. The company is acting as judge and jury, but there is money at play and it is not as straightforward as that.”According to Vinted, all appeals are handled by human reviewers, including Warrilow’s cases.View image in fullscreenVinted says all appeals are handled by human reviewers.Photograph: Timon Schneider/AlamyVictoria Chamberlain-Ralphs has built a business selling clothes for clients who do not have time to do it themselves on Vinted. She says her problems started when she was made to convert her account to a “Pro” one, which took her offline for six weeks. “They said that our wardrobe was too big: we have 700 clients, which was, at that time, 18,000 items. They said that they had no capacity to get us back on.“We were emailing constantly, and they said they ‘would get around to it’.”She adds: “I told them I have staff to pay. I have clients asking why their items are not online, and I have a building to pay for.”In three years, Chamberlain-Ralphs says she has had her account shut down about 12 times. “I got banned last Thursday,” she says. “It was a permanent ban due to ‘fraudulent activity’.”She says Vinted gave her no explanation. She had 42 outstanding orders, all of which were cancelled when her account was banned.Five hours later, she says, it was reinstated. “They said it was ‘a false alarm’,” she says. “But that has cost me.”She says her account was also banned in November 2025 after she was accused of selling a fake item of clothing. “I rang one of my clients and got a receipt from Amazon for the trousers I was selling, and proved it was not fake – but they did not remove the ban.”According to Vinted, accounts will be suspended if Pro members repeatedly breach its “catalogue rules,” which prohibit counterfeit and dangerous items, or commercial activity that is not centred on secondhand goods.James says cases such as these raise questions about what happens when a platform’s automated systems make allegations against users, and there is no obvious route for an independent review.“Things may not be the fault of the individual, but Vinted is not responding,” he says.Vinted says the company has “clear rules to protect the community and keep the marketplace safe”.It says that “98% of transactions are completed smoothly, without needing help from our support teams”.However, it adds, action is taken when rules are breached, to help “keep the marketplace safe for everyone”.It says that users can appeal against decisions.Explore more on these topicsConsumer affairsRetail industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked | Google | The Guardian
description: Great hardware let down by software flaws on these pricey machines that combine ChromeOS with Android
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Great hardware let down by software flaws on these pricey machines that combine ChromeOS with Android
Content: The new Googlebooks are premium laptops let down by underdeveloped software.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe new Googlebooks are premium laptops let down by underdeveloped software.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.GoogleReviewGooglebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbakedGreat hardware let down by software flaws on these pricey machines that combine ChromeOS with AndroidSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorTue 20 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle’s attempt to create a new type of laptop to compete with Windows and macOS machines is finally here, combining the best of ChromeOS andAndroidinto the new Googlebook. With advanced links to Android phones and the best of Google built in, can these Googlebooks really compete with a MacBook Air or Surface Laptop? I took two for a spin to find out.For years, Chromebooks have been the boss of budget laptops, but Googlebooks take a different, far more premium approach. Made by a range of traditional PC makers, including Acer, Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, they start at£999(€1,099/$899/A$2,299) – a far cry from the £160 Chromebooks.WhileGoogledoes not make these machines directly, it has set strict hardware quality standards that the laptops must reach. That includes backlit keyboards, haptic trackpads, fingerprint readers, crisp touchscreens, decent speakers and modern fast chips with at least 16GB of RAM.It is a list of specs you should expect with a premium Windows PC, but those start at a much higher price,primarily thanks to RAMageddon.View image in fullscreenThe two Intel Core Ultra Series 3-powered Googlebooks on test: the Acer Googlebook 14 (left) and the Asus Googlebook 14 (right).Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianAs such, theAcer Googlebook 14and theAsus Googlebook 14I’ve been testing have excellent hardware with satisfying keyboards, great trackpads and quality screens.The Acer is a convertible that allows the screen to fold over the back of the device turning into a tablet of sorts. It is 1.14kg and 13.9mm thick, with a glossy 14in 3K OLED screen and a smooth aluminium-magnesium body, costing£999.99.The Asus is a traditional laptop with a matt 14in 3K OLED screen and a magnesium-alloy body that weighs just 0.99kg and is 11mm thick, costing£1,199.99.Googlebook OSView image in fullscreenWith an app drawer, widgets and a taskbar at the bottom, Googlebook OS looks a lot like ChromeOS and Windows.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianTop quality hardware aside, anyone familiar with a Chromebook would be forgiven for thinking it wasChromeOSrunning on these machines. It has the familiar taskbar at the bottom, Chrome-based web apps and access to Android apps.But the software is essentially Android underneath, which means getting it up and running is just like setting up an Android phone: scan the QR code with your phone, enter a passcode and transfer your apps and accounts. It is all done and dusted in about four minutes, which is faster than setting up a modern Windows 11 machine even if you know all the shortcuts.Access to the full gamut of Android apps is the Googlebook’s biggest strength and its greatest weakness. Practically any app you have on your phone can be installed and run on the laptop. But almost all those phone apps are just that, mobile versions, with most not even aware that they are not installed on a phone.Those that have at least some tailoring to the laptop form come in a few different types, categorised by Google broadly under “compatible with desktop”, which means they should support mouse and keyboard controls; “optimised for desktop”, which means they should scale properly to the laptop’s display; and “made for desktop”, which are a handful of Android apps redesigned with the laptop in mind.Only the last category really seems to make any difference to the quality of the app, and even then most of them are still not of the same calibre as their equivalents found on Windows or macOS.View image in fullscreenGoogle Calendar can only show one account at a time, which means my schedule looks free lacking any of my work meetings.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianEven Google’s apps are a mixed bag. Google Calendar can only show one account at any one time, so you can’t see your personal, work and shared calendars on one screen like you can on Android.Google Docs starts as its own app, but when you actually open a document it just becomes anotherChromewindow hidden behind the Chrome logo on the task bar, not the Docs logo.The Files app shows your Google Drive files, but you can’t pin locations to the side bar to quickly access your commonly used folders, making it a time-consuming dig through endless folders to find things each time.Even the Chrome browser is not quite up to par with its Windows or macOS counterpart, lacking features such as split-screen tabs, the auto-hiding vertical tab bar or the ability to have multiple profiles, such as a personal and work account.Google has an app-gap problem and one that will only be solved if developers are convinced Googlebook OS is going to take off and be worth spending time and money making better apps for.Bring your Android phone into your GooglebookView image in fullscreenYou can see you phone’s apps (left), cast them (centre) and view your phone’s files (right).Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe other big selling point is deep integration with your Android phone. Google calls this “better together”, which is a collection of features that mirror capabilities of iPhones with Macs or Microsoft’s Link to Windows.Some of the features are like magic. You can search the files on your phone straight from the Files app on the laptop without plugging it in, see your notifications from your phone, continue tasks on your laptop from your phone and even use apps cast from your phone.As useful as these features sound, many are not up to scratch. Streaming apps from your phone is so slow that I feel as though I can type entire sentences before they appear on screen in chat apps, and it is restricted to one app at a time. If you click on a synced notification from your phone, it will open in a cast app, even if you have the full app installed on your Googlebook. Even viewing files on your phone from the laptop is irritatingly slow.The only apps I’ve reliably managed to get to appear with the ability to continue from where I was are Google Docs and Chrome on the phone.It also took me two hours of troubleshooting to get an up-to-dateGoogle Pixel 11 Proto actually connect with the Googlebooks, despite using the phone to set them up in the first place.GeminiView image in fullscreenWiggle the cursor to invoke Gemini and select text or images to ask questions or perform tasks on them.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe other big selling point for Google is its Gemini integration into Googlebook OS. The Gemini app is just like it ison macOS and Windows. But it is the Magic Pointer feature, which appears when you wiggle the mouse to click or highlight something on your screen to send it to Gemini, that is the most novel.You can use it to get Gemini to summarise text, explain something, search for things or generally chat. But I often hit a road block, such as Gemini refusing to generate images or saying it cannot add a date into my calendar in the mode Magic Cursor opens, which oddly isn’t within the desktop Gemini app. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t, and it is simply not joined up.Magic Cue has been imported fromGoogle’s Pixel phones, which is meant to pop up with helpful information such as calendar availability or a location in maps when you highlight a date or a place in a chat or email. But unlike on a Pixel phone, I have yet to get it to successfully activate in two weeks of testing.Google’s super-charged voice dictation systemcalled Rambler, also from the recent Pixels, does at least work as described. Press the dictation key and just speak naturally. Rambler will condense your speech into concise sentences removing filler words and errors.VerdictGooglebooks are full of excellent ideas about how a modern laptop should work. The hardware of the Acer and Asus machines I’ve tested is top notch, but the software just isn’t ready for prime time.When it works it’s great, but it is filled with limitations that might be acceptable on a super-cheap laptop but never on a £1,000 premium machine.Chrome is not as good as it is on a Mac or Windows PC. Google’s various apps are generally better on an Android phone and the third-party app ecosystem is a mess of poorly optimised mobile apps. Even the best desktop-optimised Android apps pale by comparison to their counterparts on Windows or macOS.The Android phone-linking system should be the killer feature, but it is partly broken or simply not up to scratch. Even the Gemini integration is flakey.Most of the Google-specific issues and software bugs are eminently fixable. But the app gap will take serious time, effort and money to convince third-party developers to fix.Unless you want to spend at least £1,000 to be a beta tester, your money is better spent elsewhere for now.View image in fullscreenFull wireless integration of your phone into your laptop is a great idea, but Google has some work to do to get it right.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsGoogleAlphabetLaptopsAndroidChromeComputingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The pest I’ll never forget: the maggots that rained down like hail | Insects | The Guardian
description: The record-breaking heat in London, in summer 2022, resulted in an appalling problem in my neighbourhood – which one man took on, armed only with a jet wash
Author: Jenny Stevens
Headline: The record-breaking heat in London, in summer 2022, resulted in an appalling problem in my neighbourhood – which one man took on, armed only with a jet wash
Content: Wait – those aren’t rice grains …Composite: Guardian design; Krzysztof12;ka2shka/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWait – those aren’t rice grains …Composite: Guardian design; Krzysztof12;ka2shka/Getty ImagesThe pest I’ll never forgetInsectsThe pest I’ll never forget: the maggots that rained down like hailThe record-breaking heat in London, in summer 2022, resulted in an appalling problem in my neighbourhood – which one man took on, armed only with a jet washJenny StevensTue 20 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was that terrifying summer in 2022 when London reached 40C. I was staying in a friend’s flat while she was away for a year, a former housing association property where the living room ceiling permanently had a hole in it. Each day, the air felt thicker and the leaves looked more limp. Dust clung to every surface. With no wind, the stench of the bins lingered.I’d nicknamed the guy next door “Techno Guy” because his life’s great pleasure appeared to be sitting in the driver’s seat of a parked red convertible, stereo on full volume, revving the engine but going nowhere. Maybe it was to preserve his car battery, maybe it was to get away from his wife. His music genre of choice, Shazam told me, was Romanian techno (though he was also fond of the Cher megamix). He smoked constantly, each drag like a first breath. The sound of him hawking up phlegm in the morning became a kind of alarm clock.One Sunday, I was working from home and the smell of the barbecue had been going since breakfast – long rows of sausages, chicken, chops. I popped on my noise-cancelling headphones, thinking the couple next door were settling in for a big party, but later in the afternoon I realised it was just the two of them, having a magnificent feast. “Good on them,” I thought.A few days later, the heat became unbearable – then record-breaking. I wasn’t alone in taking an umbrella with me if I left the house. It was pressing and cloying. The bins, meanwhile, had reached a crisis state – the smell from next door’s in particular was so heinous I’d learned to hold my breath when I left the front door until I’d cleared them.The day it happened was alarmingly quiet. No techno, no Cher, not a single rev of the engine. I looked out the window and saw Techno Guy, his torso hidden, elbows-deep in his wheelie bin, groaning like an animal in pain. There was a small but growing pile of bags next to him – all torn and mangled, a brownish sludge seeping out of them – the remnants of the barbecue. At first I thought the sacks were moving, before realising it was a swarm of bluebottles creating a halo. My neighbour disappeared briefly, and returned carrying a jet washer. There was splat, a yell and a blossom of what looked like rice grains were blasted into the air.With steady horror, I realised what had been breeding in the depths of my neighbour’s bin, and what had compelled him to empty it and – for some incomprehensible reason – attack it with pressurised water. Maggots. Hundreds – maybe even thousands – of maggots, propelled into flight and falling on windows, walls, cars, gardens, hedges, pavements and bins all around. I thanked the universe I’d kept my window closed, as they landed on the windowsill, still wriggling their last wriggle. Some neighbours obviously thought that rain had finally come in the form of hail. They opened their doors to see. And then they too were hit by the unfolding horror.I’m sure someone yelled, but we were all in a sort of stasis. There stood the neighbour, stray maggots in his hair and on his face, before he went inside to fetch the dustpan and brush.Explore more on these topicsInsectsThe pest I’ll never forgetSummerHomesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Houseplant hacks: will trimming brown leaf tips do any harm? | Houseplants | The Guardian
description: Cutting out dead material will make the plant look better without damaging it. But be careful not to slice into the living leaf
Author: Gynelle Leon
Headline: Cutting out dead material will make the plant look better without damaging it. But be careful not to slice into the living leaf
Content: Photograph: Firn/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Firn/Getty Images/iStockphotoHouseplant hacksHouseplantsHouseplant hacks: will trimming brown leaf tips do any harm?Cutting out dead material will make the plant look better without damaging it. But be careful not to slice into the living leafGynelle LeonTue 20 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 05.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheproblemYou can really love your plants and still be rewarded with crispy, brown leaf tips. While they won’t kill your plant, they aren’t aesthetically pleasing.ThehackThe tidy-up is simple: cut off the dry, brown parts of the leaf. The plant looks instantly better, and the theory is this does no harm because the tissue is already dead. But the worry is it will hurt the plant or make the browning worse.ThemethodUse clean, sharp scissors and cut along the leaf’s natural shape. Leave a thin sliver of the brown edge rather than cutting into the healthy green tissue, which would create a fresh wound that the plant then has to seal off, causing it to go brown again in the process.Houseplant hacks: should you water plants less in winter?Read moreThetestI trimmed the brown tips on a philodendron, following the leaf shape, and the leaves immediately looked neater and, over time, didn’t brown further along the cut. On an earlier attempt years ago, I cut back into the green part of the leaf and watched a new brown edge form within days.The verdictCutting off crispy tips doesn’t hurt the plant, so long as you only remove dead tissue. But browning tips point to a bigger problem: usually inconsistent watering, low humidity or a buildup of minerals from tap water or excessive use of fertiliser. If the tips keep browning, the real fix lies in adapting your plant care, not the scissors.Explore more on these topicsHouseplantsHouseplant hacksGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content
