title: RFK Jr’s ‘deities of vaccine research’ raided by police in Guinea-Bissau | Guinea-Bissau | The Guardian
description: Police seize doses of hepatitis B vaccine from people at center of dispute over research on African newborns
Author: Melody Schreiber
Headline: Police seize doses of hepatitis B vaccine from people at center of dispute over research on African newborns
Content: Robert F Kennedy Jr in Washington DC.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAView image in fullscreenRobert F Kennedy Jr in Washington DC.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAGuinea-BissauRFK Jr’s ‘deities of vaccine research’ raided by police in Guinea-BissauPolice seize doses of hepatitis B vaccine from people at center of dispute over research on African newbornsMelody SchreiberTue 20 Oct 2026 15.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 15.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleControversial vaccine researchers who have been praised by Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) secretary, had their offices in Guinea-Bissau raided by judicial police, who seized doses of hepatitis B vaccines, officialssaidon Facebook.The researchers have been at the heart of an ongoing dispute over research on African newborns, supported by $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and matched by the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation for a total of $3.2m.The police search took place on Monday, involving “investigative procedures aimed at clarifying the circumstances related to the said batch of vaccines”, according to the social media post, which was translated from Portuguese. The announcement noted that seizing the immunizations did not point to “irregularities in the quality, safety, or effectiveness of the vaccines”.The Bandim Health Project recently posted aletterof approval for the trial from Guinea-Bissau’s national ethics committee at the ministry of public health, dated 14 July and signed by the committee’s president, Mouhammed Djicó Ould Ahmed. A Danish research ethics committee, which had to change its rules to consider a clinical trial, alsoapprovedthe study earlier this month.Quinhin Nantote, the health minister of Guinea-Bissau’s transitional government,disputedreports that the trial would move forward.“This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese on Thursday.The study was redesigned over the summer, but it would still deny hepatitis B vaccines to 7,000 newborns in the first six weeks of life, in a country where about one in five adults have the virus. Hepatitis B kills 15% to 25% of people with chronic infections, causing cancer and liver failure, and newborns are particularly vulnerable – but vaccination within 24 hours of birth is safe and highly effective at preventing illness.Any study that would deny the vaccine to participants was “unethical and exposes newborns to serious and potentially irreversible harm”, said Tarik Jašarević, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization (WHO), calling hepatitis B vaccination at birth an “essential public health intervention”.Through its country office inGuinea-Bissau, the WHO and its partners have been advising the ministry of health on the planned introduction of the hepatitis B vaccine and the potential impact of this study, Jašarević added.The Bandim Health Project was founded by anthropologist Peter Aaby in 1978, and it is now co-led by his wife, Christine Stabell Benn, an epidemiologist.Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work,callingthem “the deities of vaccine research” at a recent anti-vaccine conference. He has several timesreferencedthe results of a study they conducted on the diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP), which the same researchers later conducted again and found completely different results. Even so, Kennedy called Aaby a “very famous” researcher on Joe Rogan’spodcastin 2023 and cited his research when he halted US funding to Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance.Stabell Benn was amemberof the hepatitis B working group of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), helping present evidence to the US committee that voted to end the universal birth recommendation before such decisions on vaccines were stayed by a federal judge. Stabell Benn also hosted a podcast with Tracy Beth Høeg, a former top official with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) whosaidshe wanted to end “unnecessary” vaccines.Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, the lead researcher on the project, did not respond to the Guardian’s questions about the trial and the police search.The Bandim organization is deeply enmeshed in Guinea-Bissau but has done little to improve the country’s health and research capacities in five decades of operation, according to areportfrom the non-profit Stand Up for Science (SUFS). The organization is nowfundraisingto help roll out the vaccines at birth to all newborns in the country.“Our investigator encountered significant distrust of Bandim by the citizenry of Guinea-Bissau,” said Colette Delawalla, an American health researcher and founder of SUFS. “However, because of the lack of public health infrastructure, Bandim is often the only option in situations where people are desperate to access medical care of any kind.”The police raid underlines the fact that Guinea-Bissau is a “fragile” nation that experienced a military coup less than a year ago, Delawalla said. The country lacks the stability needed for clinical trials, she added.“Guinea-Bissau is in the difficult situation of trying to protect their youth, their future, from exploitation by two powerful western nations and they are using what leverage they have to do so,” Delawalla said.Explore more on these topicsGuinea-BissauRobert F Kennedy JrVaccines and immunisationAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Alberta voters overwhelmingly reject plan to leave Canada in referendum | Canada | The Guardian
description: Result is a victory for prime minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: Result is a victory for prime minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity
Content: Supporters of the Forever Canadian campaign wait for results at a watch party in Edmonton.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSupporters of the Forever Canadian campaign wait for results at a watch party in Edmonton.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockCanadaAlberta voters overwhelmingly reject plan to leave Canada in referendumResult is a victory for prime minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unityLeyland Ceccoin TorontoTue 20 Oct 2026 12.24 EDTFirst published on Tue 20 Oct 2026 01.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVoters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin the process of independence, delivering a decisive victory for supporters of Canadian unity and deepening divisions within the separatist movement.With nearly 1.9m votes counted, roughly 76% people supported remaining in Canada, while 24% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.The Canadian prime minister,Mark Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, Alberta’s capital, celebrated the result.“Albertans made a clear choice. They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada.”He said the result would allow Canadians to move forward together and accelerate efforts to diversify trade, develop major infrastructure projects and make Canada a global energy powerhouse, with Alberta at its centre.The results showed an overwhelming majority of Albertans had voted to remain and one radio show hostposted: “Someone owes Albertans $130m for this theatrical waste of taxpayers’ money.”Pollster David Coletto told the Guardian that residents felt the referendum was “a distraction away” from what they wanted their government to focus on.“There was almost a general sadness about the wasted energy spent on this rather than the more real threats they see, including the Trump administration,” he said. “Most Albertans feel deep grievances with the federal government while also being proudly Canadian. The marriage may be rocky at times, and most Albertans want to see some thing changed, but very few are willing to see the marriage end.”The province’s separatists, however, saw a silver lining. “We don’t have the final results. I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better,” said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement.Others took a different view of the results. “The result is bleak. Independence feels far away and we should not pretend this was not a defeat, however, it changes nothing about the reality of the circumstances Albertans find themselves in,” David Parker, a longtime far-right organiser linked toa massive breach of voter information, wrote on social media.The Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, welcomed the early results, saying they showed widespread support for remaining in Canada. “Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith posted on social media.View image in fullscreenPeople cheer as results begin to display at a pro-Canada watch party in Edmonton.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockEven though the vote was not explicitly about independence – a point that frustrated separatists – the ballot question nonetheless exposed divisions in Alberta’s politics and raised questions about the durability of national unity.Delays at roughly 100 of the 1,400 at polling stations across the province pushed results back by more than two hours, but shortly after polls closed on Monday evening the results suggested a decisive win for those looking to remain in Canada.‘This is not poker’: Alberta goes to polls in referendum that has exposed divisions, not least among separatistsRead moreThe separation question – whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could lead to a second vote – was one of 10 put to Albertans on Monday. The others covered issues including immigration, healthcare, education and the province’s constitutional powers. Elections Alberta said the remaining results could take days to count.In the days leading up to the vote, provincial leaders and federal politicians crisscrossed the province to make the case for a unified country.Carney warned against a vote from residents of the oil-rich province simply looking to “send a message” to the federal government. “A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he told an energetic crowd last week.The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, whose parliamentary seat is in the province, told a crowd of supporters that Albertans were not “quitters”.“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation in the referendum, I say this: Canada is more than a government,” he said. “It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”Data from Elections Alberta indicated roughly 43% of eligible voters – or 1.3 million Albertans – had already cast ballots before Monday’s vote through advance voting and mail-in ballots. That figure pointed to a potentially higher turnout than the province’s last referendum in 2021.View image in fullscreenSupporters of a group that promotes independence from Canada.Photograph: Jennifer Gauthier/ReutersSmith’s tenure as leader of the United Conservative party is due in large part to separatists within the party who ousted her predecessor, Jason Kenney. In recent months she has tried to placate both the separatists and federalists in the party, in a province where a majority is not interested in secession.The referendum became a political liability for Smith’s party, whose popular support has tumbled in recent months, including with the loss of a one-time conservative stronghold in a by-election.Still, members of the separatist movementtold the Guardianthey would continue their push for independence. And in the aftermath of the results, one prominent separatist leader said he would push for a special general meeting of the party to remove Smith.Jeffrey Rath told Global News that the Alberta independence will remain nothing but a dream long as Smith, whom he called an “avowed federalist” remains in power. He said it was time for separatists to “take back ownership” of the UCP.In an interview before the results, the Calgary mayor, Jeromy Farkas, a staunch opponent of the independence movement, said the city’s “best future is here, as a Canadian city”, amid fears that uncertainty could lead to capital flight.“I am Canadian because I’m Canadian, not in a transactional way and regardless of the flavour of prime minister,” Farkas said. “And I’m going to continue to make the case for how our future is strongest together, because no result will permanently put this to bed. “The separatist movement sees this as a long-term project.”Explore more on these topicsCanadaMark CarneyAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Bad decisions’: Man convicted for taking Peachy the flamingo from Las Vegas hotel | Las Vegas | The Guardian
description: Mitchell Fairbarn found guilty of animal cruelty after prosecutors say he hurt and frightened the 27-year-old bird
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Mitchell Fairbarn found guilty of animal cruelty after prosecutors say he hurt and frightened the 27-year-old bird
Content: Security camera footage shows Mitchell Fairbarn carrying a flamingo.Photograph: LVMPDView image in fullscreenSecurity camera footage shows Mitchell Fairbarn carrying a flamingo.Photograph: LVMPDLas Vegas‘Bad decisions’: Man convicted for taking Peachy the flamingo from Las Vegas hotelMitchell Fairbarn found guilty of animal cruelty after prosecutors say he hurt and frightened the 27-year-old birdAssociated PressTue 20 Oct 2026 12.11 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 12.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Canadian man was convicted of animal cruelty charges on Monday for snatching a flamingo named Peachy from its enclosure at an iconicLas Vegashotel.Prosecutors said it was a malicious prank while a lawyer for the tourist insisted it was drunken foolishness not meant to harm the bird.Prosecutors said tourist Mitchell Fairbarn hurt and frightened the 27-year-old Chilean flamingo when he took it from its habitat at the FlamingoLas VegasHotel and Casino and carried the squawking bird to his room on 3 March. Defense attorney Josh Tomsheck told jurors at trial in a Nevada court that the man deeply regretted the “bad decisions” he made while intoxicated.Catnapped bodega cat in Brooklyn reunited with owner after intense grassroots campaignRead moreAfter about five hours of deliberations, jurors returned convictions on felony and misdemeanor animal cruelty counts against the Ontario,Canada, man.Fairbarn remains under house arrest pending a sentencing hearing set for 1 December. He faces up to four years in prison for the felony and possibly six more months for the misdemeanor conviction. Following the verdict, he declined to comment as he left the courtroom with his wife. He showed no visible emotion.His lawyer also had no comment.After the incident, the flamingo was mostly unharmed but is more anxious and nervous when being evaluated, said Peachy’s veterinarian, Tiffany Moore, medical director of Lone Mountain Animal Hospital.Prosecutors told jurors earlier that Fairbarn willfully caused the bird physical pain, noting feathers were found on the hotel floor. Video showed the bird squawking while Fairbarn handled it and prosecutors said Peachy felt pain when it was pulled by its feet.Video played at the trial showed Fairbarn holding the flamingo in an elevator and carrying it down a hotel hallway at the famous hotel. The Flamingo is one of the oldest hotels on the Las Vegas Strip, and its well-known flamingo habitat also features hummingbirds, turtles, koi and other species.Peachy was missing some feathers after being taken.Las Vegas police responded to the scene after security staff reported that someone had taken the flamingo. When Peachy was located, it was missing seven to eight feathers, had blood on its feathers and injuries to its wings, authorities said.Taking the bird was “dumb” and “fueled by drunkenness”, the defense attorney Tomsheck said. But he added that his client never intended any harm to the bird, a key element in the felony charge.“He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn’t have touched a bird, shouldn’t have taken Peachy inside,” Tomsheck said. “The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions.”Fairbarn could be seen in court at one point with head lowered, hands covering his eyes.The man had received death threats after taking the flamingo, and he was unable to leave the US when his father died while Fairbarn was awaiting trial, said Haley Willming, the Clark county prosecutor. While those events were unfortunate, the prosecutor said, “none of that would have happened had he not done what he did, had he not made the choices he made”.Jurors began deliberating shortly before midday after closing arguments on Monday morning.Nevada animal rights advocate John Waudby, who recently helped strengthen the state’s animal cruelty laws, said he believes justice was delivered on Peachy’s behalf.“I hope this sends a message to anybody else that wants to mess with our animals, that you’re not going to do it in Nevada,” he said outside the courtroom after Monday’s verdict.Explore more on these topicsLas VegasBirdsUS crimeAnimalsCanadaNevadaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Flavio Bolsonaro’s ‘corrupto’ stunt sparks viral meme before Brazil election runoff | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Far-right presidential candidate’s TV debate swipe at rival backfires as people take to social media to parody it
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Far-right presidential candidate’s TV debate swipe at rival backfires as people take to social media to parody it
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro during last Sunday’s televised presidential debate.Photograph: Allison Sales/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro during last Sunday’s televised presidential debate.Photograph: Allison Sales/NurPhoto/ShutterstockBrazilFlavio Bolsonaro’s ‘corrupto’ stunt sparks viral meme before Brazil election runoffFar-right presidential candidate’s TV debate swipe at rival backfires as people take to social media to parody itTom PhillipsLatin America correspondentTue 20 Oct 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 11.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleToFlávio Bolsonaroand his publicists, it must have seemed an ingenious idea that would expose his rival’s supposed crookedness on the eve of Brazil’s presidential election.But the far-right politician’s decision to attend a primetime television debate against his leftwing opponent,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, with the word “corrupto” (corrupt) written on the palm of his hand has backfired.Rather than drawing attention to the incumbent’s alleged misdeeds, many of the programme’s millions of viewers sarcastically took Bolsonaro’s hand-written message as an admission of his own guilt.Following Sunday night’s debate, Lula supporters from all walks of life have flooded social media with photographs of their own self-descriptions inked on their palms.John Ulhoa, the guitarist from a pop rock band called Pato Fu, jokinglydescribed himselfas a “musician (and a hunk)”.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThe Emmy-winning comedian Antonio Tabetintroduced himselfto his 2.8 million followers on X as an artist.Carlos Marcio used both palms to portray himself as a cellist and author.Carla Emanuela Sacramento, an obstetric nurse,posted a photographof herself clad in personal protective equipment and with the words “primary health care nurse” proudly written on her right palm.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueProminent politicians also jumped on the trend, including Lula’s health minister, the infectious disease specialist Alexandre Padilha,whose palm noted he was a doctor, and Tabata Amaral, whoidentifiedas a political scientist and astrophysicist.All across the country, librarians, oil workers, engineers, journalists, architects, pilots, psychologists, seamstresses, street cleaners, teachers, influencers, and police officers used ballpoint pens to inscribe their professions on to their skin.Writing on Substack, the Latin America expert James Bosworth called Bolsonaro’s stunt a “critical error” in his bid for power.“It may have seemed like an inspired pre-debate gimmick. Instead, he gave the world a meme image that will stick with him for the rest of his political career,” Bosworth said, offering politicians a word of advice.“Don’t write the word ‘corrupto’ on your hand and show it to the audience,” Bosworth suggested.Bolsonaro, who is the son of the jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, is a professional politician who has long faced corruption accusations, although he denies them and has never been convicted. The 45-year-old senator also haswell-documented tiesto members of Rio’s mafia underworld andonce employedthe relatives of the city’s most notorious contract killer, Adriano da Nóbrega. Last week two allies were arrested for alleged involvement with the Red Command drug faction, which Donald Trumprecently designateda foreign terrorist organisation. Bolsonarovoiced surpriseat those arrests and said the men had the right to prove their innocence.On Monday, Brazilian media reported that Bolsonaro was being investigated by the federal police as part of a money-laundering inquiry.Lula, whose Worker’s party (PT) has also been involved in major corruption scandals, used Sunday’s debate to throw down the gauntlet to Bolsonaro.The leftwing incumbent said he would give electoral authorities access to his banking and phone recordings, and those of close relatives, in order to prove he was not corrupt – if Bolsonaro agreed to do the same.Bolsonaro, who, polls suggest, holds a slender advantage ahead of Sunday’s second-round runoff, has yet to respond to Lula’s challenge. The rightwingerwon the 4 October first roundby more than 2m votes.Explore more on these topicsBrazilFlávio BolsonaroLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmericasThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Giving £2 a day to people in the Amazon helps protect rainforest, pilot project finds | Amazon rainforest | The Guardian
description: Researchers say almost 90% of participants in unconditional basic income scheme in Peru adopted environmentally beneficial practices
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Researchers say almost 90% of participants in unconditional basic income scheme in Peru adopted environmentally beneficial practices
Content: The experiment involved three communities in Peru’s Asháninka region.Photograph: Martín Mejía/APView image in fullscreenThe experiment involved three communities in Peru’s Asháninka region.Photograph: Martín Mejía/APAmazon rainforestGiving £2 a day to people in the Amazon helps protect rainforest, pilot project findsResearchers say almost 90% of participants in unconditional basic income scheme in Peru adopted environmentally beneficial practicesJonathan WattsTue 20 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA pioneering project to provide Indigenous people in the Peruvian Amazon with an unconditional basic income has contributed to the protection of the rainforest, according to a study.The analysisfrom the University of Bath is expected to contribute to a growing debate about the role of direct payments to communities that maintain globally important ecosystems.A two-year pilot managed by the UK-based charity Cool Earth gave 211 people in three communities in Peru’s Asháninka region six cash transfers of 1,032 Peruvian soles each – roughly equivalent to £2 a day – to spend as they wished.Over the course of the trial, researchers found almost 90% of participants adopted environmentally beneficial practices, such as collective reforestation, restoration of critical water sources and reductions of forest burning.They also noted a reduction in food insecurity, which can sometimes prompt forest people to start logging or become involved in environmental crimes. Households unable to afford nutritious food fell from 73% to 26%.Could a £2-a-day basic income be the key to protecting rainforests?Read moreAnother reported benefit was reduced migration, with the share of participants forced to leave their homes to find work falling from 43% to 18%. Researchers said this allowed more people to remain and protect the forest.Dr Nick Langridge, a co-author of the report, said: “The findings suggest that when communities have greater security and autonomy, they are better able to protect the ecosystems they depend on.”There isincreasing recognitionof the importance of Indigenous stewardship of the Amazon and other biomes that sequester carbon, shelter biodiversity and provide vital ecological services to the planet. But this role is increasingly difficult as Indigenous lands are threatened by miners, loggers, farmers and land grabbers, and as many of the young people of these often economically poor communities are exposed to the internet or lured away to wealthier cities.How to sustain, encourage and reward Indigenous stewardship is a hot debate in the international aid and environmental community. Many previous payment schemes came with strings attached, such as the Brazilian government’sbolsa família, which has child education obligations, orbolsa verde, which has conservation activity requirements.View image in fullscreenAsháninka Indigenous people from Brazil and Peru dance and sing at dawn during an annual celebration.Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/APThe authors of the new study say the project – which was drawn up with local women’s groups – is the first to offer an unconditional basic income to an Indigenous community in the Amazon.The lead author, Dr Neil Howard, said: “All of this helps ethical conservation. The incentive to exploit or abandon land is diminished, and people are put front and centre with respect and dignity, which contrasts sharply with the colonial history of conservation and Indigenous policy.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTo boost the impact, the project delivered a voluntary “cash plus” complementary programme of community-led education on finance, conservation and climate change.Other academics aremore cautiousabout the environmental impacts of cash transfers, pointing out that similar studies elsewhere have found they can lead to an increase in deforestation as people use the extra cash to expand agriculture.In some parts of the Amazon, cash payments are used to buy motorbikes and cars, which increases demand for more roads. There are also reports of Indigenous communities becoming more exposed to drugs when they visit cities to collect transfers.The authors of the new report acknowledge that wider research is needed on the ecological impacts of unconditional basic income. Their two-year study was small, covering little over 500 hectares (1,235 acres) of forest. They did not measure changes in vegetation or soil quality, nor account for the influence of any separate projects that might have been affecting community behaviour.Despite these limitations, they say the early results have excited the cash-for-conservation network of civil society organisations.“Yes, this is an experimental pilot and and we could do with something much larger,” Howard said. “But this is very pioneering. My hope is that the trade-off between scale and innovation tips in this direction.”Explore more on these topicsAmazon rainforestConservationIndigenous peoplesPeruAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I forgot to pay’: Victoria’s premier Ben Carroll drives off without paying for petrol, sparking police inquiries | Ben Carroll | The Guardian
description: After being contacted by officers, politician says, he has paid bill and is ‘grateful for the team at the servo for their understanding’
Author: Benita Kolovos
Headline: After being contacted by officers, politician says, he has paid bill and is ‘grateful for the team at the servo for their understanding’
Content: Victorian premier Ben Carroll says he has ‘fixed the bill’ for petrol after inadvertently driving away from a service station without paying.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPView image in fullscreenVictorian premier Ben Carroll says he has ‘fixed the bill’ for petrol after inadvertently driving away from a service station without paying.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPBen Carroll‘I forgot to pay’: Victoria’s premier Ben Carroll drives off without paying for petrol, sparking police inquiriesAfter being contacted by officers, politician says, he has paid bill and is ‘grateful for the team at the servo for their understanding’Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastBenita KolovosVictorian state correspondentTue 20 Oct 2026 19.05 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Tuesday night,Ben Carrollreceived a phone call: police were looking for him.The Victorian premier had met with the state’s police commissioner earlier that morning – so he wasn’t exactly hard to find.But the officers weren’t looking to speak to him about their resources, powers or investigations. They wanted to know if he had driven off from a service station without paying for his petrol on Monday night.“Late Monday night, I was running some errands and filled up the car with petrol,” Carroll said in a statement early on Wednesday morning.“[I] found out yesterday I forgot to pay. I fixed the bill straight away.”He added that he was “grateful for the team at the servo for their understanding”.It’s understood Carroll had filled up his car near his home in his electorate of Niddrie on Monday night, after spending the evening responding to thealleged attack on the federal MP Helen Hainesin regional Victoria earlier that day.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailUnbeknown to him – as he met with Victoria police commissioner, Mike Bush, the head of the Australian federal police, Krissy Barrett, and the prime minister, Anthony Albanese – officers had begun searching for him.It’s understood they contacted him through the Department of Parliamentary Services on Tuesday night.A bashful Carroll then headed back to the service station to pay up.No further action is expected to be taken.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionVictoria to become first state to make abortions free as Coalition matches Labor election promiseRead moreSpeaking at an event on Wednesday, Carroll said the former deputy premier John Thwaites had contacted him to say: “Don’t worry, Ben. I didn’t pay for the petrol, and I also drove off with the nozzle in the car.”“That made me feel a lot better,” Carrol told the Age forum. “It shows that politicians are human beings, and even premiers make mistakes.”Asked about the matter on Wednesday, Bush said the view of police was that a petrol drive-off was a “civil matter unless it’s proven otherwise”.“If someone does something accidentally, non-deliberately, it becomes a very civil matter,” the commissioner said. “That civil redress is available, and I do understand that civil redress was made.“It does occur and that’s why we’re very careful not to criminalise every petrol driver. We do understand, and I’m very empathic and sympathetic to petrol station owners who do suffer, but it’s not always criminal [behaviour].”It came months after Carroll’s predecessor, Jacinta Allan, told parliament that police were grappling with a rise inillegal drive-offs from petrol stations.“We are seeing a rise in incidents of drive-offs at service stations, and it is an illegal practice,” she said in March.Explore more on these topicsBen CarrollVictorian politicsAustralian police and policingVictorianewsShareReuse this content

title: Australian researchers identify new subtype of depression linked to body clock disruptions | Depression | The Guardian
description: Study identifies ‘circadian depression’ as affecting nearly a quarter of more than 11,000 participants
Author: Donna Lu
Headline: Study identifies ‘circadian depression’ as affecting nearly a quarter of more than 11,000 participants
Content: Individuals with circadian depression have more severe mental health symptoms, study’s author says.Photograph: milos-kreckovic/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIndividuals with circadian depression have more severe mental health symptoms, study’s author says.Photograph: milos-kreckovic/Getty ImagesDepressionAustralian researchers identify new subtype of depression linked to body clock disruptionsStudy identifies ‘circadian depression’ as affecting nearly a quarter of more than 11,000 participantsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastDonna Luassistant editor, climate, environment and scienceTue 20 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 19.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralian researchers have identified a new subtype of depression – termed “circadian depression” – linked to disruptions in the body’s internal clock, which they believe is less responsive to traditional antidepressant treatments.In a study published in British Journal of Psychiatry, involving clinical and genetic data from 11,380 Australians with mostly severe and recurrent depression, researchers identified circadian depression as affecting nearly a quarter (23%) of participants.They suggest people affected by the subtype may benefit from treatments that target the body’s circadian rhythms, such as melatonin and light therapy.Immunotherapy could be used to treat depression, early trial suggestsRead moreWhile alink between mood disorders and disrupted daily rhythmshas been known for some time, the researchers say the “study strengthens the evidence base for a circadian subtype of depression as a biologically valid and clinically useful phenotype of depression”.The study’s first author, Dr Emiliana Tonini of the University of Sydney’s Brain and Mind Centre, said the researchers defined circadian depression as being in participants who showed at least three out of six features: experiencing a seasonal pattern of illness, delayed sleep timing, sleeping longer when depressed, being a night owl, waking feeling very tired, and social jetlag – when “their sleep when they go to bed during the week or when they work is very different from the weekend or when they are free to organise their day”.“Individuals with circadian depression have more severe mental health symptoms,” Tonini said during a press briefing. “The age of onset of their depression was younger compared to those with non-circadian depression, but they also had more episodes and also more complex trajectories, more suicidality, more hypomanic and psychotic-like symptoms as well.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe researchers also found that those with circadian depression had higher genetic risk for ADHD and mood disorders, “but also a series of metabolic and inflammatory markers”, Tonini said. “This is important because that indicatesthat circadian depression is not just depression with bad sleep, but actually there is an underlying biology that is quite distinct from other forms of depression.”The researchers hope that being able to clinically diagnose circadian depression in future may help with more tailored treatments, particularly for young people seeking mental health support for the first time.Prof Ian Hickie, a psychiatrist and co-director of the Brain and Mind Centre, said: “What is critical about being in this circadian type is its poor response to the standard therapies,those which are typically recommended in the guidelines.”SSRIs and SNRIs, typical first-line antidepressant drugs, were less effective and had more side effects for people with the circadian subtype, the study found.For those with circadian depression, “chronobiological treatments – things focused on the sleep-wake cycle, particularly … to do with morning light exposure, daylight activity, regularity of sleep-wake cycles, regularity of food schedules, is critical”,Hickie said.In their study, the researchers noted that the participants were “were limited to those of genetically inferred European ancestry, which may limit generalisability”, and that “future studies are needed to replicate our findings in diverse samples”.The director of the Monash Alfred Psychiatry Research Centre, Prof Jayashri Kulkarni, who was not involved in the research, described it as a “really well-conducted study”.“They have got a polygenic risk score, which means that they’ve actually managed to tie certain types of depression to a specific genetic profile,” she said. “That will be important for onward treatment.”The research did not take into account the hormonal impacts of menopause, Kulkarni added, “which is predominantly one of the things that women describe as causing sleep disturbance … That would be another factor that might be worth considering.”Prof Andrew Coogan, a behavioural neuroscientist at Maynooth University in Ireland, said: “We have known for a long time that major depression is linked to changes in the body clock that make people later to bed and later to rise so the findings are not overly surprising.”He cited a “lack of detail as to how the cluster of features of, and the criteria for, the proposed circadian subtype of depression was arrived at”.“The results of this exploratory study are best interpreted as initial if interesting findings that warrant further examination,” he said.Explore more on these topicsDepressionHealth (Australia news)Mental healthHealth (Society)Medical researchPsychologySleepnewsShareReuse this content

title: Helen Haines loses leg as surgeons fight to save the other after alleged attack in Wangaratta | Helen Haines | The Guardian
description: Independent MP is in critical yet stable condition after man allegedly did U-turn to strike her twice with his car
Author: Tess Ikonomou
Headline: Independent MP is in critical yet stable condition after man allegedly did U-turn to strike her twice with his car
Content: The independent member for Indi, Helen Haines, remains in hospital after being struck by a car in her electorate in northern Victoria.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenThe independent member for Indi, Helen Haines, remains in hospital after being struck by a car in her electorate in northern Victoria.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPHelen HainesHelen Haines loses leg as surgeons fight to save the other after alleged attack in WangarattaIndependent MP is in critical yet stable condition after man allegedly did U-turn to strike her twice with his carBrendan Nugent’s family say Helen Haines has been their friend for more than 20 years‘I don’t want to be known as a hero’: barber who rushed to help Helen Haines praised by PMGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastTess IkonomouandTom McIlroyTue 20 Oct 2026 06.37 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 19.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe man accused of attackingHelen Hainesallegedly made a U-turn before ramming the independent MP twice in an alleged targeted attack near her electorate office, causing her to lose one of her legs.The member for Indi was airlifted from Wangaratta in northernVictoriato Melbourne’s Alfred hospital for emergency surgery on Monday night.Surgeons were on Tuesday fighting to save Haines’ other leg, as the 65-year-old remained in a critical condition.Brendan Nugent’s family say Helen Haines has been their friend for more than 20 yearsRead moreA 43-year-old Tarrawingee man alleged to have driven the Toyota LandCruiser was arrested at the scene. The alleged attacker isBrendan Nugent, Guardian Australia has confirmed.Nugent was charged on Tuesday night with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the Commonwealth offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.Victoria police confirmed in a statement that they would allege the attack was targeted. Nugent is expected to appear at Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday.9:41Australian MP Helen Haines attacked with car: what we know so far - The LatestNugent’s father, Rod Nugent, and Rod’s partner, Christine Cunningham, said in a statement that Haines had been their friend for more than 20 years.“What happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” they said.“We will be assisting Victoria Police in any way we can.”Anthony Albanese confirmed authorities believed the attack was deliberate.“Helen Haines represents the best of our political representatives,” the prime minister said on Tuesday afternoon.“Kind, compassionate, a person of integrity, totally committed to strongly representing the people of that beautiful part of Victoria.”Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereThe home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said witnesses alleged the driver completed a U-turn before the incident.“What witnesses have described is the driver doing a U-turn to get into the car park and to ram Helen against a vehicle, then to reverse and do it a second time,” he told ABC radio.“A bystander ran towards the scene, got the driver out of the vehicle and held the driver until police arrived.”3D map showing the location of helen haines office in wangaratta and the sequence of eventsRicky Jefferies, whose barbershop is next door to Haines’ office,ran from his shop to helpafter hearing the crash.“I had no choice but to take him out of the car because it was the right and safest thing to do,” he told reporters on Tuesday morning.Jefferies, who returned to work on Tuesday morning, alleged the driver had a knife on him. “He didn’t pull it out … I basically just took it out of his pocket and threw it away.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenRicky Jefferies speaks to media outside his Wangaratta barbershop, next door to Haines’ office.Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty ImagesBurke said: “I think every Australian is grateful for those moments when a hero like this runs towards the most dangerous place.”The home affairs minister said the nation’s security agencies and police would be working through what more could have been done to prevent the alleged attack and to help keep others safe.On Monday, Burke reported that there had been 1,067 reports of harassment or threats against high office holders in Australia in the last financial year, an increase from 951 the year before.“We already knew that we needed to do more to be able to keep people in public office safe and we have been,” he said.“While we don’t make public the dollar figures and the exact provision of security for obvious reasons … we had a very significant uplift in the budget.“There is a direct line between the temperature of debate and things willing people will say, and then when people are willing to take action.”View image in fullscreenA woman places flowers outside Haines’ office in Wangaratta.Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty ImagesAlbanese has been joined by leaders and parliamentarians from across the country in calling for a calming of political discourse.Helen Haines was chatting with locals at a dog park on Monday morning. By the afternoon, she was fighting for her lifeRead moreThe mayor of Wangaratta, Irene Grant, expressed gratitude to Jefferies for stepping in to stop the man.“I spoke to the barber this morning and he just shrugged his shoulders. He seemed to just take it in his stride. This was something that he had to do and he did it,” she said.“He was extraordinarily modest about the very brave action that he took yesterday … he did an amazing job.”View image in fullscreenHaines was airlifted to the Alfred hospital in Melbourne for treatment for critical injuries.Photograph: Martin Keep/AFP/Getty ImagesWangaratta, the rural city in which the incident occurred, is a tightknit community in north-east Victoria. At the last census it had a population of about 20,000 people, while the broader local government area had just under 30,000.Haines was elected to federal parliament in 2019 and has been key to the establishment of theNational Anti-Corruption Commission, as well as campaigning for rural health services, telecommunications access and pushing back on misuse of taxpayer funds, orpork barrelling.Explore more on these topicsHelen HainesVictoriaAustralian politicsIndependentsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Italy to deploy 500 troops to Milan after days of protests and looting | Italy | The Guardian
description: Government planning tougher security measures as France also says military forces will be deployed
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Government planning tougher security measures as France also says military forces will be deployed
Content: Protesters clash with police in Piazza del Duomo in Milan, Italy. The unrest followed ​clashes on Saturday in other northern cities ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin.Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenProtesters clash with police in Piazza del Duomo in Milan, Italy. The unrest followed ​clashes on Saturday in other northern cities ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin.Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/ShutterstockItalyItaly to deploy 500 troops to Milan after days of protests and lootingGovernment planning tougher security measures as France also says military forces will be deployedWhy are people protesting across Europe?Angela Giuffridain Rome andJon Henleyin ParisTue 20 Oct 2026 17.24 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 20.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleItaly’s government is sending 500 soldiers to Milan and vowed a “firm response from the state” after protests against the cost of living descended into clashes with police, vandalism and looting. Further demonstrations are planned on Saturday.The government of the far-right prime minister,Giorgia Meloni, also announced new security measures, including an offence of violent participation in ⁠a demonstration, tougher penalties for ⁠rioters, and financial liability for ​parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting..InFrance, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said on Tuesday some military forces would be deployed during ⁠protests ​planned for this Saturday, “mostly to free police and gendarmes in their mission to maintain order”.The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, told parliament that the police presence during Saturday’s demonstrations ⁠would be “massive” and that ​his ​goal was ​for an “immediate return ​to order” ‌after last weekend’s violent riots.Police in Milan, in northern Italy, detained 271 young people after hooded youths set bins ablaze, ransacked shops and smashed windows, including in the area surrounding the city’s cathedral, during the unrest on Saturday and Sunday.Police used teargas and water cannon to disperse the violent groups, who were on the fringes of an initially peaceful protest. Of those detained, 32 have been arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.View image in fullscreenIn Milan’s Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, brands including Chanel, Tiffany ‌and Dior have removed merchandise from ‌their windows as a precaution.Photograph: Stefano Porta/LaPresse/ShutterstockImages of Saturday’s clashes in France, including mobs looting shops and public buildings set on fire, prompted several countries including the US, China and Germany to issue travel advice for their citizens. Nearly 2,400 people were arrested in one of France’s most violent recent bouts of unrest.French authorities on Monday announced partial curfews in several cities, including Paris, Bordeaux, Lille and Nice, and after a night of relative calm, Lecornu said on Tuesday that new curfews would be imposed where they were needed.Authorities in Paris renewed Monday night’s curfew, which would apply from 11pm on Tuesday until 6am on Wednesday to the Place de la République, where many of the weekend clashes took place, and in the central Les Halles shopping district.Paris police ordered a temporary ban on people carrying cans or bottles of petrol or gas, and banned masks and helmets in some areas. A man was also arrested in connection with theburning down of the historic town hall in Limoges.The Italian press agency Ansa reported that one of the security measures being considered in the country was aimed at second-generation immigrant youths, known asmaranza– a slang term used to describe gangs of young people, usually from marginalised areas.Many luxury stores in Milan’s fashion district have stayed closed amid fears of further unrest. Brands including Chanel, Tiffany ‌and Dior removed merchandise from ‌their windows as a precaution.Other stores ransacked included the sports retailers Decathlon and Arc’teryx and the mobile phone operator Vodafone, footage showed.View image in fullscreenThe sports retailer Decathlon was among the stores ransacked in Milan during the protests.Photograph: Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto/Shutterstock“The government will respond firmly to these attacks on the state, ​including through measures aimed at curbing violence by minors,” the foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, who also serves as deputy prime minister, said after Meloni chaired a meeting with top security officials on Monday.Meloni’s coalition, which is facing a general election next year, is reportedly planning tougher penalties for road blockades after days of protests in southern Italy by lorry drivers over fuel prices.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhy are people protesting across Europe?Read moreMeanwhile, Milan is bracing for further protests on Saturday after a new movement, called 17 October, emerged on social media. It said it would organise demonstrations there and in other Italian cities each Saturday afternoon “until this government of thieves collapses”.“You are the violent ones,” the group said. “You, who denied us a future. Now, we are claiming that future ourselves.”Opposition politicians often accuse the government of using security as a propaganda tool, arguing that Italy’s leaders do little to address core issues such as education, housing and living conditions in marginalised areas.There were also tensions during protests at the weekend over the high cost of living in other northern Italian cities, ​including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo ​and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, police said.The protests in Italy and France have been mirrored by demonstrations in other parts ofEurope.Thousands rallied in Lisbon and other Portuguese cities on Tuesday evening, hours after police dismantled housing protest camps at dawn and arrested 55 people.Demonstrators inPortugalare protesting soaring housing costs, seeking to align themselves with similar actions in neighbouring Spain, where tents have been set up in central Madrid for weeks.In Lisbon, thousands of people gathered in the central Rossio square, where protesters voted by a show of hands to re-establish their tent camp from Wednesday.“They forced me on to the streets to shout”, read one placard. Another declared: “Lisbon is not for sale”.Anti-government demonstrations have also rocked the Albanian capital Tirana over the past week, driven by fresh demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and a controversial resort development linked to Donald Trump’s family.Clashes between the protesters and police escalated again on Tuesday amid renewed calls for prime minister Edi Rama’s resignation. Riot police used teargas and water cannon to disperse protesters who fired fireworks and hurled molotov cocktails and stones at officers.Earlier on Tuesday, Rama repeated earlier accusations that “foreign actors” were to blame for the violence, having previously accused both Russia and Iran of driving online misinformation.“It is a hybrid war that gains traction precisely because it is rooted in genuine grievances, not mere fantasy,” the prime minister said, citing the rising cost of living, housing affordability and concerns for the future.Explore more on these topicsItalyProtestEuropeGiorgia MeloniCost of living crisisFrancePortugalnewsShareReuse this content

title: US has resumed sharing intelligence with Ukraine about Russian strikes, says Zelenskyy | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Advance warnings of missile attacks were seemingly suspended last week by the White House, but Ukraine’s president says: ‘Now it works’
Author: Luke Harding
Headline: Advance warnings of missile attacks were seemingly suspended last week by the White House, but Ukraine’s president says: ‘Now it works’
Content: Zelenskyy (right) with the Finnish president (centre) and US envoy Steve Witkoff (left) in Oslo, Norway.Photograph: Heiko Junge/Pool NTB/APView image in fullscreenZelenskyy (right) with the Finnish president (centre) and US envoy Steve Witkoff (left) in Oslo, Norway.Photograph: Heiko Junge/Pool NTB/APUkraineUS has resumed sharing intelligence with Ukraine about Russian strikes, says ZelenskyyAdvance warnings of missile attacks were seemingly suspended last week by the White House, but Ukraine’s president says: ‘Now it works’Luke HardingTue 20 Oct 2026 15.32 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 19.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has resumed sharing intelligence with Kyiv about Russian missile strikes,Volodymyr Zelenskyysaid on Tuesday after a meeting with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in Norway.He saidUkrainewas again receiving advance warnings of ballistic missile attacks, which were seemingly suspended last week by the White House. “Now it works. It’s great,” he said, adding that the US move would save lives.The Ukrainian president said: “It’s very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic [missiles] is coming. So we are thankful to the American side.”Witkoff will on Wednesday meet Russian president Vladimir Putin after what a US official called “constructive” talks with Zelenskyy inNorway. The US envoy would aim to “create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations”, a US official told Reuters.The talks in Oslo took place amid the worst crisis in US-Ukraine relations since Putin’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. Donald Trump has bitterly accused Zelenskyy of failing to end the war and has said Ukraine needs a new leader.On Tuesday Trump again suggested Zelenskyy was the main obstacle to an agreement. “We want Zelensky to make a deal. He can make a deal. He could have made a deal two years ago when wehad our little chat in the Oval Office,” he said.Trump also said he had asked Putin to release Stephen Hubbard – anAmerican taken prisoner by Russian forcesin occupied Ukraine – in a further sign of his growing public alliance with Moscow.The US president’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined Witkoff and Zelenskyy by video for the talks. Norway’s prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, also took part, alongside EU and British security officials.Zelenskyy said he had held a “positive” phone call earlier with the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio. Asked if Ukraine was now losing the war, after recent hostile US actions, Zelenskyy replied: “Of course we are not losing. But we are losing people because of Russian attacks and time. It’s a pity.”He said he had raised with Rubio restrictions imposed last week on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s satellite internet service. The slowdown has crippled Ukraine’s ability to launch mid-range drone strikes on Russian battlefield positions.Zelenskyy said he had offered to stop Ukraine’s long-range attacks on Russian oil refineries – a key Trump demand – if the US provided Kyiv with Patriot missile interceptors. The Pentagon has blocked the delivery of Patriots to Kyiv paid for by other countries, leaving Kyiv more vulnerable than ever to air attacks.Speaking on Tuesday, Zelenskyy also said he opposed a trilateral summit floated by Putin, which would see the Russian leader, Trump and China’s president, Xi Jinping, meet next month to strike a Ukraine deal. Zelenskyy would be shut out, theWall Street Journal reported.“There can be nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in Oslo. He added: “If it’s about Ukraine and our future it can only be acceptable when we are at the table of negotiations.”The Washington-Kyiv crisis began 10 days ago when Trump announced he was lifting US sanctions on Russian diesel, in an attempt to lower fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections. He then announced an energy ceasefire, which Kyiv implemented for several days but Russia ignored.Despite this, Trump has bitterly rounded on Zelenskyy. He has effectively positioned the US as Russia’s ally, favouring Moscow over Kyiv, to the dismay of America’s pro-Ukrainian European and British backers. The US’s peace proposals have largely echoed Russia’s maximalist demands.The EU’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, on Tuesday questioned whether US negotiators had been honest brokers in the peace efforts. Witkoff has held numerous meetings with Putin in Moscow, while so far visiting Kyiv only once.“Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now,” Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin’s terms “because Europe has been supporting Ukraine”, Kallas said.Tuesday’s talks came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of US politicians that he believed “some political decision has been made to slow down … support for us”.US officials have denied this but have failed to explain convincingly why satellite communication services were curtailed or intelligence sharing temporarily cut off.Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio insisted nothing had changed. He said Patriot interceptors were in short supply and were needed in other parts of the world, as well as for the US’s own defence. “There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine,” he insisted.At least nine people were killed in Ukraine on Tuesday. They included passengers who were travelling on the Kyiv to Odesa highway. A Russian drone struck two vehicles, killing three people and injuring four. One of the victims was the driver of a shuttle bus, which was on its way from the capital to a military cemetery.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussiaEuropeUS foreign policyVolodymyr ZelenskyyNorwaynewsShareReuse this content

title: Nato increases Black Sea deployment amid escalating deadly Russian attacks | Nato | The Guardian
description: Mounting anxiety as Russia’s war on Ukraine reaches Nato’s borders with targeting of vessels transporting agricultural cargo
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Mounting anxiety as Russia’s war on Ukraine reaches Nato’s borders with targeting of vessels transporting agricultural cargo
Content: A Romanian air force F-16 fighter jet shoots at a drone flying over the Black Sea near Sulina on 17 October.Photograph: MAPN/Romanian Defence Ministry/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Romanian air force F-16 fighter jet shoots at a drone flying over the Black Sea near Sulina on 17 October.Photograph: MAPN/Romanian Defence Ministry/AFP/Getty ImagesNatoNato increases Black Sea deployment amid escalating deadly Russian attacksMounting anxiety as Russia’s war on Ukraine reaches Nato’s borders with targeting of vessels transporting agricultural cargoPeter BeaumontSenior international correspondentTue 20 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 14.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNato is deploying additional military assets to the Black Sea amid the recent deadly escalation of Russian attacks on merchant shipping, as five more vessels were attacked on Tuesday.Russia’s military said it ⁠struck ​three cargo vessels in Ukraine’s ⁠port of Reni and two ⁠other cargo vessels en ​route ‌to ‌Odesa.Russia’s targeting of vessels taking grain and other agricultural cargoes from Ukraine’s ports – central to the country’s economy – have brought the conflict to Nato’s borders, with a new high-risk designation used by the London shipping insurance market now covering all of the Black Sea save for the territorial waters of Romania,Bulgariaand Turkey.Witha sharply rising death toll among civilian seafarersthat has made Black Sea routes the world’s most dangerous, Nato announced the ⁠defensive military alliance would add more surveillance assets in the region.Nato’s spokesperson, Allison Hart, said: “Today,Nato‌ambassadors met in ‌the North Atlantic Council to discuss security in the Black Sea. Nato has already ​strengthened our posture along the eastern flank, including with counter-drone ⁠capabilities. Nato will ​be sending ​additional assets ​to the region, ​including ‌support for surveillance, ​reconnaissance, ​and forensics.”The deployment will include maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, drones and intelligence personnel. There is mounting anxiety about the increasing overspill from Russia’s war on Ukraine and the potential for further friction with Nato.Concern has been growing after alleged Russian attacks that have increasingly edged into the territorial waters and exclusive economic zones of Bulgaria andRomania. Romania deployed jets over the weekend to shoot down two suspected Russian drones over its territory.View image in fullscreenA vessel that was hit by a drone in the Black Sea this month.Photograph: Bulgarian Interior Ministry/ReutersRomania’s defence minister, Radu Miruță, said the drones were probably latest generation Russian drones, flying at speeds similar to fighter jets.“The ones from last night were flying ​at 450 km/h, which leads us to think they were Russian-made Geran-4 drones with a turboprop ​engine,” Miruță said. “This is the first time we’ve shot down drones like these.”Romania has recorded 35 unauthorised drone incursions so far this year, compared with nine in 2025. Romanian forces have downed six drones this year, compared with zero last year.Last week, two chemical tankers were hit by drones near Romania’s Black Sea coast, the latest ​in a series of attacks that have highlighted the risks to commercial shipping on Nato’s eastern flank. Both vessels were anchored near ​the Sulina canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea and is an export route for Ukraine.At least five other cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria in the ​past two weeks, with 23 sailors reported dead or missing. Most of those incidents ​occurred outside ⁠Nato territorial waters.View image in fullscreenFour rescued sailors arrive in Bulgaria after their vessel sank following an attack in the Black Sea this month.Photograph: Denislav Stoychev/NurPhoto/ShutterstockAmid mounting concern, Bulgaria has asked Nato for the deployment of combat aircraft and anti-drone systems to its territory. On 18 October, France sent a maritime reconnaissance aircraft to Romania.The maritime insurer and risk analyst Ambrey has said there is no end in sight to the threats to Black Sea cargo shipping, including grain and oil, and that insurance prices for passage of the waters have rocketed.Tomas Alexa, a senior analyst at Ambrey, said last week his company had noted a sharp increase in the tempo of attacks beginning in July. Russian forces are estimated to be responsible for 80% of them.The recent loss of life, he suggested, had been exacerbated by “double tap” attacks involving aerial and surface drones, the latter often carrying up to half a tonne of explosive payloads. Smaller vessels that primarily use the Danube canal system have sunk rapidly.“While attacks against merchant vessels in the Black Sea are not new, we are seeing an escalation both in terms of the number of attacks and in the geographical scope,” Alexa said.Explore more on these topicsNatoShipping industryRussiaUkraineRomaniaBulgariaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Ukraine thankful that intelligence on missile strikes ‘works now’, says Zelenskyy – as it happened | Europe | The Guardian

title: Republicans push back on Donald Trump’s wavering support for Ukraine | Republicans | The Guardian
description: GOP lawmakers threaten to pull support for president’s agenda after Russia diesel deal and sanctions pause
Author: Ariana Baio
Headline: GOP lawmakers threaten to pull support for president’s agenda after Russia diesel deal and sanctions pause
Content: Donald Trump speaks at a midterm campaign rally at the Dalton municipal airport in Georgia on 16 October 2026.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump speaks at a midterm campaign rally at the Dalton municipal airport in Georgia on 16 October 2026.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesRepublicansRepublicans push back on Donald Trump’s wavering support for UkraineGOP lawmakers threaten to pull support for president’s agenda after Russia diesel deal and sanctions pauseUS politics live – latest updatesAriana Baioin New YorkTue 20 Oct 2026 13.32 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 21.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA handful of Republicans have spoken out againstDonald Trump’ssoftening stance on Russia, threatening to pull financial support for his agenda over his “embarrassing” handling of the Ukraine war.Don Bacon, an outgoing congressman in Nebraska, condemned Trump’s actions – which include astunning agreement to buy Russian dieseland thepausing of sanctions on Moscow– as “absolutely disgraceful” and accused the US president of cozying up to a “war criminal” in Vladimir Putin, his Russian counterpart.“It really is disgraceful, and theRepublicansthat I associate with, there’s a lot of us, can’t stand it,” Bacontold CNNon Monday. “I think the president’s leverage in this Congress is shot.”US gave us no warning of Russian strikes on Kyiv power plants, Zelenskyy saysRead moreLast week, Trump waived sanctions imposed on Russia through alawnamed after his longtime ally and late senator Lindsey Graham. The legislation, which hesignedonly last month, was intended to increase financial pressure on Russia, more than four years after it invaded Ukraine.Instead, Trump announced he had struck a deal with Putin to import diesel fuel, which has become more expensive for Americans largely due to Trump’s war with Iran. Trumphas previously blamed Ukraine’s strikeson Russia.Over the weekend,Trump claimed Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy, “doesn’t care”about the impact of Ukraine’s strikes on Russia and “doesn’t want to end this war and probably never did” because Ukraine is receiving financial support from Europe.Trump also suggested Zelenskyy should step down on Monday, saying it was “time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine”.In aninterview with Bloomberg,Zelenskyysaid he believed Trump was taking steps to “convince Ukraine to capitulate” to Russian demands. On social media,Zelenskyy reaffirmed Ukraine’s partnership with the US.Darline Graham, the sister of Lindsey Graham and now a senator from South Carolina, broke with the president on his decision over the weekend,telling reporters on Saturday: “Personally, I would choose to put the pressure on Russia to end the war and get gas prices down because I don’t trust Putin, and I don’t trust Russia.”“[Ronald Reagan] and [Lindsey Graham] would be ashamed of this,” Bill Cassidy, the outgoing US senator from Louisiana,wrote on Xin response to a recentWall Street Journal editorialon the matter.Mitt Romney, a former Republican senator and presidential candidate,wrote on social mediathat if the US abandoned Ukraine, it would also “abandon liberty”.Some lawmakers had already raised concerns about the president’s support for Ukraine after Ukrainian officials said the country’s access to Starshield, a military version of the Starlink satellite internet service powered by Elon Musk’s company,was restricted last week. Muskhinted on social mediathat the US government controlled Ukraine’s access.Zelenskyyalso accused the US government ofwithholding intelligenceabout an incoming Russian missile attack on Sunday evening – the third accusation of its kind.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, plus breaking news alertsSign up toThe Stakes 2026A weekly guide to what really matters in the US midterms, plus breaking news alerts.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat is Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade Starlink system, and how will its restriction affect Ukraine?Read moreBrian Fitzpatrick, a Pennsylvania congressman,told MS Now on Mondaythat the Trump administration had not given “sufficient answers” about the recent disruptions to Starshield and the diesel deal.“This is wildly unacceptable, and it’s not going to stand,” Fitzpatrick said. “There’s going to be consequences to this. And by the way, it’s not just Starshield. It’s the diesel deal. It’s the lifting of sanctions. It’s all of this stuff.”Fitzpatrick said lawmakers would “demand accountability” and that they could take “punitive budgetary action” to force the administration to provide answers.Bacon told CNN he was unwilling to support the president’s agenda, such as building a triumphal arch or a new White House ballroom, while he withheld support for Ukraine.“Why would I want to support the president’s priorities, like the victory arch?” Bacon asked. “Frankly, what I see him doing here is surrendering.”Bacon added: “Why should we try to accommodate him and meet him halfway on funding when he is embarrassing this country so bad with what he’s doing with Putin and Zelensky?”Explore more on these topicsRepublicansDonald TrumpUkraineRussiaVolodymyr ZelenskyyVladimir PutinUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: UK to deploy fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks | Defence policy | The Guardian
description: RAF Typhoon fighters to fly defensive missions over cities and infrastructure in extension of UK support for Riyadh
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: RAF Typhoon fighters to fly defensive missions over cities and infrastructure in extension of UK support for Riyadh
Content: The Ministry of Defence said the aircraft would not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis.Photograph: Simon Maycock/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Ministry of Defence said the aircraft would not conduct offensive strikes against the Houthis.Photograph: Simon Maycock/AlamyDefence policyUK to deploy fighter jets to protect Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacksRAF Typhoon fighters to fly defensive missions over cities and infrastructure in extension of UK support for RiyadhDan SabbaghDefence and security editorTue 20 Oct 2026 14.30 EDTFirst published on Tue 20 Oct 2026 07.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRAF Typhoon fighters are to be used in efforts to protectSaudi Arabiafrom attack by Yemen’s Houthis, flying protective missions over the country’s cities and critical infrastructure as western allies increase their intervention in the escalating conflict.The operation – the most significant military mission signed off by Andy Burnham as prime minister – will involve RAF pilots attempting to shoot down Houthi missiles and drones, which attacked Saudi airports and oil facilities.The Ministry of Defence emphasised that the role of the fighters – whose number was not stated – would be limited. “These aircraft will operate in a defensive role and will not conduct offensive strikes against theHouthis,” it said.An offensive by the Iran-aligned Houthis inYementhat began in September has gradually escalated into a deadly regional conflict. This month the Houthis have attacked Saudi Arabia, the backer of Yemen’s officially recognised government.Thirteen people were killed when a missile hit King Khalid international airport in Riyadh, the deadliest incident since September in a war that has claimed 19 lives in Saudi Arabia so far.Dozens more have been killed in Yemen by the surge in fighting. The death toll from Monday’sHouthi missile strike on a Yemeni government training camphas risen to 73, a brutal demonstration of the rebel group’s military effectiveness.Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said in a TV interview the UK had agreed to help Saudi Arabia to counter the “outrageous Houthi escalation that we’ve seen in recent weeks” and said the UK was “responding to protect civilians” from attack.HA Hellyer, a Middle East expert with the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, speculated that the UK could get drawn further into the conflict in the future, asking: “What does defensive mean?”He asked what the RAF would do if a Houthi attack happened on a Saudi ship in the Red Sea and the British were in a position to stop it. “The UK might say it was defensive but the Houthis would see it as offensive,” he said.Streeting, however, said that the fighter jets’ remit was narrow. “RAF Typhoons will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles,” he said.Military advisers said the UK would also provide an Atlas A400M transport aircraft capable of transporting heavy equipment, in addition toan existing commitment to supply air-to-air refuelling for Saudi fighter jetswith an RAF Voyager. The refuelling mission has been extended by 90 days.The UK has long been a military ally of Saudi Arabia: BAE Systems has supplied it with 72 Typhoons in a deal originally worth £4.4bn. Riyadh has been considering buying another 48 in a negotiation that has dragged on for years.Though the UK only had a limited involvement in the US-Israel war against Iran, Typhoons from the RAF airbase in Akrotiri, Cyprus, and in Qatar, flew defensive missions in the spring and summer to shoot down missiles and drones launched by Iran and other proxies against Gulf states.View image in fullscreenThe UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, met his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, last week.Photograph: Finn Gomez/Getty ImagesBritain’s announcement came a few days after Streeting visited his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, at the Pentagon, where they discussed how to respond to the Houthi escalation amongst other issues.The US has so far stepped up its intelligence support and sent more than 100 military advisers to help the Saudis with targeting, but it has been cautious about providing more direct military support. Donald Trump urged Riyadh on Friday to accept help from Israel, though it was unclear what was on offer.The White House has been trying to de-escalate against Iran and in the Middle Eastbefore US midterm elections in November and with the oil price over $100 a barrel. The US envoy to Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack, told a conference in Qatar that sending in ground troops against the Houthis “seems fruitless”.The Saudi strategy for dealing with the Houthis, who have been gaining territory along the Red Sea coast, remains unclear. “Allies would be happy to help the Saudis, but they have not been very good at explaining what they want,” said Hellyer.He suggested UK military support could help free up the Saudi military to step up direct attacks on the Houthis, though in the past the Saudi air force has been accused ofusing UK- and US-made weaponsin indiscriminate bombing.Amid some concern that the UK risks being seen as closely aligned to the unpopular US war on Iran, the military intervention was partly justified because instability in the Middle East was driving up energy prices and affecting the cost of living.Explore more on these topicsDefence policyRoyal Air ForceMilitarySaudi ArabiaHouthisYemenMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Billionaire Mukesh Ambani launches India’s biggest-ever IPO | IPOs | The Guardian
description: Low-cost broadband provider Jio Platforms aims for £81bn valuation when it floats on the stock market on Wednesday
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Low-cost broadband provider Jio Platforms aims for £81bn valuation when it floats on the stock market on Wednesday
Content: Mukesh Ambani, chairman and managing director of Reliance Industries.Photograph: Amit Dave/ReutersView image in fullscreenMukesh Ambani, chairman and managing director of Reliance Industries.Photograph: Amit Dave/ReutersIPOsBillionaire Mukesh Ambani launches India’s biggest-ever IPOLow-cost broadband provider Jio Platforms aims for £81bn valuation when it floats on the stock market on WednesdayJulia KolleweTue 20 Oct 2026 05.53 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 18.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndia’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians.Indian billionaire’s payments firm plots biggest London flotation in yearsRead moreJio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential.On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.Reliance Industries said in a stock exchangefilinglast week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares.The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share.At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank.
