It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company.However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer.It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director,told investors last weekthat the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working.“What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”Explore more on these topicsIPOsIndiaSouth and central AsiaStock marketsInternet IPOsTelecommunications industryISPsnewsShareReuse this content

title: She was harassed for crude remarks about Modi at a Cockroach protest. Now she can’t leave home | World news | The Guardian
description: ​After a protest clip went viral, a teenager’s life was torn apart by threats that sent her and her family into hiding. Plus, a book on citizen journalism
Author: Niha Masih
Headline: ​After a protest clip went viral, a teenager’s life was torn apart by threats that sent her and her family into hiding. Plus, a book on citizen journalism
Content: The summer demonstrations at the Jantar Mantar protest site were widely supported.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe summer demonstrations at the Jantar Mantar protest site were widely supported.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty ImagesThis Is IndiaWorld newsShe was harassed for crude remarks about Modi at a Cockroach protest. Now she can’t leave home​After a protest clip went viral, a teenager’s life was torn apart by threats that sent her and her family into hiding. Plus, a book on citizen journalismDon’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereNiha MasihTue 20 Oct 2026 02.30 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 05.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBefore 24 July, a person I will call R was preoccupied with the ordinary routines of teenage life: experimenting with makeup,grumbling over mathematics homeworkand hanging out with friends at a tea stall.That month, as the fever of student protests spread across the country, the 15-year-old watched on her phone as young people poured into Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, demanding education reform. She went too. But an 11-second video clip from the protest site, in which she made crude and profane remarks about the prime minister, Narendra Modi, upended her life.“I feel like a criminal, as if I murdered someone,” R said in her first interview about life since the backlash. “I didn’t get a chance to make amends. In my own country, I am being treated like an enemy.”It’s been 86 days since that protest, but R doesn’t leave home over safety concerns, trapped in the reality the ordeal created.The summer agitation had for weeks demanded the ousting of the then-education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, over repeated examination paper leaks. But after aviolent police crackdownon a student march the anger spilled over to the Modi government.I went to Jantar Mantar every night that week as people from all walks of life streamed in.Protestsigns once directed largely against Pradhan now increasingly targeted Modi and his powerful deputy, Amit Shah, whose ministry controls Delhi Police.The language was oftenprofaneand sexualised, and was quickly seized on by government supporters to condemn the protesters. Pro-government media channels ran heated debates about the disrespectful language and questioned the motives of those gathered.Women were singled out; BJP supporters identified them from social media clips anddoxed them.R found herself at the centre of this storm. A police case was filed against her for insult intended to provoke a breach of the peace, and statements that could lead to public mischief and defamation. The complainant told Scroll, an independent news organisation, that she had called R and asked her to publicly apologise.After Pradhan resigned, Modi posted on Instagram about theuse of vulgar abusesagainst him by “some mischievous children”, saying: “It is a cultural shock. How can our daughters speak like this?” Modi added that the children must be forgiven, instead of being punished.Meanwhile, Rissued an apologyto Modi.In a grainy video filmed in low light, R stands against a dull white wall wearing a striped T-shirt, her hands folded in a namaste. “I am so ashamed of saying those things that I am not even able to raise my eyes. I apologise to the whole nation for it. This is my first and last mistake,” she said. (Local media reported that the complainant withdrew the police case after R’s video was posted.)“I cried after making that video,” she told me. “I was feeling so helpless.”But her apology did little to stem the abuse. She received rape and death threats, abusive phone calls, incessant warnings on text, knocks on doors and cars outside her apartment building in a Delhi suburb.“I couldn’t understand what was happening,” R said, her eyes misting up as she recalled the initial days after the incident. “People older than my mother were calling merandi(prostitute),aatankwadi(terrorist),deshdrohi(enemy of the state). Others were offering Rs11,000 to find me and Rs21,000 to beat me.”With her phone and address leaked, R and her mother were compelled to leave their home. They struggled to find landlords willing to rent them a place to stay. They found one apartment, then another and then another. Her mother, a single parent, lost the income she earned from tutoring. To pay for the repeated moves, she sold her gold jewellery. That money is keeping them afloat. She estimates it will probably last another four months. As the clock runs out, her mother is desperately searching for work.During this time, R has not been to school and can no longer imagine returning. Some friends have cut off contact, leaving her increasingly isolated.Despite her apology video, pro-government media continued to hound her, she said. In late August, frustrated and angry at yet another media crew showing up, she uploaded a video to social media laying bare what she was going through.“Modiji, my life has become hell,” R said addressing the prime minister. “Now I can’t go anywhere, neither do I have any freedom. I can’t live anywhere. I have to live hiding my face,” she said.R told me she wants people to understand how traumatising her experience has been. “To make someone homeless overnight is a big deal,” she said.Now, stuck indoors, she is watching another wave of protests unfold. This time it’s overthe controversial electoral rolls revisionthat has removed 130 million voters from the register. (If you missed it, readlast week’s newsletter about this issue.)R feels solidarity with the students getting brutalised and detained. There have been moments she has felt tempted to join them. But the thought of her mother and their uncertain housing situation have held her back.“I am not scared any more. I have gone through the worst already,” she said. But she doesn’t want to put her mother through more pain.Days before the protest, R had been planning her 15th birthday. She wanted to cut her birthday cake inside an autorickshaw, to remake a trend she had seen on social media.It’s been a couple of months since she turned 15. I asked her what she wants or hopes for now. She paused and then said: “My past is not in my hands. I can’t change that. Now, I just want to look ahead and do well in my board exams.”What else we’re reading aboutView image in fullscreenA still from award-winning film Selvi.Culture| Two Indian films won awards at theBusan international film festival. Birds in the Dark by Shashank Walia was awarded the Songwon Vision audience prize and Sailesh Rathnakumar’s Selvi won the HyLife Vision as well as the Taipei Film Commission award.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is IndiaNiha Masih takes a look at the stories, ideas and news makers of modern IndiaEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPolitics| The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, will land in Mumbai on 20 October forhis second visit to India this year. Rubio will meet foreign minister S Jaishankar and then travel to Jamnagar, home to Reliance Industries’ massive refinery.Imran Khan| Days after the Bollywood actor Imran Khanappeared at a Mumbai protestagainst the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, authorities asked him to leave the country by 28 October over what they described as a violation of the Foreigners Act. The action followed a complaint by BJP leader Kirit Somaiya against Khan, who is a US citizen.Guest shelfA recommendation from someone with great tasteView image in fullscreenMedia Ka Loktantra by Vineet Kumar.Photograph: SuppliedWith the chief justice of India criticisingcitizen journalistcovering the recent protests, veteran television reporterRavish Kumar, who now hosts a YouTube show, recommends a relevant book.“I had just finished reading Vineet Kumar’s bookMedia Ka Loktantra(Democracy of Media) when the chief justice’s statement came out, saying that if every citizen becomes a journalist, it will create problems for all of us. Published in 2024, Vineet’s book discusses the idea of do-it-yourself journalism. He shows how, when mainstream journalism began silencing the voices of ordinary people, they picked up cameras themselves and started practising journalism. They are becoming journalists to also assert their citizenship and rights guaranteed to them by the constitution. The mainstream media has a problem with journalism emerging on social media platforms because stories that it refuses to report – such as those concerning the electoral rolls – are being covered by others. The conflict between the media and DIY journalism has only now reached the courts. But it began a long time ago.”Count itA number worth knowingView image in fullscreenThe National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) plant in Dadri.Photograph: Prakash Singh/AFP/Getty Images84Close to 45% of thermal power plants in India – as many as 84 out of 191 –were critically low on coal stocks(£) as of early October. At the same time, the country’s demand for power grew by 10% this year, the highest year-on-year increase in the past 10 years.Vibe checkView image in fullscreenA felt sculpture by Sagarika Sundaram at the Henry Moore Institute.Photograph: Rob HarrisArtistSagarika Sundaramhas spent a decade working with wool, transforming it into felt for expansive sculptural pieces that feel almost otherworldly. Her latest exhibition,Reservoirrecently opened at the Henry Moore Institute, in Leeds, and runs until 10 January.“There’s a clearer commitment to sculpture in this body of work, even though I’m still working with felt. I’m thinking spatially and making large volumes that explore what cloth can do: bend, collapse, gather, turn inward and support or surrender to its own weight,” she said of her latest works. Among them is Blue Mountain, which stretches almost seven metres long, creating a cave-like space that viewers can move through. That’s what I find compelling in the way her works are presented: they are not static objects offering a single perspective.The New York-based artist finds it exciting to give up a degree of agency during the making process, allowing the material to determine, in part, how the final form will unfurl. “Wool is a wonderfully responsive material. It can be soft and pliable but also dense, strong and structural. Wool takes dye exceptionally well and I can be quite expressive with colour and mark-making,” she said.Get in touchDo you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us atthisisindia@theguardian.comand we may include your response in a future issue.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is IndiaIndiaSouth and central AsiaProtestYoung peopleStudentsActivismnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Myanmar’s ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi seen in rare photos after receiving gift from King Charles | Myanmar | The Guardian
description: Critics said images of detained former leader were a stunt by the military to end country’s diplomatic isolation
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Critics said images of detained former leader were a stunt by the military to end country’s diplomatic isolation
Content: Myanmar’s ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi talks with officials from Home Affairs Ministry as she receives two books and a sealed letter sent by Britain's King Charles III, in Naypyitaw, Myanmar.Photograph: Myanmar President Spokesperson Office/APView image in fullscreenMyanmar’s ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi talks with officials from Home Affairs Ministry as she receives two books and a sealed letter sent by Britain's King Charles III, in Naypyitaw, Myanmar.Photograph: Myanmar President Spokesperson Office/APMyanmarMyanmar’s ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi seen in rare photos after receiving gift from King CharlesCritics said images of detained former leader were a stunt by the military to end country’s diplomatic isolationOliver Holmesin BangkokTue 20 Oct 2026 01.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMyanmar has delivered presents from Britain’s ​King Charles toAung San Suu Kyi, releasing rare photos of the imprisoned former leader in what critics said was a stunt by the country’s military to end diplomatic isolation.A presidential spokesperson saidon social mediathat home ministry officials handed over two gardening books on soil, “along with one sealed envelope and a sealed diplomatic pouch”, from King Charles, who is known to have an interest in planting and the environment.Photos showed the Nobel Peace laureate smiling in a wood-panelled room, a paper calendar on the wall behind her.Suu Kyi, 81, the daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San, has spent much of her life in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements. She is now serving multiple sentences under house arrest at an undisclosed location in Naypyidaw, the capital.Over her lifetime, the country’s military rulers have been cautious about locking Suu Kyi away in prison due to her beloved domestic status and international prominence, particularly in Britain, where she lived and married an Oxford academic. Most other political prisoners languish in jail.Despite winning a 2015 election, she was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to the independent conflict monitor ACLED. Since then, Suu Kyi’s whereabouts and health have been difficult to determine untilan International Committee of the Red Cross visitin August.Coup leader and former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April afterelections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has been making efforts to rebuild regional and international diplomatic ties.Kim Aris, Suu Kyi’s son who lives in London, said in a statement that he welcomed Charles’s gifts but warned their delivery should not be exploited by the regime.“We must not allow the military regime to use such selective disclosures to create an illusion of normality or gain international legitimacy,” he said. “My mother’s fundamental human rights continue to be violated.”Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including the2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslimsthat Washington considers a genocide.The former commander-in-chief has recently conducted several regional visits to rebuild bilateral ties with neighbours, after the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) regional blocbarred him from its summitsfor not following an Asean-brokered ‌peace plan.During his most recent trip to Malaysia this month, the leader was given an official welcome and honour guard. Min Aung Hlaing earlier visited Laos, Thailand, Vietnam and Cambodia.View image in fullscreenAung San Suu Kyi pictured delivering a speech in 2020.Photograph: Aung Shine Oo/APPhil Robertson, director at the Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates (AHRLA) group, said the Suu Kyi book photo op was part of Myanmar’s “quest for global legitimacy”.“The bottom line is Asean has grown tired of arguing with Min Aung Hlaing and Myanmar’s intransigent military leaders and having nothing to show for it, and they desperately want to move the bloc on to other, more cheery issues,” he said.“So as the Asean dominoes fall to the Myanmar charm offensive, they just want to make their regional capitulation look good – and that requires Myanmar to play its part by trotting out Suu Kyi at occasional intervals to receive their latest beneficence.”Min Aung Hlaing has also made efforts to reach out to Donald Trump’s administration, saying ina September interview with Time magazinethat “it would be ideal if the US could cooperate with us”.Weeks later, Reuters reported that the US and Myanmar officials had held talks in Naypyidaw and Tokyo, in part to shut down scam centres that target Americans, but which could be broadened to exploitation of Myanmar’s mineral deposits.The US state department has said it is re-examining “the range of tools the United States has historically leveraged to promote core interests in the country”. China has become Myanmar’s key global partner.Myanmar has always denied the accusations of genocide, and Suu Kyi, who held the role of state counsellor at the time of the atrocities,defended the country at the international court of justice, disappointing many in her global support base.Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsMyanmarSouth and central AsiaAung San Suu KyinewsShareReuse this content

title: Senior Reform official cast doubt over legality of huge donations | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Admission from James Orr to undercover reporter came three months before party was given £72m
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Exclusive: Admission from James Orr to undercover reporter came three months before party was given £72m
Content: James Orr was suspended as Reform’s head of policy last month after other comments he made about political donation laws came to light.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJames Orr was suspended as Reform’s head of policy last month after other comments he made about political donation laws came to light.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesReform UKSenior Reform official cast doubt over legality of huge donationsExclusive: Admission from James Orr to undercover reporter came three months before party was given £72mRowena MasonWhitehall editorTue 20 Oct 2026 14.40 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 18.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA senior Reform UK official raised questions about whether major donations from billionaire backersChristopher Harborneand Ben Delo would be legal under the proposed new foreign donors cap three months before they gave £72m to the party.James Orr, who was then Reform UK’s head of policy and a Cambridge professor, discussed potential difficulties around future donations from Harborne and Delo in undercover footage captured by the investigative reporting group Verbatim.A reporter was posing as a potential donor when Orr talked to him about “filling the war chest in anticipation” of tougher donations rules, describing it as the establishment trying to “kneecap” the party.Orrwas suspended as Reform’s head of policylast month after Channel 4 broadcast some of Verbatim’s undercover filming in which he appeared to discuss ways to get around funding laws to allow donations from a US-based donor.The matter is under police investigation and he remains suspended, although Reform has released its own report clearing Orr and another official of wrongdoing.The new footage has been shared with the Guardian after a public debate about whether thetwo £36m donations from Harborne and Deloto Reform UK will be allowed under the cap. The party maintains the donations are legal, pointing out that the retrospective overseas donor cap has not yet been passed into law.In the footage, recorded in July this year, Orr expressed doubt about whether Delo and Harborne would still be able to donate given that, when it does become law, the £100,000 overseas donor cap is to cover party donations dating back to March this year.Orr believed Delo would probably meet the residency test as long as he was not required to have been a tax resident, in which case he would be “stuffed”. He said Harborne was “probably more of a challenge” in terms of avoiding the overseas cap and he “can’t do anything for 12 months” after moving back.Harborne had been living in Thailand until he registered to vote in Hampshire this summer, and Delo has long been resident in Hong Kong, though he has been on the UK domestic register for some years.The new law willlimit overseas donors to giving £100,000 a yearto a political party. It will apply to donations made after March 2026, and will require any domestic donor who wants to give more than £100,000 to have been resident in the UK for at least a year.In the discussion, Orr was recorded as saying the party was too reliant on Harborne and Delo as “two big whales”. He said the new law was “a retrospective law, which is unheard of. So, we’re going to challenge it in the courts.”James Orr discusses potential problems with future donations from billionaire backers – videoOrr added: “We’ll push it through judicial review. And then … so, we’ll have a big fight. But, yeah, the last few days we’ve been working hard on just filling the war chest as best we can, in anticipation of something quite brutal.”On whether the two men would be caught by the overseas cap, he said: “I mean, there’s going to be a huge fight over that. But Ben, I think it’s probably OK, because I think he is … it depends on how they legislate it, they might just say, you must have been tax domiciled here for X period of time, in which case Ben is stuffed.”Orr went on to say: “It depends what … test for moving back you apply. So, under the common law, there’s a two-limb test, which is actually quite a – not a stringent one. It’s a factual thing, a factual matrix test.“How much time you spend in England, do you have a house here, can you vote, do you have any bills that you pay, you know, it’s quite kind of, it’s not tax … So, on that test, Ben meets it, I think. And then the second then is intention. Do you intend to stay, so, evidence that you intend to stay …”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHaving debated whether Delo would meet the test, Orr said Harborne was “probably more of a challenge”. The Reform official said he would move back to the UK. “But, if he does move back, there’s 12 – he can’t pay – he can’t do anything for 12 months. And, it looks as if they will bring that in.”In his chat with the undercover reporter, Orr also referred to the “complicated backstory” ofDelo, a British-born billionairewho was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls in his cryptocurrency business. He was later pardoned by Donald Trump.0:37James Orr refers to ‘complicated backstory’ of billionaire donor Ben Delo – videoOrr also spoke about having spent time on a boat with Ben Delo in the Peloponnese this summer, talking of mixing work and a holiday in Greece, saying: “We went from Athens down to Ben’s boat in Porto Cheli.” Lawyers for Delo said he did not own a yacht.A Reform UK spokesperson said: “We are 100% confident both [donations] are legal and won’t ever have to be handed back.”Orr did not respond to a request for comment. He has previously denied wrongdoing in relation to electoral laws on overseas funding and dismissed Verbatim as “politically motivated actors trying to discredit a political opponent through dubious legal means”.Lawyers for Harborne described Orr’s comments as private speculation that would not be appropriate to comment on and did not represent established facts. Delo’s lawyers did not respond substantively, saying he would not be drawn into speculation about a conversation he was not party to, or the legal effect of a law yet to be passed. They later added that he had taken extensive legal advice on his donations and had previously set out his rationale for making them.Reform has previously said it intends to take legal action against Verbatim and its directors over the undercover filming.Explore more on these topicsReform UKParty fundingChannel 4Christopher HarbornenewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham faces climate revolt after approval of North Sea gas drilling | Fossil fuels | The Guardian
description: Jackdaw gasfield announcement signals UK’s commitment to North Sea industry but undermines green credentials
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Jackdaw gasfield announcement signals UK’s commitment to North Sea industry but undermines green credentials
Content: The Noble Endeavor oil rig in the Cromarty Firth, Scotland. Campaigners say the Jackdaw decision will exacerbate the climate crisis.Photograph: Andy Buchanan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Noble Endeavor oil rig in the Cromarty Firth, Scotland. Campaigners say the Jackdaw decision will exacerbate the climate crisis.Photograph: Andy Buchanan/AFP/Getty ImagesFossil fuelsAndy Burnham faces climate revolt after approval of North Sea gas drillingJackdaw gasfield announcement signals UK’s commitment to North Sea industry but undermines green credentialsWhat does the approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean?Kiran StaceyPolicy editorTue 20 Oct 2026 14.24 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 18.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Jackdaw gasfield will be given the go-ahead on Wednesday, signalling Andy Burnham’s commitment to the North Sea fossil fuel industry and threatening to trigger a row with climate campaigners and Labour MPs.Miatta Fahnbulleh and John Healey, the energy secretary and chancellor respectively, will make the announcement from Aberdeen on Wednesday morning after more than a year of deliberations over whether doing so would violate the UK’s climate commitments.The approval for drilling at one of the biggest undeveloped fields in the declining North Sea basin is a big boost for Britain’s oil and gas industry – and especially for Shell and the Norwegian company Equinor, which operate it.It will be met with outrage from climate campaigners, who say it undermines Labour’s green credentials and will exacerbate the climate crisis.What does the approval of the Jackdaw gasfield mean?Read moreTessa Khan, the executive director of the anti-oil campaign group Uplift, said: “Jackdaw will provide around just 2% of our gas demand for roughly 10 years. It has been oversold and won’t stop the overall decline in North Sea jobs, as it will be largely unmanned and operated remotely.”She added: “Labour’s climate credibility is on the line. No new oil and gasfields are compatible with safe climate limits.”View image in fullscreenActivists from Fossil Free London stage a protest against the Rosebank oilfield and Jackdaw gasfield outside the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockWhen fully operational, Jackdaw will account for 6% of North Sea gas production, making it one of the biggest gasfields not yet under production.Along with the Rosebank oilfield, its status has become symbolic of the government’s commitment to the oil and gas industry, which is facing heavy job losses as reserves decline and platforms become increasingly automated.The fieldwas approvedby the Conservative government in 2022, with ministers arguing it would help shield the UK from the volatility in the energy market caused by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.Labour came to power in 2024 on a promise not to grant any new licences in the North Sea, not expecting to have to make a decision on Jackdaw or Rosebank.However both fields were cast into doubt last year bya landmark rulingthat said their environmental approval had been incorrectly granted.A judge ruled that when deciding whether the two fields would violate the UK’s climate commitments, regulators should have taken into account the carbon emissions generated by burning the oil and gas they would produce.Shell and Equinor resubmitted their application for environmental consent last September. Since then, Fahnbulleh and her predecessor, Ed Miliband, have spent months deciding whether to use their ministerial power to block it.Both the prime minister and his predecessor, Keir Starmer, have come under heavy pressure to allow the fields to go ahead in recent months, not least from Donald Trump, who urged both men to “open up the North Sea”.Burnham signalled he was sympathetic to the US president’s arguments earlier this summer,promising to takea “pragmatic approach” to the decision.“There is a resource there,” he said in July. “When people are struggling – you can’t ignore that.”He told the Commons last week: “I will take a pragmatic approach on oil and gas. We will set out our decisions shortly.”Several sources have told the Guardian that Fahnbulleh has decided not to block the field, allowing the North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA), which regulates the industry, to give the go-ahead based on financial and logistical concerns.Making the announcement alongside Healey and the NSTA’s chief executive, Stuart Payne, they will say that granting the environmental approval does not violate Labour’s manifesto commitment because it is not a new licence.Fahnbulleh is understood not to have made a final decision on the larger Rosebank field, but energy department officials are looking at ways the tax proceeds from the project could go to green projects if it was given. A decision is expected later this year.The Jackdaw announcement could boost Labour’s position in north-east Scotland, where much of the industry is based and where unions have been campaigning heavily for the permits to be granted.But it is likely to cause angst among some Labour MPs, especially those in seats where they face a challenge from the Green party.A poll by Savanta for the climate group E3G and seen by the Guardian shows that nearly a third of voters say they would be less likely to vote Labour if it gives the go-ahead for more North Sea oil drilling.That includes almost exactly a third of those who voted Labour at the last election, and around half of 18- to 24-year-olds.Ellie Mae O’Hagan, the UK energy programme lead at E3G, said: “After a summer of deadly heatwaves, the public has made up its mind: more drilling is the wrong answer.“If the prime minister wants a decade in power to change the country, he should invest in heat pumps and solar, not tax breaks for the oil and gas companies driving up our bills and polluting the planet.”Officials say, however, that the Rosebank decision is likely to be the more sensitive one, partly because it will produce around seven times the CO2 emissions of Jackdaw and partly because most of the oil produced there will be exported.Khan said: “The defining test is Rosebank. Burnham must deliver on his promise and prioritise affordable bills, genuine industrial growth and a safe climate over oil profits. That means rejecting Rosebank.”Explore more on these topicsFossil fuelsEnvironment policyOil and gas companiesEnergy industryEnergyGasClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand told woman to ‘clear up the mess you’ve made’ after alleged rape, court hears | UK news | The Guardian
description: Woman says alleged assault at comedian’s London home was one of most painful experiences of her life
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Woman says alleged assault at comedian’s London home was one of most painful experiences of her life
Content: Russell Brand arriving at Southwark crown court with his wife, Laura Gallacher, on Tuesday.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAView image in fullscreenRussell Brand arriving at Southwark crown court with his wife, Laura Gallacher, on Tuesday.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAUK newsRussell Brand told woman to ‘clear up the mess you’ve made’ after alleged rape, court hearsWoman says alleged assault at comedian’s London home was one of most painful experiences of her lifeEmine SinmazTue 20 Oct 2026 14.22 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 14.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA woman has said she “couldn’t speak or breathe” when Russell Brand raped her at his London townhouse after picking her out from a crowd after one of his gigs, a court has heard.She said the comedian looked “horrified” after the alleged attack so she assumed he would apologise but instead he told her: “Clear up the mess you’ve made.”The woman said she “tortured herself” in the years that followed because it was one of the “most painful experiences” of her life.Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.The TV personality sat upright in the dock as the woman’s video-recorded police interview was played to Southwark crown court on Tuesday.The woman told officers she was a “massive fan” of Brand and “giddy” to meet him after one of his stand-up performances at the Hammersmith Apollo in 2009.She alleged he pointed to her and said “you” before inviting her, her friend and a third young woman they did not know to have drinks with him.Brand’s security guard later invited the trio backstage where the woman performed oral sex on the actor but refused to have penetrative sex. By then, the woman’s friend had left, but Brand had sex on a sofa with the third woman, who was 19.The woman said she felt “awful” and “disgusting” when she left the dressing room, which is when Brand asked her why she had refused to have sex with him. She told him she had a boyfriend, to which he replied: “We don’t belong to anyone, we’re all free, the ownership of people is sort of what we’ve been sold.”View image in fullscreenThe woman said Brand was ‘persuasive’ about her visiting his three-storey townhouse in Hampstead, west London.Photograph: Wenn Rights Ltd/AlamyBrand asked for her phone number and began messaging and calling her. She said he was “persuasive” about her visiting his three-storey townhouse in Hampstead, north-west London.Days later, the woman was picked up by Brand’s driver and taken to the star’s home knowing she would have sex with him. “I’ve really struggled for a really long time to accept what happened to me, because I went there knowingly and willingly,” she said.She alleged that when she arrived, Brand told her: “This is the best decision you’ve made.” But when they went to Brand’s bedroom, he ordered her to have a shower because her hair smelled “funny”, and made her brush her teeth.She said it made her feel “really dirty”, adding: “At the time it did feel like a thrilling thing to go to the house of this person I really fancied, and I loved comedy. But all those things didn’t feel that good.”View image in fullscreenThe woman described Brand’s dark bedroom and ‘enormous’ bed.Photograph: Metropolitan PoliceShe described his dark bedroom and “enormous” bed, and the distinctive black toilet paper in his ensuite bathroom. Pictures later shown to the jury showed a crucifix above his bed and black furnishings.The woman told how they had consensual vaginal sex but that she did not enjoy the experience, saying: “It felt very awkward. It didn’t matter who I was, and I just sort of wanted it to be over.”Then Brand anally raped the woman, she told police. “He didn’t give me a warning, he didn’t ask,” she said. “I don’t know how long it took for me between it going on and me asking him to stop. I don’t think it was very long. I felt like I couldn’t speak or breathe, the amount of pain.”She alleged she begged him to stop, at first really quietly and then more loudly, but Brand continued.She said he looked “absolutely fucking horrified” after the alleged attack, adding: “I thought he was going to say sorry … but actually what he said was: ‘You need to clear up the mess you’ve made.’”She said one of Brand’s aides later asked her to leave because the comedian had a gig.“The way I would describe that event to people after was that it was traumatic and that he hurt me and harmed me. And when I asked him to stop, he didn’t,” she said.She told the court she had gone to a sexual health clinic afterwards because she feared she had HIV, and she became unwell and anxious.“In the years that followed, if I spoke to people about it, it was was very much laced with ‘I shouldn’t have gone’, and I think I tortured myself because I think it was one of the most painful experiences I’d gone through.”Earlier on Tuesday, two women who have separately accused Brand of sexually assaulting them at work in front of his entourage gave evidence from behind a screen.The first woman said Brand laughed after “mauling” her by squeezing her breasts and kissing her sloppily while she was working at a radio station in 2004 or 2005.She told the court he “overpowered her with such strength” during the “violent” and “frenzied” attack that took place in the middle of her work day.She said she had “buried” the assault because there was such a culture of fear in the media in the 2000s and Brand was a “big star”.The second woman, who worked at Channel 4, said she was “repulsed” when Brand placed his head in her lap during a filming project after she was asked to give him a massage.She said Brand was with two men – named in court as Jack Bayles and Gareth Roy – during the alleged assault in 2009, which she reported to her line manager.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Baby who died from meningitis may have been saved if tested sooner, inquest finds | NHS | The Guardian
description: Five-month-old Esta High died at Leeds General Infirmary in November 2023 after doctors put her symptoms down to Covid-19
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Five-month-old Esta High died at Leeds General Infirmary in November 2023 after doctors put her symptoms down to Covid-19
Content: Baby Esta High with her mother Lynsey Carr.Photograph: Family Handout/PAView image in fullscreenBaby Esta High with her mother Lynsey Carr.Photograph: Family Handout/PANHSBaby who died from meningitis may have been saved if tested sooner, inquest findsFive-month-old Esta High died at Leeds General Infirmary in November 2023 after doctors put her symptoms down to Covid-19Hannah Al-Othman, North of England CorrespondentTue 20 Oct 2026 13.37 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 14.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA baby girl who died from meningitis may have been saved if doctors had tested her for the infection sooner, rather than putting her symptoms down to Covid, an inquest jury has found.Five-month-old Esta High died atLeedsGeneral Infirmary in November 2023, days after she was taken into the emergency department with a high temperature and vomiting.She had tested positive for coronavirus, and so opportunities were missed when doctors stuck with a diagnosis of Covid, the inquest found.Esta died from streptococcus pneumoniae meningitis, and her parents Lynsey Carr and Leon High told the inquest that doctors had missed vital chances to test for a bacterial infection and start vital antibiotic treatment.Carr told the inquest, at Wakefield coroner’s court, that their concerns were ignored until it was too late.On Tuesday, an inquest jury of five women and six men concluded: “Esta died of natural causes which was contributed to by neglect. Had Esta received required care, based on the balance of probabilities, it would have probably saved or prolonged her life.”Carr said she and her partner had refused advice from doctors to take Esta home, as she would not stop vomiting and had a temperature of over 40C.She said her daughter developed a rash and her arm started shaking, which she feared was a seizure. She told the jury “we were extremely worried” and “kept asking for help”, but “staff were rude and don’t listen to our concerns”.View image in fullscreenEsta High’s parents Leon High and Lynsey Carr as they listen to their solicitor reading their statement outside Wakefield coroners court.Photograph: Dave Higgens/PACarr told the inquest that the family, from Leeds, were put into a side room at the hospital’s children’s assessment and treatment (CAT) unit, adding that she believed staff were more concerned with isolating Esta due to the Covid risk than listening to her parents.She described Esta’s time on the CAT unit as “15 hours that were filled with missed opportunities”.By late afternoon on 2 November, Esta was unresponsive, and the jury heard how scans and other tests showed evidence of meningoencephalitis and streptococcus pneumoniae.She was taken to intensive care and attempts were made to save her life, but she died on 6 November.“Unfortunately, as our daughter had been left untreated for 55 hours, it was too late to save our darling girl,” Carr told the inquest, describing her daughter as “bright, beautiful and perfect from the first moment”.In a statement read by her solicitor outside court on Tuesday, Carr said: “Making the decision on the advice of the intensive care staff to withdraw Esta’s life support broke us. Esta passed away lying between me and Leon – something no parent should ever have to go through.“We felt so blessed that Esta was our daughter, and for her to be taken away so cruelly is something we’ll never get over.”She added: “Parents know their children better than anyone, and when they say something isn’t right they need to be listened to and taken seriously.”Solicitor Joe Haley, of Irwin Mitchell, said: “It’s now vital that lessons are learned to help improve patient safety and prevent others from going through the terrible suffering Esta’s family has endured.”Dr Elizabeth Garthwaite, the chief medical officer at Leeds teaching hospitalsNHStrust, said: “We are deeply sorry that we failed Esta and her family, and offer our sincere and heartfelt condolences to Lynsey and Leon following the tragic death of their daughter.”She added: “We recognise that serious failures occurred in the care provided to Esta and that these failures had devastating consequences.“We take the concerns raised by the coroner extremely seriously and will carefully consider the report’s findings and recommendations.“We are committed to responding openly and fully, and to taking any further action necessary to improve patient safety.”Explore more on these topicsNHSLeedsHealthnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ll make you famous’: court hears recording of Tommy Robinson threat to Daily Mail editor | UK news | The Guardian
description: Jurors in harassment trial told reporters who had written about far-right activist feared ‘vigilante attack’
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Jurors in harassment trial told reporters who had written about far-right activist feared ‘vigilante attack’
Content: Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, arrives at Southwark crown court, London on Tuesday.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAView image in fullscreenTommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, arrives at Southwark crown court, London on Tuesday.Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAUK news‘I’ll make you famous’: court hears recording of Tommy Robinson threat to Daily Mail editorJurors in harassment trial told reporters who had written about far-right activist feared ‘vigilante attack’Ben QuinnTue 20 Oct 2026 13.16 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 16.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTommy Robinson told the Daily Mail’s editor he would make the paper’s journalists and their families “famous”, the harassment trial of the far-right activist has been told.The threat was made in a voicemail message left on the phone of Ted Verity as Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, allegedly waged a campaign of harassment against journalists from the newspaper.One of them was scared to go to their own house and left in fear of a potential “vigilante attack”, the trial was told on Tuesday. Another said they feared Robinson’s followers would “seek revenge” on them after reporting on his activities after the 2024 Southport killings and accusations he influenced subsequent riots.Jurors at Southwark crown court were played a recording of the message Robinson left on Verity’s phone in August 2024, saying: “I’ve already located every fucking one of you. I’ve got pictures of everyone here that can go in my story.”“I’m not threatening you with violence or anything like that. What I’m promising you is I’ll make you famous and your families because that’s what you’ve done to me.”He asked Verity to get in contact, saying that he was prepared to “come knocking”. Robinson said: “Now I know you wasn’t in your house yesterday … I don’t want to do it so please make sure you answer your phone so we can chat.”Robinson, 43, is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence in 2024 to two journalists who were working for the Mail, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber. He denies the charges.A recording of Young responding to Robinson’s call after the journalists had tracked him down to Cyprus was also played to Southwark crown court.View image in fullscreenTommy Robinson on his way into court.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockThe court heard that Young’s address had been published online by an anonymous X account and unknown men started appearing outside his home and that of another journalist working with him.“My main concern was that while he may not physically harm me, he had 800,000 followers on X at the time who might have been tempted to seek revenge on me or my home or my family for what I had written,” Young said in a statement read out in court.Robinson, who attended court with a large number of supporters, was said to have become enraged after the Mail published a story about him with the headline “Stoking race riots from his sunbed”.In another witness statement read to the court, Young’s daughter said that after Robinson’s X account posted pictures of her mother and sister with their faces cropped out, they felt “very worried about our safety”.She described watching a video of Robinson saying he had photos of the wives and daughters of “the journalists involved in the article”. She also told of seeing a “lone male” waiting in a vehicle parked outside the family home and seemingly taking pictures of her with his phone.Dirnhuber said it was the Mail’s view that Robinson was working in Cyprus, since posting on X was part of how he made money, and so they felt they could legitimately report on his activity. They did not publish any identifiable images of his children.Dirnhuber and his partner had to leave their home address after Robinson shared images of the journalist online and allegedly messaged him photographs of an unknown woman, the court was told.Dirnhuber said he felt he would be “looking over my shoulder for a long time”, adding: “I have the knowledge that Tommy Robinson knows my address and my last name is very identifiable.”The alleged harassment may have had an “adverse impact” on his “willingness” to cover certain stories, he added in his witness statement.Social media messages and direct messages sent to journalists by anonymous accounts and apparent followers of Robinson after statements by him on his X account were also read out in court. They ranged from comments about their appearance to more direct messages such as an email to Dirnhuber which said he would have cause to “regret when you are in hospital”.The trial opened on Monday, with prosecutor Ben Holt saying the case was about Robinson’s reaction to what he perceived to be “an unnecessary intrusion into his holiday”. Journalists and their family members had to flee their homes after “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics” were deployed against them, Holt said.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Florida kills 77-year-old man in state’s 18th execution of year | Florida | The Guardian
description: Vietnam veteran William Reaves executed by lethal injection despite letter from fellow veterans urging halt
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Vietnam veteran William Reaves executed by lethal injection despite letter from fellow veterans urging halt
Content: Clouds hover over the entrance of the Florida state prison in Starke.Photograph: Curt Anderson/APView image in fullscreenClouds hover over the entrance of the Florida state prison in Starke.Photograph: Curt Anderson/APFloridaFlorida kills 77-year-old man in state’s 18th execution of yearVietnam veteran William Reaves executed by lethal injection despite letter from fellow veterans urging haltAssociated PressTue 20 Oct 2026 19.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlorida carried out its 18th execution of the year on Tuesday under Republican governor Ron DeSantis’s aggressive use of the death penalty in his final term.William Reaves, 77, was pronounced dead at 6.12pm following a three-drug injection at Florida state prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1986 shooting death of Indian River county deputy Richard Raczkowski.The death chamber curtain went up promptly at the 6pm execution time, and Reaves was already strapped to a gurney with an IV in his arm. Asked if he had any last statement, he said: “No, I do not.”The injection began immediately after that. About 30 seconds later, Reaves took several big breaths and then stopped moving. After a few minutes, the team warden shook Reaves’ shoulders and yelled his name, but there was no response.A medic was called into the chamber a short time later to check for a heartbeat or any other signs of life, and Reaves was pronounced dead about a minute later.Reaves was the eighth Florida prisoner over the age of 70 put to death this year, highlighting the nation’s ageing death-row population as Florida continues to far outpace the rest of country in total executions.Last year, Florida set a state record with 19 executions in a single year and it would tie that mark if another execution is carried out next month as scheduled.DeSantis, who leaves office in January after two terms, has said his goal is to deliver justice to victims’ families who have waited decades for death sentences to be carried out.Raczkowski responded to a 911 call at a Vero Beach convenience store in September 1986, according to court records. Reaves later acknowledged he had placed the call from a payphone outside the store.While Raczkowski and Reaves spoke, a gun fell out of Reaves’ shorts, officials said. The two struggled over the weapon, and Reaves eventually regained control of it. Investigators said the deputy was trying to run away when Reaves shot him four times. The deputy later died from his wounds.Reaves was convicted and sentenced to death about a year after the shooting. But the Florida supreme court overturned the conviction because of a conflict of interest with the prosecutor and ordered a new trial. Reaves was convicted again and sentenced to death in 1992, and subsequent appeals were unsuccessful.The US supreme court on Tuesday afternoon rejected Reaves’ final appeal without comment.The Florida supreme court last week also rejected Reaves’ appeals to spare his life.One issue raised by his attorneys was Florida’s method of execution. All Florida executions are carried out via lethal injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the department of corrections.The court has previously upheld this lethal injection protocol against similar challenges. It differs from the single-drug injection used by states such as Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike was rushed to the hospital last month after surviving two lethal doses of pentobarbital.Defense attorneys also argued that the jurors who recommended the death penalty for Reaves were never told that the US Department of Veterans Affairs rated Reaves – an army veteran – as 100% disabled by post-traumatic stress disorder, which was caused by his service in the Vietnam war. More than 100 veterans sent DeSantis a letter Monday urging him to stop the execution.A total of 47 people were executed in the US in 2025. Besides leading all other states last year, Florida has carried out more than half the 32 total executions in the US so far this year. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.Jesse Guardado, 64, is next scheduled to die by injection in Florida on 5 Novemner. He was convicted of robbing and killing a woman in order to buy drugs in 2004.Explore more on these topicsFloridaCapital punishmentnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alabama governor commutes sentence of prisoner on death row | Alabama | The Guardian
description: Toforest Johnson’s death penalty reduced to life in prison without parole over doubts about his conviction
Author: Dani Anguiano
Headline: Toforest Johnson’s death penalty reduced to life in prison without parole over doubts about his conviction
Content: In this undated photo provided by the Johnson family, Toforest Johnson, right, poses for a photo with his son, Robby Foster.Photograph: Johnson Family/APView image in fullscreenIn this undated photo provided by the Johnson family, Toforest Johnson, right, poses for a photo with his son, Robby Foster.Photograph: Johnson Family/APAlabamaAlabama governor commutes sentence of prisoner on death rowToforest Johnson’s death penalty reduced to life in prison without parole over doubts about his convictionDani AnguianoTue 20 Oct 2026 19.18 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 19.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleToforest Johnson, anAlabamadeath row inmate, will no longer face execution after the state’s Republican governor commuted his sentence amid increasing doubts about his conviction.Kay Ivey, the Alabama governor, commuted Johnson’s sentence to life in prison without parole in the 1995 murder of William Hardy, a Jefferson county deputy sheriff. Johnson has long maintained he is innocent, and several former public officials, as well the local district attorney, have argued he should receive a new trial.“When presented with Mr Johnson’s case, I had concerns there was not enough direct evidence to carry out the most serious punishment – death,” Ivey said in a statement. “My decision is not a determination of innocence, but a recognition that the circumstances of this case justify commuting his death sentence to life imprisonment, without possibility of parole.”Ivey has overseen 27 executions during her time as governor, and commuted the death sentence of three death row inmates. Her decision on Tuesday comes shortly after another Republican governor,Ron DeSantis, cancelled a planned execution for the first time earlier this month.Ty Alper, one of Johnson’s attorneys, said they are grateful to Ivey for “diligently reviewing Toforest’s case and taking action to spare an innocent man from execution”. Alper said the fight to overturn the conviction will continue. The governor only has the power to commute a death sentence in such cases.“Toforest Johnson is innocent. Now it is up to the courts to overturn his conviction and grant him a new trial. We will keep fighting until he is home with his family,” Alper said.Johnson was sentenced to death in 1998.Hardy was shot twice in the head while working off-duty security at a hotel in 1995. Johnson has maintained he was on the other side of town at the time of the shooting. No physical evidence tied him to the killing, and more than 10 witnesses placed him on the other side of town during the killing.Danny Carr, the Jefferson county district attorney, has called for the conviction to be overturned, as has the original prosecutor. Carr has said that “the foundation of this conviction has disintegrated” and that there are multiple reasons to doubt the key prosecution witness.The witness at Johnson’s 1998 trial testified that, while eavesdropping on a phone call, she heard a man she believed was Johnson admitting to the crime. She was paid $5,000 in 2001 for her testimony, and Johnson’s lawyers argue that the state withheld evidence of monetary motivation for the testimony.There has been a years-long legal effort to win a new trial in the case that has garnered national attention, including support from Kim Kardashian, and was the subject of a podcast. Carr wrote in a 2024 court filing that the “evidence in this case has unraveled over 20 years”.Former judges and prosecutors have joined the effort seeking a new trial for Johnson. Bill Baxley, a former Alabama attorney general, former state chief justices Sonny Hornsby and Drayton Nabers, and several former judges and prosecutors have submitted briefs or written editorials supporting a new trial.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsAlabamaUS prisonsUS justice systemnewsShareReuse this content

title: ADL condemns Trump’s antisemitic slur but fails to mention him by name | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Anti-Defamation League post decries ‘shylock’ slur but does not explain that president used it at Kansas rally on Monday
Author: Robert Mackey
Headline: Anti-Defamation League post decries ‘shylock’ slur but does not explain that president used it at Kansas rally on Monday
Content: Trump at the rally in Park City, Kansas, on Monday night.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump at the rally in Park City, Kansas, on Monday night.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpADL condemns Trump’s antisemitic slur but fails to mention him by nameAnti-Defamation League post decries ‘shylock’ slur but does not explain that president used it at Kansas rally on MondayRobert MackeyTue 20 Oct 2026 19.06 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 19.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Anti-Defamation League (ADL) denounced the use of the term “shylock” as antisemitic on Tuesday, without explaining that the slur had been used a day earlier byDonald Trumpin a speech in Kansas.Trump used the slur during a Monday night rally in support of Republican senator Roger Marshall, who is locked in a closer-than-expected re-election fight against Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton. Marshall, a doctor, as beencriticized for filing lawsuitsagainst more than 700 patients with outstanding bills, leading to 18 of them being arrested.Trump said Marshall’s critics, by highlighting the patient lawsuits in campaign ads, “made it like, oh, he was some kind of a shylock-type guy”.Trump alsofalsely claimedMarshall was “mandated by law” to “go after those people”.The ADL’s brief social media post made no mention of Trump at all. The organization, founded to combat antisemitism, offered no explanation as to why it found it necessary to explain that anyone equating an avaricious person toShylock, the villainous Jewish moneylender in Shakespeare’s Merchant of Venice, is using an antisemitic trope.“The term ‘Shylock’ is rooted in a longstanding antisemitic stereotype,” the ADLposted on Xbut not its other social media accounts. “Regardless of intent, its use can reinforce harmful tropes about Jews and normalize language that has long been used to target the Jewish community.”Critics who accuse the ADL of using accusations of antisemitism selectively, to attack people who are critical of Israel, suggested that the Jewish American civil rights group was going easy on Trump because of his support for Israel.Trump’s use of the slur came just a day after he hadendorsed Israel prime ministerBenjamin Netanyahu ahead of the country’s elections.Matt Duss, a former foreign police adviser to senator Bernie Sanders, the most prominent Jewish American politician, responded to the ADL’s failure to mention Trump by suggesting its president would have been more direct had someone else used the slur.“If a Democrat said it, [ADL CEO] Jonathan Greenblatt would be knocking people over to get in front of a camera to condemn them by name, but it was Trump, so it’s just a general public service announcement,”Duss wrote.In 2014, after then vice-president Joe Biden described people who take financial advantage of American service members as “shylocks”, the Anti-Defamation League’s national director accepted his apology and called the remarks “a teachable moment”.Trump previously used the slur during a 2025 rally in Iowa. The US president told supporters that eliminating the taxes on inherited family farms would save farmers from “going to the banks and borrowing from, in some cases a fine banker, and in some cases shylocks and bad people”.The day after that Iowa rally, the ADL called the president’s use of the term “very troubling and irresponsible”, but Trump claimed ignorance when he was asked by a reporter if he had intended to use the word “shylocks” to refer to Jews.“No, I’ve never heard it that way,”Trump replied then. “To me, a shylock is somebody that’s a, uh, a moneylender at high rates. I’ve never heard it that way. You view it differently than me. I’ve never heard that.”Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS politicsKansasDemocratsAntisemitismnewsShareReuse this content

title: United Airlines CEO faces rightwing backlash after calling for US wealth tax | United Airlines | The Guardian
description: Scott Kirby says wealth inequality is a ‘danger to society’ and calls for inheritance tax in recent interview
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Scott Kirby says wealth inequality is a ‘danger to society’ and calls for inheritance tax in recent interview
Content: Scott Kirby, the CEO of United Airlines, testifies before the Senate on Capitol Hill, on 15 December 2021, in Washington.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/APView image in fullscreenScott Kirby, the CEO of United Airlines, testifies before the Senate on Capitol Hill, on 15 December 2021, in Washington.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/APUnited AirlinesUnited Airlines CEO faces rightwing backlash after calling for US wealth taxScott Kirby says wealth inequality is a ‘danger to society’ and calls for inheritance tax in recent interviewGaya GuptaTue 20 Oct 2026 16.06 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 16.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScott Kirby, the CEO ofUnited Airlines, is under scrutiny from conservative politicians and commentators for saying wealth inequality is a “danger to society” and calling for a national wealth and inheritance tax in a recent interview.Talking to theNew York Times, Kirby was asked about the growing public distrust of CEOs and whether he felt any responsibility to quell that distrust.“We should have a national wealth tax – it won’t work by state because people will just move,” he said. “And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them.”In response, headlines fromFox Businessand theNew York Postdecried that Kirby made $32m in 2025. In response to Kirby’s comments, Glenn Beck, a former Fox News host, and other users on Xcalled fora boycott of United Airlines. Jeff Landry, Louisiana’s governor, said the statement was “audacious”.“How audacious from a guy that didn’t even build @united and makes $32 million a year,” hewroteon X, adding a link to a government website to donate money to the government. “Better yet, he should distribute his salary to the employees at the bottom of the ladder @united!”“Let’s see you step up and place your money where your mouth is!” Landry added.The comment comes just two weeks before voters in California will decide on a so-called “billionaire’s tax”, which would put a 5% tax on the state’s billionaires, that the wealthy have beenspending millionsfighting against.Kirby was also asked about the rising cost of flying and said that high prices this year were being compared to the “artificial low” prices from the pandemic, which largely halted travel and highly disrupted the airline industry.“We have to charge enough that it covers the cost of flying, and it’s expensive to fly airplanes,” he said.When asked about the $70 passengers must pay to sit in an aisle or window seat if they aren’t a frequent flyer with United, Kirby responded that “the way to give everyone what they want is to charge for the services and products that those customers want,” adding: “There are customers that pay more that get more.”Kirby also maintained that fares were still lower than in 2019 after adjusting for inflation. According to data from the labor department, the index for airline fares increased by about 20% from September 2019 to September 2026, while overall consumer prices increased by 31%.Explore more on these topicsUnited AirlinesRepublicansThe super-richAirline industryUS taxationAir transportnewsShareReuse this content

title: US judge dismisses sexual abuse lawsuit from Sam Altman’s sister | Sam Altman | The Guardian
description: Ann Altman, the Open AI CEO’s sister, accused her brother of repeatedly sexually abusing her over two decades ago
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ann Altman, the Open AI CEO’s sister, accused her brother of repeatedly sexually abusing her over two decades ago
Content: Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, speaks at the UN headquarters in New York on 23 September 2026.Photograph: Lev Radin/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, speaks at the UN headquarters in New York on 23 September 2026.Photograph: Lev Radin/ShutterstockSam AltmanUS judge dismisses sexual abuse lawsuit from Sam Altman’s sisterAnn Altman, the Open AI CEO’s sister, accused her brother of repeatedly sexually abusing her over two decades agoReutersTue 20 Oct 2026 11.34 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 11.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA judge dismissed a lawsuit filed by Sam Altman’s sister against him on Tuesday. Ann Altman accused the OpenAI CEO of repeatedly sexually abusing her more than two decades ago, which he has denied.In dismissing Ann Altman’s ⁠lawsuit, the US district judge Zachary Bluestone wrote that she had refused to appear for an independent medical examination despite warnings ⁠that failure to do so would result in the case’s dismissal.Laura Politi, ​a lawyer for Ann ‌Altman, did not immediately respond ‌to a request for comment. Santos Perez, a lawyer who previously ‌represented Ann Altman in the case but withdrew this month, said in a statement: “I am no longer authorized to comment on this case but I continue to believe in Annie.”Ann Altman brought her lawsuit ​in St Louis, Missouri, federal court in January 2025.Lawyers for Sam Altman did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Ann Altman accused her brother of sexually abusing and raping her between 1997 and 2006 at their family home in suburban Clayton, Missouri, starting when she was three ⁠and he was 12. She said the last acts of sexual ​abuse and ​rape occurred when Sam Altman ​was an adult. He is now 41.The Altman family ​has said Ann ‌Altman has mental ​health challenges and ​received financial support. Sam Altman has said she began accusing him on social media of sexual abuse after the family rejected her demands for more funds.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453 or visit their website for more resources and to report child abuse or DM for help. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. title: European air fares could rise by as much as 20% in 2027, Ryanair boss predicts | Airline industry | The Guardian
description: Conflict in Middle East is pushing jet fuel costs higher and many carriers are not hedged against such increases, Michael O’Leary says
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: Conflict in Middle East is pushing jet fuel costs higher and many carriers are not hedged against such increases, Michael O’Leary says
Content: Ryanair and many other European airlines had hedged their jet fuel requirements for 2026, O’Leary said.Photograph: Alexandros Avramidis/ReutersView image in fullscreenRyanair and many other European airlines had hedged their jet fuel requirements for 2026, O’Leary said.Photograph: Alexandros Avramidis/ReutersAirline industryEuropean air fares could rise by as much as 20% in 2027, Ryanair boss predictsConflict in Middle East is pushing jet fuel costs higher and many carriers are not hedged against such increases, Michael O’Leary saysJoanna PartridgeTue 20 Oct 2026 10.28 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 10.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRyanair’s chief executive has predicted a record increase in European air fares next year, as airlines grapple with fuel bills pushed higher by the Middle East conflict.Many carriers are not hedged against rising jet fuel costs, Michael O’Leary said, which he predicted would lead to airline bankruptcies and takeovers. He forecast these pressures would result in the price of plane tickets rising by as much as 20%.“You’re going to see air fares rise next year inEurope, I think by 10, 15, maybe 20%. You’re going to see ⁠the biggest increase in air fares, I would say, in history in Europe for the next 12 ​months,” O’Leary told a news conference ‌in Brussels.Jet fuel prices have soared in recent months, as the war on Iran has choked off fuel supplies. Jet fuel accounts for a large portion of carriers’ costs. The airlines body IATA previously predicted jet fuel prices would be70% higher across 2026– estimated toaverage $152 (£114) a barrel for the year, compared with $90 in 2025 – slashing airlines’ profits.Ryanair and many other European airlines had hedged their jet fuel requirements for 2026, O’Leary said, adding that Ryanair was 80% hedged at $67 a barrel at the time the Iran conflict began in late February.However, the boss of Europe’s largest airline said most European carriers, including Ryanair, do not have significant hedging in place from April 2027 onwards to protect them if oil prices remain high.“We’re 85% unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” O’Leary said.Ryanair’s hedging contract for 2027 covered 15% of its fuel costs at $85 a barrel, he added, whereas spot rates are currently hovering at about double that level.View image in fullscreenDuring his visit to Brussels, O’Leary announced he was cutting 20 of Ryanair’s routes and more than one million seats from Belgium from the airline’s winter schedule.Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/EPAEasyJet reported a £105m annual rise in fuel costs in July, adding it had hedged 62% of its fuel requirements for the first half of 2027 and 37% for the second half of the year. The airline announced in October it was cutting 700,000 seats from its winter schedule in an attempt to save fuel.During his visit to Brussels, O’Leary announced he was cutting 20 of Ryanair’s routes and more than one million seats from Belgium from the airline’s winter schedule, after the federal government’s decision to increase its aviation tax from €2 to €7 in January.O’Leary is the latest executive to warn of thedownbeat outlook for aviation. Industry leaders have said some carriers will struggle to survive the fuel price shock. Passenger surveys have shown travellers arebraced for higher faresand are prepared to spend more, but airlines do not know how long consumers will be able to afford pricier tickets.Explore more on these topicsAirline industryAir transportEuropeRyanaireasyJetUS-Israel war on IranMichael O'LearynewsShareReuse this content

title: Hollywood AI-listers: is the technology ready to rival flesh-and-blood film stars? | Movies | The Guardian
description: As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the corner
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the corner
Content: ‘Really, really scary’ … AI actor Tilly Norwood.Computer-generated: Particle6View image in fullscreen‘Really, really scary’ … AI actor Tilly Norwood.Computer-generated: Particle6Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.MoviesHollywood AI-listers: is the technology ready to rival flesh-and-blood film stars?As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the cornerPhil HoadTue 20 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 10.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Don’t fear the dead – and don’t fear me.” An exact facsimile of a youngVal Kilmer, not quite dead and not quite alive, utters that baiting line in the trailer for the new western As Deep as the Grave. Director Coerte Voorhees knows exactly what he is doing – this is an AI-created version of the late actor, approved by his family but bringing with it a heap of controversy about whether such technology could make flesh-and-blood thespians redundant.Not just yet, judging by theextended glimpse of the film released earlier this year: it looks like a thirtysomething Kilmer, if a robot version had been sent back to the 1920s American wilderness by Skynet and, as well as being strangely rigid, had forgotten to download his voice, let alone his signature air of spacey shrewdness. Kilmer’s estate signed off on it, citing his enthusiasm for new technology that expands storytelling, but surely he would have been dismayed by this freaky doppelganger.Many reacted with revulsion to last year’sunveiling of AI “starlet” Tilly Norwood. After her appearance in an introductory “comedy” sketch, Emily Blunt described her as “really, really scary” – underscoring the depth of feeling around the idea of synthetic performers supplanting real ones. What you might call the Norwood injunction – the feeling of a tech-driven agenda imposing something no one asked for – deepened with the announcement the AI-lister will be soon appear infeature-length film Misaligned.Tim Webber, the chief creative officer at British VFX powerhouse Framestore, is sceptical about whether fully AI-generated actors can ever capture the complexity of our inner lives. “AI models are trained on the surface of things – the pixels of internet images, if they’re image models. To get to the level where it’s a human performance, where there’s genuine emotion involved, is a long way further down,” he says. So AI acting, scraping the external texture of past performances, would seem to be the inverse of something like method acting – whose acolytes excavate their internal psyche and emotions in the interests of authenticity.Is it time to enter the Tillyverse? Seven things you need to know about AI ‘actor’ Tilly NorwoodRead moreBut AI acting is undeniably becoming more realistic. Higgsfield AI – one of many companies currently pushing the possibilities of AI video – recently claimed to have “eliminated” the uncanny valley: that nagging phoneysimilitude effect that has plagued even sophisticated recent CGI reincarnations, such as thede-aged Indiana Jones in The Dial of Destiny.Having released two full-length, entirely AI-generated features this year, Higgsfield’s content lead Adil Alimzhanov is bullish. This new frontier of completely AI-generated films is liberating for artists, he says, and shortcuts laborious Hollywood production structures. The two online-only releases –Hell Grind, a 95-minute action fantasy, and The Cully Hill Boys, a 115-minute Guy Ritchie-esque caper comedy – completed the equivalent of shooting and post-production in a fortnight and a month respectively (not counting time spent on the scripts). Despite actors’ qualms, the future can’t be resisted, says Alimzhanov, 23, who used his own face for Hell Grind’s protagonist. “We can’t fight new tools simply because they transform industries. If you draw a parallel with when cars first came out, if we’d fought that, everybody would still be riding horses today.”Hell Grind and The Cully Hill Boys are essentially extended ads for Higgsfield’s suite of AI content-creation tools. But they show swift progression on the AI acting front. In Hell Grind, released in May, the skate-rat characters only seem to be able to crank out a single emotion per 15-second shot (the limit of the Chinese video-AI model used, Seedance 2.0). The Cully Hill Boys, which came out three months later, is far more engaging, with enough convincing repartee and comic timing to qualify it as quite funny. Its lead trio of grime rappers on the lam are AI-generated likenesses of real-life streetball player Matt Kiatipis, MMA fighter Israel Adesanya and livestreamer N3on – testament to the gen Z, AI-native short-form creators Higgsfield aims to attract. Though there is something quaint about the idea of an “actor” in the age of AI. If bespoke characters can be generated for every film, why have an intermediary play a “role”?Written by a human being, Tim Planagan, The Cully Hill Boys was assembled in 30-second chunks, made possible by this summer’s release of Seedance 2.5. But prompting your way towards something dramatically convincing is labour-intensive. First, visual “assets” are created of the characters – detailed body-length shots and facial closeups that are used to establish continuity when fed into video-generation prompts. Then, using the assets as an anchor point, each 30-second segment is defined in a 4,000-word prompt (itself partly generated by an LLM) defining the key parameters: action, camera movement, lighting and, of course, the emotions on display.
