title: US bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agencies | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Use of tools ‘may result in the transfer of sensitive data’ to China, defense department says
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Use of tools ‘may result in the transfer of sensitive data’ to China, defense department says
Content: The smartphone app DeepSeek.Photograph: Andy Wong/APView image in fullscreenThe smartphone app DeepSeek.Photograph: Andy Wong/APTrump administrationUS bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agenciesUse of tools ‘may result in the transfer of sensitive data’ to China, defense department saysAgence France-PresseTue 20 Oct 2026 08.33 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 09.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUSgovernment on Monday ordered its agencies to stop using artificial intelligence (AI) tools from the Chinese startupDeepSeek, as the countries race for dominance in the fast-moving sector.A notice from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced the ban on products developed byDeepSeek– and tools created using DeepSeek by third parties – saying they must be removed from IT devices.The DHS can issue direction to civilian agencies but not the military or intelligence services. The US defense department did not respond to an AFP request for comment.“DeepSeek’s models present multiple threat vectors,” said a document attached to Monday’s notice.Use of DeepSeek AI tools “may result in the transfer of sensitive data to [China] if used by US government employees or vendors”, the department warned.Its servers are located in China, where the legal system permits the government “extensive authority” to access private company infrastructure, it said.DeepSeek has been contacted for comment.One of China’s top AI labs, DeepSeek shook up the industry in January 2025 with a low-cost, high-performance chatbot, challenging assumptions of US dominance.The firm released a long-awaited new model, V4, in April, and earlier in October updated a faster, more lightweight version of V4.The US has accused DeepSeek and other top Chinese AI firms of systematically stealing the capabilities of cutting-edge models developed by American rivals.Despite their fierce competition in the field, when their leaders Xi Jinping and Donald Trump met at the White House in September, China and the USagreedto set up a “communication channel” for AI incidents.The topic is expected to arise again at a meeting between Xi and Trump at a summit scheduled for November in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationDeepSeekUS politicsAI (artificial intelligence)ChinanewsShareReuse this content

title: Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked | Google | The Guardian
description: Great hardware let down by software flaws on these pricey machines that combine ChromeOS with Android
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Great hardware let down by software flaws on these pricey machines that combine ChromeOS with Android
Content: The new Googlebooks are premium laptops let down by underdeveloped software.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe new Googlebooks are premium laptops let down by underdeveloped software.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.GoogleReviewGooglebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbakedGreat hardware let down by software flaws on these pricey machines that combine ChromeOS with AndroidSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorTue 20 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGoogle’s attempt to create a new type of laptop to compete with Windows and macOS machines is finally here, combining the best of ChromeOS andAndroidinto the new Googlebook. With advanced links to Android phones and the best of Google built in, can these Googlebooks really compete with a MacBook Air or Surface Laptop? I took two for a spin to find out.For years, Chromebooks have been the boss of budget laptops, but Googlebooks take a different, far more premium approach. Made by a range of traditional PC makers, including Acer, Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, they start at£999(€1,099/$899/A$2,299) – a far cry from the £160 Chromebooks.WhileGoogledoes not make these machines directly, it has set strict hardware quality standards that the laptops must reach. That includes backlit keyboards, haptic trackpads, fingerprint readers, crisp touchscreens, decent speakers and modern fast chips with at least 16GB of RAM.It is a list of specs you should expect with a premium Windows PC, but those start at a much higher price,primarily thanks to RAMageddon.View image in fullscreenThe two Intel Core Ultra Series 3-powered Googlebooks on test: the Acer Googlebook 14 (left) and the Asus Googlebook 14 (right).Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianAs such, theAcer Googlebook 14and theAsus Googlebook 14I’ve been testing have excellent hardware with satisfying keyboards, great trackpads and quality screens.The Acer is a convertible that allows the screen to fold over the back of the device turning into a tablet of sorts. It is 1.14kg and 13.9mm thick, with a glossy 14in 3K OLED screen and a smooth aluminium-magnesium body, costing£999.99.The Asus is a traditional laptop with a matt 14in 3K OLED screen and a magnesium-alloy body that weighs just 0.99kg and is 11mm thick, costing£1,199.99.Googlebook OSView image in fullscreenWith an app drawer, widgets and a taskbar at the bottom, Googlebook OS looks a lot like ChromeOS and Windows.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianTop quality hardware aside, anyone familiar with a Chromebook would be forgiven for thinking it wasChromeOSrunning on these machines. It has the familiar taskbar at the bottom, Chrome-based web apps and access to Android apps.But the software is essentially Android underneath, which means getting it up and running is just like setting up an Android phone: scan the QR code with your phone, enter a passcode and transfer your apps and accounts. It is all done and dusted in about four minutes, which is faster than setting up a modern Windows 11 machine even if you know all the shortcuts.Access to the full gamut of Android apps is the Googlebook’s biggest strength and its greatest weakness. Practically any app you have on your phone can be installed and run on the laptop. But almost all those phone apps are just that, mobile versions, with most not even aware that they are not installed on a phone.Those that have at least some tailoring to the laptop form come in a few different types, categorised by Google broadly under “compatible with desktop”, which means they should support mouse and keyboard controls; “optimised for desktop”, which means they should scale properly to the laptop’s display; and “made for desktop”, which are a handful of Android apps redesigned with the laptop in mind.Only the last category really seems to make any difference to the quality of the app, and even then most of them are still not of the same calibre as their equivalents found on Windows or macOS.View image in fullscreenGoogle Calendar can only show one account at a time, which means my schedule looks free lacking any of my work meetings.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianEven Google’s apps are a mixed bag. Google Calendar can only show one account at any one time, so you can’t see your personal, work and shared calendars on one screen like you can on Android.Google Docs starts as its own app, but when you actually open a document it just becomes anotherChromewindow hidden behind the Chrome logo on the task bar, not the Docs logo.The Files app shows your Google Drive files, but you can’t pin locations to the side bar to quickly access your commonly used folders, making it a time-consuming dig through endless folders to find things each time.Even the Chrome browser is not quite up to par with its Windows or macOS counterpart, lacking features such as split-screen tabs, the auto-hiding vertical tab bar or the ability to have multiple profiles, such as a personal and work account.Google has an app-gap problem and one that will only be solved if developers are convinced Googlebook OS is going to take off and be worth spending time and money making better apps for.Bring your Android phone into your GooglebookView image in fullscreenYou can see you phone’s apps (left), cast them (centre) and view your phone’s files (right).Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe other big selling point is deep integration with your Android phone. Google calls this “better together”, which is a collection of features that mirror capabilities of iPhones with Macs or Microsoft’s Link to Windows.Some of the features are like magic. You can search the files on your phone straight from the Files app on the laptop without plugging it in, see your notifications from your phone, continue tasks on your laptop from your phone and even use apps cast from your phone.As useful as these features sound, many are not up to scratch. Streaming apps from your phone is so slow that I feel as though I can type entire sentences before they appear on screen in chat apps, and it is restricted to one app at a time. If you click on a synced notification from your phone, it will open in a cast app, even if you have the full app installed on your Googlebook. Even viewing files on your phone from the laptop is irritatingly slow.The only apps I’ve reliably managed to get to appear with the ability to continue from where I was are Google Docs and Chrome on the phone.It also took me two hours of troubleshooting to get an up-to-dateGoogle Pixel 11 Proto actually connect with the Googlebooks, despite using the phone to set them up in the first place.GeminiView image in fullscreenWiggle the cursor to invoke Gemini and select text or images to ask questions or perform tasks on them.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe other big selling point for Google is its Gemini integration into Googlebook OS. The Gemini app is just like it ison macOS and Windows. But it is the Magic Pointer feature, which appears when you wiggle the mouse to click or highlight something on your screen to send it to Gemini, that is the most novel.You can use it to get Gemini to summarise text, explain something, search for things or generally chat. But I often hit a road block, such as Gemini refusing to generate images or saying it cannot add a date into my calendar in the mode Magic Cursor opens, which oddly isn’t within the desktop Gemini app. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t, and it is simply not joined up.Magic Cue has been imported fromGoogle’s Pixel phones, which is meant to pop up with helpful information such as calendar availability or a location in maps when you highlight a date or a place in a chat or email. But unlike on a Pixel phone, I have yet to get it to successfully activate in two weeks of testing.Google’s super-charged voice dictation systemcalled Rambler, also from the recent Pixels, does at least work as described. Press the dictation key and just speak naturally. Rambler will condense your speech into concise sentences removing filler words and errors.VerdictGooglebooks are full of excellent ideas about how a modern laptop should work. The hardware of the Acer and Asus machines I’ve tested is top notch, but the software just isn’t ready for prime time.When it works it’s great, but it is filled with limitations that might be acceptable on a super-cheap laptop but never on a £1,000 premium machine.Chrome is not as good as it is on a Mac or Windows PC. Google’s various apps are generally better on an Android phone and the third-party app ecosystem is a mess of poorly optimised mobile apps. Even the best desktop-optimised Android apps pale by comparison to their counterparts on Windows or macOS.The Android phone-linking system should be the killer feature, but it is partly broken or simply not up to scratch. Even the Gemini integration is flakey.Most of the Google-specific issues and software bugs are eminently fixable. But the app gap will take serious time, effort and money to convince third-party developers to fix.Unless you want to spend at least £1,000 to be a beta tester, your money is better spent elsewhere for now.View image in fullscreenFull wireless integration of your phone into your laptop is a great idea, but Google has some work to do to get it right.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsGoogleAlphabetLaptopsAndroidChromeComputingreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Is this the beginning of the end of the AI stock market boom?  | Stock markets | The Guardian
description: After a wobble on the tech-heavy Nasdaq, some AI market observers think a reassessment of the potential value of various businesses may be under way
Author: Patrick Commins
Headline: After a wobble on the tech-heavy Nasdaq, some AI market observers think a reassessment of the potential value of various businesses may be under way
Content: Experts say recent market corrections may reflect investors taking a ‘more balanced approach’, rather than it being a sign the entirety of the AI market is at risk.Photograph: John Angelillo/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenExperts say recent market corrections may reflect investors taking a ‘more balanced approach’, rather than it being a sign the entirety of the AI market is at risk.Photograph: John Angelillo/UPI/ShutterstockStock marketsAnalysisIs this the beginning of the end of the AI stock market boom?Patrick ComminsAfter a wobble on the tech-heavy Nasdaq, some AI market observers think a reassessment of the potential value of various businesses may be under wayGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastMon 19 Oct 2026 22.29 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 02.19 EDTShareThe world is holding its breath as it waits to find out whether this year’s estimated $US1tn investment in artificial intelligence is resting on a castle made of sand.Last week, the Nasdaq 100 – an index of the 100 biggest non-financial stocks on the American tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange – dropped by 5.5%, triggeringthe usual angstthat the AI boom is about to go bust.The recent rotmay have started with the failure of Firmus, an Australian datacentre company, to list on the ASX.AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’Read moreThe multi-billion dollar initial public offering was, at one stage, on track to make Firmus worth more than Telstra – even before having delivered on its promised earnings.Thatproved to be a fever dreamof its founders and a wake-up call to investors in Australia and around the world to reconsider the potential value of similar businesses.Value of the Nasdaq technology index plotted out since Nov 2025If this is the beginning of the end of the AI boom, it is only the very beginning, and tech stocks bounced back in Wall Street trade on Monday night.Gerard Minack, of Minack Advisors, said his view was that investors were fundamentally overestimating the returns that AI providers will be able to deliver.“While I am becoming more confident that returns on AI investment will disappoint, I have no confidence calling the precise top of the AI market,” Minack said.Despite the recent wobbles, the Nasdaq 100 is still worth nearly three times more than at the start of 2023.On the S&P 500, meanwhile, tech titans Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia and Tesla now account for 35% of the American sharemarket index, up from 12% a decade ago.The total market capitalisation of the so called “magnificent seven” companies has increased by more than 50% in the past two years.Raisah Rasid, a Singapore-based global market strategist at JP Morgan Asset Management, said what she was seeing in the recent sell-off was “a valuation reset, rather than the market questioning the efficacy of AI itself”.“This is still a long-term, structural transformation trend,” Rasid said. “This is very different from the dotcom bubble.”Rasid sees two potentially more meaningful threats. First, that an open source AI model, potentially from China, could undermine the economics of AI and the hundreds of billions of dollars of investment – a concern shared by Minack.The second, said Rasid, is the risk that popular opposition gains a critical mass: for example, anger about datacentre developments or that AI will do more harm to workers and society than good.The imminent quarterly earnings season in the US will deliver the latest verdict on whether the AI companies are worth their extremely high valuations. But Minack said sharemarkets can continue to climb well after warning signs over earnings emerge.Sally Auld, NAB’s chief economist, agreed that last week’s pullback in valuations looked more like investors taking a breath rather than the entire trade running out of puff altogether.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“When you look back in time, every big new technology, from railroads to the internet, we always overbuild capacity. Why do we think this one will be any different?”“It suggests investors may be taking a more balanced approach. It doesn’t mean the whole thing is a disaster; there’s a reassessment under way.”The recent market action may also be evidence that investors are becoming more mindful of the risks associated with tech companies’ growing reliance on debt.Companies like Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Apple have gone on a borrowing binge to help pay for spending on datacentres and associated AI infrastructure. These American “hyperscalers” spent $US425bn in AI-related capital expenditure in 2025, Minack said, and are on track to invest $US800bn this year and over $US1.1tn in the next.Corporate bonds issued by these companies now account for nearly 10% of the global investment-grade credit market, from 0.5% at the end of 2024, according to the International Monetary Fund.The fast-growing financialisation of the AI story helps explain whythe IMF last weekput the bursting of the AI investment bubble at the top of a trio of risks that could threaten the global economy, alongside rapidly rising borrowing costs and the threat of a major cyber-attack.Another cause for concern in the AI market is the growing “circularity” of funding arrangements between companies – where, for example, a manufacturer agrees to help pay to build a datacentre in return for the centre owner buying its microchips.These circular financing deals are only as strong as their weakest link.“If the demand for AI is not there, then not only does the datacentre not get built, but also the chips don’t need to be made,” Auld said. “But that’s far more of an issue for the US than in Australia.”In Australia, money is pouring into datacentres to power the computing needs of the vaunted AI revolution. CBA economists have estimated there will be $150bn in datacentre investment in this country by 2030, and $260bn by the mid-2030s, creating echoes of the mining investment boom of the 2010s.The investment is meaningful, but is not a “major part” of Australia’s economy, Auld said.“We would not be at the epicentre of any AI bust.”Explore more on these topicsStock marketsTechnology sectorAI (artificial intelligence)analysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘Too big to not fail’: Google outage exposes UK reliance on a handful of cloud providers | Datacentres - UK | The Guardian
description: Our dependence on internet services of a few key tech companies leaves us vulnerable to cloud failures, bugs and more, experts say
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: Our dependence on internet services of a few key tech companies leaves us vulnerable to cloud failures, bugs and more, experts say
Content: A Google technician diagnoses an overheated CPU at a datacentre in Dalles, Oregon.Photograph: Google Handout/EPAView image in fullscreenA Google technician diagnoses an overheated CPU at a datacentre in Dalles, Oregon.Photograph: Google Handout/EPADatacentres - UK‘Too big to not fail’: Google outage exposes UK reliance on a handful of cloud providersOur dependence on internet services of a few key tech companies leaves us vulnerable to cloud failures, bugs and more, experts sayAisha DownTue 20 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt happened again. Apower outage hit a datacentre in London, and things cascaded from there: multiple banking services faltered, court hearings were put on hold and patients reported temporary glitches on the NHS app.The datacentre in question was in Google’s europe-west2-b zone, one of more than a dozen “zones” that the US search giant maintains in Europe to service its clients.The outages – which have affected, according to the website Downdetector, Royal Mail, Revolut, HSBC and Lloyds bank, among others, are so far not of the scale of a similar cascade this time last year, when Amazon Web Services went down for nearly half a day.That outage hit a far bigger node – Amazon’s us-east-1 – in a concentrated region of Virginia, which hosts the greatest density of datacentres on Earth. It saw cascading effects worldwide: taking out the Roblox game and Signal messaging app and causing smart mattresses worldwide to suddenly heat overnight and toast their occupants.It lasted about 15 hours.Today’s problems appeared to peak at about 9am, and by mid-afternoon were somewhat resolved, according to reports submitted to Downdetector. Because Google Cloud stores data and runs operations for a number of businesses, there were widespread knock-on effects – mostly confined to UK businesses.Revolut confirmed “a service disruption affecting multiple services”, but added that “all our customers’ money and data are safe”. Lloyd’s said its app was working, but “we understand some [people] are having issues with certain online services this morning”.HM Courts and Tribunal Service, which handles remote video hearings in courts across England and Wales, said it was “aware of an issue affecting Cloud Video Platform,” and was “working with our technology partners to restore service”.Like the far bigger outage last year, it’s a reminder of the physical infrastructure – often creaking and provisional – that underpins most of the virtual world.Michał “rysiek” Woźniak, an internet infrastructure expert, said the outages were a reminder of the increasing concentration of the internet and vital services on the infrastructure of a few key companies – the “hyperscalers”.“Hyperscalers have become too big to not fail. But worse, they’ve become so deeply ingrained into the very fabric of our digital lives that switching away from them seems unimaginable.”The Guardianhas reportedthat British police keep vital data on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, despite being apparently aware that this exposes sensitive information to US government insiders, hostile foreign actors and outages like today’s. Up to 60% of the UK government’s infrastructure ishostedon cloud services – mostly Amazon, Microsoft and Google.“I am sure Google’s engineers are doing everything they can to mitigate them, but it is unreasonable to have a handful of gigantic companies whose outages time and again cause public institutions or large swaths of the digital economy to stop working en masse,” said Woźniak.Last year’s AWS outage was later revealed to have been caused not by a power outage, but by a bug inautomation software. A separate outage was caused by an AI tool that Amazon hadadoptedafter laying off tens of thousands of staff last autumn.Woźniak pointed at anannouncementthis year from Google indicating that it was also embracing AI, with 75% of all new code “now AI-generated and approved by engineers”.“One can only wonder how that affects the reliability and quality of Google’s services. Multiple large outages at another hyperscaler, AWS, a year ago have been linked to internal AI tooling.”A Google spokesperson said: “We have resolved a disruption to Google Cloud services at a third-party facility in our europe-west2 cloud region due to a power event. Services have been restored. We will update ourpublic status dashboardwith an analysis of the incident.”Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - UKGooglefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Could this be a Deep Blue moment for the cryptic crossword? | Puzzles | The Guardian
description: A computer program has finally outdone humans at solving cryptic crosswords. Plus, more from around the puzzleverse
Author: Alan Evans
Headline: A computer program has finally outdone humans at solving cryptic crosswords. Plus, more from around the puzzleverse
Content: Garry Kasparov playing Deep Blue at chess in 1997.Photograph: Stan Honda/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGarry Kasparov playing Deep Blue at chess in 1997.Photograph: Stan Honda/AFP/Getty ImagesCluesletterPuzzlesCould this be a Deep Blue moment for the cryptic crossword?A computer program has finally outdone humans at solving cryptic crosswords. Plus, more from around the puzzleverseDon’t get Cluesletter, our weekly puzzles newsletter, delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereAlan EvansTue 20 Oct 2026 11.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 11.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the IBM supercomputer Deep Blue beat Garry Kasparov at chess in 1997, it was an early victory for artificial intelligence over the human mind, and the culmination of decades of attempts. Almost 30 years later, a computer program has finally outdone humans at solving cryptic crosswords.Earlier this month, a model called Darmok solved the final puzzle of the Times’s annual cryptic crossword competition about three minutes faster than Liam Hughes, 29, whobecame the contest’s youngest (human) winner.After Deep Blue’s victory, the New York Times’s puzzle editor, Will Shortz,set engineers a challenge. “Is the computer going to be able to solve the clues involving puns and wordplay? I don’t think so,” he wrote. “In a much more wide-ranging and, frankly, complex game like crosswords, we humans still rate just fine.”Less than a decade later, a computer named WebCrowbeat 75 human crosswordersat an AI conference, and by 2021 a program named Dr Fill“won” the American crossword puzzle tournament, the most prestigious of its type for American-style crosswords, which rely on a combination of general knowledge, allusion and double meanings.But cryptics are much trickier, and as recently as 2024 my colleagueAlan Connor was asking: “Will the cryptic crossword remain the last thing AI can’t conquer?”Dr Sid Chatterjee, a computer scientist at the University of Texas in Austin, thought not, and in 2025 set out to prove it. He began work on Darmok, named aftera Star Trek episodein which the crew attempt to converse with a species that speaks only in allegories – an experience akin to solving a cryptic.View image in fullscreenSid Chatterjee and Darmok after solving the final puzzle in the Times’s cryptic crossword championship.Darmok’s first tilt at the Times championship ended in failure when it gave up on the final puzzle after 18 minutes. Its triumph this year was partly as a result of successfully solving a clue that tripped up three of the five finalists, including 14-time champion Mark Goodliffe:double quotation markWolf trap missing its lowest crosspiece? (5)”The letters filled in as part of other clues gave the pattern S_A_F. Both SCARF and SNARF mean “to eat greedily” (synonyms for “wolf”) but the rest of the wordplay relied on a visual element.“Trap” indicates the synonym “SNARE”, and when the bottom line of the E is removed – “missing its lowest crosspiece” – it becomes an F, making SNARF the answer.While one might expect visual clues like these to be more difficult for an AI, Chatterjee said he couldn’t detect a pattern in the types of clues Darmok struggles most with. It does find puzzles by John Henderson (known to Guardian readers asEnigmatist) harder than most, though.If you’d like to challenge yourself against Darmok, it solvedthis Fed crosswordfrom last week in four minutes and 10 seconds. Good luck.Darmok is based on four AI models: Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Fable 5, GPT-5 and GPT-6 Astra. The solving is primarily done by the first two, with the others joining in if needed. Chatterjee attributed Darmok’s improvement this year to the extra power behind these frontier models, as well as some of his refinements, such as making Darmok wait until it had attempted all the clues before inserting answers.The next frontier for AI and cryptic crosswords – setting a satisfying puzzle – will be an even bigger jump. “It is a very, very difficult problem because you have got to make a sentence that parses both in normal English and in cryptic English smoothly, and those two grammars are very, very different,” said Chatterjee. “If [beating humans at cryptic crosswords] was the Mount Everest challenge, I call this next one the Olympus Mons challenge.”Clue of the weekdouble quotation markProportion of inspiration and perspiration? It’s roughly 45% and 42% (5)FromBluebird in the Independent. The answer, RATIO, is hidden in the clue twice, making up five of the 11 letters in “inspiration” – or roughly 45% – and five of the 12 letters in “perspiration” – roughly 42%.Readers’ cluing contestCongratulations toTony Kelly (Montano)for winning this week’s competition with his clue for the wordDEBUT:double quotation markKick-off leads to decisive early goal for PSG (5)Kick-off is the definition. “Leads to” indicates the first letters of decisive and early, ie DE, and “goal for PSG” refers to the football team Paris Saint-Germain, indicating BUT, the French word for goal.This week, as a nod to the word wrongly identified by solvers in the Times championship, we’d like you to come up with a clue for the wordSCARF. title: ‘It was so satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen’: the people sick of being spied on by their smart TV | Television | The Guardian
description: Is your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacy
Author: George Francis Lee
Headline: Is your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacy
Content: ‘It’s not intimidating, just increasingly enshittified’ … a user and their smart TV.Photograph: SimpleImages/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It’s not intimidating, just increasingly enshittified’ … a user and their smart TV.Photograph: SimpleImages/Getty ImagesTelevision‘It was so satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen’: the people sick of being spied on by their smart TVIs your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacyGeorge Francis LeeTue 20 Oct 2026 10.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 10.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Dan had had enough of his television, he threw a rock straight through the screen. The offence? His smart TV was downloading its third update in three days. “It drove me crazy with what seemed like daily software updates that never fixed anything and ‘features’ that never seemed to work,” says the 71-year-old from Illinois. “And of course, constantly trying to push me to subscribe to paid-for services when all I wanted to do was watch over-the-air TV, play a DVD or stream something from my computer.”Some may accuse Dan of being a luddite, but his master’s degree in computer science and decades of experience in telecommunications would suggest otherwise. “The tech is not intimidating,” he explains, “just increasinglyenshittified.”The first smart TVs entered the market in the late 2000s, when companies introduced operating systems, media players and apps to screens that were becoming wider and thinner. In recent years, the luxury status of smart TVs has waned and increasingly affordable options are widely available. Tom Parsons, TV and audiovisual editor at the electronics magazine What Hi-Fi?, explains that these cheaper models can struggle under more advanced features. “They’re not necessarily super-fast and responsive out of the box,” he says. “And then two, three, four years down the line, they can end up slowing down quite a lot under the weight of all that processing.”Dan is just one of a growing number of tech-savvy watchers wishing their TVs weren’t so smart. Erin McQuiston and Matthew Schroyer, a couple from Connecticut, share his smart-screen scepticism.View image in fullscreenIncreasingly hard to find … a dumb TV.Photograph: Svetlana Lazarenka/Alamy“I don’t think we’ve ever used [our TV] as anything other than just a giant display,” says McQuiston. “There was a period where we were running it through an Xbox. And that was a constant battle because that was constantly being updated and patched and then you’d have to redownload all the apps for it.”Meanwhile, Schroyer says his job as a software engineer has influenced his decision to “intentionally keep it very dumb” by keeping their TV disconnected from the internet. “A rule of the house is: don’t give things the wifi password,” he says. “It concerns me that folks increasingly have to be IT experts to get the bare minimum enjoyable experience out of this stuff.”Instead, the 41-year-old connects his screen to an Apple TV box as a streaming workaround, and cites privacy as well as “highly invasive” advertisements for doing so. “Our living room is not a billboard for sale,” he says.When asked how the couple might cope in a future where TVs may have mandatory internet, McQuiston says her husband is “handy enough to break every terms of service known to man and get in there and unsolder something to manually disconnect it”.For Helen Northmore, a 51-year-old from Wales who works in AI delivery for the UKHealthSecurity Agency, privacy is also a worry. Her grudge against smart screens began four years ago, when her faithful dumb TV broke without warning and she had to quickly find a replacement.“We had already decided that we didn’t want the smart functionality, but it became really clear that it was very hard to find one that didn’t have any,” she says. Northmore, whose partner works in cybersecurity, says the couple wanted to “keep control” over their devices, which cost them a premium. “We were willing to pay more. One of the boundaries in how we live our lives is we want to minimise the smart element. We don’t have smart speakers. We don’t enable or connect to the internet.”View image in fullscreen‘Our living room is not a billboard for sale’ … a smart TV aerial.Photograph: Zdenek Maly/AlamyToday, she watches entertainment through a Sky box connected to her dumb TV, and dreads that when her current telly breaks there won’t be any option but to get a smart model and offer up her data.More consumers are becoming worried about how their information is being used by manufacturers. “There are increasing privacy concerns around to what degree TVs are essentially scraping your data,” says Parsons. “TVs these days are full of sensors, including microphones, and that can make people nervous.”But according to Parsons, despite interest in “dumber” models from some buyers, most shoppers want their TVs to be catch-all entertainment systems. The result is that the dumb TV market is almost nonexistent. “You can buy cheap monitors for signage,” he says, “but from a features point of view, you wouldn’t get the same performance that you would from a consumer TV.”Paul, a public servant from Australia, knows just how hard finding a traditional TV can be. “When my last telly – a glorious 32-inch dumb TV – died recently, aged approximately 10 years old, I spent about three weeks scouring the city looking for something comparable. What I found is that they do not exist any more.”After much searching, Paul discovered a single 40-inch TV without any smart functionality in the back of a shop. “It had zero ways to connect to the internet – just a couple of plugs on the back for making it work with the aerial on the roof and my VHS player, and that was it.” He remembers that it “was very dusty and cost about 200 dollars. Naturally, we fell instantly in love.”“My friends all laugh at it when they come over,” he admits, “but secretly I know the joke is on them. My little telly doesn’t spy on me, and has a DVD player built in.”The punchline may eventually land on Paul, however. In September, the Australian government launched aconsultation into the future of the country’s free-to-air broadcasting, asking citizens for feedback on how TV should be accessed. One of the proposed scenarios would see traditional broadcast services cut in favour of streaming services and video on-demand apps.View image in fullscreen‘My little telly doesn’t spy on me’ … some users such as Paul are clinging hard to analogue.Photograph: Dmitriy Shironosov/AlamyIn the same month, the UK government released amedia green paperoutlining its plan to fully move away from digital terrestrial television to services provided over a broadband connection by 2034 at the earliest. Such a situation would mean viewers having to rely on broadcaster apps and streaming services.If a similar fate befell North America, James certainly wouldn’t care. He is originally from the US but now lives in British Columbia, Canada, and says traditional broadcast TV is “dead to him” and that he prefers to watch shows on streaming services or on YouTube. For the father and husband, privacy is a top priority.“No one expects an end-user licence agreement to include giving up autonomy,” he says. “Having my TV listen to any conversation and use that for monetary or any form of gain is above and beyond expectations on the loss of privacy.”In September, the YouTube channel Gamers Nexus releaseda two-hour investigationinto LG Electronics’ smart televisions, saying that the devices record audio – even when they are offline or powered down. The South Korean companydenied the allegations. In the fallout, some have taken measures to modify their smart TVs, regardless of brand or model. Some videos online show usersreplacing motherboards, cutting out Bluetooth and wifi modules and removing microphones from their TV remote controls.Amid the controversy, James read online advice that modifying a TV remote microphone was a simple procedure. So he surgically removed the sensor himself. “Removing the mic was literally as easy as using a [craft] knife to scrape it off the top,” he says, “and the remote continued to work fine.”James’s willingness to dissect his tech comes from fears for his children. “My kids are not teenagers and they have no agency to protect their private information,” he says. “Someone listening in on a TV gets to find out about my daughter’s first period without her knowing. And that is a level of invasion no one should have without explicit consent.”Frustration and controversies have sparked a DIY interest in opening up and neutering the black rectangles in our living rooms. Though the desire in the first place may lead consumers to ask themselves an important question: have our TVs become too smart for their own good?Gutting any piece of electronic equipment should be left to professionals. However, some may find that, for a complex problem, the simplest solutions are the most elegant. As Dan recalls: “It was enormously satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen.”Explore more on these topicsTelevisionPrivacyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Hollywood AI-listers: is the technology ready to rival flesh-and-blood film stars? | Movies | The Guardian
description: As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the corner
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the corner
Content: ‘Really, really scary’ … AI actor Tilly Norwood.Computer-generated: Particle6View image in fullscreen‘Really, really scary’ … AI actor Tilly Norwood.Computer-generated: Particle6Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.MoviesHollywood AI-listers: is the technology ready to rival flesh-and-blood film stars?As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the cornerPhil HoadTue 20 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 10.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Don’t fear the dead – and don’t fear me.” An exact facsimile of a youngVal Kilmer, not quite dead and not quite alive, utters that baiting line in the trailer for the new western As Deep as the Grave. Director Coerte Voorhees knows exactly what he is doing – this is an AI-created version of the late actor, approved by his family but bringing with it a heap of controversy about whether such technology could make flesh-and-blood thespians redundant.Not just yet, judging by theextended glimpse of the film released earlier this year: it looks like a thirtysomething Kilmer, if a robot version had been sent back to the 1920s American wilderness by Skynet and, as well as being strangely rigid, had forgotten to download his voice, let alone his signature air of spacey shrewdness. Kilmer’s estate signed off on it, citing his enthusiasm for new technology that expands storytelling, but surely he would have been dismayed by this freaky doppelganger.Many reacted with revulsion to last year’sunveiling of AI “starlet” Tilly Norwood. After her appearance in an introductory “comedy” sketch, Emily Blunt described her as “really, really scary” – underscoring the depth of feeling around the idea of synthetic performers supplanting real ones. What you might call the Norwood injunction – the feeling of a tech-driven agenda imposing something no one asked for – deepened with the announcement the AI-lister will be soon appear infeature-length film Misaligned.Tim Webber, the chief creative officer at British VFX powerhouse Framestore, is sceptical about whether fully AI-generated actors can ever capture the complexity of our inner lives. “AI models are trained on the surface of things – the pixels of internet images, if they’re image models. To get to the level where it’s a human performance, where there’s genuine emotion involved, is a long way further down,” he says. So AI acting, scraping the external texture of past performances, would seem to be the inverse of something like method acting – whose acolytes excavate their internal psyche and emotions in the interests of authenticity.Is it time to enter the Tillyverse? Seven things you need to know about AI ‘actor’ Tilly NorwoodRead moreBut AI acting is undeniably becoming more realistic. Higgsfield AI – one of many companies currently pushing the possibilities of AI video – recently claimed to have “eliminated” the uncanny valley: that nagging phoneysimilitude effect that has plagued even sophisticated recent CGI reincarnations, such as thede-aged Indiana Jones in The Dial of Destiny.Having released two full-length, entirely AI-generated features this year, Higgsfield’s content lead Adil Alimzhanov is bullish. This new frontier of completely AI-generated films is liberating for artists, he says, and shortcuts laborious Hollywood production structures. The two online-only releases –Hell Grind, a 95-minute action fantasy, and The Cully Hill Boys, a 115-minute Guy Ritchie-esque caper comedy – completed the equivalent of shooting and post-production in a fortnight and a month respectively (not counting time spent on the scripts). Despite actors’ qualms, the future can’t be resisted, says Alimzhanov, 23, who used his own face for Hell Grind’s protagonist. “We can’t fight new tools simply because they transform industries. If you draw a parallel with when cars first came out, if we’d fought that, everybody would still be riding horses today.”Hell Grind and The Cully Hill Boys are essentially extended ads for Higgsfield’s suite of AI content-creation tools. But they show swift progression on the AI acting front. In Hell Grind, released in May, the skate-rat characters only seem to be able to crank out a single emotion per 15-second shot (the limit of the Chinese video-AI model used, Seedance 2.0). The Cully Hill Boys, which came out three months later, is far more engaging, with enough convincing repartee and comic timing to qualify it as quite funny. Its lead trio of grime rappers on the lam are AI-generated likenesses of real-life streetball player Matt Kiatipis, MMA fighter Israel Adesanya and livestreamer N3on – testament to the gen Z, AI-native short-form creators Higgsfield aims to attract. Though there is something quaint about the idea of an “actor” in the age of AI. If bespoke characters can be generated for every film, why have an intermediary play a “role”?Written by a human being, Tim Planagan, The Cully Hill Boys was assembled in 30-second chunks, made possible by this summer’s release of Seedance 2.5. But prompting your way towards something dramatically convincing is labour-intensive. First, visual “assets” are created of the characters – detailed body-length shots and facial closeups that are used to establish continuity when fed into video-generation prompts. Then, using the assets as an anchor point, each 30-second segment is defined in a 4,000-word prompt (itself partly generated by an LLM) defining the key parameters: action, camera movement, lighting and, of course, the emotions on display. The prompts are revised and the scene regenerated until the uncanny valley is hopefully bridged.double quotation markIt becomes a case of treating the model like a marionette doll and tweaking individual stringsWhere, say, Klaus Kinski could summon torrents of rage by tapping into his personal demons, an AI programmer has to achieve the same effect in much more approximate ways. “An AI is not an actor, so how do you communicate the internal state of a character?” says Zack London, who asGossip Goblinmakes highly baroque AI-generated sci-fi shorts. “You can say: they look confused, or they say this in jest, or they say this sternly. But it’s such a broad stroke. The model will probably come out with a very over-the-top telenovela-type performance, or will just not understand.” At that point, it becomes a case of treating the model like a “marionette doll” and tweaking individual strings. “You could say: there’s a slight quiver on the left side of their lip, and then their gaze diverts slightly downwards, and they look up again and blink.”London chooses to keep a human ghost in the machine by first recording dialogue with real actors, around which he retro-fits the animation. He is candid about the shortcomings of the current prompting process, saying the results suit a certain type of film: “The acting is not going to be particularly subtle, like some grand Anthony Hopkins or Olivia Colman performance. It’s more like an old-school Terry Gilliam or Guy Ritchie performance, where the characters are larger than life.” But maybe that’s where the danger lies for actors: many blockbuster performances, meting out simple beats of easily comprehensible emotion, have a cut-and-paste quality – and are therefore susceptible to AI.Then again, a mundane magic still happens even on blockbuster sets. “Sometimes the most brilliant moment happens in the fraction of a second. And you can’t put your finger on why an actor gives a certain look,” saysTye Sheridan, the co-founder (in 2016) of Wonder Dynamics, an Autodesk company who developed the AI production tool Autodesk Flow Studio. He should know: he was the star of Steven Spielberg’s 2018 filmReady Player One, which itself patrolled the frontier between real and digital.View image in fullscreen‘You can’t put your finger on it’ … Tye Sheridan in Ready Player One.Photograph: courtesy of Warner Bros Pictures/APSheridan shares Higgsfield’s belief that AI-driven methods can democratise film-making. But he is adamant that performances should retain a human core.Flow Studiouses AI for an augmented and far cheaper version of motion capture, layering CG characters and environments on top of filmed footage. At Framestore, Webber is exploring similar AI tools that allow him to apply what he calls “digital makeup” to traditional performances, without the guesswork involved in generative prompts.He, London and Sheridan agree that this hybrid form of film-making still allows actors to make specific choices essential to authentic creation. “You have to ask, with these generative models: are they really designed to deliver legendary performances, or are they designed to cut to an average?” asks Sheridan. Alimzhanov, though, insists something akin to an actor’s internal process is achievable via AI. The prompting used on The Cully Hill Boys was different in one key regard: instead of replicating emotions by specifying the physical mechanics, the AI model generated sequences based on contextual input about what the characters were experiencing.These two camps of AI acting – technological and human-centric – are fighting the latest bout in the struggle between the forces that have shaped the craft: external v internal; reproducing v experiencing; Laurence Olivier telling Dustin Hoffman that, instead of staying awake for 72 hours, he should “try acting, dear boy”. But where Stanislavsky promoted the internal quest to revitalise acting, this could be the first time in the modern era when the formalist approach – the mannered reproduction of emotions – looks like the future.Opening the digital floodgates could lead toWilliam Gibson territory, where deathless virtual stars seduce the masses, as in his 1996 novel Idoru. But it’s still not clear whether the box office demand, and thus a true economic case, for AI cinema exists. And we’re yet to see a compelling script that crystallises the possibilities of the tech in story form, as The Matrix did for CGI. If we’re inundated with unloved AI abominations, the words of Val Kilmer in Tombstone, playing that icon of human mortality, Doc Holliday, will ring anew: “There’s just something about him. Something around the eyes reminds me of … me. I’m sure of it – I hate him.”Explore more on these topicsFilmAI (artificial intelligence)Val KilmerTilly Norwood (AI character)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Labor and the Coalition are poised to take a reckless gamble on AI. Haven’t they realised community support has collapsed? | Edward Santow and Sarah Sacher | The Guardian
description: Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand
Author: Edward Santow
Headline: Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand
Content: ‘The decisions being made now on datacentres and how we adopt AI could define our economy, environment and society for generations,’ write Edward Santow and Sarah Sacher.Photograph: James Ross/AAPView image in fullscreen‘The decisions being made now on datacentres and how we adopt AI could define our economy, environment and society for generations,’ write Edward Santow and Sarah Sacher.Photograph: James Ross/AAPOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Labor and the Coalition are poised to take a reckless gamble on AI. Haven’t they realised community support has collapsed?Edward Santowand Sarah SacherAustralian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at handGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastTue 20 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 19.08 EDTShareAustralia’s major political parties are edging towards rare consensus. Labor and theCoalitionincreasingly want to take a major bet on artificial intelligence. Yet, just as the parties are coming together, the Australian community is running the other way.Last year,only 30% of Australiansbelieved the benefits of AI outweighed the risks. In 2026, community trust in AI appears to be falling even further.It was an unusual step for our parliament to form a joint select committee on AI. It signalled that the decisions being made now on datacentres and how we adopt AI could define our economy, environment and society for generations.Calls to strengthen workplace privacy in Australia as employers turn to AI to track staffRead moreAs a fresh round of hearings starts this week, the committee members must confront the gulf between the politics of AI and the stark reality on the ground. Some parts of the business sector are urging us to prioritise innovation and AI adoption, which is often another way of saying: “Do a better job of selling the upside of AI.”Whether you’re an AI optimist or a sceptic, this is a terrible idea. Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and the other titans of Silicon Valley have a golden megaphone to spruik the benefits of their technology. Australians don’t want our elected representatives to do the same thing – especially when the technology is already bringing both opportunity and harm.This doesn’t mean being blind to the benefits of AI. On the contrary, Australia is among the highest users per capita of Anthropic’s Claude and other generative AI applications. But we must also be clear-eyed about potential risks. And, crucially, we don’t see a compelling response to our concerns from government or the AI companies themselves.Take the impact of AI on work. Our community is asking practical questions. How will AI impact our jobs and the jobs of our children? What is the government doing to ensure the AI systems used in Australian workplaces are safe?Our new report,Drawing the Line,lays out how AI is propelling the rise of harmful tech-enabled worker surveillance. Often workers are unaware of the extent to which they are being monitored – including through their work devices and phones, and via software such as Microsoft Teams.Unlike some of the hypothetical (and frankly terrifying) risks that the joint select committee on AI has already covered, such as AI-enabledbiological weaponsandengineered pandemics, this is happening today.‘Not our friends’: Victorian Coalition warns Advance’s ‘bizarre’ AI campaign may cost it majority governmentRead moreAustraliansupermarket workersare already being pushed to meet AI-generated productivity metrics that force them to work harder and faster under the threat of punitive repercussions – putting them at risk of injury and workplace accidents.Remote workersare already being subjected to intrusive surveillance software capable of watching everything they do on their screen – including audio recording conversations they have with their families.Rideshare driversare already being penalised for road conditions and customer complaints that are unrelated to their performance, which can result in their account being deactivated and days of work lost.Workers are being quietly crushed by commonplace AI-powered surveillance tools that have crept into our workplaces and home offices. And the impact is real. Think, for example, of the young woman who reported beingsexually harassedby a boss that required her to be on video at all times. Or warehouse workers driven tosuicidal ideationdue to relentless micromanagement by machine.Our workplace laws don’t protect workers from unreasonable surveillance. Nor do they give employers clarity about what types of monitoring are lawful.Unlike existential risks from AI, which are outside the Australian government’s direct control, this problem could be addressed through straightforward law reform.We urge the government to update the Fair Work Act to require any worker monitoring be “fair and reasonable”. This builds on the government’s commitment to require all personal information covered by the Privacy Act to be handled fairly and reasonably.Australian workersexpectthe government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand. This is not a hypothetical future risk – let’s address it now.Prof Edward Santow is co-director of the UTS Human Technology Institute and served as human rights commissioner from 2016-2021. Sarah Sacher is HTI’s senior responsible technology policy specialistExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionAustralian politicsLabor partyCoalitionLiberal partycommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m a chief technology officer. AI still needs your human expertise  | Madhu Shashanka | The Guardian
description: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment
Content: The people best suited for doing this new type of work aren’t computer programmers. They are the ones who know how the real work is done.Illustration: Guardian Design/Westend61/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe people best suited for doing this new type of work aren’t computer programmers. They are the ones who know how the real work is done.Illustration: Guardian Design/Westend61/Getty ImagesReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)I’m a chief technology officer. AI still needs your human expertiseMadhu ShashankaAI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgmentSupported byAbout this contentTue 20 Oct 2026 08.30 EDTShareAutonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according tothe Wall Street Journal.That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI.People expect AI to lead to fewer jobs in 34 of the 37 countries surveyed by thePew Research Center. In wealthy countries like the US, Australia and South Korea, about seven in 10 expect job losses over the next 20 years. And across countries, concern among young people is rising. While fears focus on job numbers, the bigger change will be what jobs become.The nature of human work will move towards judgment. Experts refer to AI as “jagged”, superhuman at certain tasks but weak at others, with no clear boundary between the two. AI rapidly improves where work can be automatically checked and examples are endless. But it’s shaky where no automated test can determine whether the answer is right. Even if AI is correct a majority of the time on a task, it often doesn’t tell you when it’s inaccurate. If you’ve used AI, you’ve probably experienced how it can be confidently wrong.Some of these errors will solve themselves as models get better. But jaggedness is a symptom of how these models learn. I see this often as a technology leader building with these systems.A smarter model still needs a right answer to learn from. When one gap is closed, it shows up somewhere else no one thought to check. But many business decisions don’t immediately have a clear right answer. Whether a choice is good depends on a future no one can see and data no one has. That’s where judgment comes in. So AI will keep mastering tasks that have checkable results but struggle where a person has to decide what a good outcome looks like.As a result, a new type of work is starting to appear. Someone tests whether the output of AI is correct based on real work, not just on benchmarks. Someone sets limits on what AI is allowed to do before it runs, so the worst mistakes are avoided. Someone runs and manages several agents the way a shift manager runs a crew. Picture an airport control tower. Radar and software track flight paths, with humans judging the few that matter to avoid collisions. No one is manually watching every screen. That would never scale.Setting AI’s limits is harder than it sounds. In a2026 study, after an agent was told to protect a secret, it destroyed its own email server, deleting every single email. It was given a goal, without any limits on what it could do. The researchers described it as the right values paired with terrible judgment. Deciding what is off limits and what a mistake would cost takes someone who knows the work and will answer for the result.Here is the good news for people worried about their own jobs. The people best suited for doing this new type of work aren’t computer programmers. They are the ones who know how the real work is done. Catching what a confident AI left out or got wrong takes someone who knows the complete answer. That knowledge is uncheckable, unwritten and takes the form of judgment honed over years of doing the task and watching it break.Ford recently learned the value of human expertise. In recent years, it leaned hard on automating its quality control, cutting thousands of jobs. But earlier this year, it had to rehire 350 veteran engineers to oversee the process and hunt for failure points before a part reached the factory floor. They brought the judgment of watching parts fail over years. With humans at the helm, Ford’s quality ranking then hit first among mainstream brands for the first time since 2010.But we are making a serious mistake with the jobs we’re eliminating due to AI: the entry-level, routine ones. That routine work is how judgment gets built over time. Junior employees work under the supervision of senior experts until their experience turns into instinct. AI eliminates the friction related to learning how to do the job. But the demand for judgment did not go away. We are just destroying the path to developing it.The real question is not whether machines will take over our work. It is whether we will have the people who can tell when the machines are wrong. Right now, we are automating the training ground where judgment is learned. If you have hard-earned expertise about anything, the next few years will only make you more valuable. And if you are just starting out, the old apprenticeship model will not hand it to you. You have to go and earn it, deliberately, on tasks the machines cannot yet judge.Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software companyExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedComputingJob lossescommentShareReuse this content

title: Americans, this is your chance to slap down the tech broligarchs | Rebecca Solnit | The Guardian
description: The midterms will be a referendum on the GOP’s alignment with tech overlords over the public they’re meant to serve
Author: Rebecca Solnit
Headline: The midterms will be a referendum on the GOP’s alignment with tech overlords over the public they’re meant to serve
Content: ‘Like the Trump administration, the tech overlords have proceeded on the assumption they can ignore or override the will of the people.’Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Like the Trump administration, the tech overlords have proceeded on the assumption they can ignore or override the will of the people.’Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersHow we winUS midterm elections 2026Americans, this is your chance to slap down the tech broligarchsRebecca SolnitThe midterms will be a referendum on the GOP’s alignment with tech overlords over the public they’re meant to serveTue 20 Oct 2026 15.16 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 15.17 EDTShareWelcome back to How We Win, a Guardian opinion series with leading thinkers, offering bold ideas for America’s political future. Last week,Robert Reichhighlightedthe link between corruption and affordability. Today’s edition was written by Guardian US columnistRebecca Solnit.Sign up for future editions here.“The world should accept some bad things happening,” Sam Altman, the head of OpenAI,saidrecently, “for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.” Like so many things tech oligarchs say, it’s incoherent, since Altman would like to deny the world and the people in it the agency to decide whether or not we should accept his bad things. Surveys show that most Americans would liketo pause AI; opposition to AI datacenters isa factor in many racesin the midterm elections. People are outraged and anxious about what tech hath wrought, mad enough to fight back in what is coming to seem like a human v machine battle.I’ve been a fan of the film Terminator 2forever, the one where a badass female protagonist leads the action-movie-style spectacular destruction of Skynet, the massive computer system that will otherwise go rogue and pit itself and a plethora of advanced weapons against the human race. We’re not in a film and we’re probably not going to solve the problems big tech creates through spectacular violence, although the guerrilla campaigns to take down, disable or destroy Flock cameras have some action-movie charms (wading through the bureaucratic process of getting cities to reject or take down the surveillance technology is probably more effective.)A few months ago, I was surprised to find myself using the term “beautiful hatred” to describe the nationwide revolt against datacenters, Flock cameras, AI, and tech corporations and the oligarchs (or broligarchs) they’ve spawned. It is beautiful because behind fierce opposition to a destructive force is something you’re trying to protect from destruction, something you care about, even love. Behind this revolt against big tech is concern about many things, from the climate to democracy to mental health and humanity itself.Like the Trump administration, the tech overlords have proceeded on the assumption they can ignore or override the will of the people. The will of the people is in the process of proving them wrong, at least to some extent, and the midterms will be, among other things, a referendum on the GOP’s alignment with predatory tech giants over the public they’re supposed to serve and, arguably, humanity itself. It’s sometimes said only a common enemy can unite a country, and in that sense Silicon Valley has provided something useful at last, because across the political spectrumpeople hate datacentersand are working to stop them. Datacenterwatch.orgreportsthat at least 142 activist groups across 24 states have organized to block datacenter construction and expansion.double quotation markIt’s sometimes said only a common enemy can unite a country, and in that sense Silicon Valley has provided something useful at lastOften the foregrounded concerns are about local issues – effects on land, water, electricity prices, noise – since datacenters offer a lot of negatives and, arguably, no real positives, not even more than a handful of local jobs. But behind that is beautiful hatred of the high-handed efforts to bludgeon communities into accepting something for which they’ll get little in return but trouble – and of AI itself. A nine-year-old I spend time with recently remarked: “I don’t trust AI,” more or less out of the blue, and I think she speaks for a lot of us. Never mind my nine-year-old; the pope is speaking up against it, too, saying in a recentsocial media post: “Algorithms lack the spark of humanity” and calling on us to “safeguard our humanity” against tech’s incursions.The tech leaders onstage with Trump at his second inauguration thought they’d turn him into their golden escalator up; the current revolt suggests they could follow him on the golden escalator down. In San Francisco, more than 1,000 nurses and community members came out in a march in September to demand that hospitals cut ties with Palantir, Peter Thiel’s sinister surveillance corporation that also aids Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Nurses in the march noted that the software makes significant errors, violates patient confidentiality and the president of the California Nurses Association and National Nurses Organizing Committeesaid: “The violence and destruction unleashed by immigration agents and enabled by Palantir is a total violation of nursing values of care and compassion.”Recent news stories, following former Anthropic safety employee Jacob Coxon’s statements about AI’snear-term apocalypticrisks, were further reminders of the absolute amorality of Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei. The documents for Anthropic’s IPOacknowledgedAI models could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, and the sheer arrogance of choosing to make profit-driven private decisions about the collective future is another reason to loathe and oppose them. Although there are useful and legitimate applications of this technology, the people pushing it on us are pursuing its more dangerous and corrosive uses, even as their products again and again prove harmful and unreliable. In recent weeks another AI safety employee quit, OpenAI’s David Robinson, with a statementnoting: “The future depends on wisdom that Silicon Valley lacks.”We will not see anything as dramatic and decisive as the explosion of Skynet, but we are seeing enough of a grassroots opposition going after so many aspects of tech, that maybe history will remember it as the beginning of our war against the machines. A new organization called Mothers Against Media Addiction (Mama) is going after the effects of the internet and smartphones on children. Other encouraging developments include New York City’sdecision to ban AIfor students through eighth grade, and the most recent round oflawsuits against Metafor what Instagram and Facebook do to children. Meanwhile congressional Democrats, spurred on by their constituents, are stumbling towardregulation of the tech industrythat protects human beings against machines and the owners of those machines.Another new organization, calledthe Association for Human Mathematics(AHM), founded in September, declares that it “protects mathematics as a human endeavor against the threat of artificial intelligence”. AHM seems to have been founded in response to OpenAI claiming it solved one of the longstanding problems in mathematics. Since then it has gone after many more, much to thedismay of mathematicians. The mission statement recognizes, as many creative workers do, that the process of thinking, struggling, creating, learning, writing is at least as important as the product, that in doing the work we form ourselves as well as arrive as results. “Why surrender our agency (that amazing ability we have to reach across time and space, with our strange, idiosyncratic phenomenon, and land within the sensibility of another human being) to something that, by its very design, pushes the individual sensibility aside?”saidnovelist George Saunders of AI.The spiritually bereft rhetoric of AI, like so much tech rhetoric, insists that doing things is hard and we don’t want to do hard things. As the brilliant tech critic Sherry Turklepoints out, AI as currently promoted and used threatens to “deskill” us both intellectually and emotionally, if we depend on it for a sycophantic pandering to our egos in place of the challenge of human relationships, if we make it do our mental labor for us. Like physical strength, emotional and intellectual strength are achieved through efforts tech would like us to abandon in favor of outsourcing the work to their products. A third new anti-AI organization, launched by longtime climate activist Phil Aroneanu, is calledIrreplaceable.org, and while its main goal is to regulate AI, its premise is that we need to protect our incomes, our rights, our freedom, but also our humanity against the tech corporations pushing AI.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, for twelve weeksSign up toHow we winBernie Sanders, Robert Reich, Stacey Abrams, Mehdi Hasan, Paul Krugman and other bold thinkers on how to defeat Trumpism and build a better future. From our opinion desk.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThese new developments point to something that’s going to be important in the resistance to big tech: as it seeks to literally dehumanize us and argues for replacing human beings (and at its most extreme, humanity itself), we must define and cherish and defend what does make us human and what makes being human joyful, meaningful, dignified and honorable. It’s a more nuanced, undramatic job than, say, going after Flock cameras, but not less important. I began this essay talking about beautiful hatred. It is only beautiful if it knows what it opposes because it knows what it loves and endeavors to defend. In this case, we’re defending nearly everything, including democracy, human creativity, human nature and nature itself. Terminator 2’s subtitle is Judgment Day; judgment day in 2026 will be election day, and I’ll be rooting – and voting – for humanity against oligarchical technology.Rebecca Solnitis a Guardian US columnist. She is the author of Orwell’s Roses and co-editor with Thelma Young Lutunatabua of the climate anthology Not Too Late: Changing the Climate Story from Despair to Possibility***Want to hear more from our contributors?Follow them on Substack:Stacey Abrams,Robert Reich,Paul Krugman,Naomi Klein,Mehdi Hasan,Bernie Sanders,Rebecca Solnit,Katie Phang,Judd LegumandWajahat Ali.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026How we winAI (artificial intelligence)US politicsDatacenters – USSam AltmanOpenAISurveillancecommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Alberta’s referendum: Canada holds together – against Donald Trump | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Voters’ emphatic rejection of separation strengthens Mark Carney’s energy strategy in the face of a US trade war and threats
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Voters’ emphatic rejection of separation strengthens Mark Carney’s energy strategy in the face of a US trade war and threats
Content: A pro-Canada rally in Edmonton, Alberta, on 18 October.Photograph: Timon Johnson/The Canadian Press/APView image in fullscreenA pro-Canada rally in Edmonton, Alberta, on 18 October.Photograph: Timon Johnson/The Canadian Press/APOpinionCanadaThe Guardian view on Alberta’s referendum: Canada holds together – against Donald TrumpEditorialVoters’ emphatic rejection of separation strengthens Mark Carney’s energy strategy in the face of a US trade war and threatsTue 20 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.52 EDTShareCanadians are proving to be a voice of sanity. In roundlyrejectingthe idea of separating from Canada, voters in the oil- and gas-rich province of Alberta sensibly backed thenation-buildingstrategy of the prime minister, Mark Carney. He has put Alberta at the centre of his plan to make Canada an energy superpower that is “much less dependent on the United States”.Donald Trump’s trade war and threatslast weekto make Canada the 51st US state were a fillip for Mr Carney in Alberta, a landlocked western province where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular. The stakes were high: a successful separatist campaign would have handed Mr Trump leverage over Canada’s resource belt. The result instead lets Mr Carney cast Alberta’s mineral wealth as a national asset, rather than allow separatists to define it as a regional grievance.Albertans were not offered a binding secession vote. They rejected the idea of beginning the process towards such a vote. The early result – roughly75%against 25% – looks emphatic. For all the separatists’ talk of “success”, Albertans did not buy their tactical argument: that voting for a future referendum would strengthen the province’s hand against Ottawa. However, the sense of alienation in the province is profound: polls show thatAlbertansthink most of the country does not respect the region.View image in fullscreenMark Carney.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockAddressing that alienation has come at a worrying cost, both politically and environmentally. Mr Carney, who was raised in Alberta’s capital, Edmonton, made a series of pacts with the province’s premier, Danielle Smith. Heagreedto back a new 1m-barrel-a-day oil pipeline and tear up environmental rules. Mr Carney has to deliver tangible gains, or else the sizable faction that supports separatism within Ms Smith’s United Conservative party will entrench itself and look for future opportunities to act.Whatever replaces the “Let Alberta decide” movement will have an uphill struggle. In his bookThe Republic of Alberta, the journalist Tyler Dawson wrote that it has “no charismatic leader like René Lévesque, the suave, smoke-wreathed Quebec separatist who took his province to its 1980 secession referendum. There is no culturally entrenched canon of nationalist literature to fill Alberta bookshelves. The province has no unique language or race or faith that binds its residents together.” Yet victory this month for the Lévesque-founded Parti Québécois in provincial elections reveals that separatists can win power despite their raison d’etre beingunpopular.To those who witnessed the Brexit referendum, the Albertan poll offered adepressingrerun of nationalist gripes and political fantasy. The easy assurance that sovereignty can be recovered painlessly is wearily familiar. Keith Wilson, an architect of Alberta’s separatist movement, calling the task of founding a country “super easy” will prompt a sense of deja vu. Perhaps most importantly, Blackfoot leaders saying that separatists regarded treaty nations as a “speed bump” is a sign that the sovereigntists have not caught up with the fact that First Nations’ rights are belatedly being recognised as a critical part of Canada’s constitutional makeup.Canada’s unity is a political achievement that is continually negotiated among regional interests, Québécois nationhood, Indigenous people’s rights, new arrivals and the continental pull of the US. Paradoxically, theinsecuritythat characterises Canadians keeps them in check – and holds the nation together. Or as one of the country’s most famousnovelistsput it: Canada is “not a country you love, it is a country you worry about”.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
