title: Trump’s obsession with Ilhan Omar has reached a dangerous new level | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The administration seems intent on stripping the congresswoman of her US citizenship and deporting her. It’s a terrible abuse of power, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The administration seems intent on stripping the congresswoman of her US citizenship and deporting her. It’s a terrible abuse of power, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: Omar has been repeatedly attacked by Trump.Photograph: Demetrius Freeman/The Washington Post/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOmar has been repeatedly attacked by Trump.Photograph: Demetrius Freeman/The Washington Post/Getty ImagesOpinionIlhan OmarTrump’s obsession with Ilhan Omar has reached a dangerous new levelArwa MahdawiThe administration seems intent on stripping the congresswoman of her US citizenship and deporting her. It’s a terrible abuse of powerTue 20 Oct 2026 10.56 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 12.36 EDTShareWhat do you think it is about Ilhan Omar, exactly, that seems to get under Donald Trump’s tangerine-tinted skin? The president hasclaimedhe has a problem with the progressive Democratic congresswoman because she is “unpatriotic” to the US and “disrespectful … to Israel”. However, the extent of his animus towards Omar, the first Somali American in Congress, suggests there’s more to it. Trump hasinsistedhe is “the least racist person there is anywhere in the world”, so I’m sure it has nothing to do with the fact that she’s brown and Muslim. Truly, it’s a mystery.Whatever the reason, Trump’s not a fan. The president has plenty of enemies, but few have been attacked as ferociously and consistently over the years as Omar. He’s called her “garbage”, among other nasty names, suggested (without evidence) that she married her brother, andsaidshe “should be thrown the hell out of our country”. His supporters haveechoed his callsto deport Omar, who fled war-torn Somalia as a child and became a naturalised US citizen at 17.Now Trump’s obsession with Omar has reached a dangerous new level. Trump isn’t just throwing out insults any more; his administration seems intent on stripping the congresswoman of her US citizenship and deporting her. Last Monday, 22 days before the November midterms in which Omar is seeking re-election, federal agentsraidedher house in Washington DC. Her phone was seized and grand jury subpoenas were reportedly issued to some of her relatives as part of an investigation concerning her immigration paperwork. Trump, by the way, denied anyinvolvement. Just a curious coincidence that one of his biggest nemeses is now being treated like a criminal.As House Democratic leadershave said, the raid on Omar’s house “raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponisation of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries”. But it also raises another question: is this “just” a stunt designed to embarrass and intimidate Omar before the midterms? Or is there a real possibility that the congresswoman could be denaturalised and deported?“Certainly, if the evidence points that way, that could happen,” Tom Homan, Trump’s “border czar”,told Fox Newsover the weekend when asked about Omar being deported. “We’ll let the evidence lead where it leads, but she’ll be held to the same standard you and I are held: if she violated the law, then she’ll be held accountable,”Homan added.Oh, please. I know the Mar-a-Lago set are big on Botox, but I can’t believe Homan was able to preach about accountability with a straight face. Not many people areconvictedof 34 felonies and face no jail time. Trump, however, is in the White House rather than prison because the supreme court’s conservative majority (which he helped create) found that former presidents areentitledto a degree of immunity from criminal prosecution.The US government has every right to uphold its immigration laws, but its appetite seems to vary considerably depending on the person. If Homan really is so keen on accountability, may I suggest he take a look at the Trump megadonor Elon Musk? The tech mogul’s brother, Kimbal Musk, has publicly joked about the fact that the brothers briefly worked in the US without proper documentation in the 1990s. (Elon said it was a “grey area”.) And then there’s Melania Trump: in 2016, theAssociated Pressreported the first lady was paid for 10 modelling jobs in the US before she had legal permission to work in the country. (Melania has denied ever violating the terms of her immigration status.)Omar was just a teenager when her father filled out the paperwork that led to them both being naturalised. I obviously have no idea if there were any errors in that. But I can tell you that this “investigation” is not about accountability. It is a terrifying abuse of power that reflects the way in which the Trump administration is weaponising the immigration system to stamp out dissent. We’ve already seen Trumpdeportnoncitizen student activists to crack down on pro-Palestinian speech. Now he’s applying that strategy to Omar, a sitting congresswoman. As Barack Obamawarnedat the weekend, “If this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her.” Indeed it won’t; Trump is just getting started.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Jalen Hurts played through a blood clot. Are NFL players cattle? | Philadelphia Eagles | The Guardian
description: The Eagles quarterback’s recent health issues highlight how football’s toughness culture puts its players at risk
Author: Andre Gee
Headline: The Eagles quarterback’s recent health issues highlight how football’s toughness culture puts its players at risk
Content: Jalen Hurts is set to miss the rest of the NFL season.Photograph: Ali Habib/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJalen Hurts is set to miss the rest of the NFL season.Photograph: Ali Habib/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockPhiladelphia EaglesJalen Hurts played through a blood clot. Are NFL players cattle?Andre GeeThe Eagles quarterback’s recent health issues highlight how football’s toughness culture puts its players at riskTue 20 Oct 2026 10.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 14.11 EDTShareJalen Hurts islikely to miss the rest of the NFL seasonafter an ultrasound revealed blood clots in his lungs. Thankfully, he’s now restricted from playing for the immediate future, meaning he won’t be risking serious complications – or even his life – as he did when he played in the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 5 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars in London.The quarterback complained to the Eagles’ medical staff of calf pain on 8 October,according to ESPN.The Eagles sayHurts flew to London with the rest of the team and, out of an “abundance of caution”, was given an ultrasound. The test found a superficial clot in his calf. Doing an ultrasound before the flight would’ve been the most prudent thing. The same for making him inactive after the clot was found. But instead, he played in the game on 11 October, as the medical staff and doctors in London agreed “that activity and mobility were important”. Hurts also practiced all last week before a follow-up ultrasound alsofound clots in his lungs.Brock Purdy becomes highest-rated passer in NFL history as 49ers stay perfectRead moreSome have celebrated Hurts’s performance against the Jaguarsas a feat of virility; to many it looks more like putting a player in real danger. His blood clots could have caused serious health issues during the flights or game. (One sports medicine doctortold NJ.com that Hurtswas “a walking risk”.) If his condition was dire enough that doctors reportedly told him in the early hours of Sunday morning not to sleep before the Jaguars game, he shouldn’t have been playing. Hurts’s agent, Nicole Lynn,clarified that he did get some sleepbefore facing the Jaguars, but the question remains: was the NFL’s London showcase so important that it was worth risking Hurts’s life?Asked about his decision to play Hurts,Eagles coach Nick Sirianni told reporters thathe relies on advice from medical staff. “I’m a football coach. I lean on our medical experts in every situation,” he said. “I have full trust and full faith in them. It’s not just me that has major care for our players. It’s them as well.”The Super Bowl LIX MVP is on blood thinners and hopefully on the road to healing, expected to make a full recovery. But his ordeal is the latest example of how football players are put in danger season after season.One piece of research from 2017found that a college player took hits to his head during a single game that were equivalent to multiple car crashes.A study published this yearfound that 215 of 235 brains of former NFL players donated for research showed signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease that can only be diagnosed after death. The NFL has said that it “continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing ⁠strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts” but players keep on suffering concussions, and others like Hurts find themselves in a football culture where playing through injury is commonplace.Last Wednesday, Hurtstold reportersthat his last week had been a “very unique experience” but declined to reveal the blood clot. No one has reported that he received any undue pressure from the Eagles or the league to play against the Jaguars. But it wouldn’t be shocking; this isn’t even the Eagles’ first controversial injury in London. In 2018, former Eagles tackleLane Johnson was reportedly “berated”by general manager Howie Roseman for saying he was unsure about playing because of a high ankle sprain. After suiting up, Roseman reportedly told him, “Good, you have your mouthpiece in, now you can’t say anything stupid.” Neither man has commented on the matter, but it appears to offer a glimpse of life in the good ol’ NFL, where admitting you’re impaired is stupidity. Johnson aggravated the ankle injury and suffered a knee injury during the game.Football culture demands players “tough it out” and get on the field. As former NFL receiver Bernard Berrianhas said, the tension “isn’t verbal” but is still “there” because, “as we say, you can’t make the team in the training room.” Former running back Clinton Portisechoed Berrianwhen he spoke about playing through 10 concussions in his career and rarely getting treatment: “You can’t make the club in the tub.” Portis said he was “really scared” of undergoing testing to assess his neurological health.You can see how the culture of the NFL makes players behave this way. With only61% of NFL contracts containing guarantees, andan average 56% year-to-year retention, the pressure to stay active and keep the checks coming in is rampant. Pretty much every job pressures its employees to perform in some capacity; only one entails 300lb men running full speed to tackle you for 17 games a season. Players shouldn’t be made to feel they need to be on the field, but the irrational “win now” pressure they face trickles down and paints them in two colors: as an asset or expendable. It’s inherently inhumane.The NFL has attempted to address injuries, and the threat of concussion and CTE in particular, but those efforts don’t seem to be enough. The league has changed kickoff rules and introducedoversized Guardian Capsto mitigate concussions, but football’s physical risks persist. A2018 studyin the Brain Neurology Journal revealed that subconcussive hits also contribute to CTE. And a 2025Wisconsin School of Medicine study concludedthat Guardian Caps did not reduce concussion rates in a sample of high school players. It’s unclear what seismic changes could actually address football’s inherent brutality. And the NFL’s struggles to stop it shows it is unsure – or doesn’t care enough – too.Hurts’s case also raises the specter of medical racism.Multiple studies have shownthat Black people and other minorities in the United States are less likely to receive adequate medical care than white people. It’s impossible to say whether the staff who treated Hurts looked at a strapping Black athlete and believed he could play a brutal game while suffering from blood clots. But the incident nonetheless conjureshistorical patterns and lived experiencesof Black peoplenot receiving proper care.Hopefully Hurts gets back on the field and has a long, healthy career. Regardless, the Eagles’ handling of his treatment should be a demarcation point for the league. From the top down, theNFLneeds to stop treating its labor force like cattle on a farm, as if their sole worth is in putting their bodies at risk.Explore more on these topicsPhiladelphia EaglesNFLUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m a chief technology officer. AI still needs your human expertise  | Madhu Shashanka | The Guardian
description: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment
Content: The people best suited for doing this new type of work aren’t computer programmers. They are the ones who know how the real work is done.Illustration: Guardian Design/Westend61/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe people best suited for doing this new type of work aren’t computer programmers. They are the ones who know how the real work is done.Illustration: Guardian Design/Westend61/Getty ImagesReworkedAI (artificial intelligence)I’m a chief technology officer. AI still needs your human expertiseMadhu ShashankaAI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgmentSupported byAbout this contentTue 20 Oct 2026 08.30 EDTShareAutonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according tothe Wall Street Journal.That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI.People expect AI to lead to fewer jobs in 34 of the 37 countries surveyed by thePew Research Center. In wealthy countries like the US, Australia and South Korea, about seven in 10 expect job losses over the next 20 years. And across countries, concern among young people is rising. While fears focus on job numbers, the bigger change will be what jobs become.The nature of human work will move towards judgment. Experts refer to AI as “jagged”, superhuman at certain tasks but weak at others, with no clear boundary between the two. AI rapidly improves where work can be automatically checked and examples are endless. But it’s shaky where no automated test can determine whether the answer is right. Even if AI is correct a majority of the time on a task, it often doesn’t tell you when it’s inaccurate. If you’ve used AI, you’ve probably experienced how it can be confidently wrong.Some of these errors will solve themselves as models get better. But jaggedness is a symptom of how these models learn. I see this often as a technology leader building with these systems.A smarter model still needs a right answer to learn from. When one gap is closed, it shows up somewhere else no one thought to check. But many business decisions don’t immediately have a clear right answer. Whether a choice is good depends on a future no one can see and data no one has. That’s where judgment comes in. So AI will keep mastering tasks that have checkable results but struggle where a person has to decide what a good outcome looks like.As a result, a new type of work is starting to appear. Someone tests whether the output of AI is correct based on real work, not just on benchmarks. Someone sets limits on what AI is allowed to do before it runs, so the worst mistakes are avoided. Someone runs and manages several agents the way a shift manager runs a crew. Picture an airport control tower. Radar and software track flight paths, with humans judging the few that matter to avoid collisions. No one is manually watching every screen. That would never scale.Setting AI’s limits is harder than it sounds. In a2026 study, after an agent was told to protect a secret, it destroyed its own email server, deleting every single email. It was given a goal, without any limits on what it could do. The researchers described it as the right values paired with terrible judgment. Deciding what is off limits and what a mistake would cost takes someone who knows the work and will answer for the result.Here is the good news for people worried about their own jobs. The people best suited for doing this new type of work aren’t computer programmers. They are the ones who know how the real work is done. Catching what a confident AI left out or got wrong takes someone who knows the complete answer. That knowledge is uncheckable, unwritten and takes the form of judgment honed over years of doing the task and watching it break.Ford recently learned the value of human expertise. In recent years, it leaned hard on automating its quality control, cutting thousands of jobs. But earlier this year, it had to rehire 350 veteran engineers to oversee the process and hunt for failure points before a part reached the factory floor. They brought the judgment of watching parts fail over years. With humans at the helm, Ford’s quality ranking then hit first among mainstream brands for the first time since 2010.But we are making a serious mistake with the jobs we’re eliminating due to AI: the entry-level, routine ones. That routine work is how judgment gets built over time. Junior employees work under the supervision of senior experts until their experience turns into instinct. AI eliminates the friction related to learning how to do the job. But the demand for judgment did not go away. We are just destroying the path to developing it.The real question is not whether machines will take over our work. It is whether we will have the people who can tell when the machines are wrong. Right now, we are automating the training ground where judgment is learned. If you have hard-earned expertise about anything, the next few years will only make you more valuable. And if you are just starting out, the old apprenticeship model will not hand it to you. You have to go and earn it, deliberately, on tasks the machines cannot yet judge.Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software companyExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ReworkedComputingJob lossescommentShareReuse this content

title: We can stop Trump’s assault on the international criminal court | Kenneth Roth | The Guardian
description: Here’s what we need to do to stand up for international law
Author: Kenneth Roth
Headline: Here’s what we need to do to stand up for international law
Content: ‘The sanctions are the latest step in Trump’s effort to make the world safe for American and Israeli war criminals.’Photograph: Finn Gomez/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The sanctions are the latest step in Trump’s effort to make the world safe for American and Israeli war criminals.’Photograph: Finn Gomez/Getty ImagesOpinionUS newsWe can stop Trump’s assault on the international criminal courtKenneth RothHere’s what we need to do to stand up for international lawTue 20 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 12.35 EDTShareMany applauded when Navi Pillay wasawardedthe Nobel peace prize. The South African human rights lawyer hadchairedthe UN commission of inquiry that found Israel to have committed genocide in Gaza and served forfive yearsas a judge on the international criminal court (ICC).Donald Trump responded a few hours later by imposingsanctionson the ICC. He chose a moment for celebrating the rule of law to try to undermine it.Trump had alreadysanctioned 13 ICC judgesand prosecutors,obstructingtheir access to credit cards, bank accounts and the modern economy. The new sanctions target the entire institution. If they take effect in six months asthreatened, they would effectively bar all financial transactions with the court – and more.They would starve it of cash; no banks would be able to do business with it. They could force internet companies to halt the court’s email and computer systems and telecom companies to cut its phones. And they wouldprecludehuman rights groups and victims from working with the court. Violators would risk penalties themselves.The sanctions are the latest step in Trump’s effort tomakethe world safe for American and Israeli war criminals. He wants the ICC to agree, presumably during the six-month hiatus, never to prosecute the national of a country that has not joined the court, even when the individual commits a crime on the territory of a member state.This is a battle that the US government fought and lost when the court’s founding treaty was adopted in Rome in 1998. The US position wasrepudiatedoverwhelmingly, with the treaty approved by a vote of 120 to 7.In justifying the latest sanctions in the name of American sovereignty, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state,conjuredup images of the ICC prosecuting Trump officials as they detain migrants. That is scaremongering. The court has no jurisdiction over crimes committed inside the United States and never claimed it.But other countries have a sovereign right to prosecute crimes committed on their territory, even if the perpetrator is an American or an Israeli. Ordinarily that would be done by a country’s regular courts, but if in extreme circumstances those courts were unwilling or unavailable, governments have a sovereign right to delegate that power to the ICC. That’s what joining the ICC entails.The Trump-Rubio view is that the US and Israel have a sovereign right to commit war crimes wherever they want, and no other government has a sovereign right to have them prosecuted. That is laughable.Fortunately, other governments see through the Trump-Rubio sophistry. Only Venezuela, which since Trump’scapture of former president Nicolás Madurohas become a USvassalstate, and Chad, which receivessignificantUS military aid, have heeded Washington’s call and announced plans to withdraw from the court. (Three Russian-backedmilitaryjuntasin theSahelhave also announced an intention to withdraw for their own self-protective reasons.) Even if they all follow through, that would leave a solid 120 governments fully onboard.Now they must act to defend the court.The most important step would be for the European Union to invoke its “blocking statute”, which, when activated, prohibits European companies from complying with US sanctions outside US territory. European banks would have to continue providing services to the court. So would telecom, internet and other European companies.The EU has already invoked the blocking statute in twopriorcircumstances – to limit US sanctions against Cuba and Iran. Trump’s threat to destroy one of the world’s foremost institutions of justice is a veryappropriatethird case.Why hasn’t the EU already done so? One significant obstacle seems to beDutch banks. The ICC is located in The Hague. If Dutch banks were ordered under the blocking statute to ignore Trump’s sanctions, they might faceretaliation.But Europe has tools to fight back. When Trump rattled on about seizing Greenland, European leaders responded by threatening to deploy their economic “bazooka” – officially known as theAnti-Coercion Instrument– which wouldrestrictdesignated American companies from operating in Europe. Trump backed down.The ICC also has an important tool in its arsenal. Article 70 of its foundingRome Statutemakes it a crime (with a potential prison sentence of up to five years) to obstruct justice by intimidating or retaliating against court personnel for their official duties.That’s what Trump’s and Rubio’s sanctions do. The ICC president, Judge Tomoko Akane of Japan,saidas much in responding to them.They were imposed because court personnel charged the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the former Israeli defense minister Yoav Gallant for war crimes inGazaand opened an investigation that might have included torture by US personnel under the George W Bush administration.The court had jurisdiction even though neither the United States nor Israel has joined the court because these alleged crimes took place on the territory of the member statesPalestineand Afghanistan.Trump and Rubio might try to laugh off being charged by the ICC, but their world would become much smaller. They would suddenly risk arrest if they traveled to any ICC member state. They should ask the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, facing his own ICCarrest warrant, how he felt being unable to travel to the Brics summits inSouth AfricaandBrazil. Trump’s pardon power does not extend to the ICC.Charging a US president or secretary of state would obviously be a big deal. It would take a courageous chief prosecutor to take the step. Unfortunately, the ICC currently has no chief prosecutor since Karim Khan wasoustedfor sexual misconduct.Twodeputies, Nazhat Shameem Khan and Mame Mandiaye Niang, are serving as interim leaders. While the ICC is under attack, its member states are inexplicablydawdlingin naming a successor. Urgent action is required.Meanwhile, all of us should make clear what Trump’s sanctions are really about. The ICC isfarfrom perfect, but it has done importantworkon behalf of the victims of mass atrocities in Ukraine, Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Myanmar, Afghanistan, the Philippines and elsewhere.Trump would sacrifice all of that for his lawless views on American and Israeli crimes. Supporters of selective justice might endorse his quest for impunity. No one else should.Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author ofRighting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive GovernmentsExplore more on these topicsUS newsOpinionTrump administrationUS politicsIsraelGazaInternational criminal courtPalestinecommentShareReuse this content

title: My wife Jo Cox was murdered in her constituency in 2016. The alleged attack on Helen Haines is a punch to the gut | Brendan Cox | The Guardian
description: Moments like these can reinforce our divisions or remind us of what we stand to lose when hatred and intimidation are allowed to brutalise our democracy
Author: Brendan Cox
Headline: Moments like these can reinforce our divisions or remind us of what we stand to lose when hatred and intimidation are allowed to brutalise our democracy
Content: Brendan Cox, the widower of murdered UK Labour MP Jo Cox (pictured), speaks at an event in London on 22 June 2016, on what would have been Jo’s 42nd birthday.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBrendan Cox, the widower of murdered UK Labour MP Jo Cox (pictured), speaks at an event in London on 22 June 2016, on what would have been Jo’s 42nd birthday.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionHelen HainesMy wife Jo Cox was murdered in her constituency in 2016. The alleged attack on Helen Haines is a punch to the gutBrendan CoxMoments like these can reinforce our divisions or remind us of what we stand to lose when hatred and intimidation are allowed to brutalise our democracyTue 20 Oct 2026 19.11 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 19.55 EDTShareIt’s never a good sign when you turn on your phone to find a dozen messages asking if you are OK. For reasons you will come to understand, I only get those messages when something awful has happened.So on Monday, when I came out of an all-day meeting on antisemitism and picked up the messages from friends, I clicked across to check the news with real dread. The last time I’d received a similar barrage of messages was whenformer UK MP Ann Widdecombe was killed earlier this year.As I read the news about thealleged attack on Australian MP Helen Haines, the dread I felt was followed by what I can best describe as a punch to the gut. A wave of shock. Deep sorrow. The despair that another elected representative had been so brutally injured.I knew one of us could get hurt eventually. I never thought it would be my friend Helen Haines | Zoe DanielRead moreJo Cox MP, my late wife,was murdered in 2016in her constituency in Yorkshire, England by a far-right extremist as she went about her constituency work.Helen’s story reminded me of what happened to Jo. Both incidents took placein a small townfar from the corridors of power. Helen, like Jo, clearly has a deep connection with her community. Even their names connected them (Jo’s first name was Helen – though she always used Jo as her main name).View image in fullscreenA photograph of UK Labour MP Jo Cox and her husband Brendan outside 10 Downing Street in London sits beside floral tributes to Jo, who was murdered on 16 June 2016.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesWhen something like this happens it’s impossible not to feel yourself back in the moment of your own loss. My immediate reaction was to hope to God she survives – I remembered how I prayed the same as I heard the news about Jo’s attack.I quickly worried about her family, the impact on them, and immediately recalled the impact on mine.And then of course you worry about the impact on the country, its democracy and the values that underpin it.Practically – unless you are part of her medical team – there is not much that most Australians can do to help Helen directly. Or even to comfort her family (though public solidarity really does matter). But what you can do is be part of the response.I don’t know what motivated the alleged attack on Helen, which is still under investigation. And I’m not sure I care. Whatever the motivation, it damages democracy. And there can only be one appropriate response: to work together to strengthen it.I know from bitter experience that moments like these can become turning points. They can reinforce our divisions, fuel our anger and make us more fearful of one another. Or they can remind us of what we stand to lose when hatred and intimidation are allowed to shape our public life and brutalise our democracy.After Jo was killed, I saw extraordinary acts of kindness and solidarity. People who had never met her came together to celebrate her life and the values she represented. They reached across political, religious and cultural divides. They refused to let an act of hatred have the final word.That response mattered then, and it still does today.View image in fullscreenTributes left for independent federal MP Helen Haines outside her electoral office in Wangaratta on Wednesday. Haines remains in a critical condition.Photograph: James Ross/AAPPolitical hate speech can have real-world fallout. After the alleged attack on Helen Haines, our leaders must act | Paul DaleyRead moreAcross democracies,political debate is becoming more hostile.Opponents are increasingly portrayed not merely as people who are wrong, but as enemies who must be defeated at any cost. Online, contempt is rewarded, threats are normalised and people are encouraged to see the worst in one another.We should be alarmed by that. But alarm alone is not enough.We cannot undo what happened to Jo. We cannot take away the pain of those affected by the alleged attack in Australia. But we can decide what kind of society we build in response.We can allow violence to make us more divided, more suspicious and more fearful. Or we can use this moment to reaffirm our commitment to democracy, decency and what we have in common.The measure of a society is not what shocks it experiences, but how it responds. Australians cannot undo what is done, but you can still shape what it means.Brendan Cox is the co-founder of the Together Coalition, which acts as the secretariat for the Independent Commission on Community and Cohesion. He’s also co-founder of theJo CoxFoundation, Survivors Against Terror and More in CommonExplore more on these topicsHelen HainesOpinionAustralian politicsJo CoxcommentShareReuse this content

title: Labor and the Coalition are poised to take a reckless gamble on AI. Haven’t they realised community support has collapsed? | Edward Santow and Sarah Sacher | The Guardian
description: Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand
Author: Edward Santow
Headline: Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand
Content: ‘The decisions being made now on datacentres and how we adopt AI could define our economy, environment and society for generations,’ write Edward Santow and Sarah Sacher.Photograph: James Ross/AAPView image in fullscreen‘The decisions being made now on datacentres and how we adopt AI could define our economy, environment and society for generations,’ write Edward Santow and Sarah Sacher.Photograph: James Ross/AAPOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Labor and the Coalition are poised to take a reckless gamble on AI. Haven’t they realised community support has collapsed?Edward Santowand Sarah SacherAustralian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at handGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastTue 20 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 19.08 EDTShareAustralia’s major political parties are edging towards rare consensus. Labor and theCoalitionincreasingly want to take a major bet on artificial intelligence. Yet, just as the parties are coming together, the Australian community is running the other way.Last year,only 30% of Australiansbelieved the benefits of AI outweighed the risks. In 2026, community trust in AI appears to be falling even further.It was an unusual step for our parliament to form a joint select committee on AI. It signalled that the decisions being made now on datacentres and how we adopt AI could define our economy, environment and society for generations.Calls to strengthen workplace privacy in Australia as employers turn to AI to track staffRead moreAs a fresh round of hearings starts this week, the committee members must confront the gulf between the politics of AI and the stark reality on the ground. Some parts of the business sector are urging us to prioritise innovation and AI adoption, which is often another way of saying: “Do a better job of selling the upside of AI.”Whether you’re an AI optimist or a sceptic, this is a terrible idea. Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and the other titans of Silicon Valley have a golden megaphone to spruik the benefits of their technology. Australians don’t want our elected representatives to do the same thing – especially when the technology is already bringing both opportunity and harm.This doesn’t mean being blind to the benefits of AI. On the contrary, Australia is among the highest users per capita of Anthropic’s Claude and other generative AI applications. But we must also be clear-eyed about potential risks. And, crucially, we don’t see a compelling response to our concerns from government or the AI companies themselves.Take the impact of AI on work. Our community is asking practical questions. How will AI impact our jobs and the jobs of our children? What is the government doing to ensure the AI systems used in Australian workplaces are safe?Our new report,Drawing the Line,lays out how AI is propelling the rise of harmful tech-enabled worker surveillance. Often workers are unaware of the extent to which they are being monitored – including through their work devices and phones, and via software such as Microsoft Teams.Unlike some of the hypothetical (and frankly terrifying) risks that the joint select committee on AI has already covered, such as AI-enabledbiological weaponsandengineered pandemics, this is happening today.‘Not our friends’: Victorian Coalition warns Advance’s ‘bizarre’ AI campaign may cost it majority governmentRead moreAustraliansupermarket workersare already being pushed to meet AI-generated productivity metrics that force them to work harder and faster under the threat of punitive repercussions – putting them at risk of injury and workplace accidents.Remote workersare already being subjected to intrusive surveillance software capable of watching everything they do on their screen – including audio recording conversations they have with their families.Rideshare driversare already being penalised for road conditions and customer complaints that are unrelated to their performance, which can result in their account being deactivated and days of work lost.Workers are being quietly crushed by commonplace AI-powered surveillance tools that have crept into our workplaces and home offices. And the impact is real. Think, for example, of the young woman who reported beingsexually harassedby a boss that required her to be on video at all times. Or warehouse workers driven tosuicidal ideationdue to relentless micromanagement by machine.Our workplace laws don’t protect workers from unreasonable surveillance. Nor do they give employers clarity about what types of monitoring are lawful.Unlike existential risks from AI, which are outside the Australian government’s direct control, this problem could be addressed through straightforward law reform.We urge the government to update the Fair Work Act to require any worker monitoring be “fair and reasonable”. This builds on the government’s commitment to require all personal information covered by the Privacy Act to be handled fairly and reasonably.Australian workersexpectthe government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand. This is not a hypothetical future risk – let’s address it now.Prof Edward Santow is co-director of the UTS Human Technology Institute and served as human rights commissioner from 2016-2021. Sarah Sacher is HTI’s senior responsible technology policy specialistExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionAustralian politicsLabor partyCoalitionLiberal partycommentShareReuse this content

title: After the violence and chaos in France, there’s only one beneficiary: Marine Le Pen | Paul Taylor | The Guardian
description: The far-right leader’s promise to restore order will appeal to many ahead of next year’s presidential elections – the stakes are suddenly much higher, says the European Policy Centre’s Paul Taylor
Author: Paul Taylor
Headline: The far-right leader’s promise to restore order will appeal to many ahead of next year’s presidential elections – the stakes are suddenly much higher, says the European Policy Centre’s Paul Taylor
Content: Firefighters tackled a blaze in Paris as protesters march in the background, 17 October 2026.Photograph: Firas Abdullah/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFirefighters tackled a blaze in Paris as protesters march in the background, 17 October 2026.Photograph: Firas Abdullah/Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionFranceAfter the violence and chaos in France, there’s only one beneficiary: Marine Le PenPaul TaylorThe far-right leader’s promise to restore order will appeal to many ahead of next year’s presidential elections – the stakes are suddenly much higherTue 20 Oct 2026 05.59 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 10.36 EDTShareThere is only one clear winner so far from France’s chaos: Marine Le Pen. Theviolence and riotingthat engulfed towns and cities across the country over the weekend, six months before a pivotal presidential election, is a godsend for the hard-right, Eurosceptical, anti-immigration candidate. Asbuildings burned, shops were looted and police attacked, the rioting largely drowned out peaceful mass protests over the dilapidated state of schools , fuel prices and the cost of living.Across France and the rest of Europe, people are in shock atscenes of arson and pillagein city centres, the wrecking of symbols of the republic such as the 19th-century town hall in peaceful provincial Limoges and the bust of Marianne in Marseille’s city hall, and the looting of more than 2,000 shops.Though France has along revolutionary tradition, this was not the work of egalitarian insurgents or working-class warriors, but nihilist, anarchist “black bloc” gangs, with opportunist looters and rioters along for the ride.Emmanuel Macron is a lame-duck president who has no practical answers to a crisis that is ruining his legacy. Macronexpressed his “anger and shame”at the violence and the damage to France’s global image in a Sunday-night broadcast to the nation, but he is so widely loathed, including by many who voted for him in two presidential elections, that his pleas for order and dialogue were largely ignored.Le Pen, in contrast, issued asolemn video message, looking presidential as she sat at a desk with the national tricolor (but no EU flag) and bookshelves as her backdrop. Millions of suffering French people were angry about “anarchic immigration” and the cost of living without smashing or burning anything, she said. They would have an opportunity in six months’ time to vote for a different path of “restored authority and security”.View image in fullscreenA screengrab from Marine Le Pen’s video after the riots across France.Photograph: Rassemblement NationalMacron’s minority government is trapped in a vicious circle. France’s debt and deficit squeeze leaves him no spare cash left to buy off protesters. A decade of his centre-right presidency has failed to reform a bloated public sector or improve public services. The country has a youth crisis, characterised by anxiety over aneconomically uncertain futureand amplified by social media, as well as a geopolitical crisis with Russia’s war on Ukraine spreading into acovert war against Europe.Foreign critics of progressive European social policies are fanning the flames with incendiary commentaries. Donald Trumpgloatedon social media that “France is burning!”. Blaming the situation on immigration, he urged the French to “close your borders and take control before it is too late”. Vladimir Putin’s close aide Kirill Dmitriev described events in France as“the suicidal fall of Europe”and also ascribed it in part to chaotic migration.The convergence of crises leaves little room for manoeuvre for a French government struggling to push even a mildly cost-cutting budget through a hung parliament. For now, it is trying to extinguish the violence withselective curfews. One presidential hopeful, Dominique de Villepin, who was a Gaullist prime minister 20 years ago, has even compared the situation to the eve of the fall of theancien regimein 1788, a year before the outbreak of the Revolution, when France was stricken by drought, failed harvests and empty state coffers.That may be a far-fetched parallel. But the sense of a fraying state, a discredited political class and an ossified bureaucracy unable to staunch a slow-motion financial crisis that might suddenly accelerate makes the stakes in next year’s presidential race ever-higher.Until last weekend’s explosion, the school and student protests, unrest over the cost of living and outrage at instances of police brutality against young demonstrators all seemed to be lifting the campaign of radical-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who in some opinion polls hadovertaken the centrist Edouard Philippefor second place. However, Mélenchon’s apparent refusal to clearly condemn the looting or attacks on the police, and hisbelittling of the violenceas “disorder that is part of the events in the life of a society”, may cost him support among more moderate leftwing voters who have boosted Socialist candidate Raphaël Glucksmann in the latest opinion surveys.Investors aretaking frightat the violence and political instability, selling French stocks and bonds. A deepening market run on France could yet change the dynamics of the presidential campaign, rallying a frightened middle-class behind a seasoned centrist candidate seen as a safe pair of hands in a crisis.A month after the May 1968 student-worker uprising that rocked Charles de Gaulle’s staid regime, voters scared by the spectre of civil unrest delivered a landslide victory to his party, which promised to restore order and authority. A year later, De Gaulle was disavowed in a referendum on regional devolution and resigned.Historical comparisons are risky. Last weekend’s violence has increased the likelihood of a law-and-order backlash among voters that could propel Le Pen into the Élysée Palace. But if the financial situation worsens and the campaign turns on who can save the economy, she may yet lose out to a candidate who is firm on security and more orthodox on fiscal policy. Economics is Le Pen’s weak spot.So far, neither Philippe nor other centrist and centre-right rivals have set the campaign alight. But six months is a long time in French politics.Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy CentreExplore more on these topicsFranceOpinionMarine Le PenEmmanuel MacronProtestEuropeParisJean-Luc MélenchoncommentShareReuse this content

title: Worried about what your phone is doing to your brain? This new fad will make it worse | Imogen West-Knights | The Guardian
description: I have long known that internet detritus is bad for me. But with microdramas – stories told in episodes under two minutes – I can actually feel the damage being done, says writer Imogen West-Knights
Author: Imogen West-Knights
Headline: I have long known that internet detritus is bad for me. But with microdramas – stories told in episodes under two minutes – I can actually feel the damage being done, says writer Imogen West-Knights
Content: Images from the microdrama Pregnant By My Ex’s Professor Dad.Composite: DailymotionView image in fullscreenImages from the microdrama Pregnant By My Ex’s Professor Dad.Composite: DailymotionOpinionTelevision industryWorried about what your phone is doing to your brain? This new fad will make it worseImogen West-KnightsI have long known that internet detritus is bad for me. But with microdramas – stories told in episodes under two minutes – I can actually feel the damage being doneTue 20 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 11.06 EDTShareSeven or eight years ago, a new kind of televisual entertainment was born in China. Microdramas: over-the-top, soap opera-type series with splashy, schlocky premises such as infidelity, arranged marriage and secret billionairehood, in which each episode is a mere 60-90 seconds long, took off there among an audience of the phone-addicted.And now, as with many cultural phenomena that start in China, microdramas have made it over here. The form is forecast to take in$1.5bn in revenue in the USby the end of this year. Channel 4 announced recently that it waslaunching its first microdrama, and the UK is already leading Europe in terms of microdrama-watching, with8.2 million of us tuning in to these thingsevery month.Numbers such as this give me a queasy, vertiginous feeling about the vast difference in possible human experiences existing alongside each other at the same time. What do youmean, millions and millions of people are watching this stuff that seems, to me, catastrophically brainless and objectively bad? Who? What do they eat for breakfast? What do they dream of at night?Before I read those numbers, I had only seen tiny snippets of microdramas embedded into news pieces about the phenomenon. I wanted to know what it was like to actually watch one. I downloaded ReelShort, one of the apps that hosts microdramas exclusively, and flicked through the homepage. Recommended for me wereTrapped in the Boss’s Embrace,I Had a Baby Without YouandCarrying His Triplets, Becoming His Wifey. I went to the “HOT” tab and selected the one with the most convoluted title,Pregnant By My Ex’s Professor Dad, althoughLet Me Taste Your Husbandalso appealed.In Pregnant By My Ex’s Professor Dad, it is legible right from the get-go who the bad guy is (the ex) and who the good guy is (the protagonist) and what is going to happen, not least because it is right there in the title. The question of “what is going to happen?” that is supposed to drive you into the next episode, the question that has driven all narrative since time immemorial, is rendered oddly moot.There is no setup, no world-building, no padding whatsoever, just rapidly cut dramatic denouements over and over again: someone being cheated on, someone slapping someone else, a car window getting smashed, a new love interest being introduced, a sex scene. All of this happens in the first three minutes of the series. Helpless women swoon over geometrically jawed hunks on sets lit like a morgue and say exactly what they are thinking in voiceover, so that there is no room at all for nuance to creep in and engage your brain while you watch.You can watch the first few episodes of any given series for free, and then you hit a paywall, which you can get around by watching ads for another form of phone brain rot: colour-matching mobile games. I have been told by loved ones before now that I couldn’t be a newsreader or a jury member because I can’t keep my emotions off my face. This is true. I caught sight of myself in my phone screen reflection while watching microdramas and saw there a person who looked as if they’d just spotted a pile of dog sick on the carpet.I’m not incapable of enjoying bad television. I do not come here having descended from a lofty perch of only watching heritage BBC adaptations of classic novels or whatever. My appetite for dreck is hearty enough. But, my God – and can there be such an entity in a universe producing microdramas? – this stuff is awful. Flagrantly so, though, to the degree that I start to feel there is something wrong with me for desiring quality in this format.Or I sense that I’ve done something wrong by intentionally going to watch one. In apiece for the New York Times Magazine, writer Daniel Kolitz described these shows as happening to people “like a food-borne illness”, rather than something that people elect to get into. They appear on your phone screen, and there you are, watching them in a half-conscious malaise while you wait for the day to end.I would love for this kind of thing to go the way of non-fungible tokens: something we all had to hear about for a short time and that are now patently doomed to the scrapheap of short-lived modern internet detritus.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMaybe this is partly because my own feelings about internet detritus have changed lately. Whereas in the past I had a known, but not felt, understanding that the allure of apps and games and scrolling on my phone was bad for me, nowadays I am regularly experiencing real, bodily panic that my brain is being atrophied. I am scared of my phone, and my sick want for it. So the emergence of an all-new, even more terrible way of being on your phone does provoke the reactionary in me. “Just let people enjoy things!” a better person might think. Not this time.Imogen West-Knights is a writer and journalistExplore more on these topicsTelevision industryOpinionInternetTelevisionSmartphonesDigital mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: What’s the future for the Green party? Should it be ecosocialism? | Joe Todd | The Guardian
description: The party must aspire to be more than a Labour pressure group. It should offer a vision for radical reform – and ways to implement it, says political writer and Green party member Joe Todd
Author: Joe Todd
Headline: The party must aspire to be more than a Labour pressure group. It should offer a vision for radical reform – and ways to implement it, says political writer and Green party member Joe Todd
Content: Zack Polanski at a Green party campaign event in London on 4 October.Photograph: Jacqueline Lawrie/LNPView image in fullscreenZack Polanski at a Green party campaign event in London on 4 October.Photograph: Jacqueline Lawrie/LNPOpinionGreen partyWhat’s the future for the Green party? Should it be ecosocialism?Joe ToddThe party must aspire to be more than a Labour pressure group. It should offer a vision for radical reform – and ways to implement itTue 20 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 05.40 EDTShareIt’s a strange time to be a Green. We have just held our largest conference ever, but it was overshadowed by a controversial motion that was attacked by the media as racist. Then, when welost a byelectionin a Camden seat that is so Labour it has estates named after Blair-era ministers, the headlines called for Zack Polanski to resign.It does, however, mark the end of phase one for Polanski’s Greens. Polanski burst on to the political scene in 2025 and ate up attention, enjoying an easy monopoly on hope while Labour was sucked into the black hole of Starmerism. Labour has since escaped, with Andy Burnham giving social democracy with Mancunian characteristics a half-hearted go. But Burnham’s honeymoon already seems to be ending. John Healey’sbudgetof “difficult decisions” and “fiscal responsibility” is likely to disappoint everyone but the financial markets, and a winter energy bill crisis driven by a possibleEl Niñodeep freeze is just one of many problems he’ll soon have to face.One school of thought says Polanski can carry on as before, focusing on points of difference with Labour. Healey announces a no-change budget; Polanski calls for a tax on wealth to fund public services. Angela Raynersides with landlordsover renters; Polanski proposes an emergency rent brake and explores Berlin’s plan to expropriate the properties of corporate landlords.These interventions matter, especially in our attention-driven politics. But on their own they are only tactical manoeuvres in response to the politics ofLabour. If we act like we’re only a Labour pressure group, that’s what we will become. And in doing so, we will neglect to answer the deeper question: what are society’s fundamental problems and what is our plan to fix them?In practice, Burnham’s “radical vision” promises only modest regulation of public utilities, limited devolution and reform of the voting system and of social care after the next election. Weighed against the crises we face – climate breakdown, bankrupt public services, rampant inflation, runaway rents, an epidemic of loneliness, a billionaire-owned media, a deranged elite of tech oligarchs who literally want the world to end – his vision reads more like the managed decline of a system in crisis.If phase two of Polanski’s Green party is about anything, it should be about breaking this spell. Part of this is naming capitalism as the root cause. Naomi Klein made the best-selling case more than a decade ago that the fight of our times iscapitalism v the climate– that a livable world and continued resource extraction are fundamentally incompatible.But Burnham will not go there. He namesneoliberalism as the problemand then neglects to fix it, unceremoniously dumping any intention to expand public ownership and shrink the role of the market.Polanskishouldgo there,rooting his day-to-day interventions in a credible programme to transition away from capitalism – not only imagining the end of capitalism and what might come next, but planning in painstaking detail just how we are going to get there. He must build a credibleGreen partyvision that shows Burnham’s to be meek and hollow.Don’t get me wrong, the Green party isn’t there yet, nor anywhere close. We have 5 MPs, 10% of the vote and we’re still learning to be a mass of 230,000 members. But if we don’t start taking ourselves seriously, why would anybody else? Trust in political parties is on the floor, and that affects the Greens too. Why should people put their faith in us and dare to hope if we don’t have a programme that is honest, rigorous and credible?We only need to look to the French leftwing party La France Insoumise to see what this looks like. In 2016 Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s movement published L’Avenir en Commun, which went straight into the bestseller list and has been read by hundreds of thousands of people. It is a visionary, comprehensive programme that would be written into the constitution so that companies can never take more from nature than they give. It’s a plan to provide free water and energy to every household, to redraw France’s regions around river basins, mountain ranges and forests, and to organise ecological planning. It is more extensive and detailed than any manifesto for ecological transition in Europe, and polls suggest Mélenchon could lead the French left into next May’spresidential runoffagainst Marine Le Pen.The Green party’s programme must be similarly full of strategy and vision: reckoning honestly with the forces arrayed against us and setting out precisely what we’d do in our first year of government. It should also talk about the good life and what we’re fighting for, in words that resonate with voters, rather than dry policy. Written in a big open process where lots of groups are involved: unions, community groups and thinktanks, farmers watching harvests fail, pensioners battling fuel poverty, renters priced out of homeownership and workers whose jobs are vanishing – it should become a comprehensive point of unity that can provide an answer to those who aren’t voting Green because they doubt our credibility, and fill the void currently occupied by single-issue policy motions.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPolanski is correct when he says that Burnham isn’t serious about socialism. But we have to be honest: right now, neither are we. If Burnham’s vision is meek and hollow, ours is still being formed. And as Labour faces the tests of governing, now is the time to write it.Joe Todd is a senior fellow at the Autonomy Institute, the co-host of the Life of the Party podcast and a Green party memberDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsGreen partyOpinionZack PolanskiSocialismLabourAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: Don’t be fooled. The AI that was supposed to save us time is doing just the opposite  | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: The government says it can transform the state with AI, but it is no match for the resulting stream of machine-generated slop. And we all pay the cost, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: The government says it can transform the state with AI, but it is no match for the resulting stream of machine-generated slop. And we all pay the cost, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: Since the adoption of ChatGPT, governments around the world are seeing surges in complaints and requests.Photograph: Krongkaew/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSince the adoption of ChatGPT, governments around the world are seeing surges in complaints and requests.Photograph: Krongkaew/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Don’t be fooled. The AI that was supposed to save us time is doing just the oppositeGaby HinsliffThe government says it can transform the state with AI, but it is no match for the resulting stream of machine-generated slop. And we all pay the costTue 20 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 09.06 EDTShareAnother morning, another avalanche of emails. Even after a guilty cull, my inbox is sitting at well over 7,000, but lately I’ve started subscribing to theQuentin Crisptheory of housework: why bother, when after four years or so you stop noticing the accumulating dust? Empty inboxes just fill up again anyway.In theory, email was supposed to save hours of meetings, phone calls and standing over photocopiers. Instead, we just spend hours deleting stuff people wouldn’t have bothered telling us if it had meant picking up the phone, but which they can now spam to their entire database at the click of a button. The glorious ease and convenience of being able to reach the world in seconds came, we now know, with the inconvenience of them being able to reach you right back.And therein lies the challenge to the government’s hopes of AI helping to transform the machinery of the state on the cheap, saving not only time but billions of pounds in public money. It’s early days, but AI seems not so much to be streamlining public service delivery as gumming it up – partly because, as was once the case with email, the public is using it right back at them.In aSubstack postlast week, the former civil servant Sam Freedman noted that governments around the world seem to be experiencing unusual surges in complaints, requests and responses to regulatory and official bodies since the adoption of ChatGPT. It’s the same storyin the courts, withemployment tribunal casesin England, Scotland and Wales reportedly rising by 39% in a year thanks in part to claimants using AI to draft claims, while magistrates and judges face a wave of people who can’t afford lawyers using ChatGPT to build cases that often don’t make sense. And all of this needs patient disentangling by a human, on the grounds that just because a defendant is citing precedents that don’t exist, it doesn’t mean there isn’t a genuine grievance buried in there somewhere.Whitehall special advisers complain of departments drowning in AI-generated freedom of information requests, an abuse of a system originally intended to empower individuals. MPs’ offices are similarly swamped by AI-generated letters, all of which need to be read by humans for fear of missing something important from a constituent.How long before public consultations on changing the law become so spammed by slop that they are in essence useless as a measure of what the country actually thinks? There’s a fine line between the noble aim of making it easier for individuals to interact with an otherwise remote state, and making it so easy that the result is an uncontrollable firehose of meaningless machine-generated guff.The obvious answer to this kind of AI flooding is getting AI tools to detect or sift it, but that doesn’t always work when dealing with potentially vulnerable human beings. Constituents who use AI to express themselves in more fancy-sounding language when writing to their MP, for example, still have the right to expect a personal response from a human being.Employers who thought they were being smart by getting AI to sift job applications, meanwhile, are reaping what they sowed, as resentful applicants automate their end of things too and spray-gun applications across the board, rather than concentrating on the jobs they really want. Now neither side can separate the wheat from an avalanche of chaff.The risk of paralysis is likely only to increase if the public startsadopting agentic AIin the kind of numbers big tech fondly imagines. Early adopters might well find agents save them time and hassle. But shortcuts stop being shortcuts once everyone else is using them too, and risk turning into bottlenecks instead. Think of cars, which have vastly shortened journey times compared with travelling by horseback, except in cities at rush hour when too many other people are also trying to shorten theirs. By 2018, central London daytime traffic was moving on average atjust over 7mph– about the same speed as a trotting pony.Historically, humans have always learned to develop ways around problems of our own making. We have spam filters for email, congestion charges to keep cars out of cities, and in the long term we could well figure out what kind of frictions we need to put back in the system to make it possible to live with the impact of AI.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut for now a useful rule of thumb, if improbable claims start to be made for savings due to AI, will be that more isn’t always better; faster and easier isn’t always more convenient; and time saved in one section of public services has a horrible habit of popping up in another one. Let the Whac-A-Mole begin.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionChatGPTOpenAIComputingEmployment lawEmployment tribunalscommentShareReuse this content

title: I knew one of us could get hurt eventually. I never thought it would be my friend Helen | Zoe Daniel | The Guardian
description: There will now be a flood of rhetoric about who is to blame. Don’t fall for the political opportunism from left or right. We are all responsible
Author: Zoe Daniel
Headline: There will now be a flood of rhetoric about who is to blame. Don’t fall for the political opportunism from left or right. We are all responsible
Content: People lay flowers outside the office of Helen Haines in Wangaratta, Victoria on Tuesday. The independent MP for Indi remains in a critical condition after what is believed to be a targeted attack near her electorate office.Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople lay flowers outside the office of Helen Haines in Wangaratta, Victoria on Tuesday. The independent MP for Indi remains in a critical condition after what is believed to be a targeted attack near her electorate office.Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionHelen HainesI knew one of us could get hurt eventually. I never thought it would be my friend HelenZoe DanielThere will now be a flood of rhetoric about who is to blame. Don’t fall for the political opportunism from left or right. We are all responsibleMon 19 Oct 2026 23.27 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 06.47 EDTShareIt was obvious to those of us who work in and around politics, that eventually, someone would get physically hurt.The fact that it’sHelen Haines, arguably the best of all of us, not just as a politician but a person, is unbearable.Some of us community indies have T-shirts that say, “What would Helen do?”Political hate speech can have real-word fallout. After the alleged attack on Helen Haines, our leaders must act | Paul DaleyRead moreThey were a gift from the member for Kooyong, Dr Monique Ryan, a few years ago.And while it was a bit funny at the time, it’s not a joke.Helen is the one you go to when you’re grappling with the moral quandaries that arise frequently as an MP, in a job when a binary yes/no vote sometimes feels impossible. With intelligence, warmth and deeply held ethics, she represents the very backbone of the parliament.In the footsteps of Cathy McGowan, Helen has carved a path to a different kind of politics out of the hills and valleys of Indi in north-east Victoria.She has gathered people looking for integrity, honesty, empathy and direct engagement under her community-generatedBeechworth principleswhich helped underpin her successful push for a National Anti-Corruption Commission.She has showed that a local member can both represent community and shift generational national policy.Without her, and Zali Steggall’s work on climate, I doubt that theteal wave of 2022would have happened.But with it came something else.Call it a sign of the times; the apparent spillover of online behaviour into the real world, egged on by global political influences, the fracturing caused by Covid, the endemic mental health issues in our communities, the isolation and aggravation, the widening wealth gap, the outright anger, the threats.double quotation markMainstream media’s business model is built almost entirely on mortal combat and clickbait. Social media drives outrage for profitAs Women for Electionrecently reported, these are outsized risks for women in politics.After the 2025 election, Helen and I spoke about our shared concerns.As I told the Age after a torrid campaign involving doxing, abuse and threats, “one of us is going to get hurt eventually”.But never for a moment did I expect that would become realityon a street in Wangaratta.It is sickening to have been right, and to see my friend the target.View image in fullscreenThe independent federal member for Indi, Helen Haines, on her property near Wangaratta, Victoria in November 2021.Photograph: Mike Bowers/The GuardianTo suggest “this is not us” as some commentators are – as if politically motivated violence is an exclusively international phenomenon – is naive.Trumpism and everything it has enabled, social media and everything it has exploited, including populism and extremism across the spectrum, are global influences. Our island status does not protect us.There will now be a flood of rhetoric about who is to blame here. Don’t fall for the political opportunism from left or right. This is spectrum-wide.Already the gaslighting from commentators, politicians and media calling for a return to reasoned debate having actively done the opposite for so long is breathtaking.Helen Haines was chatting with locals at a dog park on Monday morning. By the afternoon, she was fighting for her lifeRead moreLet’s be honest: much of the political strategy that has been deployed in recent history has weaponised anger and division for one reason only – to win. Mainstream media’s business model is built almost entirely on mortal combat and clickbait.Social mediadrives outrage for profit.So, spare me.Social media needs managing with an enforceable duty of care that includes transparency around how destructive algorithms deploy fake news, manipulate public opinion, damage mental health and compound mental illness.And everyone else has to take a good hard look at what they’ve done or not done.It’s a dark day when a community representative, a wife, a mother, a grandmother, a colleague and a friend is allegedly violently attacked when she was just being what we all seek to be: a damn fine person.We are all responsible.So, what are we all going to do about it, together?I am so sad to have to write this about my beautiful friend.Zoe Daniel is a three-time ABC foreign correspondent and former independent member for GoldsteinExplore more on these topicsHelen HainesOpinionAustralian politicsIndependentsAustralian mediaSocial mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: Political hate speech can have real-world fallout. After the alleged attack on Helen Haines, our leaders must act | Paul Daley | The Guardian
description: Social media amplify the worst excesses of what passes for public discourse, while some media outlets foment polarisation
Author: Paul Daley
Headline: Social media amplify the worst excesses of what passes for public discourse, while some media outlets foment polarisation
Content: ‘In times of crisis our federal and some state parliaments do national introspection well,’ Paul Daley writes. ‘But too often nothing comes of it.’Photograph: Mike Bowers/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘In times of crisis our federal and some state parliaments do national introspection well,’ Paul Daley writes. ‘But too often nothing comes of it.’Photograph: Mike Bowers/The GuardianOpinionAustralian politicsPolitical hate speech can have real-world fallout. After the alleged attack on Helen Haines, our leaders must actPaul DaleySocial media amplify the worst excesses of what passes for public discourse, while some media outlets foment polarisationMon 19 Oct 2026 21.18 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 22.18 EDTShareIf the increasingly vituperative tenor of our public discourse, online and verbal, has fully trailed America’s into the murky dungeon of political violence with the appallingalleged attackon Helen Haines, Australia’s political class has only itself to blame.Amid outpourings of concern from across the political spectrum (including from peoplewho have fosteredconsiderable vicious personal animus online and in the parliament) for the gravely injured and much-respectedmember for Indi, it is blindingly evident that the political square has long been utterly incapable of self-regulation.There are no consequences for the abuse hurled across the chambers by Australia’s elected representatives beyond brief parliamentary suspension amid the invariably blokey guffaws. There are no consequences for political operatives here – students of the US experts of weaponising political hatred – who pursue their opponents and critics online with the most vicious, cruel and offensive personal attacks, sometimes under the purported guise of humour.‘I don’t want to be known as a hero’: barber who rushed to help Helen Haines praised by PMRead moreThe ongoing traditional political race-call, for all of its marketability of conflict, meanwhile, reports both the anguish of the attack targets and the dismissive calls for them to effectively harden TF up. It’s just a bit of a joke, don’t you know, snowflakes? All’s fair in the tinderbox of politics. It’s not for the faint-hearted, after all.Do the worst public excesses of personal invective by elected representatives seep into the broader community and license them to do the same? Undoubtedly. But do they transmogrify into actual political violence?What has happened to Haines is still being investigated buthas of course given elected representatives pause to stop and think. The question is, how will they act to change things?The last fortnight or so in Australian politics is a particular a case in point – a burning example of the need to“turn the temperature down”in line with the prime minister’s repeated entreaties to parliamentary colleagues.There have been verbalevocations of violence(of public execution) in the House of Representatives (defended by senior mainstream politicians) and (of a murder fantasy) at a major conference of purportedly “conservative’’ leading thinkers.Social media echo and amplify the worst excesses of what passes for public/political discourse. It also too often contorts it into ideations and outright threats of violence against politicians and sometimes their staff, too often gendered and sexual. Security authorities have beenconsistently warningabout the increasing threats to MPs, especially women.Meanwhile media – old and new – have their own onerous responsibilities in this increasingly polarised space. Too many outlets are far from immune to picking sides and fomenting polarisation, given the marketability of political hate and division that drives the internet in times of news media convergence.double quotation markIt’s impossible to legislate tolerance and kindness – although that is what’s needed most right nowThe federal government has shown a world-leading willingness to take on the major tech companies (albeit with limited efficacy, perhaps) toprotect childrenfrom the worst excesses of social media. But is there a willingness to take on the same powerful forces to curb the no-less-insidious pervasion of political hate speech, whether from the elected or the hordes of nameless trolls and bot-factories swamping the online world?The extremities of left and right will converge where there is any real – or perceived – threat to what passes as political speech freedom but too often lands into the purview of hate and violent threat.Regardless of whether the hate speech which evokes or potentially spurs violence emanates from the extreme left or right – it is virulently pervasive in both – now is not the time for inertia.Actions speak louder than words. And in coming weeks and days there will be a lot of words spoken by politicians about the tragic violence inflicted on perhaps federal parliament’s most respected and loved lower house member.In times of crisis our federal and some state parliaments do national introspection well. But too often nothing comes of it. Now, amid all the calls for determined countermeasures to the hate and evocations of violence that have inveigled almost every medium of our body politic, it is time for leaders to act.It’s impossible to legislate tolerance and kindness – although that is what’s needed most right now as more and more heat, more opinions and more anger flood the national discourse in the wake of this national tragedy.If Haines’ terrible experience represents the moment of “national reckoning’’ that our political class and media insist it is, then it’s truly time for the paradigm shift to redemptive action.Paul Daley is a Guardian Australia columnistExplore more on these topicsAustralian politicsOpinionHelen HainesSocial mediaAustralian mediacommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’ll keep doing this if people pay us!’ The cast of TV hit Ghosts on making a movie – and maybe a caveman spinoff | Comedy films | The Guardian
description: As the haunters of Button House hit the big screen with a plot about an escaped phantom, we hear how the team just missed each other too much – and why grunting Robin may get his own show
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: As the haunters of Button House hit the big screen with a plot about an escaped phantom, we hear how the team just missed each other too much – and why grunting Robin may get his own show
Content: ‘It was like being at a party’ … Mathew Baynton, Martha Howe-Douglas, Jim Howick and Ben Willbond in Ghosts: The Possession of Button House.Photograph: Mandozzi Photography/PAView image in fullscreen‘It was like being at a party’ … Mathew Baynton, Martha Howe-Douglas, Jim Howick and Ben Willbond in Ghosts: The Possession of Button House.Photograph: Mandozzi Photography/PAComedy films‘We’ll keep doing this if people pay us!’ The cast of TV hit Ghosts on making a movie – and maybe a caveman spinoffAs the haunters of Button House hit the big screen with a plot about an escaped phantom, we hear how the team just missed each other too much – and why grunting Robin may get his own showStuart HeritageTue 20 Oct 2026 10.14 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 11.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the final episode of Ghosts was aired in December 2023, the sitcom felt as if it had reached a definitive conclusion. The show’s central relationships, between Charlotte Ritchie’s Alison and the ghosts who haunt her tumbledown inherited manor house, were neatly tied up, as they encouraged her to sell the place to a hotel developer. It was a tearjerker of an episode for the millions of people who watched it, as well as for the cast and crew behind the scenes.“We had stopped the series with genuinely no intention of coming back,” explains the show’s co-creator Mathew Baynton, who also stars as the callow romantic poet Thomas. “We were all in tears on the last day of filming,” he says, now perched on the uncomfortable end of a chaise lounge in a London hotel suite.“I was so upset that it finished,” addsLolly Adefope, who plays the excitable Kitty, from the better structured end of the chaise. “It was like being at a party and you guys were leaving.”“It was a clear ending, and the guys felt like they had fully explored all of the characters,” says director Simon Hynd, “but I did notice a look of regret in some of their eyes.”All of which is to say that Ghosts is now back.
