Although the television series remains over, the story will continue in the new film Ghosts: The Possession of Button House. So the question is, who blinked first?“Alison Carpenter, our executive at Monumental, had started to say, ‘We could get the funding for a film if you guys want to do that,’” explains Baynton. “But we just batted it away.”“The fear was that you’d end up making a 90-minute episode of a TV show, and it would feel like, Please Sir! The Movie,” says co-creator and star Laurence Rickard, who plays both caveman Robin and decapitated nobleman Sir Humphrey Bone. “Which I love, by the way.”Eventually Carpenter convinced the show’s six creators and stars (the others being Simon Farnaby, Martha Howe-Douglas, Jim Howick and Ben Willbond, not present) to at least get into a room and discuss the prospect. “We all talked through what we didn’t want it to be, and what it sort of had to be to be a film,” explains Baynton. “That led us very quickly to the concept of possession, which would allow one of the ghosts to get out of the grounds.”double quotation markWhen Ghosts ended, it was the first time that we hadn’t done something together in 18 years“It was the fastest turnaround ever,” laughs Rickard. “We went in at 9:30am going ‘I mean, it’s nice to see everyone, but I think the answer is probably no’ – and then by 11 o’clock, we were going, ‘We have to do this.’”The resulting film is still very much Ghosts, with its unique mix of sharp absurdity (at one point a Ouija board spells out ‘Leave’ to make a point about Brexit) and near-debilitating emotional notes (you may never again look at a scotch egg without crying). But it is undoubtedly a movie, with stakes and a ticking clock and big set pieces.“The possession idea immediately invites a body swap sort of thing, which reminded us of Big,” says Baynton. “Then we were talking about, what if the possession doesn’t last and his spirit is fading, which reminded us of Back to the Future. The group of kids breaking into the house felt like The Goonies. All our touchstones for this were films we loved in our youth.”The film is an astonishing feat, not just because of its quick turnaround – Hynd only learned of the film late last year – but because every member of its ensemble has a vital part to play in the plot.“With the series, we got so used to writing multi-thread narratives,” explains Baynton. “In any episode, the actual stories are told in two or three brief moments, so that had become our mode of writing anyway.”View image in fullscreen‘I was the Gen Z member of the cast’ … Lolly Adefope in the film.Photograph: Mandozzi Photography/PAThis approach meant that, despite no longer living in Button House, Alison and her husband Mike, played by Kiell Smith-Bynoe, find themselves swept up in the action. Smith-Bynoe seems especially pleased with his arc. “Mike gets to prove himself in this one,” he explains, “which felt good after spending a few years not getting to do that.”Smith-Bynoe has arguably always had the hardest acting job on Ghosts, as Mike is often the only person on screen who isn’t a ghost and can’t interact with them. This challenge was doubled for the film’s climax when, without giving too much away, a roomful of characters old and new flit in and out of tangibility. “It took me a minute,” he says. “I had to keep asking Simon who I was supposed to be able to see.”Much of the cast this time around are new, in the form of the aforementioned kids. It takes a lot to steal a film out from underneath a cast as talented as this, but Scott Ellis Watson, who played the young John Davidson in I Swear, is phenomenal here, largely because he spends a lot of time doing a bang-on impersonation of a dead middle-aged Tory MP.The new additions were something that Adefope in particular appreciated. “It was so fun having Scott around,” she says. “I was sort of the Gen Z member of the cast, so we talked a lot about memes and TikTok.”“You were the child whisperer, weren’t you?” says Rickard.“Yes, exactly. I was translating for you,” she smiles back.With the show, the six creators were able to break off and write individual episodes in various permutations of their troupe. But the film is credited to all six of them. Was that a hard thing to accomplish? “It was just a process of who was around at what time,” says Baynton. “So sometimes it was two of us, sometimes three or four. What is lovely about that is that the person who’s absent for a little period of time then becomes your fresh pair of eyes when they return. You get to a point at times where all you can see is A or B and both of them are problematic, but then someone who’s been away for a couple of weeks comes in and goes, ‘Well, what about C?’ And you go, ‘Oh yeah!’”A lot of this is simply muscle memory. The Ghosts team are now veterans, having met while making theHorrible HistoriesTV show almost two decades ago, and continued with the sitcomYonderlandand the 2015 Shakespeare comedy film Bill. It’s hard to think of any writing and performing group this large who have managed to stay intact for so long. Even Monty Python ran out of films and shows in less time, their work together now largely consisting of tweeting hatred at each other.View image in fullscreenWhat a pickle … Baynton and Howick in the Shakespeare comedy Bill (2015).Photograph: Bbc Films/Allstar“Oh, we’ve got that phase to look forward to,” laughs Rickard. “I’ve been drafting some of that stuff.”Rickard is the one who seems to have most keenly felt the absence of Ghosts: “The first year after the series stopped was the first time that we hadn’t done something together in 18 years.” You get the sense that this film exists in part because its creators missed hanging out with each other.So why stop the party now? Will there be anything else to look forward to from the gang? “There isn’t something secretly being developed,” insists Baynton. “But we’ve always had the same feeling, which is that we love working together and we’ll keep doing it if people will pay us to do it.”Does that mean more Ghosts films? That prompts a slightly more uneasy response. “This does sort of feel like, you know, the big swan song,” replies Rickard.“Yes, but we said that before, so no one can take our word for it,” adds Baynton. “But there’s no intention. Also, ghosts can’t age, and I’m rapidly getting way too old to play Thomas.”“But Robin could definitely have a spinoff, and that wouldn’t be a problem,” cracks Rickard, noting that he’s looking more and more like a long-dead caveman with every passing year. “It would be great. My makeup call would get shaved right down.”Ghosts: The Possession of Button House is in cinemas on Friday 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsComedy filmsTV comedyTelevisionLolly AdefopefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I had no plan. Just total scorched earth’: how Kiran Leonard survived teen success to make songs of full-body joy | Experimental music | The Guardian
description: Hailed as a prodigy at 16, the Saddleworth singer-songwriter was patronised in the press and lost his musical path. Now courted by imaginative new bands, he explains his route back
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: Hailed as a prodigy at 16, the Saddleworth singer-songwriter was patronised in the press and lost his musical path. Now courted by imaginative new bands, he explains his route back
Content: ‘I couldn’t really find another manager – never have since, actually’ … Kiran Leonard.Photograph: Ben BeauvalletView image in fullscreen‘I couldn’t really find another manager – never have since, actually’ … Kiran Leonard.Photograph: Ben BeauvalletExperimental musicInterview‘I had no plan. Just total scorched earth’: how Kiran Leonard survived teen success to make songs of full-body joyShaad D'SouzaHailed as a prodigy at 16, the Saddleworth singer-songwriter was patronised in the press and lost his musical path. Now courted by imaginative new bands, he explains his route backTue 20 Oct 2026 09.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 09.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKiran Leonard presses the tips of his fingers together and looks at me solemnly across the table. “I don’t know if I’m doing a very good job,” he says, “But I’m trying really,reallyhard not to swear.”A decade ago, he explains,he was interviewed by the Guardian, got too drunk, and “swore all the way through the interview”. When the piece came out, his grandfather was thrilled. “But he couldn’t show any of his friends because I just sounded really aggressive,” he tells me sheepishly.It’s true that, the last time Leonard had a profile in this paper, he sounded a lot like a twentysomething trying hard to shed the preciousness of his former status as a teenage wunderkind. Hailed as a prodigy at age 16, upon the release of baroque, bonkers 2012 debut Bowler Hat Soup, a lot of Leonard’s early press plays up his age in a way that now reads as embarrassingly trite. “I think, unconsciously, I was probably quite defensive about how I was written about,” he says. “It’s not nice for journalists to fetishise the density or the ambitiousness of the music – it [was] obviously meant in a slightly patronising way.”The Leonard sitting across from me at a pub near his home in south-east London speaks calmly and carefully, like someone with nothing to prove – because, perhaps, he has so thoroughly proved himself over the interceding decade. In the past five or so years, Leonard has emerged as one of Britain’s most consistently fascinating experimental musicians. His recent slate includes 2024’s Real Home, a rangy pop record that touches on ramshackle country, menacing prog and Jonathan Richman-esque romanticism; last year’s Small Brown Bed/With You Waltz, a surrealist album of live takes recorded at notable DIY venues such as the Golden Lion in Todmorden and Delicious Clam in Sheffield with a group of musicians he calls No Tailgate; and credits on acclaimed records by Eli Winter, Caroline and My New Band Believe.His music is certainly far less wordy these days, far less likely to garner comparisons to Captain Beefheart or Joanna Newsom. But that’s because at this point, he says, he’s searching more for a sense of pure feeling: “I’m strongly driven by a very physical thing – which might seem quite broad, but it’s what distinguishes what I’m interested in and what I’m not.”Leonard was born and raised in Saddleworth, near Manchester, the son of a community midwife and John Leonard, a folk musician who worked for BBC Radio 1 and 2 in Manchester in the 80s and 90s. Although it’s clear he was making music from a young age, it’s less clear how he ended up signed, with a manager and booking agent, before he could legally drink. “The short answer is: I don’t know,” he says. “I was very ignorant and sheltered from a lot of it. I made Bowler Hat Soup and put it on Bandcamp. I think I sent it to a load of blogs, and a blog wrote about it, which was then read by [the people who ran the label] Hand of Glory. I didn’t really come up through like, gigging.”From there, Leonard was set up with that dreaded industry mechanism: a team. He got a publicist and a radio plugger and, through his management, a band, thankfully comprised of Manchester musicians who were at least making music that felt aligned with Leonard’s own. “I was fortunate to work with really good people and great musicians and have all this support, but the context was wrong,” he says.View image in fullscreenFinding his groove, Leonard performing in 2024.Photograph: Ben BeauvalletDuring that period, he made and released four albums, but increasingly felt as if he wasn’t in the right zone. Enamoured by fuck-the-industry icons such as Steve Albini, he began tanking his commitments because the music was the one thing he had control over. He moved to London and then, one day, ditched his entire team. “It was a disaster – just total scorched earth,” he says with a sheepish smile. “I had no plan, had no idea what I was doing.”Leonard found London “really alienating and difficult”, a feeling that was compounded by the fact that, he soon realised, he didn’t really know how much his team had sheltered him. “I couldn’t really find another manager – never have since, actually. And couldn’t get gigs,” he says.Leonard “gradually found a groove in London, found a way to find it really stimulating and engaging”. That came through booking more shows and from befriending the post-rock band Caroline, who are the nexus of some of the country’s most vital experimental music. “I’m sure many people in this community would say the same thing,” he says. The band have become “a centre of activity in a lot of the work that I do because there’s so many of them, the quality of what they do is such a high standard and they’re operating at a level that everyone is very proud of and impressed by.”Leonard quickly realised that his work could comprise “different investigations” – that he didn’t have to feel pinned down by one style, and that he didn’t have to be haunted by the music he made as a teenager. “I wanted to articulate myself more clearly and with less pomposity, less adolescent over-the-top-ness,” he says. “With the teenagery records, a lot of them were coming out much later than they’d been made. The difference between 15 and 18 is really massive, so playing those songs, I’d feel a bit of a dissonance, which made me more conscious of wanting to move past [them].”Leonard says that most of his work now is extremely solitary, although he occasionally plays in Caroline, and enjoys playing in a project where he doesn’t have to add his own compositional voice to the mix. An exception to that solitary work is Or Sobre Blau, Leonard’s duo with Catalan guitarist Andreu G Serra. Their remarkable second album, Making Friends, released earlier this year, is a heady mix of ambient guitar primitivism, oddball samples and scratched-up found sound. “Or Sobre Blau is really thrilling because it’s in a totally different voice,” he says. “It’s the voice of that friendship, which is really thrilling because for my stuff, I’m just in my head, which is sometimes horrible.”My New Band Believe review – beautiful ideas burst from ex-Black Midi man’s lovable debut albumRead moreIf there’s a common link between all Leonard’s work now, it’s that it often comes from a desire to make sounds that conjure full-body sensations. He often gets there. “I remember having a conversation with someone about the Caroline song Total Euphoria,” says Leonard. “They were like, I don’t know how often I feel total euphoria. I’m like: ‘I feel it quite a lot.’”Kiran Leonard istouring the UK, Europe and US, including dates as Or Sobre Blau, into January 2027Explore more on these topicsExperimental musicinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was so satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen’: the people sick of being spied on by their smart TV | Television | The Guardian
description: Is your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacy
Author: George Francis Lee
Headline: Is your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacy
Content: ‘It’s not intimidating, just increasingly enshittified’ … a user and their smart TV.Photograph: SimpleImages/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It’s not intimidating, just increasingly enshittified’ … a user and their smart TV.Photograph: SimpleImages/Getty ImagesTelevision‘It was so satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen’: the people sick of being spied on by their smart TVIs your television listening to every conversation? Filling your home with highly invasive ads? Some viewers have had enough of tech violating their privacyGeorge Francis LeeTue 20 Oct 2026 10.42 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 10.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Dan had had enough of his television, he threw a rock straight through the screen. The offence? His smart TV was downloading its third update in three days. “It drove me crazy with what seemed like daily software updates that never fixed anything and ‘features’ that never seemed to work,” says the 71-year-old from Illinois. “And of course, constantly trying to push me to subscribe to paid-for services when all I wanted to do was watch over-the-air TV, play a DVD or stream something from my computer.”Some may accuse Dan of being a luddite, but his master’s degree in computer science and decades of experience in telecommunications would suggest otherwise. “The tech is not intimidating,” he explains, “just increasinglyenshittified.”The first smart TVs entered the market in the late 2000s, when companies introduced operating systems, media players and apps to screens that were becoming wider and thinner. In recent years, the luxury status of smart TVs has waned and increasingly affordable options are widely available. Tom Parsons, TV and audiovisual editor at the electronics magazine What Hi-Fi?, explains that these cheaper models can struggle under more advanced features. “They’re not necessarily super-fast and responsive out of the box,” he says. “And then two, three, four years down the line, they can end up slowing down quite a lot under the weight of all that processing.”Dan is just one of a growing number of tech-savvy watchers wishing their TVs weren’t so smart. Erin McQuiston and Matthew Schroyer, a couple from Connecticut, share his smart-screen scepticism.View image in fullscreenIncreasingly hard to find … a dumb TV.Photograph: Svetlana Lazarenka/Alamy“I don’t think we’ve ever used [our TV] as anything other than just a giant display,” says McQuiston. “There was a period where we were running it through an Xbox. And that was a constant battle because that was constantly being updated and patched and then you’d have to redownload all the apps for it.”Meanwhile, Schroyer says his job as a software engineer has influenced his decision to “intentionally keep it very dumb” by keeping their TV disconnected from the internet. “A rule of the house is: don’t give things the wifi password,” he says. “It concerns me that folks increasingly have to be IT experts to get the bare minimum enjoyable experience out of this stuff.”Instead, the 41-year-old connects his screen to an Apple TV box as a streaming workaround, and cites privacy as well as “highly invasive” advertisements for doing so. “Our living room is not a billboard for sale,” he says.When asked how the couple might cope in a future where TVs may have mandatory internet, McQuiston says her husband is “handy enough to break every terms of service known to man and get in there and unsolder something to manually disconnect it”.For Helen Northmore, a 51-year-old from Wales who works in AI delivery for the UKHealthSecurity Agency, privacy is also a worry. Her grudge against smart screens began four years ago, when her faithful dumb TV broke without warning and she had to quickly find a replacement.“We had already decided that we didn’t want the smart functionality, but it became really clear that it was very hard to find one that didn’t have any,” she says. Northmore, whose partner works in cybersecurity, says the couple wanted to “keep control” over their devices, which cost them a premium. “We were willing to pay more. One of the boundaries in how we live our lives is we want to minimise the smart element. We don’t have smart speakers. We don’t enable or connect to the internet.”View image in fullscreen‘Our living room is not a billboard for sale’ … a smart TV aerial.Photograph: Zdenek Maly/AlamyToday, she watches entertainment through a Sky box connected to her dumb TV, and dreads that when her current telly breaks there won’t be any option but to get a smart model and offer up her data.More consumers are becoming worried about how their information is being used by manufacturers. “There are increasing privacy concerns around to what degree TVs are essentially scraping your data,” says Parsons. “TVs these days are full of sensors, including microphones, and that can make people nervous.”But according to Parsons, despite interest in “dumber” models from some buyers, most shoppers want their TVs to be catch-all entertainment systems. The result is that the dumb TV market is almost nonexistent. “You can buy cheap monitors for signage,” he says, “but from a features point of view, you wouldn’t get the same performance that you would from a consumer TV.”Paul, a public servant from Australia, knows just how hard finding a traditional TV can be. “When my last telly – a glorious 32-inch dumb TV – died recently, aged approximately 10 years old, I spent about three weeks scouring the city looking for something comparable. What I found is that they do not exist any more.”After much searching, Paul discovered a single 40-inch TV without any smart functionality in the back of a shop. “It had zero ways to connect to the internet – just a couple of plugs on the back for making it work with the aerial on the roof and my VHS player, and that was it.” He remembers that it “was very dusty and cost about 200 dollars. Naturally, we fell instantly in love.”“My friends all laugh at it when they come over,” he admits, “but secretly I know the joke is on them. My little telly doesn’t spy on me, and has a DVD player built in.”The punchline may eventually land on Paul, however. In September, the Australian government launched aconsultation into the future of the country’s free-to-air broadcasting, asking citizens for feedback on how TV should be accessed. One of the proposed scenarios would see traditional broadcast services cut in favour of streaming services and video on-demand apps.View image in fullscreen‘My little telly doesn’t spy on me’ … some users such as Paul are clinging hard to analogue.Photograph: Dmitriy Shironosov/AlamyIn the same month, the UK government released amedia green paperoutlining its plan to fully move away from digital terrestrial television to services provided over a broadband connection by 2034 at the earliest. Such a situation would mean viewers having to rely on broadcaster apps and streaming services.If a similar fate befell North America, James certainly wouldn’t care. He is originally from the US but now lives in British Columbia, Canada, and says traditional broadcast TV is “dead to him” and that he prefers to watch shows on streaming services or on YouTube. For the father and husband, privacy is a top priority.“No one expects an end-user licence agreement to include giving up autonomy,” he says. “Having my TV listen to any conversation and use that for monetary or any form of gain is above and beyond expectations on the loss of privacy.”In September, the YouTube channel Gamers Nexus releaseda two-hour investigationinto LG Electronics’ smart televisions, saying that the devices record audio – even when they are offline or powered down. The South Korean companydenied the allegations. In the fallout, some have taken measures to modify their smart TVs, regardless of brand or model. Some videos online show usersreplacing motherboards, cutting out Bluetooth and wifi modules and removing microphones from their TV remote controls.Amid the controversy, James read online advice that modifying a TV remote microphone was a simple procedure. So he surgically removed the sensor himself. “Removing the mic was literally as easy as using a [craft] knife to scrape it off the top,” he says, “and the remote continued to work fine.”James’s willingness to dissect his tech comes from fears for his children. “My kids are not teenagers and they have no agency to protect their private information,” he says. “Someone listening in on a TV gets to find out about my daughter’s first period without her knowing. And that is a level of invasion no one should have without explicit consent.”Frustration and controversies have sparked a DIY interest in opening up and neutering the black rectangles in our living rooms. Though the desire in the first place may lead consumers to ask themselves an important question: have our TVs become too smart for their own good?Gutting any piece of electronic equipment should be left to professionals. However, some may find that, for a complex problem, the simplest solutions are the most elegant. As Dan recalls: “It was enormously satisfying when I threw a rock through the screen.”Explore more on these topicsTelevisionPrivacyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Hollywood AI-listers: is the technology ready to rival flesh-and-blood film stars? | Movies | The Guardian
description: As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the corner
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the corner
Content: ‘Really, really scary’ … AI actor Tilly Norwood.Computer-generated: Particle6View image in fullscreen‘Really, really scary’ … AI actor Tilly Norwood.Computer-generated: Particle6Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.MoviesHollywood AI-listers: is the technology ready to rival flesh-and-blood film stars?As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the cornerPhil HoadTue 20 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 10.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Don’t fear the dead – and don’t fear me.” An exact facsimile of a youngVal Kilmer, not quite dead and not quite alive, utters that baiting line in the trailer for the new western As Deep as the Grave. Director Coerte Voorhees knows exactly what he is doing – this is an AI-created version of the late actor, approved by his family but bringing with it a heap of controversy about whether such technology could make flesh-and-blood thespians redundant.Not just yet, judging by theextended glimpse of the film released earlier this year: it looks like a thirtysomething Kilmer, if a robot version had been sent back to the 1920s American wilderness by Skynet and, as well as being strangely rigid, had forgotten to download his voice, let alone his signature air of spacey shrewdness. Kilmer’s estate signed off on it, citing his enthusiasm for new technology that expands storytelling, but surely he would have been dismayed by this freaky doppelganger.Many reacted with revulsion to last year’sunveiling of AI “starlet” Tilly Norwood. After her appearance in an introductory “comedy” sketch, Emily Blunt described her as “really, really scary” – underscoring the depth of feeling around the idea of synthetic performers supplanting real ones. What you might call the Norwood injunction – the feeling of a tech-driven agenda imposing something no one asked for – deepened with the announcement the AI-lister will be soon appear infeature-length film Misaligned.Tim Webber, the chief creative officer at British VFX powerhouse Framestore, is sceptical about whether fully AI-generated actors can ever capture the complexity of our inner lives. “AI models are trained on the surface of things – the pixels of internet images, if they’re image models. To get to the level where it’s a human performance, where there’s genuine emotion involved, is a long way further down,” he says. So AI acting, scraping the external texture of past performances, would seem to be the inverse of something like method acting – whose acolytes excavate their internal psyche and emotions in the interests of authenticity.Is it time to enter the Tillyverse? Seven things you need to know about AI ‘actor’ Tilly NorwoodRead moreBut AI acting is undeniably becoming more realistic. Higgsfield AI – one of many companies currently pushing the possibilities of AI video – recently claimed to have “eliminated” the uncanny valley: that nagging phoneysimilitude effect that has plagued even sophisticated recent CGI reincarnations, such as thede-aged Indiana Jones in The Dial of Destiny.Having released two full-length, entirely AI-generated features this year, Higgsfield’s content lead Adil Alimzhanov is bullish. This new frontier of completely AI-generated films is liberating for artists, he says, and shortcuts laborious Hollywood production structures. The two online-only releases –Hell Grind, a 95-minute action fantasy, and The Cully Hill Boys, a 115-minute Guy Ritchie-esque caper comedy – completed the equivalent of shooting and post-production in a fortnight and a month respectively (not counting time spent on the scripts). Despite actors’ qualms, the future can’t be resisted, says Alimzhanov, 23, who used his own face for Hell Grind’s protagonist. “We can’t fight new tools simply because they transform industries. If you draw a parallel with when cars first came out, if we’d fought that, everybody would still be riding horses today.”Hell Grind and The Cully Hill Boys are essentially extended ads for Higgsfield’s suite of AI content-creation tools. But they show swift progression on the AI acting front. In Hell Grind, released in May, the skate-rat characters only seem to be able to crank out a single emotion per 15-second shot (the limit of the Chinese video-AI model used, Seedance 2.0). The Cully Hill Boys, which came out three months later, is far more engaging, with enough convincing repartee and comic timing to qualify it as quite funny. Its lead trio of grime rappers on the lam are AI-generated likenesses of real-life streetball player Matt Kiatipis, MMA fighter Israel Adesanya and livestreamer N3on – testament to the gen Z, AI-native short-form creators Higgsfield aims to attract. Though there is something quaint about the idea of an “actor” in the age of AI. If bespoke characters can be generated for every film, why have an intermediary play a “role”?Written by a human being, Tim Planagan, The Cully Hill Boys was assembled in 30-second chunks, made possible by this summer’s release of Seedance 2.5. But prompting your way towards something dramatically convincing is labour-intensive. First, visual “assets” are created of the characters – detailed body-length shots and facial closeups that are used to establish continuity when fed into video-generation prompts. Then, using the assets as an anchor point, each 30-second segment is defined in a 4,000-word prompt (itself partly generated by an LLM) defining the key parameters: action, camera movement, lighting and, of course, the emotions on display. The prompts are revised and the scene regenerated until the uncanny valley is hopefully bridged.double quotation markIt becomes a case of treating the model like a marionette doll and tweaking individual stringsWhere, say, Klaus Kinski could summon torrents of rage by tapping into his personal demons, an AI programmer has to achieve the same effect in much more approximate ways. “An AI is not an actor, so how do you communicate the internal state of a character?” says Zack London, who asGossip Goblinmakes highly baroque AI-generated sci-fi shorts. “You can say: they look confused, or they say this in jest, or they say this sternly. But it’s such a broad stroke. The model will probably come out with a very over-the-top telenovela-type performance, or will just not understand.” At that point, it becomes a case of treating the model like a “marionette doll” and tweaking individual strings. “You could say: there’s a slight quiver on the left side of their lip, and then their gaze diverts slightly downwards, and they look up again and blink.”London chooses to keep a human ghost in the machine by first recording dialogue with real actors, around which he retro-fits the animation. He is candid about the shortcomings of the current prompting process, saying the results suit a certain type of film: “The acting is not going to be particularly subtle, like some grand Anthony Hopkins or Olivia Colman performance. It’s more like an old-school Terry Gilliam or Guy Ritchie performance, where the characters are larger than life.” But maybe that’s where the danger lies for actors: many blockbuster performances, meting out simple beats of easily comprehensible emotion, have a cut-and-paste quality – and are therefore susceptible to AI.Then again, a mundane magic still happens even on blockbuster sets. “Sometimes the most brilliant moment happens in the fraction of a second. And you can’t put your finger on why an actor gives a certain look,” saysTye Sheridan, the co-founder (in 2016) of Wonder Dynamics, an Autodesk company who developed the AI production tool Autodesk Flow Studio. He should know: he was the star of Steven Spielberg’s 2018 filmReady Player One, which itself patrolled the frontier between real and digital.View image in fullscreen‘You can’t put your finger on it’ … Tye Sheridan in Ready Player One.Photograph: courtesy of Warner Bros Pictures/APSheridan shares Higgsfield’s belief that AI-driven methods can democratise film-making. But he is adamant that performances should retain a human core.Flow Studiouses AI for an augmented and far cheaper version of motion capture, layering CG characters and environments on top of filmed footage. At Framestore, Webber is exploring similar AI tools that allow him to apply what he calls “digital makeup” to traditional performances, without the guesswork involved in generative prompts.He, London and Sheridan agree that this hybrid form of film-making still allows actors to make specific choices essential to authentic creation. “You have to ask, with these generative models: are they really designed to deliver legendary performances, or are they designed to cut to an average?” asks Sheridan. Alimzhanov, though, insists something akin to an actor’s internal process is achievable via AI. The prompting used on The Cully Hill Boys was different in one key regard: instead of replicating emotions by specifying the physical mechanics, the AI model generated sequences based on contextual input about what the characters were experiencing.These two camps of AI acting – technological and human-centric – are fighting the latest bout in the struggle between the forces that have shaped the craft: external v internal; reproducing v experiencing; Laurence Olivier telling Dustin Hoffman that, instead of staying awake for 72 hours, he should “try acting, dear boy”. But where Stanislavsky promoted the internal quest to revitalise acting, this could be the first time in the modern era when the formalist approach – the mannered reproduction of emotions – looks like the future.Opening the digital floodgates could lead toWilliam Gibson territory, where deathless virtual stars seduce the masses, as in his 1996 novel Idoru. But it’s still not clear whether the box office demand, and thus a true economic case, for AI cinema exists. And we’re yet to see a compelling script that crystallises the possibilities of the tech in story form, as The Matrix did for CGI. If we’re inundated with unloved AI abominations, the words of Val Kilmer in Tombstone, playing that icon of human mortality, Doc Holliday, will ring anew: “There’s just something about him. Something around the eyes reminds me of … me. I’m sure of it – I hate him.”Explore more on these topicsFilmAI (artificial intelligence)Val KilmerTilly Norwood (AI character)featuresShareReuse this content

title: TS Eliot’s Murder in the Cathedral review – gather in wonder at David Suchet’s excellent archbishop | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The poet’s 1935 verse drama has its eccentricities but the meticulous star plays Thomas Becket with a Shakespearean relish
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: The poet’s 1935 verse drama has its eccentricities but the meticulous star plays Thomas Becket with a Shakespearean relish
Content: Mass appeal … David Suchet as Thomas Becket in Murder in the Cathedral at St John the Divine church.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenMass appeal … David Suchet as Thomas Becket in Murder in the Cathedral at St John the Divine church.Photograph: Marc BrennerTheatreReviewTS Eliot’s Murder in the Cathedral review – gather in wonder at David Suchet’s excellent archbishopSt John the Divine church, LondonThe poet’s 1935 verse drama has its eccentricities but the meticulous star plays Thomas Becket with a Shakespearean relishMark LawsonTue 20 Oct 2026 07.50 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 15.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAstriking example of site-specific theatre, TS Eliot’sMurder in the Cathedralwas first performed in 1935 at Canterbury Cathedral. This was the location, in 1170, for its pivotal event: the killing by Henry II’s knights of Archbishop Thomas Becket during a dispute over the powers of church and state.Subsequently, audiences have been more likely to enter a production via a church nave than a theatre aisle. The latest host venue is St John the Divine, opposite theOrange Tree theatre, whose boss, Tom Littler, co-directs with Francesca Ellis.David Suchet’s Becket, in gilded vestments, preaches from the pulpit. Dozens of candles on the altar and lining a marbled walkway between pews (design by Rob Jones, lighting by Peter Mumford) cast shadows on the walls around stained glass windows.The overall classiness of the show is extended by a programme essay by an actual former archbishop of Canterbury,Rowan Williams, covering Eliot’s concern with whether priests, in 1930s England and Germany, served or resisted politicians.View image in fullscreenHard lesson … (from left) David Yelland, Ben Caplan, David Suchet, Nick Sampson and Jyuddah Jaymes.Photograph: Marc BrennerNo staging can disguise the eccentricities of a text that begins classically with a Greek-like chorus of Canterbury women (Eliot’s four swollen to a dozen by a community ensemble) but concludes with a precociously postmodern coda where the slaughtering quartet engage the audience in an emergency seminar about whether the churchman deserved it.Like Pinter heavies in black leather jackets and polo sweaters, Jyuddah Jaymes, Ben Caplan, Nick Sampson and David Yelland memorably double the murderous knights with the four tempters who offer Becket varieties of earthly and heavenly riches. Less successfully, the women’s choruses are musicalised (composer Orlando Gough) more than Eliot indicated, muffling some of the poetry in a piece with lines (“Human kind cannot bear very much reality”) directly rehearsing Eliot’s Four Quartets.His verse dramas often feel more written for page than stage; of seven plays, only this one is regularly revived and his biggest theatrical hit was, inadvertently, the musical Cats. Becket is a role with difficult rhythms for an actor. Initially listening to lengthy speeches by women, priests and tempters with minimal responses, the character then speaks unbroken for six pages.Listen out for Lanny: can Max Porter’s mythic tale of a mulch-guzzler really be heard in this woodland?Read moreAlways a meticulous actor, Suchet makes each gesture and syllable precise and shows the making up of Becket’s mind in the responsive phase and then brings the clarity and verbal relish of the best Shakespearean soliloquies to the Christmas Day sermon in which the turbulent priest accepts that he must be killed.Eliot, raised in the austere Unitarian church in St Louis, seems, on converting to Anglo-Catholicism in 1927, to have been enthralled by its tradition of martyrs and the play challenges each age with the balance between conviction and fanaticism, belief and futile sacrifice. If everything in churches were as dramatic and atmospheric as this, Becket’s current successor would not have to worry about declining congregations.AtSt John the Divine church,London, until 7 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreOrange Tree theatreDavid SuchetTS EliotReligionPoetryAnglicanismreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Taylor Swift tells us to take the lead!’ Could highly organised pop fans clinch victory for Brazil’s Lula? | Music | The Guardian
description: Brazil’s famously outspoken fandoms have near-unanimously rallied behind the leftwing presidential candidate. On the streets of São Paulo, they explain their mission
Author: Felipe Maia
Headline: Brazil’s famously outspoken fandoms have near-unanimously rallied behind the leftwing presidential candidate. On the streets of São Paulo, they explain their mission
Content: Two pop fans at a pro-Lula demonstration in São Paulo.Photograph: Felipe MaiaView image in fullscreenTwo pop fans at a pro-Lula demonstration in São Paulo.Photograph: Felipe MaiaMusic‘Taylor Swift tells us to take the lead!’ Could highly organised pop fans clinch victory for Brazil’s Lula?Brazil’s famously outspoken fandoms have near-unanimously rallied behind the leftwing presidential candidate. On the streets of São Paulo, they explain their missionFelipe MaiaTue 20 Oct 2026 06.23 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 06.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier this month, Brazil’s presidentLuiz Inácio Lula da Silvaled a rally in São Paulo, as he aims to be re-elected to a fourth presidential term, and faces serious opposition from right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro. Taking the mic before a crowd on Avenida Paulista that organisers put at more than a million, the former union leader began: “I’m not sure whether to open this speech with ‘comrades’ or ‘fandoms from all over Brazil’.” The rally was organised by Lula’s Workers’ party (PT) and a string of other leftwing groups – but the spark came from pop music fandoms.More than 600 Brazilian fanbase groups forBillie Eilish, Lady Gaga, Katseye, Demi Lovato, Harry Styles, Katy Perry, Selena Gomez, as well as Brazilian stars such as Anitta, Marina Sena and Ludmilla among others, all came together to back Lula, waging an intense online campaign as soon as Lula’s rival, son of imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro, came out on top in the first round on 4 October. Neither candidate earned more than 50% of the vote, so a runoff is now scheduled for 25 October to decide between the two.When the first round results came in, “I had this feeling I’d seen it all before with Jair Bolsonaro, and that was really frustrating,” says V, a Billie Eilish fan who helps run Info Billie Brasil, one of the country’s biggest fan communities dedicated to the US singer. “So my first reaction was to use the only communication tool we have and get our community to embrace the cause: Lula’s re-election.”View image in fullscreenAnother pro-Lula demonstrator.Photograph: V-Info Billie BrasilThe account posted a short open letter to Lula on X and Instagram: “Our social media pages are open for you and your team”. Within hours, a wave of fan accounts had shared the same message. “We knew social media had always been a weak spot for his campaign, so for the second round we’ll do everything we can to get the word out about Lula’s government,” says V (their name, and others in this report, have been anonymised). The initiative eventually grew into Fandoms Pelo Brasil, a website explaining to pop music fans how to mobilise for Lula. “Our frustration with the election turned into something massive, uncontrollable.”Amid the crowd on Paulista, São Paulo’s main avenue, supporters carried the familiar symbols of the left, from the hammer and sickle to Palestinian flags, but there were newcomers too: Beyhive T-shirts, BTS merch andTaylor Swiftmotifs.“We’re inspired by these artists, and Taylor is always talking about how young people should take the lead,” said Josiane, a Swiftie. Her friend Giovanna, a member of the Army fandom for K-poppersBTS, agrees: “We need to step up and make ourselves heard.”“A lot of people don’t keep up with politics, but they do follow fanclubs and fan accounts, so I think fandoms can bring this kind of discussion to more people,” said Raissa, a Beyoncé fan. “She’s a pop diva who talks about LGBTQ+ freedom and freedom of speech, and that matters to us too.”Pop stars’ mostly progressive politics, however tempered by the commercial interests of the music industry, are the main convergence point for these fandoms. And the influence can run the other way, too. After Info Billie Brasil reached out to him, Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and collaborator, endorsed the movement with a story on his Instagram account.“Our views clearly line up with those of the Blackpink members,” says W, one of the people who run a leading Blackpink fan account inBrazil. “Some of them are ambassadors for Unicef or the UN, and they stand up for the environment and women’s rights. We can’t speak for them, but our ideas are aligned.”Pop music is a huge business in Brazil, and the country’s fans are globally famed – even notorious – for the intensity of their fandom, imploring artists to tour from overseas via hundreds of comments on their social media pages.View image in fullscreenA fan with a bag featuring bespoke BTS stickers.Photograph: Felipe MaiaLula’s government has cannily courted these vociferous, campaign-minded fans. In August, he signed a “fan decree” cracking down on ticket-scalping bots and requiring free drinking water at all large public events. Some fandom representatives attended a meeting with the president. “There was no political coordination in regards to the election on our side back then, but ticketing is a huge part of fan life,” says W.Fandoms aren’t unanimously leftwing.NJZ Brasil, a fan page for the K-pop group NewJeans, is openly pro-Bolsonaro; W says they have “noticed comments and messages from rightwing voters in the Blackpink fan community”.Shakira Brasilhas stayed out of political campaigns, following an earlier instruction from Shakira’s team restricting the use of the singer’s image in political content online.But V rejects that stance: “I remember congresswoman Erika Hilton once saying that everything is political, so a party or a concert can be political too.” Hilton, who was re-elected this month as the most-voted woman in the history of Brazil’s lower house, joined forces with fandoms in 2024 to campaign against a bill that would have equated abortion after 22 weeks of pregnancy with homicide, even in cases of rape. The bill stalled after a public backlash.“We’ll wage a digital guerrilla campaign, but we’ll be on the streets as well,” Hilton said in avoice notesent to the fandoms the day after the first round. “Lula will be president again. That’s our mission, and we’re in this together – count on me.”The Info Billie Brasil team has told its followers that, until the runoff, politics will take priority over Billie Eilish news, “because we can get our issues seen,” says V. “We want to win rightwing voters over to the left. We won’t stop.”Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaFlávio BolsonaroAmericasTaylor SwiftfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The CO2-absorbing building made of old sinks, windscreens and toilets: Ghent’s £17m design museum is a green marvel | Architecture | The Guardian
description: Inspired by a gothic cathedral partly built using human bones, this gleaming monument to recycling boasts 82,000 bricks derived from construction waste – following a two-day brick-making festival
Author: Oliver Wainwright
Headline: Inspired by a gothic cathedral partly built using human bones, this gleaming monument to recycling boasts 82,000 bricks derived from construction waste – following a two-day brick-making festival
Content: Even its loos have QR codes … the building lit up for its opening party.Photograph: Behangmotief for Design Museum GentView image in fullscreenEven its loos have QR codes … the building lit up for its opening party.Photograph: Behangmotief for Design Museum GentArchitectureThe CO2-absorbing building made of old sinks, windscreens and toilets: Ghent’s £17m design museum is a green marvelInspired by a gothic cathedral partly built using human bones, this gleaming monument to recycling boasts 82,000 bricks derived from construction waste – following a two-day brick-making festivalOliver WainwrightTue 20 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMuseums often try to reflect the world around them, but rarely are they made so literally of their surroundings as thenew design museum in Ghent. Rising above the Belgian city’s medieval tiled rooftops like an angular white watchtower, the new building has vacuumed up the city’s condemned concrete frames, windows, car windscreens, sinks and old toilets, and transformed them, phoenix-like, into a gleaming monument to recycling.“There’s nothing new about reuse,” says Andy Groarke, co-founder ofCarmody Groarke, the London-based architects who designed the €20m (£17m) project with local firmsAtamaandRe-st. “We’ve just forgotten how to do it.”double quotation markFor €10, you can take a brick home from the museum shopHe says the team drew inspiration from Ghent’s 16th-century gothic cathedral, Saint Bavo’s, which was partly built using the white limestone blocks of the 10th-century romanesque basilica that had stood on the same site (recent renovations also ghoulishly uncoveredwalls made of human bones, femurs and tibias apparently having particularly useful structural properties, with crushed skulls for infill).View image in fullscreenEarthy layers of rubble … Design Museum Ghent.Photograph: Oliver WainwrightThe new design museum doesn’t quite go that far in its nose-to-tail approach, but almost. The toilet cubicles are a smorgasbord of “biomaterials”, each featuring different tiles made of seaweed, flax, wood terrazzo and volcanic ash (you can scan a QR code for more info while you’re sitting on the loo). Some walls are plastered with local clay, while a chunky column in the entrance hall revels in its earthy layers of rubble dug straight from the building site.But thereal innovation is the brick, which was specially developed, tested and certified for the project (funded by a grant from Circular Flanders and Sogent, the city’s development agency). Each brick is made of 63% construction waste, sourced from within 8km of the museum, pulverised and compressed with hydrated lime, saving two-thirds of the embodied carbon of a regular fired clay brick. And the lime will continue to absorb CO2 from the atmosphere as it cures over the coming months and years.“We’re not claiming this is a panacea, or a solution to the climate crisis,” says architect Sian Ricketts, Carmody Groarke’s sustainability lead. “But it is a sort of 82,000-brick proof of concept that you can do something different, with the right collaborators and the right clients.” Developed by East Sussex firmLocal Works Studioand Brussels groupBC Materials, the bricks were made in a former railway depot nearby, with the public invited to mix the ingredients and press their own blocks during a two-day festival of brickmaking. For €10, you can take one home from the museum shop.Public participation extended to defining the very essence of the museum, too. In keeping with Belgium’s democratic traditions, a“citizens’ panel”of 40 people, drawn from a wide variety of Ghent residents, was established to inform what the museum should be. Their 100+ recommendations ranged from incorporating unticketed areas, to being able to see work-in-progress, and having plenty of seating, as well as ensuring that the “chic” building didn’t put people off. The result is as locally sourced and collaboratively created as big civic buildings come. “This expansion and renovation are not about creating more museum,” says the outgoing director, Katrien Laporte, “but about creating more than a museum: a community sense-making museum with real social relevance.”View image in fullscreenAngular geometries … Design Museum Ghent.Photograph: Johan DehlinThe extension fills a leftover plot on the museum’s site, uniting the galleries that were previously spread between an 18th-century rococo mansion, called the Hotel de Coninck, and a troublesome 1990s addition – designed with a moving glass floor that rarely moved, now thankfully banished. The new building stands with the presence of a grand Ghent house, rising in five large storeys, and turning as it climbs to face the city centre, with big picture windows looking out in different directions on each floor. “We wanted it to feel domestic, industrial and civic at once,” says Groarke. It certainly has a bold presence.Not everyone has welcomed its industrial bulk. Concerns have been raised about how the boxy white mass lumbers into view from the city’s quaint historical centre, and there is something slightly clumsy about the form on the skyline, topped with multiple roofs angled in different directions. Silicone joints between stretches of brick don’t help either, reading as unsightly seams from a distance. The museum defended the height as providing never-before-seen views of the city, and it’s true: when you’re on the top floor – a freely accessible public loft – or the roof terrace below, the panoramic vistas of Ghent’s castle and church spires are a treat.View image in fullscreenLumbers into view … Design Museum Ghent.Photograph: Michiel De Cleene/Design Museum GhentSkyline concerns also fade away as you approach the museum at street level. Agate in the form of a billowing metallic curtain, frozen in motion, signals the new entrance in a delightfully surreal touch. Designed by Antwerp studio Unfold and 3D-printed in aluminium, it is a welcome change from the previously off-putting carriage entrance of the historical hotel down the sidestreet. The striking gate is one of a series ofspecial projectscommissioned by curator Siegrid Demyttenaere that have been dotted throughout the building, from a cast street number to a reception desk and lockers, making functional parts of the museum exhibits in themselves.A lobby lined with timber salvaged from a tobacco factory in Brussels leads into thestadskamer, or city room, opening through big sliding windows on to the museum courtyard on one side, and the street on the other. It was thronging with visitors during the opening weekend, with the feeling of a true public square. The chubby earthen column (a commission byGrond Studio) rises to support an intersection of the deep wooden beams that crisscross the ceiling, the first glimpse of the building’s sculptural timber frame. The architects say it is the biggest mass timber public building in Belgium, featuring walls and floors of spruce CLT (cross-laminated timber) and chunky beams of beech LVL (laminated veneer lumber), imported from Austria. A beautiful oak staircase connects the floors, with joinery details in darker walnut, its angular geometries lending a Piranesian air.View image in fullscreen‘The feeling of a true public square’ … the stadskamer (city room).Photograph: Johan DehlinThe new building is “a stack of five rooms”, says Groarke, “each with a particular identity”. The stairs lead to the Forum, for lectures and events; the Atelier, a light-flooded studio for education workshops; and the Vitrine for temporary exhibitions – before arriving at the Loft, a grand event space with spectacular views. Its balcony became an urban-scale DJ booth for the opening party, when local duo2manydjsperformed above the rooftops to 5,000 revellers dancing in the streets below.Spectacle aside, one of the building’s most useful achievements is connecting the museum’s pre-existing wings in a continuous, accessible loop for the first time. Visitors can now move from the chandelier-bedecked suites of the Hotel de Coninck, through to the 90s wing – from which 60% of the columns have been removed and voids filled in to create more display space for the permanent collection – to the light, woody world of the new tower. It was made possible by a wise use of funds: while competing architects proposed taller towers and deeper basement levels, the winning team suggested a better use of some of the tight budget would be to refurbish and renew what was already there.View image in fullscreen‘Functional parts of the museum are exhibits in themselves’ … the entrance gate by Unfold.Photograph: Johan Dehlin“The competition was such a great process,” says Groarke, singing the praises of the renownedFlemish Open Callrun by the Vlaams Bouwmeester (the government architect), with a jury that included five international museum directors alongside architects and planners. You can stillsee all the entries online. “Architecture is in the public consciousness here in a way that it’s not in the UK,” Groarke continues. “Back home, it’s seen as an extension of the property industry, with a pyramid scheme of mediocrity in the way.”He’s got a point. It would be hard to imagine a building of such quality and imagination being realised on British shores, where contractors rule all and architects are forced to compete on fees in a self-sabotaging race to the bottom. Public procurement rules also mean architects generally have to have built several buildings of the type they are bidding for before they can even qualify to compete, meaning few opportunities for young practices.Our bureaucrats might do well to spend some time in the museum’s opening exhibition,Public Matter(s): Design and Democracy. Curated by Amelie Klein and Vera Sacchetti, it is a fascinating exploration of the design of democratic decision-making, examining everything from ballot papers to the layout of parliament buildings, to how nature might be given a seat at the table. One particularly revealing project,The Flemish Scrollersby artist Dries Depoorter, uses AI to track distracted politicians scrolling on their phones during parliamentary sessions, and automatically posts screenshots of the live stream to social media, asking the elected officials to do better.Perhaps a similar algorithm could be used to name and shame each time a public tender is awarded to the same old suspects, with dismal results for our built environment. Once again, the Flems are leading the way.Explore more on these topicsArchitectureBelgiumMuseumsDesignGreen buildingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘If the lion does not tell its story, the hunter will’: a century of thrilling Cameroonian art | Art | The Guardian
description: Key players in the country’s art history feature in a hefty new tome that covers everything from royal-carvers to bronze-smiths to work inspired by a horrific video smuggled out of a torture chamber
Author: Eromo Egbejule
Headline: Key players in the country’s art history feature in a hefty new tome that covers everything from royal-carvers to bronze-smiths to work inspired by a horrific video smuggled out of a torture chamber
Content: La salle à manger (The Dining Room) by Roxane Mbanga.Photograph: (c) Studio VanssayView image in fullscreenLa salle à manger (The Dining Room) by Roxane Mbanga.Photograph: (c) Studio VanssayArt‘If the lion does not tell its story, the hunter will’: a century of thrilling Cameroonian artKey players in the country’s art history feature in a hefty new tome that covers everything from royal-carvers to bronze-smiths to work inspired by a horrific video smuggled out of a torture chamberEromo Egbejulein AbidjanTue 20 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne Sunday last year, the Cameroonian-Guadeloupean-French artistRoxane Mbangawas relaxing in bed when she received a message that made her sit up. It was about working on an art history project.Growing up in Paris, she had been a regular at Maasai Mara, the now defunct restaurant owned by her father, where Africans in the diaspora, including the artists whom he helped organise exhibitions, convened to eat and chat. Thus the concept of a book, attempting for the first time to comprehensively compile and document key players in Cameroon’s vast visual art history, made obvious sense to her.“It’s a magical reconnaissance, being recognised by my peers and being in the same book as people I look up to,” says the 30-year-old artist. “This idea of creating spaces, as with the book, is incredibly important because it allows us to build from there and leave traces for people that will come after. I really lacked that growing up … spaces like books, podcasts or whatever, where I could really see people that resemble me, that do things similar to me.”View image in fullscreenThe first African woman to curate the Venice Biennale … Koyo Kouoh.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesShe is one of 180 artists who appear inÔ Cameroon!, a 424-page volume that launches at the1-54 Contemporary African Art Fairin London in October, with planned stops in Côte d’Ivoire’s Abidjan, Paris and the Cameroonian cities of Douala and Yaoundé. Posthumous additions include the painter-sculptorKoko Komégné, who died three weeks after submitting his contribution to the book, and the first African woman to curate the Venice Biennale, Koyo Kouoh whodied of cancerlast year.The book was curated and conceived by Cameroonian national Ozong Agborsangaya-Fiteu, an Abidjan-based collector and development finance executive. During her travels, she kept encountering artists from her homeland of different generations and in different places, and realised that there was also no single archive or directory to find out more about them.“There was a sense of absence or loss … I became increasingly conscious that if we did not document these artists’ works, some could just simply disappear,” she says. “At some point, my own curiosity became a feeling of urgent responsibility. I began to feel that if we did not gather these histories right away, we might lose them for ever.”In 1919 , a year after Germany was defeated in the first world war, its former colony of Kamerun was split into two unequal halves between the French and British. Despite the profound transformation – and as European colonial administrators looted thousands of artefacts from the country – societies of artists continued their intellectual and cultural work underground. Royal carvers and bronze-smiths in the ancient walled city of Foumban, for example, thrived under the reign of Sultan Njoya, famed for his promotion of the arts.Ô Cameroon!covers from then until 2025, a century of diverse art from east to west and between anglophone and francophone regions, presented in non-chronological order. “The book is an act of cultural recovery and restitution,” says Agborsangaya-Fiteu. “Art for Cameroon is not a new story. Before Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso and Constantin Brâncuși, there were big sculptors likeAteu Atsa, who is Cameroonian” – from the 19th century. “Many of these artists influenced European modernism.View image in fullscreenSymphonie by Koko Komégné.Photograph: Courtesy the artist“If the lion does not tell its story, the hunter will,” she adds. “This is an attempt for the lion to tell its own story, and given that Cameroon is so complex, it was very important that the story be told by multiple voices so that there could be multiple interpretations and perspectives shaping the book.”In 1961, a UN plebiscite led to English-speaking Southern Cameroons rejoining the country after almost four decades as part of neighbouring Nigeria, while Northern Cameroons voted to remain in Nigeria. That reunion laid the foundation for a civil war between the anglophones and the state security apparatus, while deepening regional tensions. In that time, some on the art scene who didn’t leave earlier under the repressive, four-decade rule of Paul Biya, who remainsthe world’s oldest head of state, emigrated.The most recent chapter of Cameroon’s art history has been tough to document. Among those included in the book isEm’kal Eyongakpa, an Amsterdam-based botanist turned artist, who has worked on subjects focusing on the Cameroon volcanic line. He had plans for building a physical art space in his native south-west Cameroon, but they were disrupted by the anglophone conflict.“I think [the book is] mainly for historicity and because there is a need for accuracy, especially with respect to people from my side of the Cameroons, as Cameroon is two colonial entities that came together,” says Eyongakpa, who now runs creative spaces in camp settlements in southern Nigeria hosting refugees who fled Cameroon.One of his projects documented in the book is sǒbàtú“to cleanse one’s ears” (in the Kenyang language), inspired by a horrific video smuggled out of a torture chamber as the crisis intensified. He hopes it can fill a gap. “There had not been any discussions within the academia that really looks at this conflict that has taken the lives of so many people and it really felt like kind of a big betrayal,” he says.For Agborsangaya-Fiteu, this book is only a start. She wants to inspire more exhibitions and research including elsewhere in Africa. “This was a very emotional project and I’m getting goosebumps as I reflect,” she says, sobbing quietly. “It’s a love story since we are all immigrants. We all left to go out to find things to do, to find our dignity and get education, to find our purpose. But I was born in Cameroon, so you cannot [but] love where you’re from.”Mbanga, who has been on a lifetime quest for identity, believes that the book can help broaden the scope for young artists like her in the diaspora: “I think it can allow people to dream bigger.”Explore more on these topicsArtArt and design booksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Vast Beatles museum, hailed as ‘extraordinary’ by Paul McCartney, to open in Liverpool in 2028 | Music | The Guardian
description: City’s Beatles Story museum to move to 100,000 sq ft new home and official ownership, along with Yellow Submarine makeover of Liverpool’s second-tallest building
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: City’s Beatles Story museum to move to 100,000 sq ft new home and official ownership, along with Yellow Submarine makeover of Liverpool’s second-tallest building
Content: ‘Liverpool was, and still is, a music city’ … the Beatles in 1962.View image in fullscreen‘Liverpool was, and still is, a music city’ … the Beatles in 1962.MusicVast Beatles museum, hailed as ‘extraordinary’ by Paul McCartney, to open in Liverpool in 2028City’s Beatles Story museum to move to 100,000 sq ft new home and official ownership, along with Yellow Submarine makeover of Liverpool’s second-tallest buildingBen Beaumont-ThomasTue 20 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLiverpool is to unveil a new 100,000 sq ft visitor attraction about the Beatles, in plans hailed as “extraordinary” byPaul McCartney, and by Andy Burnham as having “the kind of ambition I want to see more of across Britain”.Opening in 2028, the project is a huge upgrade for the Beatles Story, a museum which opened in Liverpool’s Royal Albert Dock in 1990. Ownership will now pass to the Beatles company Apple Corps, making the Beatles Story the band’s first official fan experience in their home city.It will also move across the city to the former shopping centre St John’s Market, close to Liverpool’s Lime Street railway station, which has lain unused since closing in 2024. The new site will allow the museum to become four times bigger than its current home.Apple Corps has also announced it will take over and renovate Liverpool’s second-tallest building: St Johns Beacon, a 450ft tower that has also remained unused since 2024, when its viewing gallery closed and its radio station tenants vacated. Neighbouring the redeveloped museum, the tower will become a separate attraction themed around the Beatles’ whimsical and psychedelic animated film Yellow Submarine.View image in fullscreenSt Johns Beacon pictured earlier this year.Photograph: Chris Chambers/AlamyThe new iteration of the Beatles Story is being billed as a “multi-hour experience” which will recreate settings from the group’s history, from their childhood homes in Liverpool to the city’s Cavern venue and the nightclubs where they cut their teeth in Hamburg, and on to Abbey Road, New York’s Shea Stadium – where Beatlemania provoked such fevered screaming that the band couldn’t hear themselves play – and the building on London’s Savile Row where they played their final rooftop concert in 1969.McCartney said: “I find it incredible and humbling that people are still interested in our story and it’s very exciting to me that the Beatles Story and the Beacon are being transformed in such an exciting way in the heart of Liverpool city. I love Liverpool. It’s part of who I am, it’s part of who the Beatles are. If you’d told us this was going to happen when we were hanging out and getting started, we’d never have believed it.”Ringo Starr also celebrated the plans, saying: “It is great to be part of this – deep down I am still a scouser.“Liverpool was, and still is, a music city. And now we are expanding the Beatles Story … how far out. The beat goes on.”A new charity, the Apple Corps Liverpool Trust, has also been founded. It will receive a portion of every ticket sold, and use that revenue to fund initiatives for local musicians.Andy Burnham praised the Liverpool plans as having “the kind of ambition I want to see more of across Britain: backing the things our great cities do best and turning that global reputation into jobs, opportunity and growth”. He hailed the charitable arm as helping “the next generation of young artists, wherever they grow up, to believe there is a route from their bedroom, rehearsal room or local venue to the very top of the world.”View image in fullscreenSt John’s shopping centre pictured in 2019, part of which will house the new Beatles Story museum.Photograph: Greg Balfour Evans/AlamyLiverpool’s mayor Steve Rotheram said: “People already travel halfway around the globe to visit the birthplace of four lads that shook the earth. These plans take that extraordinary pull to another level – creating a world-class destination that will give millions more fans a reason to make the pilgrimage to their spiritual home and experience the city, its music and its culture for themselves.”The project is being helmed by Apple Corps in tandem with Liverpool city council and Liverpool City Region Combined Authority, with UK government support. Financial details of the project and its partnerships have not been disclosed.Apple Corps’ chief executive Tom Greene compared the plans with Elvis Presley’s Graceland in Memphis or Dolly Parton’s Dollywood in Tennessee: “A world-class destination for fans to visit in the centre of the city where the story started.”Greene is already overseeing the development of another official Beatles attraction: a renovation of 3 Savile Row where that final rooftop concert took place. The seven-floor museum, due to open in 2027, will allow visitors to access the rooftop and will also recreate the building’s in-house studio where they recorded the Let It Be album, alongside showcases of Apple Corps’ archive and temporary exhibitions.The plans come amid sustained and varied efforts to carry the Beatles’ legacy forward, not least with an ambitiousfour-film biopic project helmed by director Sam Mendes, telling the stories of each band member. Currently in production, those films will also arrive in 2028, and sets and props will be reused for the recreated environments in the new iteration of the Beatles Story.The band’s Hamburg era is being separately told in Hamburg Days, a forthcoming BBC drama scripted by Succession writer Jamie Carragher, and a reissue programme of the Beatles’ catalogue continues: an expanded version of 1965’s Rubber Soul reached No 2 in the UK charts earlier this month.View image in fullscreenThe current iteration of The Beatles Story, in Liverpool’s Albert Dock.Photograph: David A Eastley/AlamyThe Beatles are a big tourism draw in Liverpool, with a 2016 study suggesting the band added £82m to the local economy each year.The current iteration of the Beatles Story has helped to drive that success, with exhibits such as George Harrison’s first guitar and John Lennon’s glasses. The museum has won VisitEngland awards for excellence in each of the last two years.Explore more on these topicsMusicThe BeatlesLiverpoolMerseysidePop and rockPaul McCartneyRingo StarrnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s important that Michael’s voice is heard’: Jaafar Jackson says second biopic of his uncle will cover sexual abuse allegations | Movies | The Guardian
description: The star of Michael, the most commercially successful biopic of all time, has said sequel will give airtime to point-of-view of late singer
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: The star of Michael, the most commercially successful biopic of all time, has said sequel will give airtime to point-of-view of late singer
Content: Screen debut … Jaafar Jackson as Michael Jackson in Michael.Photograph: Glen Wilson/LionsgateView image in fullscreenScreen debut … Jaafar Jackson as Michael Jackson in Michael.Photograph: Glen Wilson/LionsgateMovies‘It’s important that Michael’s voice is heard’: Jaafar Jackson says second biopic of his uncle will cover sexual abuse allegationsThe star of Michael, the most commercially successful biopic of all time, has said sequel will give airtime to point-of-view of late singerCatherine ShoardTue 20 Oct 2026 11.15 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 11.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOf all the criticisms levelled at the authorised biopic ofMichael Jacksonreleased earlier this year, the most persistent was that Antoine Fuqua’s film failed to mention the sexual abuse allegations against the singer.In part, this was due to a legal clause, only spotted late in production, which stipulated that one of the men who accused Jackson of abusing them as a boy could never be depicted in a fictionalised account of the period.A sequence involving a police raid at the Neverland ranch was cut, $50m (£37m) of reshoots were funded by the Jackson family, and the narrative was curtailed early.However, the enormous box office response to the film, which recently overtook Oppenheimer as the highest-grossing biopic of all time, has meant a sequel is inevitable.Speaking to Variety, star Jaafar Jackson – the nephew of the man he plays – downplayed the first film’s production woes, saying: “I’ve heard many stories from other actors about how much you shoot on a project that doesn’t make it into the final picture.“In the editing room, you go through scenes looking for specific performances or takes and things change constantly. So going in, I knew not everything we shot would make it into the final picture.”Speaking toGQ Middle East, the actor, who made his screen debut in Michael, also suggested the sequel would address the allegations, albeit from the accused’s standpoint.“I think the second film will give even more insight from [Michael Jackson’s] point of view, because at the end of the day, [the allegations] are always from someone else’s [point of view],”he said. “It’s someone else’s story. It’s someone else’s idea of what it is …”“And that’s really the issue we’ve been having as a family – not having Michael’s voice being heard. I think that’s very, very important, especially in [his later] years.”The actor continued by saying that he felt there was considerable continuity of his uncle’s character between the time periods covered by the films.“He never changed that purity, that sense of always wanting to find the good in other people. And no matter all the stuff he went through, how he was treated, what things were said about him, he never stopped treating people with kindness. He never stopped believing in and wanting to look for the good in people … even though he was broken, his heart still stayed the same.”Earlier this year, Fuqua said the sequel to the film would not “sensationalise” details of Jackson’s life. “I think the key is, like, who was he as a human being? Stay on that path and then we’ll be OK, because that’s what it’s about. It’s a biopic, it’s about a human being, he’s a real person.”‘A false narrative around a paedophile’: Michael Jackson biopic criticised by Leaving Neverland directorRead moreOne of thebestselling music artistsof all time, Jackson’s solo sales topped 500m records. He was first accused of sexually assaulting a child in 1993 and settled out of court the following year. In 2005, he was tried and acquitted on other child sexual abuse charges, and died from an accidental propofol overdose in 2009, aged 50.The 2019 documentaryLeaving Neverlanddetailed further child sexual abuse allegations against Jackson; its director, Dan Reed, criticised the biopic on its release as containing “zero insight into what makes Jackson tick”, saying: “He’s this asexual plastic action doll of a figure in the film. And of course, the issue of his relationship with children is completely distorted by the fact that they portray him as an eccentric, overgrown child, which we know is not the full story.”Reed added: “The film just flips the truth on its head – black is white, white is black, and two and two make five … it’s a movie that’s impossible to take seriously.“He’s become part of the collective imagination, and the collective imagination can never include the fact that he’s a paedophile.”Explore more on these topicsFilmBiopicsMichaelMichael JacksonLeaving NeverlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Actor Christina Applegate reveals she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis | Christina Applegate | The Guardian
description: The Married … With Children actor says the news is ‘unnerving’ and ‘really confusing’
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: The Married … With Children actor says the news is ‘unnerving’ and ‘really confusing’
Content: Christina Applegate at the 29th annual Screen Actors Guild awards on 26 February 2023 in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Gilbert Flores/Variety/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChristina Applegate at the 29th annual Screen Actors Guild awards on 26 February 2023 in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Gilbert Flores/Variety/Getty ImagesChristina ApplegateActor Christina Applegate reveals she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosisThe Married … With Children actor says the news is ‘unnerving’ and ‘really confusing’Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter emailRichard LuscombeTue 20 Oct 2026 09.51 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 12.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter becoming a prominent advocate formultiple sclerosisawareness and chronicling her struggles in anemotional memoirpublished in March, the Emmy-winning actor Christina Applegate has revealed she does not have the debilitating autoimmune disease after all.Applegate, 54, made the stunning announcement in an episode of her podcast MeSsy, recorded with fellow actor Jamie-Lynn Sigler, postedto YouTubeon Tuesday.“I’m back at square one – that I don’t know what’s going on with me,” she said through tears.Applegate recalled the moment she found out about the misdiagnosis in a visit to her doctor.“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations – you don’t have MS.’ I was not happy at all.“You don’t get misdiagnosed, and all of a sudden I’m better. I haven’t gotten better, Jamie. If anything, I’ve gotten worse in some ways.“I still have to use wheelchairs when I go to the doctor’s office. I can’t walk from the car to the room. I’m still in this. Nothing magical happened when she said, ‘You don’t have MS.’ Nothing magical happened.“It’s weird because I feel like I let everybody down. It’s this weird feeling of like I became this, you and I, the poster children for MS.
