All that I did, everything that I was doing, I had a fucking reason as to why my day sucked every day.“And now I don’t have a reason. It’s very unnerving and it’s really confusing for me.”Applegate had revealed in 2021 that she was diagnosed with MS. In aninterviewwith People magazine promoting her memoir, You With the Sad Eyes, she said was largely confined to bed because of her diagnosed condition.She is known for her roles in the TV series Married … With Children and Dead to Me – as well as the films Anchorman: The Legend of Ron Burgundy and Don’t Tell Mom the Babysitter’s Dead.Applegate also worked on the TV show Friends and won a 2002 Emmy for outstanding guest acting in a comedy series.She retired from acting two years after the 2021 MS diagnosis, when she wrapped up her role on Dead to Me.Applegate had also stepped back over the last six months from the podcast with Sigler, whorevealed in 2016her own diagnosis of relapsing MS (RMS).During that period, Applegate said in Tuesday’s episode, “a lot of interesting things happened to me”.She recalled originally receiving her diagnosis in 2021, when a doctor showed her images of dozens of lesions on her brain and confirmed she had MS. “That was it, right? That was my answer to everything going on,” she said, saying she began to feel safe and welcome in the MS community as her treatment moved on.“I had every symptom of someone with MS. Every single one.”She said a study into her diagnosis began “a couple of years ago” after cell testing produced curious results. Now that she knows she does not have the disease, she said: “That’s going to be an online investigation my doctors are going to get into just to find out what has been happening since 2021. Why did this happen?”Later in the episode, Sigler and Applegate discuss what they say is a trend of misdiagnoses.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We have come to learn this is not that rare of an occurrence, especially when it comes to MS,” Sigler said.Applegate added: “There’s a pretty damn high number of misdiagnoses with MS, and that’s after people have been going through the process of it, with the infusions, for many years.“It’s clear now they’re finding something different, that something else is going on.”Applegate said learning she doesn’t have the disease was challenging mentally.“I’m sure people are saying like, ‘Crybaby, you don’t have MS, you know, that’s a good thing’ – but no, no, no,” she said.“I’m sitting here having slept all day yesterday, feeling like absolute crap because of the heat. My legs aren’t working. You know, all the same stuff is happening to me, and yet I have this thing of like, well, you don’t have that, so maybe you’re faking it.“In my head I’m like, what can I be doing differently? This is what I’m sure a lot of people start thinking when they get their misdiagnoses. It’s like, ‘Well, what have I done wrong? What am I doing?’”Sigler told Applegate that she never let anybody down.“Everything you did, and shared, and were, and are to so many people doesn’t go anywhere,” she said.“Because of this misdiagnosis or this new information that you have in your life, that doesn’t take away anything that you did. You didn’t mislead anyone. In no way should you feel bad or uneasy about your continuing to share your journey with people.”A2024 Swiss-led study, published in the Multiple Sclerosis Journal, found “high-level evidence for high proportions of misdiagnosis and underdiagnoses of MS” – including a 15% misdiagnosis rate in cases it looked at.Explore more on these topicsChristina ApplegateMultiple sclerosisnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Oh God, I can’t bear it’: Judi Dench says Cats film was ‘a waste of goodwill and talent’ | Movies | The Guardian
description: The actor’s forthcoming memoir Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? says the makers had honourable intentions but the elements ‘didn’t coalesce’
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: The actor’s forthcoming memoir Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? says the makers had honourable intentions but the elements ‘didn’t coalesce’
Content: Feline bad … Judi Dench in Cats.Photograph: Working Title Films/AllstarView image in fullscreenFeline bad … Judi Dench in Cats.Photograph: Working Title Films/AllstarMovies‘Oh God, I can’t bear it’: Judi Dench says Cats film was ‘a waste of goodwill and talent’The actor’s forthcoming memoir Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? says the makers had honourable intentions but the elements ‘didn’t coalesce’Catherine ShoardTue 20 Oct 2026 07.28 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 15.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDame Judi Dench has long made her feelings clear about Cats, the doomed 2019 adaptation of theAndrew Lloyd Webbermusical. In an interview the year after release, she said she had so far declined to watch the movie – in which she played wise moggy Old Deuteronomy – and described the orange fur coat she had to wear as looking like “five foxes fucking on my back”.In her forthcoming memoir, Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It? Dench reflects further on her involvement in the movie, which was universally panned and whose director,Tom Hooper, has not made a film since.“Oh God, I can’t bear it,” she writes in the book, “and [Lloyd Webber] had waited so long for it to be made. What a waste of all that goodwill and talent.“I understand the critics were rather hostile to the film. I never saw the final cut so I can’t judge. All I’ll say is nobody sets out to give a poor performance or make a bad film. You do your best, offer something up and hope that people will get on board and join the party.”Old Deuteronomy with human hand and wedding ring.Photograph: TwitterAmong the aspects of the film most energetically criticised on release was the film’s erratic CGI, which erased every animal’s anus but retained, in the case of Dench, a human hand, complete with wedding ring.In her book, Dench writes that she felt “ill at ease from the beginning – I just didn’t feel right in the role”. Nor, she continues, did she “like the way the young dancers were left hanging at the end of each take. They’d stand there exhausted and be completely ignored.”However, Dench says she did enjoy discovering “I could still lift my leg in the air” and playing Bananagrams with her vocal coach on set. She also liked meeting co-star Taylor Swift and, on the final day of filming, was given 50 everlasting roses, spraypainted gold, by Jason Derulo, who played Rum Tum Tugger.“There were no villains in the making ofCats,” writes Dench. “And if something isn’t a success, then there are always things you can say you’ve learned.“Sometimes things just don’t work out: the timing’s wrong, the cast don’t gel, the elements don’t coalesce. But people’s intentions are mostly honourable.”Lloyd Webber has vociferously criticised the film, saying Hooper did not consult those involved in the original West End show and saying “the whole thing was ridiculous”.In 2021, he called it “off-the-scale all wrong” and said the experience left him so “emotionally damaged” he became a dog owner in an effort to recover.“There wasn’t really any understanding of why the music ticked at all. I saw it and I just thought, ‘Oh, God, no.’ It was the first time in my 70-odd years on this planet that I went out and bought a dog. So the one good thing to come out of it is my little Havanese puppy.”The composer said that he had to prove to an airline that he required the companion as an emotional support animal in order to travel with him. “I said: ‘Just see what Hollywood did to my musical Cats.’ Then the approval came back with a note saying, ‘No doctor’s report required.’”Explore more on these topicsFilmCatsJudi DenchAndrew Lloyd WebberTom HoopernewsShareReuse this content

title: Getting Ziggy with it: David Bowie’s alter egos inspire dance show that will transform his songs | Stage | The Guardian
description: Subject to Change: A Dance for David Bowie will explore how the musician ‘practised a form of artistic reincarnation’, says choreographer Marcos Morau
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Subject to Change: A Dance for David Bowie will explore how the musician ‘practised a form of artistic reincarnation’, says choreographer Marcos Morau
Content: Not a ‘nostalgic tribute’ … David Bowie as Ziggy Stardust in 1973.Photograph: Ilpo Musto/AlamyView image in fullscreenNot a ‘nostalgic tribute’ … David Bowie as Ziggy Stardust in 1973.Photograph: Ilpo Musto/AlamyStageGetting Ziggy with it: David Bowie’s alter egos inspire dance show that will transform his songsSubject to Change: A Dance for David Bowie will explore how the musician ‘practised a form of artistic reincarnation’, says choreographer Marcos MorauChris WiegandStage editorTue 20 Oct 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Let’s dance,” sangDavid Bowiein 1983, commanding: “Put on your red shoes and dance the blues.” That call is to be answered – with footwear TBC – by an international dance production featuring new choral arrangements of songs from throughout his career.Subject to Change: A Dance for David Bowiewill be staged at Sadler’s Wells in London in autumn 2028 after a world premiere in Luxembourg. It will visit Tokyo in 2029. The show will explore how Bowie “practised a form of artistic reincarnation” according to Spanish choreographer Marcos Morau who is taking inspiration from the superstar’s transformations into personas such as Aladdin Sane and the Thin White Duke.“One of the greatest dangers for an artist is ending up resembling themselves too much,” said Morau. “Bowie turned change into a way of remaining true to himself. That inspires me deeply. I believe every new work should force us to let go of some certainty. Art shouldn’t serve to confirm who we are, but rather to accept that life transforms us, that we change over time, and that our own contradictions help us grow.”View image in fullscreen‘What happens when his songs leave behind the voice we all know?’ … Bowie in his Thin White Duke era in 1976.Photograph: Jorgen Angel/RedfernsOrchestrations of pop and rock classics have powered recent hit dance productions such asBlack Sabbath: The Balletanda reworking of The Who’s Quadrophenia, bringing in new audiences. In Subject to Change, Bowie’s songs will be interwoven with choral sounds from around the world and the voice of Spanish singer Maria Arnal. “I’m not interested in reproducing Bowie or creating a nostalgic tribute,” said Morau, who wants to explore “what happens when his songs leave behind the voice we all know and travel towards other voices, other cultures and other generations”. By employing different choral traditions, he hopes to “transform something deeply individual into a collective experience. I like to think that a work of art remains alive as long as we are able to transform it, and that perhaps the best way to remain faithful to Bowie is to dare to change him.”Over his career, Bowie collaborated with significant choreographers including Édouard Lock and Annie-B Parson. He was taught dance by the great mime Lindsay Kemp who recalled him taking part in improvisations such as sailors drowning at sea. Kemp directed Bowie in a 1967 theatre show, Pierrot in Turquoise, and tried – but failed –to get him to play Puss in Boots.The pierrot became one of Bowie’s alter egos – others included Halloween Jack from his Diamond Dogs era and, most famously, Ziggy Stardust, the intergalactic rockstar who “took it all too far but, boy, could he play guitar”. A black vinyl jumpsuit with stripes known asTokyo Pop, designed by Kansai Yamamoto for Bowie to wear as Ziggy in 1973, is used in the promotional image for Subject to Change.View image in fullscreenThe Subject to Change promotional image featuring the Tokyo Pop costume designed by Kansai YamamotoPhotograph: Kazuyoshi ShimomuraEach of his alter egos ushered in a new musical direction and a fresh look for Bowie but also brought out a different physicality, said Morau. “For Bowie, the body was just as important as the music or the costumes. It wasn’t simply a matter of appearance, but of how he inhabited space. What fascinates me is that he managed to turn his own body into a territory of fiction, allowing those fictions to become part of reality. When you can transform yourself with that kind of freedom, you can also find new ways of living. In a world obsessed with categorising us and making us follow certain patterns, Bowie turned his body into an act of defiance.”View image in fullscreen‘Perhaps the best way to remain faithful to Bowie is to dare to change him’ … Marcos Morau.Photograph: Kazuyoshi ShimomuraMorau is an in-demand choreographer whose works includeHorses(2024), created for Nederlands Dans Theater, which featured animalistic dancers prowling around mean streets to music by contemporary classical composer Caroline Shaw.Étude, performed earlier this year by the Paris Opera Ballet, upended the conventions of ballet. The former piece featured dancers wielding giant lamp posts; the latter used a swinging replica of the chandelier in the auditorium of Paris’s Palais Garnier. Both sets were designed by Max Glaenzel who will work on Subject to Change. The costumes will be by another of Morau’s regular collaborators, Silvia Delagneau, and the musical direction is by Alex Röser Vatiché and Ben Meerwein. It is co-produced by Sadler’s Wells, Bunkamura in Japan and Morau’s company La Veronal.Ten years after Bowie’s death, the musician continues to fascinate. Earlier this year, a3D documentaryabout him was unveiled at the Venice film festival.David Bowie: You’re Not Alone, an hour-long immersive portrait, is running at Lightroom in London and the V&A’s Bowie archive, featuring Yamamoto’s costumes for Ziggy Stardust,goes on tour next month.Last weekend, Let’s Dance inspireda paso doble on Strictly. What is Morau’s favourite Bowie song to dance to? “Space Oddity – it’s probably not the most obvious choice for dancing, but that’s precisely why I like it,” he said. “There’s something profoundly choreographic about imagining a body losing gravity and drifting away from everything familiar.”Explore more on these topicsStageDanceTheatreDavid BowieSadler's WellsJapanLuxembourgnewsShareReuse this content

title: Royal Exchange boss unveils new plays two years after damaging censorship row | Royal Exchange | The Guardian
description: Selina Cartmell announces season including Stockport-set version of Phaedra myth by Simon Stephens
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Selina Cartmell announces season including Stockport-set version of Phaedra myth by Simon Stephens
Content: Cartmell is interested in northern stories with an international reach, such as a new play about the 1958 Munich air disaster.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCartmell is interested in northern stories with an international reach, such as a new play about the 1958 Munich air disaster.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianRoyal ExchangeRoyal Exchange boss unveils new plays two years after damaging censorship rowSelina Cartmell announces season including Stockport-set version of Phaedra myth by Simon StephensMark BrownNorth of England correspondentTue 20 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 03.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA theatre boss has promised to channel the “pioneering spirit of Manchester” and be “brave and fearless” as she unveiled a new season of work, two years after a deeply damaging censorship row.Selina Cartmell, the artistic director of theRoyal Exchange in Manchester, revealed details of 2027-28 productions that include a retelling of the Munich air disaster and a modern Stockport-set version of the ancient Greek myth Phaedra.Cartmell took over at the theatre two years ago, during what was one of the biggest crises in its 50-year history.A production of A Midsummer Night’s Dream was cancelled in a dispute over one of the production’s songs, which referenced transgender rights and contained the phrase “free Palestine”.There were accusations of censorship, although an independent review did not find that butdid highlight “significant leadership failures”. The play’s director, Stef O’Driscoll, talked of a growing “fear-driven decision-making in the arts”.Cartmell told the Guardian it had been “a very challenging time” for the theatre, and the board at the time took “full responsibility”. All the review recommendations were now in place, with “artists firmly back at the centre of the theatre”, she said.“It was an incredibly complex and difficult period of our time, but we are absolutely, as a theatre, moving forward into the next chapter.”Cartmell said she was interested in northern stories with an international reach, adding that risks would be taken – “all part of the pioneering spirit of Manchester”.She said the theatre would reopen its 100-seat studio space next year, which has remained closed since the Covid pandemic.She said the closure had been a “real loss to Manchester” and reopening it would allow the theatre “to nurture local talent and to tell really urgent stories”.The first studio show since March 2020 will be Talking to Boys, by Abbi Greenland, which explores “what happens to one woman’s mind through 14 conversations with the men in her life”.The reopening will coincide with a six week-long closure of the main 750-seat in-the-round space for refurbishment, including the seats, which have been in place for 30 years.Season highlights in 2027 will include the world premiere of a new play by Olivier and Tony award-winningSimon Stephens, The First Blue Thing.Directed by Cartmell, it is a reimagining of the Greek myth of Phaedra – a princess who falls in love with her stepson, leading to terrible consequences – and will be set in Stephens’s home town of Stockport.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKing Lear review – David Threlfall makes a moving Lear, but why is he playing the Fool too?Read moreThere will also be a new production of Guys and Dolls, and Much Ado About Nothing with the soul singer and West End star Beverley Knight.In 2028, 70 years after one of the defining moments in the history of Manchester – the Munich air disaster – the theatre will stage the world premiere of an adaptation ofDavid Peace’s novel Munichs.Munichs brings to life the story and aftermath of the air crash that killed 23 out of 44 passengers, including eight Manchester United players, three of its staff and eight journalists.It has been adapted for the stage by Ben Power and will, Cartmell said, explore the “religion of football” and how a club, a community and a country were all changed by events on 6 February 1958.TheRoyal Exchangeis one of the UK’s leading regional theatres and has a proud history, Cartmell said, “of doing things differently, dancing to their own drum beat.“I think Manchester has that spirit as well, that punky, edgy feeling of going: right, we need to take risks. We need to act with courage. We need to be brave and fearless. And this is the moment … Manchester, as we know, is going through an extraordinary moment in time.”This article was amended on 20 October 2026. Beverley Knight will appear in Much Ado About Nothing, not A Midsummer Night’s Dream as an earlier version said.Explore more on these topicsRoyal ExchangeTheatreManchesterNorth of EnglandMunich air disasterGreater ManchesterCensorshipnewsShareReuse this content

Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Jack Seale,Ali CatterallandEllen E JonesTue 20 Oct 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStacey Dooley: Down the K-Hole9pm, BBC ThreeTo be clear, Stacey Dooley says she has never taken ketamine. But it is one of the most popular recreational drugs among those under 24, so she is meeting some of the long-term users who are living with the consequences. From learning about “ket bladder” (passing blood or parts of an eroding bladder in the urine) to hearing how much the drug helps them to “dissociate”, the conversations are eye-opening and often heartbreaking.Hollie RichardsonThe Great British Bake Off8pm, Channel 4It’s dessert week in the tent, which brings newness in round one: the bakers tackle a signature challenge with staggered starts, so letting one’s errors melt into the general chaos isn’t an option. After a technical bake set by Nigella Lawson, the showstopper is a retro confection demanding classic puddings worthy of a squeaky-wheeled dessert trolley.Jack SealeOnly Fools and Horses: The Lost Archive9pm, U&GoldView image in fullscreenAnd cut … David Jason as Del Boy and Nicholas Lyndhurst as Rodney in a clip from Only Fools And Horses Christmas Special 1996.Photograph: © BBCA lovely jubbly watch for fans of the beloved sitcom. David Jason, Gwyneth Strong and Tessa Peake-Jones are among those who sit down to watch never-before-seen cut clips. Episodes include A Royal Flush, Chain Gang and, everybody’s favourite, The Jolly Boys’ Outing – and they all agree they should have been kept in.HRBlue Lights9pm, BBC OneIt’s finally here: the resurrection (well, flashback episode) of lovely, gravelly voiced Gerry (Richard Dormer) we were promised. And it shows how his relationship with Sandra (Andi Osho) started with a molotov cocktail. Expect plenty of police action, a Chaka Khan rendition, lots of wise words from the man himself – and a romance for the ages.HRJohn le Carré: A New Life9pm, Sky ArtsA psychoanalytical biography of the bestselling novelist, examining how his books reflect the worldview and personal life of the real David Cornwell. The juiciest sections see the talking heads speculate about the late writer’s interactions with women, and whether a serial philanderer was perfectly placed to create fiction about duplicitous people.Jack SealeSaving Lives at Sea9.30pm, BBC Two“Craziest 10 minutes of my life,” recalls Australian surfer Gavin Bowden, saved from drowning last year by 14-year-old Oscar McCrae, a member of the Saunton Sands Surf Life Saving Club. That’s just one of the cockle-warmers here, along with the fearless RNLI rescue of a pair of paddleboarders swept more than a mile out to sea.Ali CatterallFilm choiceA Want in Her (Myrid Carten, 2024),10pm, BBC FourView image in fullscreenElusive … Myrid Carten’s mother, Nuala, in A Want in Her.Photograph: Publicity imageMyrid Carten’s mother, Nuala, is a character, a charmer and an elusive mystery. She is also a woman struggling to get a grip on her addiction issues and the mum that Carten has spent a lifetime trying to find – sometimes when she was missing, presumed on a bender in Belfast, and sometimes when she was right there, smoking rollies in the same room. Carten’s Bafta-nominated debut feature is about this search, involving interviews with other eccentric relatives around rural Donegal. title: Gilgamesh by Simon Armitage review – an ancient epic is brilliantly translated for our times | Poetry | The Guardian
description: The poet laureate’s visceral take on the legendary Mesopotamian hero’s wild adventures is a tour de force
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The poet laureate’s visceral take on the legendary Mesopotamian hero’s wild adventures is a tour de force
Content: An orthostate depicting Gilgamesh between two minotaur demigods holding up a sun disc.Photograph: Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn orthostate depicting Gilgamesh between two minotaur demigods holding up a sun disc.Photograph: Fine Art Images/Heritage Images/Getty ImagesBook of the dayPoetryReviewGilgamesh by Simon Armitage review – an ancient epic is brilliantly translated for our timesThe poet laureate’s visceral take on the legendary Mesopotamian hero’s wild adventures is a tour de forcePhilip TerryTue 20 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 02.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe poet laureate is paid a salary of £5,750 per annum plus a barrel of sherry. No specific duties are attached to the role, but there is an expectation that poets will write verse for public occasions and royal events, a duty that Simon Armitage has fulfilled by writing a poem on the death of Elizabeth II, Floral Tribute, and another to mark the coronation of Charles and Camilla in 2023. Though it’s an awkward time for the royals, no laureate is going to write about them behaving badly (it wasn’t John Dryden, the first laureate, who wrote about Charles II’s bedroom habits, but John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester). And yet with Gilgamesh, Armitage does deliver a poem about royalty’s misdeeds, at least in part.The epic originated in ancient Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq) at least 4,000 years ago, and it begins with the eponymous demigod, king of Uruk, lording it over his subjects. Among other bad habits, he exercises the “right of the first night”, which allows him to bed newlywed brides before their husbands. To check his powers, the gods create his counterpart, the wild man Enkidu, who confronts Gilgamesh outside the house of one of these brides. The two rivals turned comrades then embark on a series of extraordinary adventures, including battles with Humbaba, guardian of the Cedar Forest, and with the winged Bull of Heaven, sent by the goddess Ishtar in revenge after Gilgamesh rejects her marriage proposal. Following Enkidu’s death, Gilgamesh sets out alone on a desperate quest for immortality that leads him to the very edge of the world.In his introduction Armitage draws our attention to the poem’s rich modern resonance, including its frankness about sex workers, who play a key role in bringing Enkidu to Uruk, its ecological dimension – Enkidu’s death is a punishment for cutting down the forest guarded by Humbaba – and the way the relationship of Gilgamesh and Enkidu can be seen as a celebration of same-sex physical love (Gilgamesh loves his companion “like a wife”). Most striking of all is the way the heroes’ fight with Humbaba echoes modern resource wars. The Gulf wars took place in the same geographical region, though the commodity in question was not timber – the prime building material at the time of the poem – but oil.double quotation markSome of the finest passages have a sumptuousness you can almost taste and touchThe poem’s uniquely fragmented history makes it both ancient and modern. Sumerian sources date back to 2000BC, but it remained lost until fragments of cuneiform tablets in a later Akkadian form were discovered by archaeologists in the 19th century. A tablet on display in the British Museum drew the attention of George Smith, employed by a firm that designed bank notes, and he repeatedly visited the museum in his lunch hour to gaze at it. When the keeper of Babylonian antiquities asked him what he was doing, Smith replied that he was reading it. Later, now in the employ of the British Museum, Smith was excited to discover a tablet describing a great flood. Crying “I am the first person to read that after 2000 years of oblivion,” he rushed about the room in a state of great excitation, and to the astonishment of those present began to undress. The passage Smith had deciphered comes towards the end of the poem, where Gilgamesh visits the now-immortal flood survivor Uta-napishtim – the poem’s Noah character – in an attempt to find immortality himself. It caused a sensation in Victorian England because of its similarity to the flood story in the Book of Genesis: here perhaps was evidence of the historical veracity of the event.This fragmented history of the poem is reflected in the way it has come down to us in broken tablet form, which Armitage compares to a vast jigsaw with pieces still missing. Readers who see this fragmentation as integral to the poem may be disappointed with Armitage’s approach, which is generally to paper over the cracks, as he puts it (though he does present passages that have been restored from later sources in prose, and occasionally leaves gaps whose contents he speculates on in detailed footnotes). One feature Armitage is very faithful to is the incantatory use of repetition, as in the journey to meet Humbaba – “After forty leagues they stopped and broke bread. / After sixty leagues they stopped and pitched camp” – which he says “enacts the mundane regularity of a long slog across featureless terrain”. Generally, the results are fresh and impressive, as in the poem’s opening lines, as solid as the rock they were once carved on:He witnessed great depths, saw the land’s bedrock.Astute in all subjects, wise in every matter,Gilgamesh glimpsed the foundations of life.Nothing escaped him; he possessed all knowledge,had learned each discipline in equal measure,understood completely the ways of the world.He uncovered secrets, revealed what was hidden,brought back word from before the Great Flood,trudged distant paths, earned his rest.He carved his trials and travails in a stone.Armitage wisely avoids rhyme, unlike some recent versions – there is no evidence of rhyme in the original text – but he knits his poem together tightly with a standard four-beat line, a fine-spun mixture of the modern and the archaic, and a smattering of the alliteration he employed inhis translation of Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. Some of the finest passages have a sumptuousness you can almost taste and touch – Gilgamesh’s mother Ninsun, “She-Wild-Cow”, purifies herself with “tamarisk and soapwort”. Others have a delicious contemporaneity, as Humbaba calls Enkidu, created by the gods out of a lump of clay, a “half-wit”, a “crossbred freak” who “never sucked milk from his mother’s tit”. Of all the scenes, it is those in the forest, as the heroes make their way towards the home of Humbaba, that bring out Armitage’s best poetry, which sings and clatters its way through the undergrowth:The canopy was knitted and knotted with creepers;sap and resin came raining downand flowed away through channels and gorges.A bird called out, then the forest echoedwith the racket of more birds calling in answer.A lone cicada sounded its note,triggering a chorus of piping and hymning.A turtle dove answered the cries of a pigeon.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe register of Gilgamesh remains one of the great unknowns of the poem. Given the nature of its content – often violent, mocking and sexually explicit – there is no reason to assume it should, as it generally is, be translated into elevated language. Armitage tackles this head on by mixing different registers and idiolects. His tactile, visceral version is a tour de force, combining careful scholarship with poetic verve and deft linguistic meldings, and it is likely to become one of the standard renditions in English. It cannot, though, be the last word on this continuingly resonant poem, whose fragments are still coming to light in museum collections, fresh excavations and accidental finds.Philip Terry is the author of Dictator: A Free Version of the Epic of Gilgamesh in Globish (Carcanet, £12.99). Gilgamesh: A New Verse Translation by Simon Armitage is published by Faber (£14.99).To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Children of the Wicker Man review – how the folk-horror classic haunted the family that made it | Movies | The Guardian
description: Director Robin Hardy’s children lay bare the sometimes agonised family background to a movie that went from ruinous flop to cult favourite
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Director Robin Hardy’s children lay bare the sometimes agonised family background to a movie that went from ruinous flop to cult favourite
Content: Spawning a monster hit … Children of the Wicker Man.Photograph: Courtesy of Hardy PicturesView image in fullscreenSpawning a monster hit … Children of the Wicker Man.Photograph: Courtesy of Hardy PicturesMoviesReviewChildren of the Wicker Man review – how the folk-horror classic haunted the family that made itDirector Robin Hardy’s children lay bare the sometimes agonised family background to a movie that went from ruinous flop to cult favouriteLeslie FelperinTue 20 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 08.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis documentary is a collaboration between Justin Hardy and Dominic Hardy, two of film director Robin Hardy’s children (he had seven in all, and was married five times), and it delves into the legacy of both their father and his most enduring work, 1973 folk-horror classicThe Wicker Man. The latter still stands today, for all its imperfections and peculiarities, as one of the most unsettling and paradoxically influential British films of all time, despite being a box-office flop on its initial release. This latest work is partly an account of The Wicker Man’s troubled production – a story that’s been told in books and journalism a fair few times already – and its strange reemergence as a cult movie-cum-fetish object, and partly a therapeutic exercise for the brothers themselves, full of raw feeling that’s sometimes painful to watch.However, while the brothers’ willingness to share their pain remains admirable, their film feels hampered by omissions and silences. On some level it is haunted by the ghosts of significant players in the story who have passed away, including Hardy himself and screenwriter Anthony Shaffer, as well as other key figures who are alive but aren’t interviewed here. Where, for example, are the brothers’ other siblings? Allan Brown, author of Inside The Wicker Man: How Not to Make a Cult Classic, is mentioned in several juicy anecdotes but is also absent, while somewhat bafflingly there’s a fair amount of an interview with Scottish actor Bill Paterson, who was almost cast in the original film but wasn’t.Of the two brothers, Justin’s is the more prominent voice;he died in Augustjust before the festival premiere of Wrath of the Gods, a long-nurtured semi-sequel to The Wicker Man he made with Dominic. Justin comes across as a choleric, clenched figure, understandably simmering with rage at a father who walked out of his life when he was still a child, leaving him and his sister in the care of their alcoholic mother, who was effectively bankrupted by the financial failure of The Wicker Man. Dominic, born to a different mother and raised in Canada, comes across as more tender-hearted, more forgiving of his father, thanks perhaps to both physical distance and the detachment of his training as an art historian.There’s a little, possibly unintentional, comedy to be had at one point when Dominic goes missing during filming and we see Justin raging over it to the film’s producers. The vignette stands as a salutary reminder that film-making is bloody hard work and it’s almost a miracle anything ever gets made, let alone an accidental masterpiece like The Wicker Man.Children of the Wicker Man is in UK cinemas from 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsThe Wicker ManHorror filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Explosive births, talking foxes and the devil in a trenchcoat – the Sitges fantastic film festival in all its creepy glory | Movies | The Guardian
description: Olivia Colman goes vulpine, Rupert Grint’s newborn is a monster and Joko Anwar makes a warmhearted violent ghost story set in an Indonesian prison
Author: Anne Billson
Headline: Olivia Colman goes vulpine, Rupert Grint’s newborn is a monster and Joko Anwar makes a warmhearted violent ghost story set in an Indonesian prison
Content: Indecently entertaining … (l-r) Andrea Genovese, Adriano Giannini, Jasmine Trinca and Gabriella Telegrafo in The Spiral.Photograph: Andrea MiconiView image in fullscreenIndecently entertaining … (l-r) Andrea Genovese, Adriano Giannini, Jasmine Trinca and Gabriella Telegrafo in The Spiral.Photograph: Andrea MiconiMoviesExplosive births, talking foxes and the devil in a trenchcoat – the Sitges fantastic film festival in all its creepy gloryOlivia Colman goes vulpine, Rupert Grint’s newborn is a monster and Joko Anwar makes a warmhearted violent ghost story set in an Indonesian prisonAnne BillsonTue 20 Oct 2026 10.10 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 10.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf I’d ever wanted children, the films showing at the 59th edition of the International Fantastic film festival of Catalonia in the coastal town of Sitges, south of Barcelona, would have soon set me straight. This year’s recurring themes were explosive parturition, chewed-up nipples and the fruit of the womb turning out to be at best sociopathic, at worst inhuman.The theme was celebrated in an evil-kiddy exhibition at the Miramar Cultural Centre, marking the 50th anniversary ofNarciso Ibáñez Serrador’s “fantaterror” classic Who Can Kill a Child?, some of which was filmed in Sitges itself. The expo traced the subgenre from 1956’s The Bad Seed, via Rosemary’s Baby and The Exorcist, tothis year’s Nightborn, in which poor Rupert Grint, as the hapless husband, is no match for the developing folk-horror bond between his depressed wife, their newborn “child”, and the spooky forest surrounding their house. Finnish director Hanna Bergholm, in her introduction, confessed it was inspired by her experiences of motherhood. Only up to a point, one hopes.Postpartum depression reared its head again in Mutter: The Diary of a Mother from Turkish director Alphan Eşeli, which begins with a father taking one look at his newborn offspring and fleeing into the woods. Hazar Ergüçlü’s terrific central performance keeps the focus on the social and economic plight of being a single parent, even when your baby resembles the one in Eraserhead.View image in fullscreenSpooky … Seidi Haarla and Rupert Grint in Nightborn.Photograph: Pietari PeltolaAs usual, a third of the titles in competition here were directed by women. Indeed, winner of this year’s best feature film award was Marion Le Coroller’s Sanguine (AKA Species), which followed in the gloopy French body horror footsteps of Julia Ducournau (Raw) and Coralie Fargeat (The Substance) with a medical intern developing a disfiguring skin condition that will have anyone who ever squeezed a pimple squirming in sympathy. The festival’s award for best female performance went to Jasmine Trinca as a mother who enters into a diabolical pact in Paolo Strippoli’s indecently entertaining The Spiral, though it is supporting actor Valeria Bruni Tedeschi who steals all her scenes as a soigné Mephistopheles in a trenchcoat.Meanwhile, best actor went to Benoît Magimel, oozing menace in one of his sleazy white suits in Léa Mysius’s The Birthday Party, a finely wrought home invasion thriller, and another of the films pivoting on a fraught mother-child relationship. It was heartening to see so many female protagonists in genre films, even ones by male directors such as Casey Affleck, whoseCompany, with its Russian doll structure, slowly morphs from a frontier western into a spine-tingling tale of the supernatural.Elsewhere, young women train as mermaids (Titanic Ocean, which teases the possibility of a mermaid-shark face-off, but fails to deliver), or bond with their abductors (The Daughters), or face off against a sociopathic youngster who infiltrates her snowed-in scout troop (11).Warmhearted …Ghost in the Cell.Photograph: Come and See PicturesAlas, I was so busy watching these that I missedthe 4K restoration of Jimmy Wang Yu’s Master of the Flying Guillotinefrom 1976 with its glorious krautrock soundtrack. But I did get to pay my respects to the late, great Sam Neill, who provided the voice of a magpie in Dario Russo’s bawdy, unabashedly full-frontalAustralian folk yarn The Fox. The stacked cast includes Jai Courtney and Olivia Colman as the voice of a wily talking fox.My favourite films of the festival included Javier Ruiz Caldera’s 5 More Minutes, which manages to put a new spin on the time-loop subgenre, its early lighthearted tone sliding into darker Timecrimes territory. Then there was The Mouths, about a cursed tree, a return to J-horror form from Takashi Shimizu (The Grudge) that gets more sinister and disorientating as it goes on, plus Sabu’s Taiwanese-Japanese co-production Arrested Memory, in which a traumatised Taipei cop suffering from Guy-Pearce-in-Memento syndrome bumbles his way through kidnapping, drug deals and car chases, to deadpan but ultimately hilarious effect.But best of all was Joko Anwar’s Ghost in the Cell, in which all the usual prison tropes – rioting, brutal guards, shivs, the threat of sexual violence – are supplemented by a supernatural curse, arty splatter, interpretative dance, a commentary on Indonesian corruption, and – best of all – an unexpectedly warmhearted vibe. Fortunately for everyone, it hasa UK release on digital platforms from 26 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmScience fiction and fantasy filmsHorror filmsThrillersSpainEuropeOlivia ColmanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Listen out for Lanny: can Max Porter’s mythic tale of a mulch-guzzler really be heard in this woodland? | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Every sun-dappled object is an instrument as composer Dom Coyote and sound designers Elena Peña and Dave Price conjure trip-hop-inspired rhythms in the Mendips for a new stage adaptation
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: Every sun-dappled object is an instrument as composer Dom Coyote and sound designers Elena Peña and Dave Price conjure trip-hop-inspired rhythms in the Mendips for a new stage adaptation
Content: A microphone placed in Stockhill Wood on the Mendip Hills.Photograph: Courtesy Dom CoyoteView image in fullscreenA microphone placed in Stockhill Wood on the Mendip Hills.Photograph: Courtesy Dom CoyoteTheatreListen out for Lanny: can Max Porter’s mythic tale of a mulch-guzzler really be heard in this woodland?Every sun-dappled object is an instrument as composer Dom Coyote and sound designers Elena Peña and Dave Price conjure trip-hop-inspired rhythms in the Mendips for a new stage adaptationKate WyverTue 20 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 02.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe woodland is stuck to our skin. Sound designers Elena Peña and Dave Price are hunched next to me, burying a microphone into mossy ground. Composer Dom Coyote is listening on headphones, crunching out a rhythm with his boot before shucking his shoes for a subtler sound. “It’s got to be socks off, Dom,” says Price. Coyote obliges, the balls of his feet soon covered in dead conifer needles. “Do you wish you’d had a pedicure now?” Peña asks.It’s a short drive from Bristol to this patch on the Mendip Hills, where pine cones and rowan berries scatter at the entrance to the trees. We’re on the hunt for sounds to orchestrate a staging of Max Porter’s novelLanny. The adaptation by Somerset-based Bea Roberts moves the spectral story of a lost boy and a mulch-guzzling creature from commuting-distance-to-London to commuting-distance-to-Bristol, with director Nancy Medina wanting the show’s sound to exist within the city’s historical music scene. “A kind of trip-hop world,” says Coyote, who is exploring this idea by replacing electronic beats with those of the natural world. “So we need to go and play the forest.” Every sun-dappled object becomes an instrument. Up on his feet, Price tests out a rhythm on a deep-timbred trunk. He points to the tree. “Any notes for the snare drum department?”View image in fullscreenElena Peña, Dave Price and Kate Wyver attempt to make the sound of deer running.Photograph: Courtesy Dom CoyoteLanny is a story that lends itself to the ear. On the page, which uses experimental typography, Porter’s text curls as Dead Papa Toothwort – an ancient creature who is myth, fable, scapegoat and threat – inhales the sounds of the village. “Music is so part of the book,” says Coyote, who describes the novel as like a spell. “You can already hear this village voice, where Dead Papa Toothwort is almost feeding off the language and culture and thoughts.” The team shake and rustle the trees, listening for sounds to bring the audience into Dead Papa Toothwort’s mystical world. Coyote’s aim is for the audience to ask: “Is the world making music, or am I just making sense of it?” As he and Peña are changing a microphone’s settings, Price appears with a blackberry plucked for each of us. “To enter the other realm,” he smiles.The human world is hard to escape. They worry the road is too close. A little further in, we come to a contained ring of spruce trees, where Peña places a stethoscope-like contact mic – so called because they only record what they’re in contact with – against a trunk. Every angle she taps and twists gives a different quality of sound. “Infinity,” she whispers. One tree sounds remarkably like bongos. “Too cheery,” Coyote frowns. Lanny is a tale of warning: a boy is lost, a village turns against itself and a family is torn apart. “When we do our job well, people don’t notice it,” says Coyote. “But it’s drawing you in, sharpening the lens.” He hopes this show’s music will “give the audience wonder”, he says, “to counteract the absolute tragedy of the tale”.A folk song laces through Roberts’ adaptation, which Coyote has put to the tune ofSumer Is Icumen In. “Dead Papa Toothwort is living outside of our human arrow of time,” he says. “He’s in the past, present and future.” Coyote is hoping to capture the natural, folkloric feel, which runs stream-like through Porter’s story, within his compositions. “I’m not particularly interested in a trained voice,” he says. “I like rawness. Rough magic.”View image in fullscreenRough magic … Dom Coyote in rehearsals for Lanny.Photograph: Helen MurrayCoyote never officially studied music. Instead, he learned guitar and acted, made anarchic music with Kneehigh in Cornwall, then continued doing theatre. Cracking open his laptop, he gives us a taste of his work-in-progress, made from recording sounds at home, in his garden and using the rattles of his child’s toys. “I used to feel very self-conscious about the fact that I couldn’t read music,” he says, “but now I see people want something more. For it to be led by ear. To feel really human.”Tilting back his head, Coyote begins to sing. It’s a song about a mother calling to her lost son, which the composer has been teaching to the cast in a round. Peña and Price start tapping and crunching out rhythms in the leaves. Even in this rough form, the raw folk song and cathedral-like synths from his laptop sound like the breath of the woodland. The treetops seem to sing it back and pass it on, starting a round of their own. “It’s a temple,” Coyote says, “isn’t it?” Now their job is to bottle this rough magic and bring it back inside.Lanny is atBristol Old Vicuntil 7 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreBristol Old VicMax PorterExperimental musicBristolSomersetMassive AttackfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Devil Woman: why does gen Z suddenly love Cliff Richard? | Cliff Richard | The Guardian
description: His 1970s banger is climbing up the streaming charts, with some young listeners tracking it down on vinyl. How did he become the voice of youth, again, aged 86?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: His 1970s banger is climbing up the streaming charts, with some young listeners tracking it down on vinyl. How did he become the voice of youth, again, aged 86?
Content: Like he never went away … Cliff Richard.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreenLike he never went away … Cliff Richard.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyPass notesCliff RichardDevil Woman: why does gen Z suddenly love Cliff Richard?His 1970s banger is climbing up the streaming charts, with some young listeners tracking it down on vinyl. How did he become the voice of youth, again, aged 86?Tue 20 Oct 2026 09.12 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 13.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Devil Woman.Age:50.Popularity:Never bigger.DevilWoman, the song by SirCliff Richard?That’s right, his most famous song.Well now, that’s hardly fair. Sir Cliffhas been aniconsince the birth ofpopularmusic.Yes, that’s true. His 68-year-old song Move It was potentially the first British rock’n’roll record.He’s had so manyNo 1s, too.True. Living Doll in the 50s, Summer Holiday and The Young Ones in the 60s, We Don’t Talk Any More in the 70s, Mistletoe and Wine in the 80s, The Millennium Prayer in the 90s.And what number didDevilWoman get to?No 9.So it’s far from his mostfamoussong,then?I rebut this. In terms of pure cultural cut-through, Devil Woman represents the pinnacle of Sir Cliff’s career.Cultural cut-through how?The song formed the centrepiece of the video game trailerGrand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look, which has gained 32m views on YouTube since it launched last month.Oh wow. What footage did it soundtrack?Variously: scuba diving, basketball, kayaking, stripping, VR pornography, kidnapping and armed robbery.And how does thefamouslyChristianSir Cliff feel about his song being used for such depravity?He may be stuffing his ears with money as we speak.Outrageous.Yes, but also extremely cool. The song fits the game perfectly. It’s corny and sleazy in equal measure, and as a result people are falling for it again.So this is why it’swildlypopular?Exactly. Streams on Spotify are up 325%, and gen Z is making a big thing of tracking it down on vinyl. The success is being compared to when Kate Bush’s Running Up That Hill surged back up the charts after being featured on Stranger Things.This tends to happen a lot, doesn’t it?In the streaming age, where all music is permanently accessible, yes. Even Murder on the Dancefloor got a bump after it soundtracked Barry Keoghan’s genitals at the end of Saltburn.Well, this is great.It is. Not only is the Devil Woman resurgence a timely validation for a song about being poisoned by a woman who sometimes transforms into a cat, but for Sir Cliff as a whole.How so?The man is 86 years old. It’s only natural that his career should wane a little as he ages. Lately he’s become more famous for his novelty calendars than his music, so this resets the clock a little.How does he plan to capitalise upon this hip resurgence?He’s about to release a reggae version of The Lord is My Shepherd.Sorry I asked.Yeah, me too.Do say:“Cliff Richard is cool again.”Don’t say:“Quick, hide the video where herollerskates around a Milton Keynes shopping centre.”Explore more on these topicsCliff RichardPass notesGrand Theft AutoGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘How green are our valleys?’: in the footsteps of miners on south Wales’s new forest trail | Wales holidays | The Guardian
description: The first stage of an ambitious new hiking route that will link woodlands across Wales takes walkers into the wild hills above the valleys’ old mining villages
Author: Rhiannon Batten
Headline: The first stage of an ambitious new hiking route that will link woodlands across Wales takes walkers into the wild hills above the valleys’ old mining villages
Content: On the climb up to Tarren y Fforch plateau, looking back to Nant-y-Moel.Photograph: Rhiannon BattenView image in fullscreenOn the climb up to Tarren y Fforch plateau, looking back to Nant-y-Moel.Photograph: Rhiannon BattenWales holidays‘How green are our valleys?’: in the footsteps of miners on south Wales’s new forest trailThe first stage of an ambitious new hiking route that will link woodlands across Wales takes walkers into the wild hills above the valleys’ old mining villagesRhiannon BattenTue 20 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Tue 20 Oct 2026 02.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBracken and heather ripple across the plateau. I exhale into the chill autumn air and my breath mists a view that reaches all the way to Gower and the ochre peaks of Bannau Brycheiniog (formerly the Brecon Beacons). Far below, the Ogmore valley’s terrace houses look like tiny constellations but up here on Tarren y Fforch, it’s just me and a few sheep taking springy steps between tufts of bilberries. If this corner of the south Wales valleys feels a long way from its coal mining past, that is, partly, the point.I’m hiking the newLlwybr Coedwig Cymru Trail, or Wales Forest Trail. Running from Porthkerry Park, near Barry, to Pont Walby, close to Glynneath, this 50-mile (80km) pilot route is the first section of what theNational Forest for Waleshopes will eventually be a trail linking woodlands across the length and breadth of Wales: a sylvan counterpart to theWales Coast Path.My father grew up in one of the valleys’ mining villages and, when I visited relatives there as a child, the disconnection of those post-industrial communities from the wild hills that loomed above them was striking. Mountain bikers have long discovered the region’s potential, but walkers still tend to head for the more obvious trails that wind through thenational parksor along the coast. This pilot trail seems a good excuse to explore untapped footpaths.View image in fullscreenThe trail starts near the viaduct in Porthkerry Park.Photograph: Freespiritarchitecture/AlamyWith the sea behind me, I set off from the oak leaf sculpture that marks the trail’s start. The viaduct ahead once carried coal to Barry docks, but today it stands overCaffe Matteo, busy with dog walkers sipping cappuccinos. Leaving them behind, I cross the park between the soft greens of birch and oak trees.I swerve on to a fern-fringed path and follow a stream to the outskirts of Barry. The next section is less lovely – a long stretch of roadside pavement until I enterHensol Forest. The sunshine splinters through ancient pine trees and their needles cushion the ground. Weaving in and out of forest and fields, I soak up all the calm this long-distance forest-bathing exercise can offer until theVale Resortcomes into sight.This vast hotel is popular with golfers, but also holds two trump cards for walkers: aspawhere weary hikers can swim, sauna and steam their muscles limber again, and abarserving energy-boosting Welsh rarebit spiked with ale mustard, Dragon cheddar and charred leeks.Restored, I rejoin the trail the next morning, dipping along leafy lanes and footpaths as the roar of the M4 gets louder. I cross beneath it to enter Coedwig Gellihir, a small broadleaf woodland, then continue north into Pontyclun, before clambering down to the river at Ynysmaerdy Forest to pick up an old railway path to Coedely.double quotation markParts of the trail follow the paths miners took. I’m glad they had this antidote to the darkness and danger undergroundThe trail has been designed to offer stretches for cyclists, pushchair users and horse riders, with more pavement-pounding and, in Thomastown, a reminder of the challenges faced by post-industrial communities. Leaving the village behind, the trail opens out again on to a little rocky path with soaring views of Ogwr Fach Valley.One of the National Forest for Wales’s aims is to help communities connect with nearby woodlands. In Blackmill, the next village I come to, the trail passes Coed Bach Dimbath, a small community woodland where local groups have come together to build an otter hide, outdoor classroom and accessible paths.“The woodland there had been inaccessible for decades, and now people can access it,” says Rhodri Hewitt of Natural Resources Wales, the trail’s project lead. “The valleys can feel desperately poor in places, but the River Ogmore is another world entirely.”Continuing north to Nant-y-Moel, I come to Blaenogwr Farm, a Georgian farmstead marooned in the village, where I’m staying in ahomely holiday cottage. I drop off my backpackand head across the road for fish with buttery potatoes and laverbread (made from edible seaweed) and cockle sauce at theBlaenogwr Hotel.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe holiday cottage at Blaenogwr Farm.Photograph: Rhiannon BattenMy final day’s walking starts with a climb up to that extraordinary plateau on Tarren y Fforch. Hewitt tells me that parts of the trail follow the paths miners took across these hills to work in pits in neighbouring valleys. I’m glad they had this antidote to the darkness and danger underground. Today’s route feels uplifting. I slip through an ancient gate on to open moorland and pick my way up the escarpment, meadow pipits chirruping around me.Crossing the plateau, I enterAfan Forest park, a large commercial woodland that’s also home to a forest of wind turbines, a peat restoration project and a network ofmountain-biking trails. I have an urge to be inside the forest rather than tracing its edges and detour on to a footpath leading up to the trig point at Craig y Llyn, the highest point of the valleys at 600m.Continuing beneath branches dripping velvety lichen, I come to another spectacular viewpoint, as the land drops away to the waters of Llyn Fach and Llyn Fawr, with the peaks ofCorn Du and Pen y Fan shrouded in soft-focus drizzle behind them. Soon I dip into the loveliest stretch of forest along the whole trail.The valley of Cwm Gwrelych is a designated geological site of special scientific interest because of the near complete 300m-year-old strata exposed here. But it’s also rainforest-like, cut through with waterfalls, a dark, glossy river and dense, broadleaf woodland. I feel completely enveloped in green as I hike the last couple of miles to the trail’s current end, the Isambard Kingdom Brunel-designed viaduct at Pont Walby. As I continue toSgwd Gwladyspub with rooms in nearby Pontneddfechan, I remind myself that this is not a finished trail but the beginning of one.View image in fullscreenSgwd Gwladys waterfall.Photograph: Liquid Light/AlamyThe next morning, I pull on my boots one last time and set out in search of the waterfall the pub is named after. Mist rises from the river, shafts of sunlight turn the leaves amber and a heron glides past in cinematic slow-mo. When we spoke about the trail, Hewitt mentioned an old Welsh proverb:Dod yn ôl at fy nghoed, meaning “To return to my trees”, or finding your way back to a balanced state of mind. As I sit and admire SgwdGwladys’ thundering cascade, I realise this leafy trail has delivered exactly that.The trip wasprovided by theNational Forest for WalesandNatural Resources Wales.Vale Resorthasdoubles from£104room-only. The Airbnb cottage costs from£87 a night.Sgwd Gwladyshasdoubles from£65.55, room only. title: Fridge or not? What’s the best way to store bread? | Chefs | The Guardian
description: Our experts have some airtight advice to stop your loaf from going stale
Author: Anna Berrill
Headline: Our experts have some airtight advice to stop your loaf from going stale
Content: That greaseproof paper your loaf came in is the best way to store it.Photograph: Nazgul Anarbekova/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThat greaseproof paper your loaf came in is the best way to store it.Photograph: Nazgul Anarbekova/Getty ImagesKitchen aideChefsFridge or not? What’s the best way to store bread?Our experts have some airtight advice on stopping your loaf from going stale – and even freshening it up again – but whatever you do, keep it out of the fridgeAnna BerrillTue 20 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat’s the best way to store bread? Beeswax wraps, plastic bags, fridge – I’ve tried everything except a bread bin.Nancy, by email“When bread is baked, what happens is that all the starch in the flour expands and takes in all the water,” saysSophia Handschuh, co-founder ofSourdough Sophiain London. That’s why the crumb turns all soft and fluffy. “When you pull the bread out of the oven, as soon as it touches any surface it will start to dry up, which is why bread goes stale; the starch doesn’t like being kept in the air.”To combat this, Handschuh stores her loaf at room temperature in a greaseproof paper bag (ie, the one you bring it home in): “That’s probably the best way – no plastic. And, yes, you can use beeswax wrap, but that’s expensive and you shouldn’t have to go and buy some just for storing bread.”A paper bag is also Rachel Morgan’s preference: “I’d avoid a bread bin, though,” says the co-founder ofTwelve Trianglesin Edinburgh. “That can trap moisture, so the bread gets a bit sweaty, which softens the crust and encourages mould.”As for the fridge, that’s a hard no, says Florin Grama ofTarn Bakeryin north London: “It’s the worst thing you can do,” he says. “Your bread will go stale in about a day.” (As Harold McGee discovered in an experiment for his masterworkOn Food & Cooking, “bread stored in the refrigerator at 46F/7C staled as much in one day as bread held at 86F/30C did in six days”.)Reheating is your gateway to regaining freshness: “Warming bread enables the water to evaporate and for the starch to reactivate,” Handschuh says. So, if your bread is a couple of days’ old, “stick it in the oven for five to 10 minutes, and it should stay fresh for a day or two longer”.If you’re not planning to eat that loaf within a few days of buying it, meanwhile, freezing is by far the best option, Grama says – especially if you’re planning to toast it anyway. “Slice it, so you can later take out only what you need, then wrap tightly, freeze and toast from frozen.” Alternatively, freeze the loaf whole and intact, Handschuh says: “Let that defrost, then stick it in the oven at a low temperature [about 160C] to warm through.”If your bread’s almost on the turn, however, Handschuh recommends tearing it into pieces, and tossing it with “loads” of olive oil, flaky sea salt, a bit of garlic and fresh thyme. “Whack that in the oven for 10-20 minutes, until browned, and you’ll have a batch of chunky croutons for salads.”Equally worthy of consideration are sourdough crisps, especially as we head into soup season, Handschuh adds: “Slice the bread really thinly, drizzle with olive oil and pop in the oven to dry out completely.” Morgan, meanwhile, keeps a bag of stale ends knocking about to turn into breadcrumbs, which will improve all manner of meals: fried in olive oil and used to top pasta; to coat chicken breasts for schnitzels; or to mix into fritters, meatballs and cakes. Alternatively, says Grama, simply refresh an old loaf with a sprinkle of water, then slice it and stuff with “loads of herby, garlic butter, maybe some cheese, too – that will give more life to your bread”. And probably to Nancy, too.Got a culinary dilemma? Emailfeast@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsChefsKitchen aideBreadFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sami Tamimi’s recipes for lamb meatballs with spinach and chickpea stew, and red rice | Food | The Guardian
description: A comforting stew that’s made to be shared
Author: Sami Tamimi
Headline: A comforting stew that’s made to be shared
Content: Sami Tamimi’s lamb meatballs with spinach and chickpea stew and red rice.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Emma Cantlay. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.View image in fullscreenSami Tamimi’s lamb meatballs with spinach and chickpea stew and red rice.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Emma Cantlay. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.FoodSami Tamimi’s recipes for lamb meatballs with spinach and chickpea stew, and red riceServe this warm and juicy meatballsabanekhwith Iraqi tomato rice for a comforting meal that’s made to be sharedSami TamimiTue 20 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is the kind of meal I love for its generosity and simplicity. A comforting spinach and chickpea stew (sabanekh), scattered with tender lamb meatballs and finished with a bright squeeze of lemon. And, alongside, Iraqi red rice (timman ahmar) brings warmth, colour and a gentle sweetness from the tomato, and soaks up the rich, savoury juices of the stew. Together, they form a hearty meal made for sharing.Lamb meatballs, spinach and chickpea stew (sabanekh)View image in fullscreenSami Tamimi’s lamb meatballs with spinach and chickpea stew.Sabanekh is a beloved spinach stew across the Levant, and here I’ve added lamb meatballs to make it a more substantial meal. The combination of cumin, coriander and garlic gives warmth and depth, while a generous squeeze of lemon brightens everything. Serve with rice or warm flatbread to soak up the delicious, fragrant sauce.Prep10 minCook1 hrServes4-6500glamb minceSalt and black pepper1 tspbaharatmix4 tbsp olive oil30g pine nuts1 large onion, peeled and finely chopped (180g)600g frozen whole-leaf spinach400g tin chickpeas, drained and rinsed500ml water or chicken stockRice and/or flatbread, to serve2 tbsp lemon juice, plus lemon wedges, to serveFor theadhagarnish60ml olive oil5 garlic cloves,peeled and crushed20g fresh coriander, finely chopped½ tspaleppo chilli flakesPut the mince in a medium bowl, add a teaspoon of salt, half a teaspoon ofbaharatand a third of a teaspoon of black pepper, and mix well. Shape the meat into 25 balls (about 20g each) and set aside.Heat two tablespoons of olive oil in a large saucepan on a medium heat. Add the pine nuts and cook, stirring constantly, for three to four minutes, until golden brown. Spoon the pine nuts into a bowl.Add the meatballs to the pan in two batches and cook until brown all over. Remove the meat from the pan and add the remaining two tablespoons of oil and the onion, and cook, stirring occasionally, for seven minutes, until soft and translucent. Add the spinach, chickpeas, water/stock, lemon juice, one teaspoon of salt, a good grind of black pepper, and the remaining half-teaspoon of baharat. Bring to a boil and cook for five minutes, until the spinach is soft. Return the meatballs to the pan, cover and cook on a low heat, stirring occasionally, for 20 minutes, until the stew has thickened slightly.To make the adha garnish, put the oil and garlic in a small frying pan on a medium heat. Cook, stirring often, for two to three minutes, until the garlic is lightly golden, then take off the heat and stir in the coriander and chilli. Pour the adha over the stew, cover and leave for five minutes.Scatter over the toasted pine nuts and serve hot with the red rice below, or plain steamed rice, and lots of lemon wedges.Red rice (timman ahmar)View image in fullscreenSami Tamimi’s red rice.A simple and deeply comforting rice dish, known for its rich colour and savoury flavour. Traditionally made by cooking rice with tomato, onion and spices, it’s the kind of everyday dish that sits naturally at the centre of the Iraqi table. The gentle sweetness of the tomato is balanced by warm spices, while the rice remains light and fluffy. Serve alongside stews, grilled meats or vegetables.Prep15 minSoak20 minCook50 minServes4–6300g basmati rice3 tbsp vegetable oil120g vermicelli, broken into small pieces1 medium onion, peeled and finely chopped (120g)3 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed1 green chilli, finely chopped (seeds removed if you want less heat)2 tbsp tomato puree1½ tbsp pomegranate molasses1½ tsp ground cumin¾ tsp ground allspice½ tsp ground cinnamon1 large tomato(140g), finely chopped1 green pepper, stalk, pith and seeds removed, fleshfinely chopped (160g)600mlhot vegetable stock25g unsalted butterSalt and black pepperRinse the rice under cold running water several times, until the water runs clear. Leave the rice to soak in fresh water for 20 minutes, then drain well.Heat a tablespoon of the oil in a medium saucepan on a medium heat. Add the vermicelli, cook, stirring, for five minutes, until golden brown, then tip on to a plate.Add the remaining two tablespoons of oil and the onion to the pan, and cook, stirring occasionally, for seven minutes, until soft and lightly golden. Stir in the garlic and chilli, and cook for a minute. Add the tomato puree, pomegranate molasses and spices, and cook for another minute, until fragrant.Stir in the tomato and green pepper, and cook for three minutes. Add the drained rice and toasted vermicelli, and stir gently for a minute, making sure all of the grains are coated in the tomato sauce.Pour in the hot stock and add the butter, one and a quarter teaspoons of salt and a good grind of black pepper. Bring to a boil, then cover the pan and leave to cook on a very low heat for 15 minutes. Take off the heat and leave covered for 10 minutes. Gently fluff the rice with a fork, then serve.Explore more on these topicsFoodMiddle Eastern food and drinkRiceMain courseHerbs and spicesMeatStewfeaturesShareReuse this content
